Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. # PREFACE.

In this work, of which the present volume is one installment <note>original: "instalment"</note>, my goal has been to present to the reader a coherent explanation of the theory of sound. This explanation includes the most important modern advances made by mathematicians and physicists. I believe those qualified to judge will agree that the goal I have pursued is important. Currently, many of the most valuable contributions to science are found only in scattered journals and the published proceedings of various societies. These are printed in different parts of the world and in several languages; they are often virtually impossible to access for those who do not live near large public libraries. In these circumstances, the practical obstacles to study create a great deal of unproductive labor. This hinders the progress of science to a degree that is difficult to overstate.

Since the well-known article on "Sound" in the *Encyclopædia Metropolitana* <note>The *Metropolitan Encyclopedia*, a major 19th-century reference work.</note> by Sir John Herschel (1845), no complete work has been published that treats the subject mathematically. With the early death of Professor Donkin, the scientific world lost a man whose mathematical skills—combined with a practical knowledge of music—uniquely qualified him to write about sound. The first part of his book *Acoustics* (1870), though it is little more than a fragment, is enough to show <note>original: "shew"</note> that my own work would have been unnecessary if Professor Donkin had lived to finish his.

<summary>The author explains the need for a modern, comprehensive mathematical text on the theory of sound, noting that previous research is scattered and difficult for many to access. He also pays tribute to the unfinished work of Professor Donkin, whose death left a void in the field of acoustics.</summary>
<keywords>theory of sound, acoustics, mathematics, physics, scientific literature, Sir John Herschel, Prof. Donkin, Encyclopædia Metropolitana</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface, shifting from the general need for the book to the specific scope of the topics covered, the technical contents of the first and second volumes, and acknowledgments for the first and second editions.</meta>

# PREFACE.

In choosing the topics to be addressed in a work on sound, I have mostly followed the example of those who wrote before me. To a large extent, the theory of sound, as it is commonly understood, covers the same territory as the general theory of vibrations. However, unless some limits were set, we would have to include the study of subjects like the tides, not to mention optics <note>The branch of physics that studies light.</note>. As a general rule, we will limit ourselves to those types of vibrations for which our ears provide a ready-made and incredibly sensitive instrument of study. Without ears, we would likely care no more about vibrations than we would care about light if we were without eyes.

The current volume includes chapters on the vibrations of systems in general. In these chapters, I hope the reader will find some new approaches and results. This is followed by a more detailed look at specific systems, such as stretched strings, bars, membranes, and plates. The second volume, much of which is already written, will begin with the study of aerial <note>original: "aërial"</note> vibrations.

I owe my best thanks to Mr. H. M. Taylor of Trinity College, Cambridge, who was kind enough to read the proofs. With his generous help, several errors and confusing passages were removed, and the volume as a whole has been made more complete than it otherwise would have been.

I would greatly appreciate any corrections or suggestions for improvement that my readers might offer.

->**Terling Place, Witham,**<-
->**April 1877.**<-

---

In this second edition, all important corrections are noted. New material appears either as fresh sections (for example, § 32 *a*) or is enclosed in square brackets [ ]. Two new chapters, X A and X B, have been inserted, focusing on *curved plates or shells* and *electrical vibrations*. Much of the added material deals with the more difficult parts of the subject; first-time readers may choose to skip these sections during their first reading.

<meta>This page concludes the preface to the second edition (1894), continuing the author’s discussion on the mathematical methods used in the book and providing final acknowledgments for the revision process.</meta>

# PREFACE.

In my mathematical investigations, I have usually used methods that come naturally to a physicist. A pure mathematician might complain—and I must admit, sometimes with good reason—about a lack of rigor <note>In mathematics, "rigor" refers to the strict adherence to logical proof and absolute precision.</note>. However, there are two sides to this issue. While it is important to maintain a consistently high standard in pure mathematics, a physicist may sometimes be justified in being satisfied with arguments that are fairly convincing and conclusive from their perspective. To a mind trained in a different way of thinking, the stricter procedures of the pure mathematician may seem less, rather than more, conclusive. Furthermore, in many difficult cases, insisting on the highest level of mathematical proof would mean leaving the subject out entirely because of the large amount of space that would be required to explain it.

In the first edition, I placed great emphasis on establishing general theorems using Lagrange’s method <note>A powerful mathematical technique for describing the motion and energy of complex systems, named after the mathematician Joseph-Louis Lagrange.</note>, and I am more convinced than ever of the benefits of this approach. It is not uncommon for a theorem to be proven in its most general form using fewer mathematical tools <note>original: "apparatus"</note> than those needed to handle specific cases using specialized methods.

During the revision of the final drafts <note>original: "proof-sheets"</note>, I once again had the great advantage of cooperating with Mr. H. M. Taylor, until he was unfortunately forced to stop <note>original: "desist"</note>. I owe my thanks to him and to several other friends for their valuable suggestions.

*July 1894.*

<summary>In this conclusion to the preface, the author defends his use of "physicist's logic" over strict mathematical rigor and emphasizes the efficiency of Lagrange’s method for proving general theorems.</summary>

<keywords>mathematical physics, rigor, Lagrange’s method, H. M. Taylor, mathematical proof, scientific methodology</keywords>

# CHAPTER I.

### INTRODUCTION.

1. THE sensation of sound is a thing *unique in its own kind* <note>original: *sui generis*</note>, not comparable with any of our other sensations. No one can express the relationship between a sound and a color or a smell. Directly or indirectly, all questions connected with this subject must come to the ear, as the organ of hearing, for a decision; and from its judgment, there can be no appeal. But we should not, therefore, infer that all acoustical investigations are conducted with the unassisted ear. Once we have discovered the physical phenomena that constitute the foundation of sound, our explorations are largely transferred to another field lying within the domain of the principles of Mechanics. In this way, important laws are reached to which the sensations of the ear must necessarily conform.

2. Very brief <note>original: "cursory"</note> observation often suffices to show that sounding bodies are in a state of vibration, and that the phenomena of sound and vibration are closely connected. When a vibrating bell or string is touched by the finger, the sound ceases at the same moment that the vibration is dampened. However, to affect the sense of hearing, it is not enough to have a vibrating instrument; there must also be an uninterrupted communication between the instrument and the ear. A bell rung *in a vacuum* <note>original: *in vacuo*</note>, with proper precautions to prevent the communication of motion, remains inaudible. In the air of the atmosphere, however, sounds have a universal vehicle capable of conveying them without a break from the most variously structured sources to the inner recesses of the ear.

3. The passage of sound is not instantaneous. When a gun is fired at a distance, a very perceptible interval separates the 

<summary>This page introduces sound as a unique physical sensation governed by the laws of mechanics. It establishes that sound is produced by vibration and requires a medium like air to travel, as demonstrated by the silence of a bell in a vacuum.</summary>
<keywords>acoustics, sensation of sound, vibration, vacuum, mechanics, sound transmission, physics of sound</keywords>

--- Page 21 ---
<meta>This page continues the introduction to the physical properties of sound, moving from the basic necessity of a medium (air) to the experimental measurement of the speed of sound and its behavior across different pitches and intensities.</meta>

<page-type>text</page-type>
<page-num>2 [3.]</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION</header>

report from the flash. This represents the time sound takes to travel from the gun to the observer. The delay of the flash itself, caused by the limited <note>original: "finite"</note> speed of light, is so small that it can be completely ignored. The first accurate experiments were conducted by members of the French Academy in 1738. They fired cannons and observed the delay of the reports at various distances. The most important precaution is to alternate the direction in which the sound travels; this cancels out the influence of the wind <note>original: "motion of the air in mass"</note>. For instance, when traveling with the wind, sound moves faster relative to the earth than its normal rate, because the velocity of the wind is added to the speed of sound in still air. In still, dry air at a temperature of 0ºC, the French researchers found a velocity of 337 meters per second. Similar observations were made by François Arago and others in 1822; by the Dutch physicists Gerrit Moll, Abraham van Beek, and Kuytenbrouwer in Amsterdam; by Bravais and Martins between the summit of the Faulhorn <note>A mountain in the Bernese Alps</note> and a station below; and by others. The general result has provided a slightly lower value for the speed of sound—about 332 meters per second. We will best consider how changes in temperature and pressure affect the travel <note>original: "propagation"</note> of sound later, when we discuss mechanical theory.

**4.** Observation shows that, within wide limits, the speed of sound is independent—or at least nearly independent—of its intensity <note>loudness</note> and its pitch. If this were not the case, a fast piece of music heard from a distance would seem hopelessly confused and discordant. However, when the sound waves <note>original: "disturbances"</note> are extremely violent and sudden, so that the changes in air density are significant compared to the overall density of the air, this simple law may no longer apply.

**5.** Victor Regnault <note>original footnote: *Mémoires de l'Académie de France*, volume 37 (Memoirs of the French Academy)</note> conducted an extensive series of experiments on how sound travels through long tubes, specifically water pipes. He used an automatic setup similar in principle to those used for measuring the speed of bullets <note>original: "projectiles"</note>. At the moment a pistol is fired at one end of the tube, the shock breaks <note>original: "ruptures"</note> a wire carrying an electric current. This causes a stylus <note>original: "tracing point"</note>, which was previously marking a line on a revolving drum, to be pulled away. At the far end of the pipe is a stretched membrane; when the sound arrives and the membrane moves in response to the—

In these experiments, the speed <note>original: "velocity"</note> of sound appeared to be slightly affected by the diameter of the pipe, which ranged from 0.108 to 1.100 meters <note>original: "0^m^·108 to 1^m^·100"</note>. This difference is perhaps due to friction, which has a greater influence in smaller pipes.

**6.** Although air is usually the medium <note>original: "vehicle"</note> for sound in practice, other gases, liquids, and solids are equally capable of carrying it. In most cases, however, we lack the equipment to measure the speed of sound directly, and we are not yet ready to discuss indirect methods. But in the case of water, the same difficulty does not exist. In the year 1826, Daniel Colladon and Charles Sturm investigated how sound travels in Lake Geneva. The striking of a bell at one station was timed to coincide with a flash of gunpowder. An observer at a second station measured the interval between the flash and the arrival of the sound by pressing his ear to a tube held beneath the surface. At a temperature of 8°C, the speed of sound in water was found to be 1,435 meters per second.

**7.** The way solids carry sound may be shown by an elegant <note>original: "pretty"</note> experiment designed by Charles Wheatstone. One end of a metal wire is connected to the soundboard of a piano, and the other end is taken through walls or floors into another part of the building where nothing would normally be heard. If a sounding board <note>original: "resonance-board"</note>—such as a violin—is now placed in contact with the wire, a tune played on the piano is easily heard, and the sound seems to come directly from the violin. <insert>Mechanical telephones based on this principle have been introduced into practical use for transmitting speech.</insert> <note>These "mechanical telephones," also known as lovers' telephones or string telephones, used vibrations in a wire or string rather than electricity.</note>

**8.** In an open space, the volume <note>original: "intensity"</note> of sound decreases very quickly as the distance from the source increases. The same amount of energy <note>original: "motion"</note> must spread over surface areas that grow larger according to the square of the distance <note>This is the inverse square law: if you double the distance, the sound is four times quieter</note>. Anything that traps or confines the sound will tend to reduce this loss of volume. For instance, sound carries further over the flat surface of still water than over rough...

**9.** Before proceeding further, we must consider a distinction which is of great importance, though not free from difficulty. Sounds may be classified as musical and unmusical; for convenience, the former may be called *notes* and the latter *noises*. The most obvious cases will not be disputed; everyone recognizes the difference between the note of a piano <note>original: "pianoforte"</note> and the creaking of a shoe. But it is not so easy to draw a clear line between them. In the first place, few notes are entirely free from unmusical accompaniment. With organ pipes especially, the hissing of the air as it escapes at the mouth may be heard alongside the proper note of the pipe. Secondly, many noises have enough of a musical character to have a definite pitch. This is more easily recognized in a sequence—giving, for example, a <term>common chord</term> <note>A basic musical chord consisting of three notes: the root, a third, and a fifth.</note>—than by listening closely to a single instance. This experiment can be made by pulling corks from bottles that have been "tuned" by pouring water into them, or by throwing wooden sticks of specific sizes down onto a table. But, although noises are sometimes not entirely unmusical, and notes are usually not quite free from noise, there is no difficulty in recognizing which of the two is the simpler phenomenon. There is a certain smoothness and continuity to a musical note. Moreover, by sounding a variety of notes together—for example, by striking many consecutive keys on a piano simultaneously—we get something close to a noise; however, no combination of noises could ever blend into a musical note.

**10.** We are therefore led to focus our attention, at first, mainly on musical sounds. These arrange themselves naturally in a certain order according to pitch—a quality that everyone can appreciate to some degree. Trained ears can recognize an enormous number of variations—more than a thousand, probably, within the range <note>original: "compass"</note> of the human voice. These levels of pitch are not like the degrees of a thermometer scale <note>original: "thermometric scale"</note>, which lack special relationships to one another. <page-num>5</page-num>

-># PITCH<-

musicians can identify specific notes that have a fixed relationship to the first note, known as its <term>octave</term>, <term>fifth</term>, and so on. The resulting differences in pitch are called ***intervals***, and they are considered constant for each specific relationship. Therefore, no matter where they appear in the musical scale, a note and its octave are always separated by the ***interval of the octave***. Later, we will aim to explain the origin and nature of these harmonious <note>original: "consonant"</note> intervals as much as possible, but for now, we must examine the physical side of the issue.

Because sounds are produced by vibrations, it is natural to assume that simpler sounds—namely, musical notes—correspond to ***periodic vibrations***. These are vibrations that repeat themselves with perfect regularity after a certain amount of time, known as the ***period***. As we will see, this is true, though there is one exception to be discussed later.

**11.** Many devices <note>original: "contrivances"</note> could be suggested to demonstrate how a musical note is created. One of the simplest is a spinning wheel with a ridged <note>original: "milled"</note> edge pressed against a card. Each ridge produces a light tap as it strikes the card. As the wheel spins, the regular repetition of these taps creates a note of a specific pitch. This pitch rises in the scale as the speed of rotation increases.

However, the best instrument for basic experiments on musical notes is undoubtedly the Siren, invented by Baron Cagniard de la Tour <note>Charles Cagniard de la Tour (1777–1859) was a French physicist who invented this acoustic device in 1819.</note>. It consists primarily of a rigid disc that can spin around its center. This disc is pierced with one or more sets of holes arranged at equal distances around the circumferences of circles sharing the same center <note>original: "concentric"</note> as the disc. An air pipe connected to a set of bellows is positioned perpendicular to the disc, with its open end facing one of the circles of holes. When the bellows are operated, the stream of air escapes freely whenever a hole passes in front of the pipe; otherwise, the air is blocked. As the disc spins, a series of air puffs escape through it. When the speed is fast enough, these puffs blend into a single note. The pitch of this note rises continuously as the puffs become more frequent. Later, we will describe more complex versions of the Siren, but this simple design is enough for our current purpose.

**12.** The Siren demonstrates one of the most fundamental facts in all of science: the pitch of a note depends on the period <note>The time taken for one complete cycle of vibration.</note> of its vibration. The size and shape of the holes, the force of the air, and other factors...

## INTRODUCTION.

varied; but if the number of puffs in a given time, such as one second, remains unchanged, the pitch also remains the same. We may even do away with the wind entirely and produce a note by allowing the corner of a card to tap against the edges of the holes as they rotate; the pitch will still be the same. Observing other sources of sound, such as vibrating solids, leads to the same conclusion, although the difficulties involved often make it necessary to use more refined experimental methods.

However, in saying that pitch depends upon the period, there is an ambiguity that deserves careful consideration, as it will lead us to a point of great importance. If a variable quantity is periodic over any time $\tau$ <note>$\tau$ is the Greek letter tau, used here by the author to represent a specific duration of time.</note>, it is also periodic at the times $2\tau$, $3\tau$, etc. Conversely, a recurrence within a given period $\tau$ does not exclude a more rapid recurrence within periods that are the <term>aliquot parts</term> <note>original: "aliquot parts"; these are parts of a number that divide into it exactly without a remainder, such as 2 and 3 being aliquot parts of 6.</note> of $\tau$. Accordingly, it would appear that a vibration actually repeating in the time $\frac{1}{2}\tau$ (for example) may be regarded as having the period $\tau$, and therefore—by the law just established—as producing a note of the pitch defined by $\tau$. The weight of this consideration cannot be entirely avoided by defining the period as the *shortest* <note>original: "least"</note> time required to bring about a repetition.

In the first place, the necessity of such a restriction is in itself almost enough to show <note>original: "shew"</note> that we have not reached the root of the matter; for although the right to the period $\tau$ may be denied to a vibration that repeats itself exactly within a time $\frac{1}{2}\tau$, it must still be allowed for a vibration that differs from it by an infinitesimally small amount. In the Siren experiment, suppose that in one of the circles of holes containing an even number, every other hole is shifted <note>original: "displaced"</note> along the arc of the circle by the same amount. This shift may be made so small that no change can be detected in the resulting note, even though the periodic time on which the pitch depends has been doubled. 

And secondly, it is evident from the nature of <term>periodicity</term>, that the <term>superposition</term> <note>original: "superposition"; in physics, this refers to the way different waves or vibrations layer on top of one another to form a new pattern.</note> of other vibrations having periods of $\frac{1}{2}\tau$, $\frac{1}{3}\tau$, etc., onto a vibration of period $\tau$ does not disturb the period $\tau$ itself. Yet, it cannot be supposed that the addition of these new elements has left the quality of the sound unchanged. Moreover, since the pitch is not affected by their presence, how do we know that elements of these shorter periods were not there from the beginning?

**13.** These considerations lead us to expect remarkable relationships between the notes whose periods are the reciprocals of the...

# MUSICAL INTERVALS.

<meta>catchword: 13.]</meta>

Natural numbers. Nothing can be easier than to investigate this question by means of the Siren <note>The Siren is an acoustic instrument used to measure sound frequency by passing air through holes in a rotating disc.</note>. Imagine two circles of holes: the inner circle containing any convenient number, and the outer containing twice as many. Then, at whatever speed the disc may turn, the period of the vibration created <note>original: "engendered"</note> by blowing through the first set will necessarily be double that of the vibration from the second set. On making the experiment, the two notes are found to stand to each other in the relation of octaves; and we conclude that *in passing from any note to its octave, the frequency of vibration is doubled.* A similar method of experimenting shows <note>original: "shew"</note> that to the ratio of periods 3 : 1 corresponds the interval known to musicians as the *twelfth*, made up of an octave and a fifth; to the ratio of 4 : 1, the double octave; and to the ratio 5 : 1, the interval made up of two octaves and a *major third*. In order to obtain the intervals of the fifth and third themselves, the ratios must be 3 : 2 and 5 : 4 respectively.

**14.** From these experiments, it appears that if two notes stand to one another in a fixed relation, then, no matter at what part of the scale they may be situated, their periods are in a certain constant ratio characteristic of that relation. The same may be said of their *frequencies*¹, or the number of vibrations which they execute in a given time. The ratio 2 : 1 is thus characteristic of the octave interval. If we wish to combine two intervals—for instance, starting from a given note, to take a step of an octave and then another of a fifth in the same direction—the corresponding ratios must be combined <note>original: "compounded"</note>:

->$\frac{2}{1} \times \frac{3}{2} = \frac{3}{1}.$<-

The twelfth part of an octave is represented by the ratio $\sqrt[12]{2} : 1$ <note>This is the twelfth root of two, used in "equal temperament" tuning to divide an octave into twelve equal semitones.</note>, for this is the step which, repeated twelve times, leads to an octave above the starting point. If we wish to have a measure of intervals in the proper sense, we must take not the characteristic ratio itself, but the logarithm of that ratio. Then, and only then, will the measure of a combined <note>original: "compound"</note> interval be the *sum* of the measures of the components.

¹ A single word to denote the number of vibrations executed in a unit of time is indispensable. I know no better term than ‘frequency,’ which was used in this sense by Young <note>Thomas Young (1773–1829), a polymath who made significant contributions to the fields of vision, light, and solid mechanics.</note>. The same word is employed by Prof. Everett in his excellent edition of Deschanel’s *Natural Philosophy* <note>Augustin Privat-Deschanel's "Traité Élémentaire de Physique" was a standard physics textbook in the late 19th century, translated and edited by J.D. Everett.</note>.

# INTRODUCTION.

**15.** From the intervals of the octave, fifth, and third discussed above, other intervals known to musicians can be derived. The difference between an octave and a fifth is called a **fourth**, and it has a mathematical ratio of $2 \div \frac{3}{2} = \frac{4}{3}$. This process of subtracting an interval from the octave is called **inverting** it. By inverting the major third, we obtain the minor sixth. Similarly, by subtracting a major third from a fifth, we obtain the minor third; and by inverting that minor third, we get the major sixth. The following table shows the names of these intervals alongside their corresponding vibration ratios:

| Interval | Ratio of Frequencies |
| :--- | :--- |
| Octave | 2 : 1 |
| Fifth | 3 : 2 |
| Fourth | 4 : 3 |
| Major Third | 5 : 4 |
| Minor Sixth | 8 : 5 |
| Minor Third | 6 : 5 |
| Major Sixth | 5 : 3 |

These are all the consonant <note>original: "consonant intervals"; refers to intervals that sound stable and pleasant to the ear rather than clashing.</note> intervals found within the span of a single octave. You will notice that the corresponding ratios are all expressed using small whole numbers, and this is especially true for the most harmonious intervals.

Notes whose frequencies are multiples of a starting note are called its **harmonics**, and the entire series makes up a **harmonic scale**. As violinists know well, these harmonics can all be produced from a single string by touching it lightly with the finger at specific points while drawing the bow.

The establishment of this connection between musical intervals and specific vibration ratios—a fundamental principle in **Acoustics**—is credited to Marin Mersenne in 1636 <note>original: "Mersenne (1636)"; Marin Mersenne was a French polymath often called the "father of acoustics."</note>. While the ancient Greeks knew the ratios by which string lengths must be changed to produce an octave or a fifth, Mersenne was the first to demonstrate the physical law connecting a string's length with its vibration period. He also made the first measurement of the actual vibration rate of a known musical note.

**16.** Using any note as a key-note, or **tonic**, we can build a **diatonic scale** <note>The standard seven-note scale (like Do-Re-Mi) used in Western music.</note>, the derivation of which we will now explain. If the key-note—regardless of its actual pitch—is called **Do**, then the fifth above it (the dominant) is **Sol**, and the fifth below it...

The **common chord** <note>original: "common chord"; today more commonly called a major triad, consisting of a root, a major third, and a perfect fifth.</note> on any note is produced by combining it with its major third and fifth, giving the vibration ratios of $1 : \frac{5}{4} : \frac{3}{2}$ or $4 : 5 : 6$. Now, if we take the common chord on the **tonic** [the first note], on the **dominant** [the fifth note], and on the subdominant [the fourth note], and transpose them when necessary into the octave lying immediately above the tonic, we obtain notes whose frequencies, arranged in order of magnitude, are:

->**Do**&emsp;**Re**&emsp;**Mi**&emsp;**Fa**&emsp;**Sol**&emsp;**La**&emsp;**Si**&emsp;**Do**<-
->$1, \quad \frac{9}{8}, \quad \frac{5}{4}, \quad \frac{4}{3}, \quad \frac{3}{2}, \quad \frac{5}{3}, \quad \frac{15}{8}, \quad 2.$<-

Here the common chord on **Do** is **Do**—**Mi**—**Sol**, with the ratios $1 : \frac{5}{4} : \frac{3}{2}$; the chord on **Sol** is **Sol**—**Si**—**Re**, with the ratios $\frac{3}{2} : \frac{15}{8} : 2 \times \frac{9}{8} = 1 : \frac{5}{4} : \frac{3}{2}$; and the chord on **Fa** is **Fa**—**La**—**Do**, still with the same ratios. The scale is completed by repeating these notes above and below at intervals of octaves.

If we take as our **Do**, or keynote, the lower C of a tenor voice, the **diatonic scale** <note>original: "diatonic scale"; the standard seven-note scale of Western music.</note> will be:

->c&emsp;d&emsp;e&emsp;f&emsp;g&emsp;a&emsp;b&emsp;c'.<-

Usage differs slightly as to the method of distinguishing different octaves; in what follows, I adopt the notation of Helmholtz <note>Hermann von Helmholtz (1821–1894), a German physicist who standardized the way we name musical octaves.</note>. The octave below the one just referred to is written with capital letters—C, D, etc.; the next below that with a subscript—C₁, D₁, etc.; and the one beyond that with a double subscript—C₂₁, etc. On the other side, accents denote elevation by an octave—c', c'', etc. The notes of the four strings of a violin are written in this notation as g—d'—a'—e''. The middle C of the pianoforte is c'. [In French notation, c' is denoted by ut₃ <note>original: "ut"; the original name for the note "Do" in the solfège system.</note>.]

**17.** With respect to an absolute standard of **pitch** <note>original: "pitch"; the perceived highness or lowness of a sound, determined by its frequency.</note>, there has been no uniform practice. At the Stuttgart conference in 1834, c' = 264 complete vibrations per second was recommended. This corresponds to a' = 440. The French pitch makes a' = 435. In Handel's time, the pitch was much lower. If c' were taken at 256 or $2^8$, all the C notes would have frequencies represented by powers of 2. This pitch is usually adopted by physicists and acoustical instrument makers, and it has the advantage of mathematical simplicity.

<header>INTRODUCTION.</header>

The principle involves using the **Siren** <note>original: "Siren"; an acoustic instrument invented in the 19th century that measures the frequency of a sound by passing air through a rotating perforated disc.</note>, which is driven at a speed that produces a note in unison with the one being measured. The number of rotations completed by the disc in one second is recorded by a counting device, which can be engaged or disengaged at the beginning and end of a measured interval of time. This number, multiplied by the number of active holes in the disc, provides the required frequency. The consideration of other methods that allow for greater accuracy must be postponed.

**18.** As long as we stick to the **diatonic scale** <note>original: "diatonic scale"; the standard seven-note scale of Western music (e.g., C Major).</note> of C, the notes written above are all that are required in a musical composition. However, it is frequently desired to change the **key-note** <note>original: "key-note"; the "home" note or tonic of a scale.</note>. Under these circumstances, a singer with a good natural ear, accustomed to performing without accompaniment, starts from an entirely new point, constructing a new diatonic scale based on the new key-note. In this way, after a few changes of key, the original scale will be quite far behind, and an immense variety of notes will be used. On an instrument with fixed notes like the piano or organ, such a multiplication of notes is impossible, and some compromise is necessary to allow the same note to perform different functions. This is not the place to discuss the question at length; we will therefore take as an illustration the simplest, as well as the most common case—**modulation** <note>original: "modulation"; the process of changing from one key to another.</note> into the key of the **dominant** <note>original: "dominant"; the fifth note of the scale.</note>.

By definition, the diatonic scale of C consists of the common chords founded on C, G, and F. In the same way, the scale of G consists of the chords founded on G, D, and C. The chords of C and G are then common to both scales; but the third and fifth notes of D introduce new notes. The third of D, written as **F#** [F-sharp], has a frequency of $\frac{9}{8} \times \frac{5}{4} = \frac{45}{32}$, and is quite different from any note in the scale of C. But the fifth of D, with a frequency of $\frac{9}{8} \times \frac{3}{2} = \frac{27}{16}$, differs very little from **A**, whose frequency is $\frac{5}{3}$. On ordinary keyed instruments, the tiny interval between the two—represented by the ratio $\frac{81}{80}$ and called a **comma** <note>original: "comma"; specifically the Syntonic Comma, a small interval representing the difference between a "perfect" tuning and a practical tuning.</note>—is ignored. Through a suitable compromise or **temperament** <note>original: "temperament"; a system of tuning that slightly adjusts the mathematical purity of intervals so that instruments can play in different keys.</note>, the two notes are treated as the same.

**19.** Various systems of temperament have been used; the simplest and most generally used today (or at least aimed for) is **equal temperament**. By referring to the table of frequencies for the diatonic scale, it will be seen that the intervals from Do to Re, from Re to Mi, from Fa to Sol, from Sol to La, and from La...

From these twelve notes, the **diatonic scale** <note>original: "diatonic scale"; the familiar seven-note major or minor scale</note> for any key may be selected according to the following rule: taking the key-note as the first, complete the series with the third, fifth, sixth, eighth, tenth, twelfth, and thirteenth notes, counting upwards. In this way, all difficulties of **modulation** <note>original: "modulation"; the process of changing from one musical key to another</note> are avoided, as the twelve notes serve just as well for one key as for another. 

But this advantage is obtained at the cost of **true intonation** <note>original: "true intonation"; tuning based on the natural mathematical ratios of sound frequencies rather than compromise</note>. The equal temperament "third," being one-third of an octave, is represented by the ratio $\sqrt[3]{2} : 1$, or approximately 1.2599, while the "true" third is 1.25. The tempered third is thus higher than the true one by the interval ratio of 126:125. The ratio of the tempered fifth may be calculated by considering that seven semitones make a fifth, while twelve make an octave. The ratio is therefore $2^{\frac{7}{12}} : 1$, which equals 1.4983. The tempered fifth is thus slightly too low, in the ratio of 1.4983 to 1.5, or approximately 881:882. This error is insignificant; and even the error of the third is not of much consequence in fast music played on instruments like the **piano** <note>original: "pianoforte"</note>. But when the notes are *sustained* <note>original: "held"</note>, as they are on the harmonium and organ, the **consonance** <note>original: "consonance"; the degree to which notes sound harmonious or "stable" when played together</note> of chords is significantly damaged.

**21.** Returning now for a moment to the physical aspect of the question, we will assume—which we shall later prove to be true within wide limits—that when two or more sources of sound agitate the air simultaneously, the resulting disturbance at any point in the external air, or in the ear canal, is the simple sum (in the extended geometrical sense) of what would be caused by each source acting separately. 

Let us consider the disturbance due to a simultaneous sounding of a note and any or all of its harmonics. By definition, the complex whole forms a note having the same period (and therefore pitch) as its lowest <term>original: "gravest"</term> element. We currently have no standard by which the two can be distinguished, or the presence of the higher harmonics recognized. 

And yet—at least in cases where the component sounds have an independent origin—it is usually not difficult for the ear to detect them, so as to analyze the mixture. This is as much as to say that a strictly periodic vibration may give rise to a sensation which is not simple, but capable of further analysis. In fact, it has long been known to musicians that under certain circumstances the harmonics of a note may be heard along with it, even when the note comes from a single source, such as a vibrating string; however, the significance of this fact was not understood. 

Since attention has been drawn to the subject, it has been proved (mainly by the work <note>original: "labours"</note> of Ohm <note>Georg Ohm, who proposed that the ear performs a mathematical Fourier analysis on sound</note> and Helmholtz <note>Hermann von Helmholtz, whose 1863 work "On the Sensations of Tone" revolutionized musical acoustics</note>) that almost all musical notes are highly complex <note>original: "compound"</note>, consisting in fact of the notes of a harmonic scale, from which in particular cases one or...

<header>NOTES AND TONES.</header>

**22.** The kind of note that the ear cannot break down further is called a "ton" by Helmholtz in German. Tyndall and other recent writers on Acoustics have adopted "tone" as the English equivalent—a practice that will be followed in this work. The concept is so important that a convenient word is almost a necessity. *Notes*, therefore, are generally made up of *tones*; the pitch of a note is defined by the lowest <term>original: "gravest"</term> tone it contains.

**23.** Strictly speaking, the quality of pitch must be assigned first only to simple tones; otherwise, the problem of discontinuity mentioned earlier arises. The slightest change in a note’s nature might lower its pitch by a full octave, as shown in the example of the Siren <note>A device used to measure frequency by passing air through holes in a rotating disk</note>. We should now say that the effect of slightly displacing the alternate holes in that experiment was to introduce a new, faint tone an octave lower than any tone previously present. This is enough to change the timing <term>original: "period"</term> of the whole sound, but the bulk of the sound remains very nearly the same as before.

In most musical notes, however, the fundamental or lowest <term>original: "gravest"</term> tone is loud enough to give its character to the whole note. The effect of the harmonic overtones <note>Higher-frequency tones that occur naturally along with a fundamental pitch</note> is then to modify the *quality* or *character*¹ of the note, regardless of its pitch. It is well known that such a distinction exists. The notes of a violin, a tuning fork, or the human voice with its various vowel sounds can all have the same pitch and yet differ in ways other than loudness. Although part of this difference is due to accompanying noises that are not strictly part of the musical notes, there is still a part of the difference that cannot be explained that way.

Musical notes can thus be classified by three variables: First, *pitch*, which we have already considered in detail. Second, *character*, which depends on the proportions in which the harmonic overtones are mixed with the fundamental tone. And third, *loudness*. Loudness is listed last because the ear is not capable of accurately comparing the loudness of two notes that differ greatly in pitch or character. In a future chapter, we will provide a mechanical measurement for the intensity of sound that includes all levels of pitch in one system, but that is not relevant here.

<header>INTRODUCTION.</header>

We are concerned here with the intensity of the sensation of sound, not with measuring its physical cause. We immediately recognize the difference in loudness as a matter of degree; therefore, we have little choice but to view it as dependent—all other things being equal <note>original: *cæteris paribus*</note>—on the size <term>original: "magnitude"</term> of the vibrations involved.

**24.** We have seen that a musical note is caused by a vibration that is necessarily periodic (repeating at regular intervals); however, it is clear that the opposite is not always true. A periodic repetition of a noise once every second—for instance, the ticking of a clock—would not result in a musical note, no matter how perfect the repetition. In such a case, we may say that the fundamental tone <note>The lowest and usually strongest frequency in a complex sound</note> lies outside the limits of human hearing. Although some of the harmonic overtones would fall within those limits, they would not create a musical note or even a chord; instead, they would produce a noisy mass of sound like what you hear when striking all twelve notes of the chromatic scale at once. This experiment can be performed with a Siren <note>A device used to measure frequency by passing air through holes in a rotating disk</note> by spacing the holes irregularly around the edge of a circle and spinning the disk at a moderate speed. Because of how the instrument is built, the entire pattern repeats after every full rotation.

**25.** The main remaining difficulty in the theory of notes and tones is explaining why the ear sometimes breaks notes down into individual tones and sometimes does not. If a note is actually complex, why isn't that fact immediately and clearly perceived, and why aren't its parts separated? The weakness of the harmonic overtones is not the reason; as we will see later in our study, they are often surprisingly loud and play a major role in music. Conversely, if a note is sometimes perceived as a single whole, why doesn't that happen every time? These questions were carefully examined by Hermann von Helmholtz¹ with fairly satisfactory results. This difficulty is not unique to acoustics but can be found in the related science of physiological optics <note>The study of how the eyes and brain perceive light</note>.

The knowledge we gain about external things from our senses is mostly the result of logical deduction <term>original: "inference"</term>. When an object is in front of us, specific nerves in our retinas are triggered, and certain sensations are produced. We are used to associating these sensations with the object and immediately conclude it is there. In the case of an unknown object, the process is much

<header>ANALYSIS OF NOTES.</header>

...perceives them as the same. We interpret the sensations we experience to form a reasonably clear idea of what causes them. From the slightly different perspectives seen by each of our two eyes, we figure out—often through a highly complex process—the actual depth <term>original: "relief"</term> and distance of an object. Without this, we might have no clue about its position. We make these conclusions extremely quickly and entirely unconsciously. 

Our entire lives are an ongoing lesson in interpreting the signals presented to us and drawing conclusions about the reality of the world outside. Our sensations are only useful in everyday life as long as we succeed in doing this. Because of this, it is no surprise that studying the sensations themselves takes a backseat, making what we call **subjective phenomena** <term>Internal experiences or perceptions unique to the individual, rather than the external object itself</term> very difficult to observe. 

As an example, we can look at the "blind spot" on the retina <term>The light-sensitive layer at the back of the eye where the optic nerve attaches, which lacks photoreceptors</term>. One might theoretically <note>original: *a priori*</note> expect this to be a very obvious phenomenon. However, in reality, probably not one person in a hundred million would discover it on their own.

How these observations apply to the topic at hand is fairly clear. In our daily use of hearing, our goal is to separate the specific sounds we are interested in from the overall mass of sound reaching our ears. When listening to a friend speak, we focus on the sound of their voice and try to understand it as a single whole. At the same time, we ignore other sounds as much as possible, treating them as distractions. 

There are usually enough clues to help us perform this kind of partial analysis. When a person speaks, the entire sound of their voice rises and falls in unison, so we have no trouble recognizing it as a single unit. It would not be helpful—and in fact, would cause great confusion—if we tried to analyze the sound even further by breaking it down into its individual component tones. While we might expect our senses to break sound down into these tones, the demands of our situation and the habits of our lives lead us to stop the analysis at the point where it is no longer useful for understanding what our sensations tell us about external objects¹.

When a note and its octave are sounding close together and with perfect uniformity, there is nothing in our sensations to enable us to distinguish whether the notes have a double or a single origin. In the **mixture stop** <term>An organ stop that connects several pipes of different pitches to a single key to create a richer, brighter sound</term> of the organ, pressing down each key admits the wind to a group of pipes, giving a note and its first three or four **harmonics** <term>Higher-frequency tones that are whole-number multiples of the fundamental frequency; they give a sound its specific "color" or timbre</term>. The pipes of each group always sound together, and the result is usually perceived as a single note, although it does not proceed from a single source.

**26.** The resolution of a note into its component tones is a matter of very different difficulty for different individuals. A considerable effort of attention is required, particularly at first; and, until a habit has been formed, some external aid—in the form of a suggestion of what is to be listened for—is very desirable.

The difficulty is very similar to that of learning to draw. From the mechanics of vision, it might have been expected that nothing would be easier than to make a representation of surrounding solid objects on a flat surface; but experience shows <note>original: "shews"</note> that much practice is generally required.

We shall return to the question of the analysis of notes at a later stage, after we have treated the vibrations of strings, which helps clarify the topic best. However, a very instructive experiment, originally developed by **Ohm** <note>Georg Ohm (1789–1854), the physicist who discovered the law of electrical resistance, also proposed that the ear hears complex sounds as a collection of simple tones</note> and improved by **Helmholtz** <note>Hermann von Helmholtz (1821–1894), a pioneering scientist who mapped out the physics of sound and the psychology of how we hear it</note>, may be given here. Helmholtz took two bottles of the shape represented in the figure, one about twice as large as the other. These were blown by streams of air directed across the mouth and issuing from **gutta-percha** <term>A natural, rubber-like latex used in the 19th century for insulation and tubing</term> tubes, whose ends had been softened and pressed flat so as to reduce the opening to the form of a narrow slit; the tubes were connected to the same bellows. By pouring in water when the note is too low and by partially obstructing the mouth when the note is too high, the bottles may be made to give notes with the exact interval of an octave, such as *b* and *b'*. The larger bottle, blown alone, gives a somewhat muffled sound similar in character to the vowel *U*; but, when both bottles are blown, the character of the resulting sound is sharper, resembling rather the vowel *O*. For a short time after the notes had been heard separately, Helmholtz was able to distinguish them in the mixture.

### PENDULOUS VIBRATIONS.

but as the memory of their separate impressions faded, the higher note seemed by degrees to blend <note>original: "amalgamate"</note> with the lower. **27.** Since we can now see that musical notes are usually "compound" (made of multiple parts), and that only a specific type called **tones** are impossible to break down further, we are led to ask: what is the physical quality of tones that makes them unique? What sort of repeating <note>original: "periodic"</note> vibration produces a simple tone? Using what mathematical formula does the air pressure change within the ear canal over time? No question in **Acoustics** <term>The branch of physics concerned with the properties of sound</term> can be more important.

The simplest repeating mathematical formulas known to mathematicians are **circular functions**, expressed by a **sine** or **cosine** <term>Trigonometric functions that describe smooth, repetitive oscillations, like the movement of a pendulum</term>; indeed, there are no other formulas that come close to them in simplicity. They may have any length of time for one cycle, and since they cannot vary in any way except in their size (magnitude), they seem well-suited to produce simple tones. Moreover, it has been proved by the mathematician **Fourier** <note>Joseph Fourier (1768–1830) proved that any complex repeating signal can be mathematically broken down into a series of simple sine waves</note> that even the most complex repeating signal can be broken down into a series of these circular functions, which have cycles that are fractions of the original signal's cycle.

Furthermore, it is a consequence of the general theory of vibration that this specific type of movement—now suggested to be a simple tone—is the only one capable of keeping its shape <note>original: "preserving its integrity"</note> despite the various changes and obstacles it may encounter. Any other kind of vibration is likely to be physically broken down, with one part being affected differently than another. If the way the ear processes sound followed different rules than the laws governing inanimate matter outside the ear, a sound that started out simple might become complex on its way to the listener. There is no reason to suppose that anything of this sort actually happens. When we consider that the internal mechanisms of the ear must follow the same physical laws as the world outside, it is clear that a strong case has been made for regarding "tones" as vibrations described by these circular mathematical functions.

However, we are not left entirely to these general ideas. In the chapter on the vibration of strings, we shall see that in many cases, scientific theory tells us in advance about the nature of—

# CHAPTER 2.

### HARMONIC MOTIONS.

**28.** The vibrations expressed by a circular function <note>original: "circular function"; this refers to trigonometric functions like sine and cosine that repeat in a cycle.</note> of time—variously called *simple*, *pendulous* <note>original: "pendulous"; motion that swings back and forth with the regular rhythm of a pendulum.</note>, or *harmonic*—are so important in Acoustics that we should dedicate a chapter to their consideration before entering into the dynamical <note>original: "dynamical"; the branch of physics dealing with forces and their effect on motion.</note> part of our subject. The quantity whose variation constitutes the "vibration" might be the displacement of a particle measured in a specific direction, the pressure at a fixed point in a fluid medium, and so on. In any case, representing this quantity as $u$, we have:

-> $u = a \cos \left( \frac{2\pi t}{\tau} - \epsilon \right) \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (1),$ <-

In this formula, $a$ represents the **amplitude**, or the maximum value of $u$; $\tau$ <note>The Greek letter 'tau'.</note> is the **periodic time**, or **period**, after which the values of $u$ repeat; and $\epsilon$ <note>The Greek letter 'epsilon'.</note> determines the **phase** of the vibration at the moment from which time ($t$) is measured.

Any number of harmonic vibrations of the *same period* that influence a variable quantity will combine <note>original: "compound into"</note> into another vibration of the same type. The properties <note>original: "elements"</note> of this new vibration are determined as follows:

-> $u = \Sigma a \cos \left( \frac{2\pi t}{\tau} - \epsilon \right)$ <-

-> $= \cos \frac{2\pi t}{\tau} \Sigma a \cos \epsilon + \sin \frac{2\pi t}{\tau} \Sigma a \sin \epsilon$ <-

-> $= r \cos \left( \frac{2\pi t}{\tau} - \theta \right) \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (2),$ <-

| | | |
|---|---|---|
| **where** | $r = \{(\Sigma a \cos \epsilon)^2 + (\Sigma a \sin \epsilon)^2\}^{\frac{1}{2}}$ | $\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(3),$ |
| **and** | $\tan \theta = \Sigma a \sin \epsilon \div \Sigma a \cos \epsilon$ | $\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(4).$ |

<vocab>Harmonic Motions, Acoustics, vibration, amplitude, periodic time, period, phase</vocab>

# HARMONIC MOTIONS.

For example, let there be two components:
-> $u = a \cos (\frac{2\pi t}{\tau} - \epsilon) + a' \cos (\frac{2\pi t}{\tau} - \epsilon')$; <-
then the combined amplitude $r$ is:
-> $r = \{a^2 + a'^2 + 2aa' \cos (\epsilon - \epsilon')\}^{\frac{1}{2}} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(5),$ <-
and the new phase angle $\theta$ is found by:
-> $\tan \theta = \frac{a \sin \epsilon + a' \sin \epsilon'}{a \cos \epsilon + a' \cos \epsilon'} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(6).$ <-

Specific cases can be observed. If the phases of the two components are the same <note>original: "agree"</note>, the formula simplifies to:
-> $u = (a + a') \cos (\frac{2\pi t}{\tau} - \epsilon).$ <-

If the phases differ by half a period:
-> $u = (a - a') \cos (\frac{2\pi t}{\tau} - \epsilon),$ <-
so that if $a'$ and $a$ are equal, $u$ vanishes <note>original: "vanishes"; in this context, it means the vibrations cancel each other out completely, resulting in zero movement or silence.</note>. In this case, the vibrations are often said to **interfere**, but this expression is somewhat misleading. Two sounds may very properly be said to "interfere" when they combine to cause silence; however, the simple superposition <note>The placing of one thing (like a wave) on top of another so that they combine.</note> of two vibrations (whether they result in rest or not) cannot strictly be called interference. After all, if this is called interference, it is difficult to define what "non-interference" would be. It will become clear later in this work that when vibrations exceed a certain intensity, they no longer combine <note>original: "compound"</note> by simple addition; *this* mutual interaction might more properly be called interference, as it is a phenomenon of a completely different nature from what we are discussing here.

Furthermore, if the phases differ by a quarter or by three-quarters of a period, the cosine of the phase difference $\cos (\epsilon - \epsilon')$ equals zero, and the resulting amplitude is:
-> $r = \{a^2 + a'^2\}^{\frac{1}{2}}.$ <-

Harmonic vibrations of a specific period can be represented by lines drawn from a central point <note>original: "pole"</note>. The lengths of these lines are proportional to the amplitudes, and their angles <note>original: "inclinations"</note> correspond to the phases of the vibrations. The combined result <note>original: "resultant"</note> of any number of harmonic vibrations is then represented by the geometric sum of these corresponding lines. For example, if the lines are arranged symmetrically around the center point, their combined total (the vibration) is zero.

**29.** If we map out distances proportional to time along a horizontal axis (the x-axis) and use $u$ as the vertical coordinate <note>original: "ordinate"; the vertical coordinate in a graph.</note>, we obtain the **harmonic curve**, or **sine wave** <note>original: "curve of sines"</note>.

It also introduces the geometric representation of vibrations and the concept of the sine wave graph.</summary>

->COMPOSITION.<-

->$$u = a \cos \left( \frac{2\pi x}{\lambda} - \epsilon \right),$$<-

where $\lambda$, called the **wavelength**, replaces $\tau$. Both quantities represent the range of the independent variable required for the function to complete one full cycle <note>original: "complete recurrence"</note>. The harmonic curve is therefore the path <note>original: "locus"</note> of a point experiencing both a steady forward motion and a harmonic vibration moving at a right angle. In the next chapter, we will see that the vibration of a tuning fork is a simple harmonic motion. Therefore, if a vibrating <note>original: "excited"</note> tuning fork is moved at a steady speed parallel to its handle, a tip <note>original: "tracing point"</note> attached to one of its prongs will draw a harmonic curve. This can be recorded permanently by letting the tip rest lightly on a piece of smoked paper. **30. If two harmonic vibrations with different periods occur together,**

->$$u = a \cos \left( \frac{2\pi t}{\tau} - \epsilon \right) + a' \cos \left( \frac{2\pi t}{\tau'} - \epsilon' \right).$$<-

In this case, the total movement <note>original: "resultant"</note> cannot be represented as a simple harmonic motion just by changing its parts. If $\tau$ and $\tau'$ are incommensurable <note>Meaning they cannot be expressed as a simple fraction or a ratio of whole numbers.</note>, the value of $u$ never repeats. However, if $\tau$ and $\tau'$ form a ratio of two whole numbers, $u$ repeats after a length of time equal to the least common multiple of $\tau$ and $\tau'$. Even so, the resulting vibration is not a simple harmonic motion. For example, when a note and its fifth <note>In music, a "fifth" is an interval where the frequencies are in a 3:2 ratio; for example, the notes C and G.</note> are played together, the vibration repeats after a duration equal to twice the period of the lower note <note>original: "graver"</note>.

<page-num>22 [30.</page-num>
<header>HARMONIC MOTIONS</header>

One specific case involving the combination <note>original: "composition"</note> of harmonic vibrations with different periods deserves special discussion: when the difference between the periods is small. If we observe what happens over a short time interval covering only a few periods, we see that the two vibrations behave almost as if their periods were identical. In that case, as we already know, they would be equivalent to a single simple harmonic vibration of that same period. For a few cycles, then, the combined <note>original: "resultant"</note> motion is approximately a simple harmonic one, but this same harmonic pattern will not represent the movement for long. The vibration with the shorter period steadily pulls ahead of the other, thereby changing the phase difference upon which the elements of the combined motion depend. 

To keep the explanation simple, let us assume that the two components have equal amplitudes and frequencies represented by $m$ and $n$ (where the difference $m - n$ is small), and that their phases match when we first observe them. At this moment, their effects combine <note>original: "conspire"</note>, and the resulting vibration has an amplitude twice that of the individual components. However, after a time interval of $1 \div 2 (m - n)$, vibration $m$ will have gained half a cycle <note>original: "period"</note> relative to the other. Now, being in complete opposition <note>original: "disagreement"</note>, they cancel <note>original: "neutralize"</note> each other out. After another equal time interval, $m$ will have gained a full vibration, and they will be completely in sync <note>original: "accordance"</note> once again. 

The combined motion is therefore approximately simple harmonic, but with an amplitude that is not constant; instead, it varies from zero to twice that of the components. The frequency of these changes is $m - n$. If two tuning forks with frequencies of 500 and 501 Hz are struck with equal force <note>original: "equally excited"</note>, there is a rise and fall in the sound every second, corresponding to the vibrations being in or out of sync <note>original: "coincidence or opposition"</note>. This phenomenon is called <term>beats</term>. 

We will not fully discuss here how the ear reacts to vibrations with nearly identical frequencies, but it is obvious that if the movement of air near the ear almost stops for a significant fraction of a second, the sound must seem to fade away. For reasons that will be explained later, beats are most easily heard when the interfering sounds are pure <note>original: "simple"</note> tones. Adjacent notes on the stopped diapason <note>An organ stop that produces a soft, flute-like sound by closing the top of the pipes.</note> of an organ show this phenomenon very well, at least in the lower registers <note>original: "parts of the scale"</note>. A continuous interference between two notes can be created by mounting two identical stopped organ pipes of the same pitch side by side on the same wind chest <note>The pressurized box in an organ that holds the air for the pipes.</note>. The vibrations of the two pipes

<summary>This page explains the phenomenon of "beats," which occurs when two sounds of slightly different frequencies interfere with each other, causing the volume to rise and fall as the waves move in and out of sync.</summary>

<page-num>23</page-num>
<header>30.] OF NEARLY EQUAL PERIOD.</header>

...adjust themselves to be perfectly out of phase <note>original: "complete opposition"</note>, so that at a short distance nothing can be heard except the soft hissing of the air. If a solid wall were placed between the two pipes to block one sound, the other would immediately become audible again. Or, the delicate balance that creates this silence can be disrupted by connecting the ear to a tube, with the other end placed close to the opening of just one of the pipes.

By listening for "beats"—the pulsing sound caused by interference—two notes can be tuned to the exact same pitch <term>unison</term> with great precision. The goal is to make these pulses as slow as possible, because the number of beats per second is equal to the difference between the frequencies of the two notes. In ideal conditions, beats as slow as one every 30 seconds can be detected; this would indicate that the higher note gains only two vibrations *per minute* over the lower one. Or, one might simply want to determine the difference in frequency between two notes that are nearly in sync, in which case one only needs to count the number of beats. It should be remembered that the difference in frequencies does not determine the musical *interval* between two notes; that interval depends instead on the ratio of their frequencies. For example, the speed of the beats produced by two notes nearly in unison is doubled when both notes are raised by exactly one octave.

Mathematical Analysis
->**u = a cos (2πmt - ε) + a' cos (2πnt - ε')**,<-
where the difference between frequencies **m - n** is small.

The term **cos (2πnt - ε')** can be rewritten as
->**cos {2πmt - 2π (m - n) t - ε'}**,<-
which gives us the resulting motion:
->**u = r cos (2πmt - θ)** ........................ (1),<-
where
->**r² = a² + a'² + 2aa' cos {2π (m - n) t + ε' - ε}** ...... (2),<-
->**tan θ = (a sin ε + a' sin {2π (m - n) t + ε'}) / (a cos ε + a' cos {2π (m - n) t + ε'})** ......... (3).<-

The resulting vibration <note>original: "resultant vibration"</note> can therefore be viewed as a harmonic motion where the elements **r** and **θ** are not fixed, but instead change slowly over time at a frequency of **m - n**. The amplitude <term>amplitude</term> (the strength or peak of the wave) **r** is at its maximum when
->**cos {2π (m - n) t + ε' - ε} = + 1**,<-
and at its minimum when
->**cos {2π (m - n) t + ε' - ε} = - 1**,<-
the corresponding values being **a + a'** and **a - a'** respectively.

# HARMONIC MOTIONS.

## 31.
Another case of great importance is the composition of vibrations corresponding to a tone and its harmonics. It is known that the most general single-valued finite periodic function can be expressed by a series of simple harmonics—

-> $u = a_0 + \sum_{n=1}^{n=\infty} a_n \cos \left( \frac{2\pi nt}{\tau} - \epsilon_n \right) \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (1),$ <-

a theorem usually quoted as Fourier’s <term>Fourier's theorem: a mathematical principle stating that any complex periodic wave can be represented as the sum of simple sine and cosine waves</term>. Mathematical proofs will be found in Isaac Todhunter’s *Integral Calculus* and the work of William Thomson (Lord Kelvin) and Peter Guthrie Tait, *Treatise on Natural Philosophy*; and a line of argument almost if not quite amounting to a proof <note>original: "demonstration"</note> will be given later in this work. A few remarks are all that will be required here.

Fourier’s theorem is not obvious. It is a common but vague notion that the infinite number <note>original: "infinitude"</note> of arbitrary constants in the series naturally grants it the capacity to represent any periodic function. It becomes clear that this is an error when one considers that the same argument would apply equally if one term of the series were removed; yet in that case, the expansion would generally be impossible.

Another point worth noting is that simple harmonics are not the only functions through which it is possible to expand an arbitrarily chosen function into a series. Instead of the simple elementary term

-> $\cos \left( \frac{2\pi nt}{\tau} - \epsilon_n \right),$ <-

we might take

-> $\cos \left( \frac{2\pi nt}{\tau} - \epsilon_n \right) + \frac{1}{2} \cos \left( \frac{4\pi nt}{\tau} - \epsilon_n \right),$ <-

formed by adding a similar vibration in the same phase but with half the amplitude and period. It is evident that these terms would serve just as well as the others; for

-> $\cos \left( \frac{2\pi nt}{\tau} - \epsilon_n \right) = \left\{ \cos \left( \frac{2\pi nt}{\tau} - \epsilon_n \right) + \frac{1}{2} \cos \left( \frac{4\pi nt}{\tau} - \epsilon_n \right) \right\}$ <-
-> $- \frac{1}{2} \left\{ \cos \left( \frac{4\pi nt}{\tau} - \epsilon_n \right) + \frac{1}{2} \cos \left( \frac{8\pi nt}{\tau} - \epsilon_n \right) \right\}$ <-
-> $+ \frac{1}{4} \left\{ \cos \left( \frac{8\pi nt}{\tau} - \epsilon_n \right) + \frac{1}{2} \cos \left( \frac{16\pi nt}{\tau} - \epsilon_n \right) \right\}$ <-
-> $- \dots \dots \text{to infinity <note>original: "ad infin."</note>},$ <-

so that each term in Fourier’s series, and therefore the total sum of the series, can be expressed by means of this double elementary term.

<summary>This page introduces Fourier's theorem, explaining that complex periodic vibrations can be broken down into a series of simple harmonic components. It clarifies common misconceptions about the theorem and demonstrates that simple harmonics are the standard, though not the only possible, building blocks for these mathematical expansions.</summary>

# FOURIER'S THEOREM.

terms now suggested. This is mentioned here because students, not being familiar with other expansions, may imagine that simple harmonic functions are by nature the only ones capable of serving as the building blocks <note>original: "elements"</note> in the expansion of a periodic function. The reason for the preeminent importance of Fourier's series in acoustics is the mechanical one referred to in the preceding chapter—which will be explained more fully later—namely, that, in general, simple harmonic vibrations are the only kind that are propagated through a vibrating system without being broken down <note>original: "suffering decomposition"</note>.

**32.** As in other similar cases (for example, Taylor's theorem <note>A formula used in calculus to represent a function as an infinite sum of terms calculated from the values of its derivatives at a single point</note>), if the possibility of the expansion is known, the coefficients may be determined by a relatively simple process. We may write equation (1) from section 31 as:

-> $u = A_0 + \sum_{n=1}^{n=\infty} A_n \cos \frac{2n\pi t}{\tau} + \sum_{n=1}^{n=\infty} B_n \sin \frac{2n\pi t}{\tau} ......(1).$ <-

By multiplying by $\cos (2n\pi t/\tau)$ or $\sin (2n\pi t/\tau)$, and integrating over a complete period from $t = 0$ to $t = \tau$, we find:

-> $\left. \begin{aligned} A_n = \frac{2}{\tau} \int_0^\tau u \cos \frac{2n\pi t}{\tau} dt \\ B_n = \frac{2}{\tau} \int_0^\tau u \sin \frac{2n\pi t}{\tau} dt \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (2).$ <-

An immediate integration gives:

-> $A_0 = \frac{1}{\tau} \int_0^\tau u dt \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(3),$ <-

indicating that $A_0$ is the mean value of $u$ throughout the period.

The degree of convergence <note>original: "convergency"</note> in the expansion of $u$ depends in general on the continuity of the function and its derivatives. The series formed by successive differentiations of equation (1) converge less and less rapidly, but still remain convergent and serve as numerical representations of the differential coefficients of $u$, as long as these latter are everywhere finite. Thus (according to Thomson and Tait <note>William Thomson (Lord Kelvin) and Peter Guthrie Tait, authors of the influential *Treatise on Natural Philosophy* (1867)</note>, § 77), if all the derivatives up to the $m^{th}$ inclusive are free from infinite values, the series for $u$ is more convergent than one with

-> $1, \quad \frac{1}{2^m}, \quad \frac{1}{3^m}, \quad \frac{1}{4^m}, \dots\dots \text{etc.},$ <-

for coefficients.

# HARMONIC MOTIONS

**32 *a*.** The general explanation of the beats heard when two pure tones at nearly the same pitch <note>original: "nearly in unison"</note> are sounded simultaneously was discussed in section 30. However, the occurrence of beats is not limited to cases of approximate unison, at least when dealing with compound notes <note>Musical tones consisting of a fundamental frequency and several overtones or harmonics</note>. Suppose, for example, that the interval is an octave. The lower <note>original: "graver"</note> note then usually includes an overtone that matches the pitch of the fundamental tone of the higher note. If the interval is slightly altered, the previously matching tones separate from one another and produce beats of the same frequency as if they existed alone. There is usually no difficulty in observing these beats; however, if one or both of the component tones involved are very faint, a resonator <note>An instrument or hollow chamber designed to vibrate at a specific frequency, used to amplify specific tones</note> may be used to help hear them.

In general, we may consider that each consonant interval <note>A musically pleasing interval, such as a fifth or a third, where the frequencies of the two notes have a simple ratio</note> is characterized by the coincidence of certain component tones; if the interval is slightly changed, the previously matching tones give rise to beats. Of course, it may happen in any particular case that the tones which would normally match in pitch are absent from one or the other of the notes. In that case, according to the theory above, the alteration of the interval would not be accompanied by beats. In practice, faint beats are usually heard anyway; but the discussion of this phenomenon, about which authorities are not entirely agreed, must be postponed for now.

**33.** Another class of combined vibrations—interesting because of how easily they can be observed optically—occurs when two harmonic vibrations acting on the same particle are performed in perpendicular directions. This is especially notable when the periods are not only commensurable <note>original: "commensurable"; meaning they can be expressed as a ratio of whole numbers</note>, but are in the ratio of two *small* whole numbers. The motion is then completely periodic, with a total period not many times greater than those of the individual components, and the path described is a closed loop <note>original: "re-entrant"</note>. If *u* and *v* are the coordinates, we may represent them as:

->*u* = *a* cos (2$\pi$*nt* - $\epsilon$), *v* = *b* cos 2$\pi$*n't* ............(1).<-

First, let us suppose that the periods are equal, so that *n'* = *n*. Eliminating the time variable *t* gives the following equation for the curve described:

->$\frac{u^2}{a^2} + \frac{v^2}{b^2} - \frac{2uv}{ab} \cos \epsilon - \sin^2 \epsilon = 0$ ............(2),<-

This represents, in general, an ellipse whose position and dimensions depend upon the amplitudes of the original vibrations and upon...

### IN PERPENDICULAR DIRECTIONS

...the difference of their phases <note>The specific point in a cycle of a wave or vibration</note>. If the phases differ by a quarter period, then the cosine of $\epsilon = 0$, and the equation becomes:

->$\frac{u^2}{a^2} + \frac{v^2}{b^2} = 1.$<-

In this case, the axes of the ellipse coincide with those of the coordinates. If, furthermore, the two components have equal amplitudes <note>The maximum extent of a vibration, measured from its center position</note>, the path degenerates into a circle:

-> $u^2 + v^2 = a^2,$ <-

which is described with uniform velocity. This shows <note>original: "shews"</note> how a uniform circular motion may be analyzed into two rectilinear <note>moving in a straight line</note> harmonic motions whose directions are perpendicular to each other.

If the phases of the components agree ($\epsilon = 0$), the ellipse collapses into coincident straight lines:

-> $(\frac{u}{a} - \frac{v}{b})^2 = 0;$ <-

or, if the difference of phase amounts to half a period, into:

-> $(\frac{u}{a} + \frac{v}{b})^2 = 0.$ <-

When the unison <note>The state of two vibrations having exactly the same frequency</note> of the two vibrations is exact, the elliptical path remains perfectly steady. However, in practice, there will almost always be a slight difference between the periods. Consequently, although a fixed ellipse represents the curve described with sufficient accuracy for a few periods, the ellipse itself gradually changes as the value of $\epsilon$ alters. It therefore becomes a matter of interest to consider the system of ellipses represented by equation (2), assuming $a$ and $b$ are constants, but $\epsilon$ is variable.

Since the extreme values of $u$ and $v$ are $\pm a$ and $\pm b$ respectively, the ellipse is in all cases inscribed in the rectangle whose sides are $2a$ and $2b$. Starting with the phases in agreement ($\epsilon = 0$), we have the ellipse coinciding with the diagonal $\frac{u}{a} - \frac{v}{b} = 0$. As $\epsilon$ increases from $0$ to $\frac{1}{2}\pi$ <note>a quarter of a cycle</note>, the ellipse opens out until its equation becomes:

-> $\frac{u^2}{a^2} + \frac{v^2}{b^2} = 1.$ <-

From this point, it closes up again, ultimately coinciding with the other diagonal $\frac{u}{a} + \frac{v}{b} = 0$, corresponding to the increase of $\epsilon$ from $\frac{1}{2}\pi$ to $\pi$ <note>half a cycle</note>. After this, as $\epsilon$ ranges from $\pi$ to $2\pi$, the ellipse retraces...

<header>34.] LISSAJOUS' CYLINDER.</header>

*AA'B'B* represents the cylinder, of which *AB'* is a flat section <note>original: "plane section"</note>. When viewed from an infinite distance in the direction of the common tangent at *A* to the flat sections, the cylinder is projected onto a 2D surface as a rectangle, and the ellipse is projected as its diagonal line. Suppose now that the cylinder turns on its axis, carrying the flat section with it. Its own projection remains a constant rectangle within which the projection of the ellipse is inscribed. Figure 6 shows the position of the cylinder after it has rotated through 90 degrees <note>original: "a right angle"</note>.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram labeled FIG. 6. It shows a cylinder with a solid elliptical top and bottom. A diagonal ellipse is inscribed within the cylinder, shown with a solid line on the front face and a dashed line on the rear face. Points are labeled A', P, and A along the top edge, and B' and B along the bottom edge.</image-desc>

->*FIG. 6.*<-

It appears, therefore, that by turning the cylinder, we can see in sequence all the ellipses that represent the paths of a point moving with two harmonic vibrations <term>harmonic vibrations: smooth, repetitive back-and-forth motions, like a swinging pendulum</term> of equal duration <note>original: "period"</note> and fixed heights <note>original: "amplitudes"</note>. Furthermore, if the cylinder is turned continuously at a steady speed <note>original: "uniform velocity"</note>—which ensures a harmonic motion for point *P*—we get a full representation of the changing orbit described by the point when the durations of the two components differ slightly. In this case, each full revolution represents the gain or loss of a single vibration¹. The cylinder's revolutions are thus synchronized <note>original: "synchronous"</note> with the "beats" <note>Beats are the rhythmic pulsations heard or seen when two vibrations of slightly different frequencies interfere with one another.</note> that would result from combining the two vibrations if they were moving in the same direction.

**35.** Vibrations of the kind discussed here are very easy to demonstrate experimentally. A heavy pendulum-weight <note>original: "pendulum-bob"</note>, hanging from a fixed point by a long wire or string, moves in ellipses under the force of gravity. Depending on how it is originally pushed <note>original: "circumstances of projection"</note>, these paths may, in certain cases, become straight lines or circles. 

However, to see these orbits most clearly, they must be traced so quickly that the image made on the eye's retina by the moving point does not have time to fade before the point completes its circuit and begins again. ->*u = a* cos (4*nπt - ε*), *v = b* cos 2*nπt*.<-

->$v^2 = \frac{b^2}{2} \left( 1 \pm \frac{u}{a} \right),$<-
