**37.** It is easy to set up a vibrating system where the motion of a point consists of two harmonic vibrations occurring in perpendicular planes, with their periods set at any specific ratio. The simplest version is known as **Blackburn's pendulum**. A wire *ACB* is fastened at two fixed points, *A* and *B*, which are at the same level. The bob *P* <term>bob: the weight at the end of a pendulum</term> is attached to the middle of this wire by another wire, *CP*. For vibrations occurring within the plane of the diagram, the point of suspension is effectively *C*, as long as the wires are pulled tight. However, for motion perpendicular to this plane, the bob swings from point *D*, moving the wire *ACB* along with it. The periods of vibration in

**38.** Another contrivance called the <term>kaleidophone</term> <note>A device consisting of a vibrating rod with a reflective bead at the end; when it vibrates in two directions, the bead traces luminous patterns.</note> was originally invented by <term>Wheatstone</term> <note>Sir Charles Wheatstone (1802–1875), an English scientist and inventor.</note>. A straight, thin bar of steel carrying a bead at its upper end is fastened in a vice, as explained in a previous paragraph. If the cross-section of the bar is square or circular, the period of vibration is independent of the plane in which it is performed. But let us suppose that the cross-section is a rectangle with unequal sides. The stiffness of the bar—the force with which it resists bending—is then greater in the plane of greater thickness, and the vibrations in this plane have the shorter period <note>Stiffer materials vibrate faster; therefore, the thicker dimension of the rod produces a higher frequency.</note>. By a suitable adjustment of the thicknesses, the two periods of vibration may be brought into any required ratio, and the corresponding curve can be displayed.

The defect in this arrangement is that the same bar will give only one set of figures. In order to overcome this objection, the following modification has been devised. A slip of steel is taken whose rectangular section is very elongated, so that as regards bending in one plane, the stiffness is so great that it is practically rigid. The bar is divided into two parts, and the broken ends are reunited, with the two pieces turned against one another at a right angle, so that the plane containing the small thickness of one contains the great thickness of the other. When this compound rod is clamped in a vice at a point below the junction, the period of the vibration in one direction—depending almost entirely on the length of the upper piece—is nearly constant. However, the period in the second direction may be controlled by varying the point at which the lower piece is clamped.

**39.** In this arrangement, the luminous point itself performs the vibrations which are to be observed. But in <term>Lissajous'</term> <note>Jules Antoine Lissajous (1822–1880), a French physicist who studied sound and light.</note> form of the experiment, the point of light remains actually fixed, while its *image* is thrown into apparent motion by means of successive reflections from two vibrating mirrors. A small hole in an opaque screen placed close to the flame of a lamp provides a point of light, which is observed after reflection in the mirrors by means of a small telescope. The mirrors, usually made of polished steel, are attached to the prongs of stout tuning forks, and the whole apparatus is arranged so that when the forks are set into vibration, the luminous point appears to describe harmonic motions in perpendicular directions, due to the angular motions of the reflecting surfaces. The amplitudes and periods of these harmonic motions depend upon those of the corresponding forks, and may be adjusted to produce...

**41.** The auxiliary harmonic motion is generally obtained optically, by means of an instrument called a <term>vibration-microscope</term> <note>An instrument used to observe the path of a vibrating object by mounting part of a microscope onto a tuning fork.</note> invented by **Lissajous**. One prong of a large tuning fork carries a lens, whose axis is perpendicular to the direction of vibration; this may be used either by itself or as the objective lens of a compound microscope formed by adding an independently supported eyepiece. In either case, a stationary point appears to move in a harmonic motion along a line parallel to the direction of the fork's vibration.

The vibration-microscope may be applied to test the strictness and universality of the law connecting *pitch* and *period* <note>In acoustics, the "period" is the time it takes to complete one full vibration cycle.</note>. For example, any point of a vibrating body that produces a pure musical note will appear to describe a <term>re-entrant curve</term> <note>A closed loop where the path returns to its starting point.</note> when examined with a vibration-microscope whose own note is in strict unison with it. By the same means, the ratios of frequencies characteristic of <term>consonant intervals</term> <note>Musical intervals that sound stable or pleasant, such as an octave or a perfect fifth.</note> may be verified; however, for this latter purpose, a more purely acoustical method—which will be described in a future chapter—may be preferred.

**42.** Another method of examining the motion of a vibrating body depends upon the use of intermittent illumination <note>This is the principle of the stroboscope, where flickering light makes a moving object appear stationary or slow-moving.</note>. Suppose, for example, that by using suitable apparatus, a series of electric sparks are produced at regular intervals $\tau$. A vibrating body, whose period is also $\tau$, will appear to be at rest when examined by the light of the sparks because it is only visible in one position. If, however, the period of the vibration differs from $\tau$ even slightly, the illuminated position varies, and the body will appear to vibrate slowly. Its frequency will appear to be the difference between the frequency of the spark and the frequency of the body. The specific type of vibration can then be observed easily.

The series of sparks can be obtained from an induction coil <note>An early type of electrical transformer used to produce high-voltage pulses.</note> whose primary circuit is periodically broken by a vibrating fork or by some other interrupter of sufficient regularity. But a better result is provided by sunlight rendered intermittent with the aid of a fork whose prongs carry two small metal plates, which are close together and parallel to the plane of vibration. In each plate, there is a slit.

# INTERMITTENT ILLUMINATION

On the opening so formed, a beam of sunlight is concentrated by means of a magnifying lens <note>original: "burning-glass"</note>, and the object under examination is placed in the cone of rays diverging on the further side¹. When the fork is made to vibrate by an electromagnetic arrangement, the illumination is cut off except when the fork is passing through its position of equilibrium <note>The central position where the fork is at rest</note>, or nearly so. The flashes of light obtained by this method are not as instantaneous as electric sparks (especially when a capacitor <note>original: "jar," likely a Leyden jar</note> is connected with the secondary wire of the induction coil), but in my experience, the regularity is more perfect. Care should be taken to cut off extraneous light as far as possible, and the effect is then very striking.

A similar result may be arrived at by looking at the vibrating body through a series of holes arranged in a circle on a revolving disc. Several series of holes may be provided on the same disc, but the observation is not satisfactory without some provision for securing uniform rotation.

Except with respect to the sharpness of definition, the result is the same when the period of the light is any multiple of that of the vibrating body. This point must be attended to when the revolving wheel is used to determine an unknown frequency.

When the frequency of intermittence is an exact multiple of that of the vibration, the object is seen without apparent motion, but generally in more than one position. This condition of things is sometimes advantageous.

Similar effects arise when the frequencies of the vibrations and of the flashes are in the ratio of two small whole numbers. If, for example, the number of vibrations in a given time be half as great again as the number of flashes, the body will appear stationary, and in general double.

# HARMONIC MOTIONS

The precise manner in which the phases <note>The "phase" refers to the specific point in a cycle that a vibration has reached at a given time.</note> are distributed may vary, resulting in an intensity ranging from $n^2$ to zero. But is there a definite intensity that becomes more and more probable when $n$ <note>Here, $n$ represents the total number of vibrations being combined.</note> is increased without limit?

The nature of the question raised here is well illustrated by the special case in which the possible phases are restricted to two opposite phases. We may then conveniently set aside the idea of phase and regard the amplitudes <note>The maximum extent of a vibration or oscillation, measured from the position of equilibrium.</note> as being randomly positive or negative. If all the signs are the same, the intensity is $n^2$; if, on the other hand, there are as many positive as negative values, the result is zero. But although the intensity may range from $0$ to $n^2$, the smaller values are more probable than the larger ones.

The simplest part of the problem relates to what is called in the theory of probabilities the "expectation" <note>In modern terms, this is the "expected value" or the weighted average of all possible outcomes.</note> of intensity—that is, the mean intensity to be expected after a great number of trials, in each of which the phases are taken at random. The chance that all the vibrations are positive is $(\frac{1}{2})^n$, and thus the expectation of intensity corresponding to this possibility is $(\frac{1}{2})^n \cdot n^2$. In like manner, the expectation corresponding to the number of positive vibrations being $(n - 1)$ is:

->$(\frac{1}{2})^n n (n - 2)^2,$<-

and so on. The whole expectation of intensity is thus:

->$\frac{1}{2^n} \left\{ 1 \cdot n^2 + n (n - 2)^2 + \frac{n (n - 1)}{1 \cdot 2} (n - 4)^2 \right.$<-
->$\left. + \frac{n (n - 1) (n - 2)}{1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3} (n - 6)^2 + \dots \right\} \dots \dots (1).$<-

Now the sum of the $(n + 1)$ terms of this series is simply $n$, as may be proved by a comparison of coefficients of $x^2$ in the equivalent forms:

->$(e^x + e^{-x})^n = 2^n (1 + \frac{1}{2} x^2 + \dots)^n$<-
->$= e^{nx} + n e^{(n-2)x} + \frac{n (n - 1)}{1 \cdot 2} e^{(n-4)x} + \dots$<-

The expectation of intensity is therefore $n$, and this remains true whether $n$ is large or small.

The same conclusion holds good when the phases are unrestricted. From (3) § 28, if $a_1 = a_2 = \dots = 1$:

->$r^2 = (\cos \epsilon_1 + \cos \epsilon_2 + \dots)^2 + (\sin \epsilon_1 + \sin \epsilon_2 + \dots)^2$<-
->$= n + 2 \Sigma \cos (\epsilon_2 - \epsilon_1) \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (2),$<-

where under the sign of summation <note>original: "$\Sigma$"</note> are to be included the cosines of the $\frac{1}{2} n (n - 1)$ differences of phase. When the phases are...

random, the sum is just as likely to be positive as negative, and thus the mean value of $r^2$ <note>Here, $r$ represents the resultant amplitude, and $r^2$ represents the intensity.</note> is $n$.

The reader should be on guard here against a fallacy that has misled some prominent authors. We have not proven that when $n$ <note>The number of individual vibrations or components.</note> is large, there is any tendency for a single combination to result in an intensity equal to $n$. Instead, we have proven the quite different proposition that in a large number of trials—in each of which the phases are distributed at random—the *mean intensity* <note>The average intensity across all trials.</note> will tend closer and closer to the value of $n$. It is true that even in a single combination, there is no reason why any of the cosines in equation (2) should be positive rather than negative. From this, we can conclude that as $n$ increases, the sum of the terms tends to become insignificant in comparison to the number of terms; however, since the number of terms is of the order $n^2$, we cannot draw any conclusions about the value of the sum of the series when compared to $n$.

So far, this is straightforward; but a complete investigation of this subject requires an estimate of the relative probabilities of resultants <note>The "resultant" is the final amplitude or vector sum produced by combining all the individual vibrations.</note> falling within specific ranges of magnitude. For example, we should be able to determine the probability that the intensity produced by a large number ($n$) of equal components is less than $\frac{1}{2}n$. This problem can be conveniently considered here, although it is naturally beyond the reach of basic methods. We will begin by examining it under the restriction that the phases are of only two opposite types <note>Meaning the vibrations are restricted to being either positive or negative along a single line.</note>.

Adopting a statistical method of description, let us suppose that there is a massive number $N$ of independent combinations, each consisting of $n$ unit vibrations <note>Vibrations with an amplitude of 1.</note>, either positive or negative, combined randomly. When $N$ is sufficiently large, the statistics become regular, and the number of combinations in which the resultant amplitude is found to be equal to $x$ may be denoted by $N \cdot f(n, x)$, where $f$ is a definite function of $n$ and $x$. Now, suppose that each of the $N$ combinations receives another random contribution of $\pm 1$, and let us ask how many of them will subsequently possess a resultant of $x$. It is clear that only those which originally had amplitudes of $x - 1$ or $x + 1$ can do so. *Half* of the former and *half* of the latter will acquire the amplitude $x$, so that the required number is:
->$\frac{1}{2}N f(n, x - 1) + \frac{1}{2}N f(n, x + 1)$.<-
But this must be identical to the number corresponding to $n + 1$ and $x$, so that:
->$f(n + 1, x) = \frac{1}{2}f(n, x - 1) + \frac{1}{2}f(n, x + 1) .........(3).<-

This equation of differences <note>original: "equation of differences"; a mathematical tool used to describe how a quantity changes in discrete steps rather than continuously.</note> holds true for all whole-number values of $x$ and for all positive whole-number values of $n$. If $f(n, x)$ is given for one value of $n$, the equation is sufficient to determine $f(n, x)$ for all higher whole-number values of $n$. For our current purpose, the starting value of $n$ is zero. In that case, we know that $f(x) = 0$ for all values of $x$ other than zero, and that when $x = 0$, $f(0, 0) = 1$.

The problem proposed in the above form is perfectly definite; however, for our immediate goal, it is enough to limit ourselves to the case where $n$ is large. We can then treat $f(n, x)$ as a continuous function of the continuous variables $n$ and $x$, much like the similar problem discussed in sections 120, 121, and 122.

By writing equation (3) in the form
-> $f(n + 1, x) - f(n, x) = \frac{1}{2} f(n, x - 1) + \frac{1}{2} f(n, x + 1) - f(n, x) \dots (4),$ <-
we can see that the term on the left side may be identified as the derivative $df/dn$, and the terms on the right as $\frac{1}{2} d^2f/dx^2$. Under these circumstances, the difference equation (3) reduces to a differential equation <note>A mathematical equation that relates a function with its derivatives, used here to model how the distribution "spreads" as the number of components increases.</note> of the well-known form:
-> $\frac{df}{dn} = \frac{1}{2} \frac{d^2f}{dx^2} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (5).$ <-

The comparison with the conduction of heat <note>Rayleigh is pointing out that the way random phases "spread out" their possible intensities follows the same mathematical laws as heat spreading through a metal bar.</note> is indeed very close; consequently, the methods developed by Fourier <note>Jean-Baptiste Joseph Fourier (1768–1830), a French mathematician who developed the theory of heat flow.</note> for the solution of problems in that subject can be applied here immediately. The specific condition here is that initially—that is, when $n = 0$—the function $f$ must vanish (become zero) for all values of $x$ except zero. As can be verified by differentiation, the specific solution to equation (5) is then:
-> $f(n, x) = \frac{A}{\sqrt{n}} e^{-x^2/2n} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (6),$ <-
where $A$ is an arbitrary constant <note>A value that does not change with the variables $n$ or $x$, but must be calculated to fit the specific physical situation.</note> to be determined by the fact that the total number of combinations is $N$. Thus, if the change in $x$ (denoted as $dx$) is large compared to one, the number of combinations that have amplitudes between $x$ and $x + dx$ is:
-> $\frac{AN}{\sqrt{n}} e^{-x^2/2n} dx;$ <-
while
-> $\frac{AN}{\sqrt{n}} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{-x^2/2n} dx = N,$ <-
so that by using the known mathematical equality
-> $\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{-z^2} dz = \sqrt{\pi} \text{ <note>original: Latin symbol for pi</note>},$ <-
we find that
-> $A \cdot \sqrt{2\pi} = 1.$ <-

# PHASES AT RANDOM

<margin>42 *a*.</margin>

The final result for the number of combinations that have amplitudes between $x$ and $x + dx$ is therefore:
->$\frac{N}{\sqrt{(2\pi n)}} e^{-x^2/2n} dx$ ........................ (7).<-

The average intensity <note>In physics, intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude. This calculation shows that on average, the total intensity of $n$ combined vibrations is simply the sum of their individual intensities ($n \times 1$).</note> is expressed by:
->$\frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi n)}} \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} x^2 e^{-x^2/2n} dx = n,$<-
as before.

We will now move on to the more significant problem, where the phases of the $n$ unit vibrations are spread randomly over the entire period <note>A "period" refers to a full cycle of a vibration, from 0 to 360 degrees (or $2\pi$ radians).</note>. In each combination, the resulting amplitude is represented by $r$ and the phase (measured from a specific starting point <note>original: "epoch"</note>) by $\theta$. We use rectangular coordinates so that:
->$x = r \cos \theta, \quad y = r \sin \theta.$<-

Therefore, any point $(x, y)$ on the coordinate plane represents a vibration with amplitude $r$ and phase $\theta$. The entire system of $N$ vibrations is shown as a distribution of points, and our goal is to find the density of these points. Because no single phase is more likely than another, we know in advance that the density of this distribution will not depend on the phase angle $\theta$.

Out of the infinite number of points $N$, we assume that
->$N f(n, x, y) dx dy$<-
are located within an incredibly small <note>original: "infinitesimal"</note> area $dx dy$. Just as before, we will investigate how this number changes when we add one more unit vibration with a random <note>original: "accidental"</note> phase to the $n$ existing components. Any vibration that reaches the point $(x, y)$ after the addition must have previously been at the point:
->$x' = x - \cos \phi, \quad y' = y - \sin \phi,$<-
where $\phi$ represents the phase of the additional unit vibration. If we temporarily assume $\phi$ is fixed, the area $dx dy$ corresponds to an identical area $dx' dy'$. Furthermore, since all values of $\phi$ are equally likely, the mathematical factor required for this calculation is $d\phi/2\pi$. Accordingly, the total number of points found in the area $dx dy$ after adding (superimposing) the extra unit is:
->$N dx dy \int_{0}^{2\pi} f(n, x', y') d\phi/2\pi ;$<-
and this is set equal to:
->$N dx dy f(n + 1, x, y);$<-
so that:
->$f(n + 1, x, y) = \int_{0}^{2\pi} f(n, x', y') d\phi/2\pi$ ......... (8).<-

# HARMONIC MOTIONS

The value of $f(n, x', y')$ is found by substituting the values of $x'$ and $y'$ and expanding the formula:

->$f(x', y') = f(x, y) - \frac{df}{dx} \cos \theta - \frac{df}{dy} \sin \theta + \frac{1}{2} \frac{d^2f}{dx^2} \cos^2 \theta$<-
->$+ \frac{d^2f}{dx dy} \cos \theta \sin \theta + \frac{1}{2} \frac{d^2f}{dy^2} \sin^2 \theta + \dots,$<-

leading to:

->$\int_0^{2\pi} f(n, x', y') d\phi / 2\pi = f(n, x, y) + \frac{1}{4} \frac{d^2f}{dx^2} + \frac{1}{4} \frac{d^2f}{dy^2} + \dots \dots$<-

Furthermore, since $n$ is a very large number,

->$f(n + 1, x, y) - f(n, x, y) = df/dn;$<-

and equation (8) reduces to

->$\frac{df}{dn} = \frac{1}{4} \left( \frac{d^2f}{dx^2} + \frac{d^2f}{dy^2} \right) \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (9),$<-

which is the standard equation for the conduction of heat in two dimensions.

In addition to equation (9), $f$ must satisfy the special condition of <term>vanishing</term> <note>original: "evanescence"; in mathematics, this means the value of the function becomes zero.</note> when $n = 0$ for all points except the origin. The correct solution must be symmetrical around the origin and takes the following form:

->$f(n, x, y) = An^{-1} e^{-(x^2+y^2)/n} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (10),$<-

as can be confirmed by differentiation. The constant $A$ is calculated based on the requirement that the total number of vibrations is $N$. Thus:

->$N = NAn^{-1} \iint e^{-(x^2+y^2)/n} dx dy = NA 2\pi n^{-1} \int_0^\infty e^{-r^2/n} r dr = \pi AN;$<-

and the number of vibrations within the area $dx dy$ becomes

->$\frac{N}{\pi n} e^{-(x^2+y^2)/n} dx dy \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (11).$<-

To determine the number of vibrations with amplitudes between $r$ and $r + dr$, we must use <term>polar coordinates</term> <note>A coordinate system where each point is determined by a distance from a central point and an angle from a fixed direction.</note> and integrate with respect to the angle $\theta$. The resulting number is:

->$2Nn^{-1} e^{-r^2/n} r dr \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (12)^1.$<-

The result may also be expressed by saying that the <term>probability</term> of a combined amplitude being between $r$ and $r + dr$, when a large number $n$ of unit vibrations are combined at random, is:

->$2n^{-1} e^{-r^2/n} r dr \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (13).$<-

<margin>
$^1$ *Philosophical Magazine* <note>original: "Phil. Mag."</note>, August 1880.
</margin>

<summary>This page derives the probability distribution for the combined amplitude of many random vibrations, demonstrating that the statistical spread follows the same mathematical laws as two-dimensional heat conduction. The final result (Equation 13) provides the mathematical probability of a specific resulting amplitude when many individual vibrations are mixed randomly.</summary>

### PHASES AT RANDOM

The <term>mean intensity</term> <note>The average power or brightness resulting from the combined vibrations.</note> is given by:

->2$n^{-1} \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-r^2/n} r^3 dr = n$,<-

as was to be expected. 

The probability of a <term>resultant amplitude</term> <note>The total height or strength of the combined wave.</note> less than $r$ is:

->2$n^{-1} \int_{0}^{r} e^{-r^2/n} r dr = 1 - e^{-r^2/n}$ .................... (14),<-

or, which is the same thing, the probability of a resultant amplitude greater than $r$ is:

->$e^{-r^2/n}$ ........................................(15).<-

The following table gives the probabilities of **intensities** less than the fractions of $n$ named in the first column. For example, the probability of the intensity being less than $n$ is 0.6321.

| Fraction of $n$ | Probability | Fraction of $n$ | Probability |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 0.05 | 0.0488 | 0.80 | 0.5506 |
| 0.10 | 0.0952 | 1.00 | 0.6321 |
| 0.20 | 0.1813 | 1.50 | 0.7768 |
| 0.40 | 0.3296 | 2.00 | 0.8647 |
| 0.60 | 0.4512 | 3.00 | 0.9502 |

It will be seen that, however great $n$ may be, there is a reasonable chance of considerable relative fluctuations of intensity in different combinations.

If the amplitude of each component is $a$, instead of one (as we have assumed until now for the sake of brevity), the probability of a resultant amplitude between $r$ and $r + dr$ is:

->$\frac{2}{na^2} e^{-r^2/na^2} r dr$ ............................(16).<-

The result is thus a function of $n$ and $a$ only through the product $na^2$. It would remain unchanged if, for example, the amplitude became $\frac{1}{2}a$ and the number of vibrations became $4n$. From this, it follows that the law is not altered even if the components have different amplitudes, provided always that the total number of each kind is very great. Therefore, if there are $n$ components of amplitude $a$, $n'$ of amplitude $\beta$, and so on, the probability of a resultant between $r$ and $r + dr$ is:

->$\frac{2}{na^2 + n'\beta^2 + ...} e^{-\frac{r^2}{na^2 + n'\beta^2 + ...}} r dr$ .........(17).<-

That this is the case may perhaps be made clearer by considering a specific example. Let us suppose, in the first place, that $n + 4n'$ unit vibrations are compounded at random.

<summary>This page calculates the probability distribution of combined wave intensities, showing that even with many vibrations, significant fluctuations in brightness or loudness still occur. It also demonstrates that the total intensity depends on the sum of the squares of individual amplitudes.</summary>

## HARMONIC MOTIONS

The appropriate law is immediately provided by equation (13) when we substitute $n + 4n'$ for $n$. That is:

-> $2(n + 4n')^{-1} e^{-r^2/(n+4n')} r dr$ ....................(18). <-

We can view the combination of $n + 4n'$ unit vibrations as being reached by merging a random combination of $n$ unit vibrations with a second random combination of $4n'$ units. This second random combination is the same as one resulting from a random combination of $n'$ vibrations, each with an <term>amplitude</term> <note>The maximum displacement or strength of a vibration.</note> of 2. Therefore, equation (18) applies just as well to a random combination of $(n + n')$ vibrations, where $n$ vibrations have an amplitude of one and $n'$ vibrations have an amplitude of two.

While this result does not apply to the theory of vibrations, it is worth noting that a similar method can be used for the composition of <term>unit vectors</term> <note>A direction in space with a fixed length of one unit.</note> in *three dimensions* when their directions are random. The equation equivalent to (8) provides the following instead of (9):

-> $\frac{df}{dn} = \frac{1}{6} \left( \frac{d^2f}{dx^2} + \frac{d^2f}{dy^2} + \frac{d^2f}{dz^2} \right)$. <-

The corresponding solution, similar to equation (13), is:

-> $3 \sqrt{\left( \frac{6}{\pi n^3} \right)} e^{-r^2/\frac{2}{3}n} r^2 dr$ ....................(18), <-

which expresses the probability of the resulting amplitude falling between $r$ and $r + dr$.

Once again, the <term>mean value</term> <note>The average or expected value over many trials.</note> of $r^2$ expected across a large number of independent combinations is $n$.

# CHAPTER III.

### SYSTEMS HAVING ONE DEGREE OF FREEDOM.

**43.** The physical systems that the study of <term>Acoustics</term> <note>The branch of physics that deals with the study of all mechanical waves in gases, liquids, and solids including topics such as sound, vibration, and ultrasound.</note> is concerned with are usually quite complex. They are capable of many different modes of **vibration**, any or all of which might occur at the same time. In fact, in some of the most important musical instruments—such as strings and organ pipes—the number of independent modes is theoretically infinite. Considering several of these modes is essential to understanding practical questions about the nature of musical chords. However, cases often arise where one mode is of primary importance. Even if this were not the case, it is still best to begin the general problem by looking at the simplest scenario: a system with one <term>degree of freedom</term> <note>The number of independent ways or directions in which a system can move.</note>. We do not need to assume that the mode we are studying is the only one possible; as long as other modes of vibration do not occur, their theoretical possibility under different circumstances is not important.

**44.** The state of a system possessing one degree of freedom is defined by the value of a single coordinate *u*. We can set the starting point (the origin) of this coordinate to correspond to the system's position of <term>equilibrium</term> <note>The state in which a system is at rest and all forces acting upon it are balanced.</note>. The <term>kinetic and potential energies</term> <note>Kinetic energy is the energy an object has due to its motion; potential energy is the energy stored in an object due to its position or state.</note> of the system for any given position are proportional to the square of the velocity ($\dot{u}^2$) and the square of the position ($u^2$) respectively:

-> $T = \frac{1}{2} m \dot{u}^2, \quad V = \frac{1}{2} \mu u^2 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (1),$ <-

In these equations, $m$ and $\mu$ are generally functions of $u$. However, if we limit ourselves to considering positions in the *immediate neighborhood of the equilibrium position*, $u$ is a very small quantity, and $m$ and $\mu$ are effectively constant. With this understanding, we—

<summary>Lord Rayleigh introduces the study of systems with one degree of freedom as a simplified starting point for understanding complex acoustic vibrations. He defines the mathematical relationship between kinetic and potential energy near a point of equilibrium.</summary>

<keywords>acoustics, vibrations, musical instruments, degree of freedom, equilibrium, kinetic energy, potential energy, mathematical modeling</keywords>

--- Page 63 ---
<meta>This page continues the mathematical derivation of motion for a system with one degree of freedom, moving from the definitions of energy to the specific equation for harmonic vibration and the concept of periodic time.</meta>

# ONE DEGREE OF FREEDOM.

Let us now proceed. If there are no forces—either resulting from internal friction or viscosity, or applied to the system from the outside—the total energy remains constant. Thus:

->*T* + *V* = constant.<-

By substituting the values for *T* (kinetic energy) and *V* (potential energy) and differentiating with respect to time, we obtain the equation of motion:

->*mü* + *μu* = 0 ..............................(2)<-

The <term>complete integral</term> <note>In modern calculus, this is referred to as the general solution to a differential equation, representing all possible paths of motion.</note> for this is:

->*u* = *a* cos (*nt* - *α*) ........................(3)<-

where *n*² = *μ* ÷ *m*, representing a <term>harmonic vibration</term> <note>original: "harmonic vibration"; a periodic motion where the restoring force is directly proportional to the displacement, like a swinging pendulum.</note>. It will be seen that the period alone is determined by the nature of the system itself; the <term>amplitude</term> <note>The maximum extent of a vibration or displacement, measured from the equilibrium position.</note> and <term>phase</term> <note>The specific point reached in a cycle of periodic motion, measured as an angle or time.</note> depend on collateral circumstances <note>That is, the starting conditions or how the vibration was initially triggered.</note>. 

If the differential equation were exact—that is to say, if *T* were strictly proportional to *u̇*² (the square of the velocity) and *V* to *u*² (the square of the displacement)—then, without any restriction, the vibrations of the system around its <term>configuration of equilibrium</term> <note>The state in which the system is at rest and all forces are balanced.</note> would be accurately harmonic. But in the majority of cases, this proportionality is only approximate, depending on an assumption that the <term>displacement</term> *u* is always small. How small depends on the nature of the particular system and the degree of approximation required; and then, of course, we must be careful not to apply this solution beyond its proper limits.

But, although it must be stated with this limitation, the principle that the vibrations of a system around a configuration of equilibrium have a period depending on the structure of the system—and not on the particular circumstances of the vibration—is of supreme importance, whether regarded from the theoretical or the practical side. If the pitch and the loudness of the note given by a musical instrument were not independent within wide limits, the art of the performer on many instruments, such as the violin and pianoforte, would be revolutionized.

The <term>periodic time</term> <note>The time taken to complete one full cycle of vibration.</note> is:

->$\tau = \frac{2\pi}{n} = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{\mu}}$ ........................(4)<-

so that an increase in *m*, or a decrease in *μ*, extends the duration of a vibration. By a generalization of the language employed in the case of a material particle pushed toward a position of equilibrium by a spring, *m* may be called the <term>inertia</term> <note>The resistance of any physical object to any change in its velocity.</note> of the system, and...

<summary>This page derives the equation of motion for a system with one degree of freedom, identifying it as a harmonic vibration where the period is determined by the system's structural properties (inertia and restoring force) rather than the vibration's intensity.</summary>
<keywords>harmonic vibration, equation of motion, periodic time, inertia, equilibrium, displacement, amplitude, phase, acoustics, Lord Rayleigh</keywords>

--- Page 64 ---
<meta>This page continues the mathematical analysis of a system with one degree of freedom. It concludes the discussion on how mass and spring stiffness affect the timing of vibrations before moving into the effects of friction and air resistance.</meta>

$\mu$ represents the force of the equivalent spring. Thus, an increase in mass or a loosening <note>original: "relaxation"</note> of the spring increases the **periodic time** <term>periodic time</term> <note>The time it takes to complete one full cycle of a vibration.</note>. By using this principle, we can sometimes establish limits for the value of a period that cannot be easily calculated with exact math.

# DISSIPATIVE FORCES

**45.** The complete absence of all frictional forces is an ideal scenario. It is never actually achieved in the real world but is only approximated in practice. The original energy of a vibration is always eventually lost <note>original: "dissipated"</note> by being converted into heat. 

However, there is another source of loss which, although not strictly a "dissipative force" like friction, produces very similar results. Consider the case of a tuning fork vibrating **in a vacuum** <note>original: *in vacuo*</note>. Internal friction within the metal will eventually stop the motion, and the original energy will turn into heat. 

But now, suppose the tuning fork is moved into an open space. Strictly speaking, the fork and the surrounding air form a single system whose parts cannot be studied separately. However, trying to find an exact mathematical solution for such a complicated problem would be nearly impossible. In any case, an approximate solution is more useful. 

The effect of the air during just a few vibration cycles is almost unnoticeable; it only becomes significant as it accumulates over time. We are therefore led to view the air's effect as a "disturbance" of the motion that would otherwise happen in a vacuum. This disturbing force is periodic (repeating at the same rate as the vibrations) and can be divided into two parts:

1.  One part is proportional to the acceleration. This acts like a simple change in the mass of the fork, which we do not need to address further here.
2.  The other part is a force directly <note>original: "arithmetically"</note> proportional to the velocity. This force always acts in the opposite direction of the motion, producing the same effects as friction. 

In many similar cases, the loss of motion caused by transferring energy to the surrounding environment can be treated the same way as actual friction. In the <term>differential equation</term> <note>A mathematical equation that describes how a physical quantity changes over time.</note> used for acoustics, this is represented by a term proportional to the velocity. Thus:

->$\ddot{u} + \kappa\dot{u} + n^2u = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (1)$<-

This is the equation of vibration for a system with **one degree of freedom** <term>degree of freedom</term> <note>A system that can be described by a single measurement or coordinate, such as the position of a pendulum.</note> that is subject to frictional forces. The solution is:

->$u = Ae^{-\frac{1}{2}\kappa t} \cos \{ \sqrt{n^2 - \frac{1}{4}\kappa^2} \cdot t - \alpha \} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (2).$<-

<summary>This page explains how real-world factors like friction and air resistance—known as dissipative forces—dampen vibrations, and provides the mathematical equation used to describe this decaying motion.</summary>
<keywords>dissipative forces, friction, tuning fork, air resistance, differential equation, periodic time, damping, one degree of freedom</keywords>

--- Page 65 ---
<meta>This page continues the mathematical analysis of a system with one degree of freedom, moving from the basic laws of vibration into the effects of friction and external forces.</meta>

<page-num>46 [45.</page-num>
->ONE DEGREE OF FREEDOM.<-

If the friction is so great that $\frac{1}{4}\kappa^2 > n^2$, the solution changes its form and no longer corresponds to an **oscillatory motion** <term>oscillatory motion</term> <note>back-and-forth movement around a center point, like a swinging pendulum</note>; however, in all acoustical applications, $\kappa$ is a very small quantity. Under these circumstances, equation (2) may be regarded as expressing a harmonic vibration whose **amplitude** <term>amplitude</term> <note>the maximum distance the vibration moves from its resting position</note> is not constant, but diminishes in a geometric progression <note>it decreases by a consistent ratio or percentage over time rather than by a flat amount</note> when measured at equal intervals of time. The difference between the logarithms of successive peak displacements <note>original: "extreme excursions"</note> is nearly constant and is called the **Logarithmic Decrement**. It is expressed by $\frac{1}{2}\kappa\tau$, where $\tau$ represents the **periodic time** <term>periodic time</term> <note>the time it takes to complete one full cycle of the vibration</note>.

The frequency, which depends on $n^2 - \frac{1}{4}\kappa^2$, involves only the second power of $\kappa$. This means that, to the first order of approximation, *friction has no effect on the period*—a principle of very general application.

The vibration considered here is called the *free vibration*. This is the motion performed by the system when it is disturbed from its **equilibrium** <term>equilibrium</term> <note>the state in which all forces are balanced and the system is at rest</note> and then *left to itself*.

**46.** We must now turn our attention to another problem, which is no less important: the behavior of the system when subjected to an external force that varies as a **harmonic function** <term>harmonic function</term> <note>a mathematical function, like a sine wave, that describes smooth, periodic motion</note> of time. To avoid repetition, we can immediately consider the more general case that includes friction. If there is no friction, we simply set $\kappa = 0$ in our results. The **differential equation** <term>differential equation</term> <note>an equation that describes how a physical system changes over time</note> is:
->$\ddot{u} + \kappa\dot{u} + n^2u = E \cos pt$ ........................ (1).<-
Assume ->$u = a \cos (pt - \epsilon)$ ........................ (2),<-
and substitute:
->$a (n^2 - p^2) \cos (pt - \epsilon) - \kappa pa \sin (pt - \epsilon)$<-
->$= E \cos \epsilon \cos (pt - \epsilon) - E \sin \epsilon \sin (pt - \epsilon);$<-
from which, by setting the coefficients of $\cos (pt - \epsilon)$ and $\sin (pt - \epsilon)$ equal to each other, we obtain:
->$\left. \begin{aligned} a (n^2 - p^2) &= E \cos \epsilon \\ a \cdot p\kappa &= E \sin \epsilon \end{aligned} \right\}$ ........................ (3),<-
so that the solution may be written as:
->$u = \frac{E \sin \epsilon}{p\kappa} \cos (pt - \epsilon)$ ........................ (4),<-
where ->$\tan \epsilon = \frac{p\kappa}{n^2 - p^2}$ ........................ (5).<-

This is called a *forced vibration*; it is the response of the system to a force imposed upon it from the outside and is maintained by the continuous operation of that force. The amplitude is proportional—

<summary>This page explains how friction causes vibrations to decay (free vibration) and introduces the mathematical framework for how a system responds to an external periodic force (forced vibration).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the mathematical discussion of forced vibrations from page 46, specifically focusing on how the energy of a vibrating system responds when the period of an external force is varied.</meta>

<page-num>47</page-num>
<header>FORCED VIBRATIONS.</header>

to $E$—the magnitude of the force—and the period is the same as that of the force.

Let us now assume $E$ is given and trace the effect that varying the period of the force has on a specific system. The effects produced in different cases are not strictly identical because the frequency of the resulting vibrations always matches the frequency of the force; therefore, the frequency is a variable in the comparison we are about to make. We may, however, compare the energy of the system in different cases at the moment it passes through its position of **equilibrium** <term>equilibrium</term> <note>the central resting position where all internal forces are balanced</note>. It is necessary to specify the moment at which the energy is calculated because the total energy does not remain constant throughout the vibration. During one part of the period, the system receives energy from the **impressed force** <note>the external force being applied to the system</note>, and during the remainder of the period, it returns that energy.

From equation (4), if $u = 0$,
->energy $\propto \dot{u}^2 \propto \sin^2 \epsilon$,<-

and the energy is therefore at a maximum when $\sin \epsilon = 1$, or, according to equation (5), when $p = n$. If the maximum **kinetic energy** <term>kinetic energy</term> <note>the energy an object possesses due to its motion</note> is represented by $T_0$, we have:
->$T' = T_0 \sin^2 \epsilon$ .................................(6).<-

The kinetic energy of the motion is therefore the greatest possible when the period of the force matches the period in which the system would vibrate freely under the influence of its own **elasticity** <note>the property that allows the system to return to its original shape or position</note> (or other internal forces) *without friction*. According to equations (4) and (5), the vibration is then:
->$$u = \frac{E}{n \kappa} \sin nt ;$$<-

and, if the friction ($\kappa$) is small, its **amplitude** <term>amplitude</term> <note>the maximum distance the vibration moves from its resting position</note> is very great. Its **phase** <term>phase</term> <note>the timing of the vibration relative to the force</note> is a quarter of a period behind that of the force.

The case where $p = n$ <note>this condition is known as resonance</note> may also be treated independently. Since the period of the actual vibration is the same as the natural period of the system,
->$\ddot{u} + n^2 u = 0$,<-

so that the **differential equation** <term>differential equation</term> <note>a mathematical equation that describes how a physical quantity changes over time</note> (1) reduces to:
->$\kappa \dot{u} = E \cos pt$,<-

from which, by **integration** <term>integration</term> <note>a mathematical process used to find a function from its rate of change</note>, we find:
->$$u = \frac{E}{\kappa} \int \cos pt \ dt = \frac{E}{p \kappa} \sin pt,$$<-

as determined before.

<summary>This page explains the principle of resonance, showing that a system reaches its maximum kinetic energy and amplitude when the period of an external force matches the system's natural period of vibration. It also notes that in this state, the system's motion lags behind the force by a quarter of a cycle.</summary>
<keywords>forced vibrations, resonance, kinetic energy, equilibrium, phase lag, differential equations, amplitude, elasticity</keywords>

--- Page 67 ---
<meta>This page continues the mathematical analysis of forced vibrations, specifically examining how the timing (phase) and size (amplitude) of a vibration change depending on whether the driving force is faster or slower than the system's natural frequency.</meta>

<page-num>48 [46.]</page-num>
<header>ONE DEGREE OF FREEDOM.</header>

If $p$ <note>the frequency of the external force</note> is less than $n$ <note>the natural frequency of the system</note>, the **phase delay** <term>phase delay</term> <note>the time lag between the application of a force and the resulting movement</note> relative to the force lies between zero and a quarter-cycle. When $p$ is greater than $n$, the delay is between a quarter-cycle and a half-cycle.

In the case of a system without friction, the solution is:

-> $u = \frac{E}{n^2 - p^2} \cos pt \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (7).$ <-

When $p$ is smaller than $n$, the phase of the vibration matches that of the force. However, when $p$ is greater, the direction of the vibration is reversed. This change of phase from complete agreement to complete disagreement—which happens gradually when friction is present—occurs instantly here as $p$ passes the value of $n$. At the same time, the mathematical expression for the **amplitude** <term>amplitude</term> <note>the maximum distance the system moves from its resting position</note> becomes infinite. Of course, this simply means that when the periods are equal, friction *must* be taken into account, no matter how small it may be or how insignificant its effect is when $p$ and $n$ are not nearly equal. We must also keep in mind the physical limits on the size of the vibration that we have assumed throughout this work.

It is sometimes considered a paradox that the displacement should be at its maximum in one direction while the driving force is at its maximum in the opposite direction; this happens, for example, in the **canal theory of the tides** <note>a mathematical model that treats the ocean's tides as waves moving through a narrow channel</note>. Any difficulty in understanding this will be removed by considering the extreme case where the "spring" (the restoring force) vanishes, so that the natural period is infinitely long. In fact, we only need to consider the force acting on the weight of a common pendulum swinging freely: in this case, the displacement on one side is greatest when the action of gravity is at its maximum in the opposite direction. When, on the other hand, the **inertia** <term>inertia</term> <note>the resistance of a physical object to any change in its velocity</note> of the system is very small, we have the other extreme case where the **equilibrium theory** <note>a theory where the system is assumed to be in constant balance with the external forces</note> becomes applicable, and the force and displacement move in the same phase.

When the period of the force is longer than the natural period, the effect of increasing friction is to introduce a delay in the phase of the displacement, varying from zero up to a quarter-cycle. If, however, the period of the natural vibration is the longer one, the original half-cycle delay is reduced by nearly a quarter-cycle; in this case, the effect of friction is to *accelerate* the phase of the displacement compared to how it would move without friction. In either case, the influence of friction brings the system closer to the state that would exist if friction were the dominant force.

<summary>This page explains how the timing of a vibration (phase) shifts relative to the driving force, illustrating the concept of resonance where amplitude theoretically becomes infinite without friction. It clarifies the "paradox" of displacement moving opposite to force using the examples of tides and pendulums.</summary>
<keywords>forced vibrations, phase delay, resonance, amplitude, friction, canal theory of tides, equilibrium theory, natural period, inertia</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the mathematical relationship between an external driving force and the resulting vibration of a system, focusing on the timing of peak displacements and the Principle of Superposition.</meta>

<page-num>49</page-num>
<header>PRINCIPLE OF SUPERPOSITION.</header>

If a force with a period nearly equal to that of the system's free vibrations increases slowly to a maximum and then slowly decreases, the displacement does not reach its maximum until after the force has already begun to diminish. Under the operation of the force at its maximum, the vibration continues to increase until a certain limit is approached; this increase continues for a time even though the force, having passed its maximum, has begun to decrease. It is by this principle that the delay of **spring tides** <note>the exceptionally high tides that occur after a new or full moon</note> following the days of the new and full moon has been explained¹.

**47.** From the **linearity of the equations** <note>the mathematical property where the total response to multiple forces is equal to the sum of the responses to each force individually</note>, it follows that the motion resulting from the simultaneous action of any number of forces is simply the sum of the motions caused by each force taken separately. Each force causes its own specific vibration without regard to whether any other forces are present. The specific characteristics of a force are thus essentially transmitted into the motion of the system. For example, if the force is periodic over a certain time $\tau$, the resulting vibration will be as well. Each harmonic element of the force will trigger a corresponding harmonic vibration in the system. 

However, since the phase delay $\epsilon$ and the ratio of the amplitudes $a : E$ are not the same for different components, the resulting vibration—though it repeats in the same amount of time—is different in *character* from the force. For instance, it may happen that one of the components is **isochronous** <term>isochronous</term> <note>having the exact same period or frequency</note>, or nearly so, with the free vibration. In this case, that component will show up in the resulting motion with an intensity far beyond its original importance. As another example, we may consider a system acted on by two forces with nearly equal periods. The resulting vibration, being composed of two vibrations nearly in unison, is intermittent <note>this refers to the phenomenon of "beats," where the sound or vibration grows louder and softer</note>, according to the principles explained in the last chapter.

To the motions which are the immediate effects of the **impressed forces** <term>impressed forces</term> <note>external forces applied to the system from the outside</note>, we must always add the term expressing free vibrations if we wish to obtain the most complete mathematical solution. Thus, in the case of one impressed force:

-> $u = \frac{E \sin \epsilon}{p\kappa} \cos (pt - \epsilon) + Ae^{-\frac{1}{2}\kappa t} \cos \{\sqrt{n^2 - \frac{1}{4}\kappa^2} \cdot t - \alpha\} \dots\dots\dots (1),$ <-

where $A$ and $\alpha$ are arbitrary values.

<page-num>50</page-num>
## ONE DEGREE OF FREEDOM. [48.]

The period <note>the time taken for one complete cycle of vibration</note> of the former (the forced vibration) is determined solely by the force supposed to act on the system from the outside. In contrast, the period of the latter (the free vibration) depends only on the internal makeup of the system itself. Another difference is that as long as the external force continues to act, a forced vibration is permanent and is represented strictly as a **harmonic function** <note>a mathematical formula, like a sine or cosine wave, that describes smooth, repeating motion</note>. A free vibration, however, gradually dies away and becomes negligible after a short time. 

Suppose, for example, that the system is at rest when the force $E \cos pt$ begins to operate. We must assign specific values to the constants $A$ and $\alpha$ in equation (1) of § 47, so that both the displacement $u$ and the velocity $\dot{u}$ start at zero. At first, the free vibration is just as significant as the forced vibration. However, after a time, **friction** <note>original: "friction"; here referring to any resistance that dissipates energy</note> reduces the free vibration to insignificance, leaving the forced vibration as the only motion remaining. This state will continue as long as the force is applied. When the force is removed, there is no sudden break in the values of $u$ or $\dot{u}$, but the forced vibration is immediately converted back into a free vibration. At that moment, the timing of the force is replaced by the natural period of the system.

During the period when both vibrations exist together at the start of the motion, the curious phenomenon of **beats** <note>a pulsing sound or movement caused by two vibrations of slightly different frequencies interfering with each other</note> may occur if the two periods differ only slightly. Because $n$ and $p$ are nearly equal and the damping factor $\kappa$ is small, the initial conditions are approximately satisfied by:

-> $u = a \cos (pt - \epsilon) - ae^{-\frac{1}{2}\kappa t} \cos \{\sqrt{n^2 - \frac{1}{4}\kappa^2} \cdot t - \epsilon\}$ <-

There is thus a rise and fall in the motion as long as the mathematical term $e^{-\frac{1}{2}\kappa t}$ remains detectable. This pulsing is very noticeable in the early stages of the motion of tuning forks driven by **electromagnetism** (§ 63). [This effect may be used when one wishes to adjust the frequencies $n$ and $p$ to be exactly equal. The initial beats should be made slower and slower until they can no longer be felt or heard. The vibration then increases steadily to its maximum.]

**49.** Vibrating systems with one degree of freedom can vary in two ways, according to the values of the constants $n$ (frequency) and $\kappa$ (damping). The distinction of **pitch** <note>the perceived highness or lowness of a sound, determined by the frequency of vibration</note> is easy enough to understand; however, it is worthwhile to examine more closely the results of a greater or lesser degree of **damping** <note>the reduction in the size of vibrations over time due to energy loss</note>. The most obvious result is the more or less rapid extinction of a free vibration. This effect can be measured by the number of vibrations that must pass before the **amplitude** <note>the maximum distance the system moves from its equilibrium or resting position</note> is reduced by a specific ratio. If we take the starting amplitude as 1, after a time $t$, let the amplitude be $\theta$. Initially, $\theta = e^{-\frac{1}{2}\kappa t}$.

# VARIOUS DEGREES OF DAMPING.
<sig>4—2</sig>

If $t = x\tau$, we have $x = -\frac{2}{\kappa\tau} \log \theta$. In a system subject to only a moderate degree of damping <note>the process where energy is dissipated from a vibrating system, usually through friction or air resistance</note>, we may use the approximation:

->$\tau = 2\pi \div n$;<-

so that

->$\displaystyle x = -\frac{n}{\kappa\pi} \log \theta \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(1).$<-

This equation gives the number of vibrations that are performed before the amplitude <note>the maximum distance a vibration moves from its central rest position</note> falls to the ratio $\theta$.

The influence of damping is also powerfully felt in a forced vibration when there is a near approach to isochronism <note>original: "isochronism"; the state where the frequency of the external force matches the natural frequency of the system, often called resonance</note>. In the case of an exact equality between $p$ (the frequency of the force) and $n$ (the natural frequency), it is the damping alone which prevents the motion from becoming infinite. We might easily anticipate that when the damping is small, a comparatively slight deviation from perfect isochronism would cause a large falling off in the magnitude of the vibration; however, with larger damping, the same precision of adjustment would not be required. From the equations:

->$T = T_0 \sin^2 \epsilon, \quad \tan \epsilon = \frac{\kappa p}{n^2 - p^2}, $<-

we get:

->$\displaystyle \frac{n^2 - p^2}{\kappa p} = \sqrt{\frac{T_0 - T}{T}} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(2);$<-

so that if $\kappa$ is small, $p$ must be very nearly equal to $n$ in order to produce a motion that is not significantly less than the maximum.

The two principal effects of damping may be compared by eliminating $\kappa$ between equations (1) and (2). The result is:

->$\displaystyle \frac{\log \theta}{x} = \pi \left( \frac{p}{n} - \frac{n}{p} \right) \sqrt{\frac{T}{T_0 - T}} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(3),$<-

where the sign of the square root must be chosen so as to make the right-hand side negative.

If, when a system vibrates freely, the amplitude is reduced in the ratio $\theta$ after $x$ vibrations, then when it is acted on by a force $(p)$, the energy of the resulting motion will be less than in the case of perfect isochronism in the ratio $T : T_0$. It does not matter whether the forced or the free vibration frequency is the higher; everything depends on the *interval* <note>the difference between the two frequencies</note>.

In most cases of interest, the interval is small; and then, by setting $p = n + \delta n$, the formula may be written as:

->$\displaystyle \frac{\log \theta}{x} = \frac{2\pi\delta n}{n} \sqrt{\frac{T}{T_0 - T}} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(4).$<-

It demonstrates that while damping prevents infinite motion at perfect resonance, it also determines how quickly the energy of the vibration drops when the forcing frequency deviates from the natural frequency.</summary>

**50.** By observing forced vibrations <note>vibrations maintained by a continuous external periodic force</note> caused by known forces, the natural period and damping of a system may be determined. The formulas are:

-> $u = \frac{E \sin \epsilon}{p \kappa} \cos (pt - \epsilon),$ <-

where

-> $\tan \epsilon = \frac{p \kappa}{n^2 - p^2}.$ <-

According to the equilibrium theory <note>a simplified model that assumes the system responds instantly to the force without considering the effects of inertia or timing delays</note>, we should have:

-> $u = \frac{E}{n^2} \cos pt.$ <-

The ratio of the actual amplitude <note>the maximum extent of the vibration</note> to this theoretical value is:

-> $\frac{E \sin \epsilon}{p \kappa} : \frac{E}{n^2} = \frac{n^2 \sin \epsilon}{p \kappa}.$ <-

If the equilibrium theory is known, comparing the amplitudes tells us the value of $\frac{n^2 \sin \epsilon}{p \kappa}$, which we can call $a$:

-> $\frac{n^2 \sin \epsilon}{p \kappa} = a,$ <-

**51.** As previously stated, the distinction between forced and free vibrations is important. However, it should be noted that most of the forced vibrations we will consider originate from the motion of a second system, which influences the first and is, in turn, influenced by it. A vibration might be considered "forced" when looking at a system with arbitrarily defined boundaries, even if that system helps determine the period of the force acting upon it. From a broader perspective that includes both systems, the vibration in question is recognized as "free." 

An example may make this clearer. A tuning fork vibrating in air is part of a combined system consisting of the fork and the air together; regarding this combined system, the vibration is free. But while the fork is influenced by the reaction of the surrounding air, that influence is very small. For practical purposes, it is convenient to treat the motion of the fork as a given "force" and the resulting motion of the air as "forced." No error occurs if the *actual* motion of the fork (as influenced by its surroundings) is used as the basis for calculation. The main advantage of this perspective is seen when an approximate solution is needed. In such cases, it may be sufficient to replace the actual motion with what the motion of the fork would be in a vacuum, and later apply a correction if necessary.

# METHOD OF DIMENSIONS

The variables related to the three fundamental units—length, time, and mass—are $a$ <note>half the length of the string</note>, $M$ <note>the mass</note>, and $T$ <note>the tension</note>. Let the solution to the problem be written as:

->$\tau = f(a, M, T)........................(3).$<-
<note>Here, $\tau$ (the Greek letter tau) represents the periodic time.</note>

This equation must remain unchanged regardless of which fundamental units are used to express the four quantities numerically. This is evident because, in deriving the equation, no assumptions are made about the specific size of those units. Now, among all the quantities that the function $f$ depends on, $T$ <note>tension, which is a force</note> is the only one involving time. Since its <term>dimensions</term> <note>the basic physical units that compose a measurement</note> are (Mass) (Length) (Time)$^{-2}$, it follows that when $a$ and $M$ are constant, $\tau \propto T^{-\frac{1}{2}}$ <note>$\tau$ is proportional to the inverse square root of the tension</note>. If this were not the case, a change in the unit of time would necessarily disrupt the balance of equation (3).

Accepting this, it is easy to see that for equation (3) to be independent of the unit of length, we must have $\tau \propto T^{-\frac{1}{2}} \cdot a^{\frac{1}{2}}$ when $M$ is constant. Finally, to ensure the equation is independent of the unit of mass, the relationship must be:

->$\tau \propto T^{-\frac{1}{2}} \cdot M^{\frac{1}{2}} \cdot a^{\frac{1}{2}}.$<-

To determine these <term>indices</term> <note>exponents or powers</note>, we might proceed by assuming:

->$\tau \propto T^x \cdot M^y \cdot a^z;$<-

Then, by considering the dimensions of time, space (length), and mass, we obtain the following equations respectively:

->$1 = -2x, \quad 0 = x + z, \quad 0 = x + y,$<-

from which we find, as shown above: $\quad x = -\frac{1}{2}, \quad y = \frac{1}{2}, \quad z = \frac{1}{2}.$

We must be careful not to mistake what this argument does and does not prove. We have assumed there is a definite periodic time that depends only on the quantities mentioned above (mass, length, and tension). For example, we have not proved that $\tau$ is independent of the <term>amplitude of vibration</term> <note>the maximum distance the string moves from its resting position</note>. That independence, as far as it is true, is actually a result of the "linearity" <note>the mathematical property where the response is directly proportional to the input</note> of the approximate <term>differential equation</term> <note>an equation involving derivatives that describes how a system changes over time</note>.

Because it requires a complete list of every quantity that might affect the result, the method of dimensions can be somewhat risky; however, when used with proper care, it is unquestionably a tool of great power and value.

**55.** As another example of a system possessing practically only one degree of freedom <note>a system that can be defined by a single measurement or coordinate</note>, let us consider the vibration of a spring. In this setup, one end is clamped in a vice or otherwise held fast, while the other end carries a heavy mass.

<image-desc>A technical diagram labeled FIG 12. It depicts a vertical rod or spring fixed at the bottom by a clamp (represented by a jagged horizontal shape and two bolts). At the top of the vertical rod is a circular mass.</image-desc>

Strictly speaking, this system—like the previous one—has an infinite number of independent modes of vibration. However, when the mass of the spring itself is relatively small, the vibration that is mostly independent of the spring's inertia <note>the resistance of the spring's mass to changes in motion</note> becomes so much more important than the others that they can be ignored. Pushing this idea to its limit, we may view the spring merely as the source of a force that pulls the attached mass back toward its position of equilibrium <note>the resting position where all forces are balanced</note>. As long as the spring is not stretched beyond a certain point, this force is in simple proportion to the displacement. The result is a harmonic vibration, with a period that depends on the stiffness of the spring and the mass of the load.

Two identical springs and weights may be mounted on the same frame in a symmetrical way. If the two weights vibrate with the same range of motion (amplitude) but in such a way that their movements are always in opposite directions—or, as it may otherwise be described, with a phase difference of half a cycle—the center of mass <note>original: "centre of inertia"</note> of the entire system remains still. Consequently, there is no force acting to make the support frame vibrate. We will see in a later chapter that this specific relationship between the movements (phases) will naturally establish itself, regardless of how the system was originally disturbed. In fact, any part of the motion that does not result in the center of mass remaining still is quickly stopped by damping <note>the process where energy is lost from a vibrating system, usually through friction or air resistance</note>, unless the supports of the system are exceptionally rigid.

**57.** Just as our first example provided a basic illustration of the fundamental vibration <note>the lowest frequency at which a system naturally vibrates</note> of a musical string, we can compare this spring and attached weight to a uniform strip or bar of elastic material with one end securely fixed. An example of this is the reed of a wind instrument. It is true, of course, that the weight of a reed is not concentrated at one end but is spread throughout its entire length. However, because there is very little movement near the point where it is supported, the mass (inertia) of that part of the bar is of little importance. 

We can conclude that the fundamental vibration of a uniform rod is very similar in nature to the spring-and-weight system we have been studying. While these two systems are different enough to require separate math for exact calculations, when the goal is to form a clear mental picture, we can often trade extreme precision for simplicity.

In this same spirit, we may view the combination of two springs and weights shown in Fig. 13 as a model for a tuning fork. This instrument, which has been much improved in recent years, is essential for anyone studying sound (acoustics). For basic purposes on a large scale, it can be made by welding a cross-piece to the middle of a steel bar to form a "T" shape and then bending the bar into a horseshoe shape. A screw thread should be cut into the handle. However, for high-quality tuning forks, it is better to forge the entire instrument from a single piece of steel.

<header>TUNING FORKS</header>

<margin>Section 57.</margin>To create a tuning fork, a cut is first made from one end down the middle of a metal bar. The two resulting parts are then bent outward to form the prongs of the fork, and the entire piece is shaped using a hammer and file. The two prongs must be perfectly symmetrical around a plane passing through the center of the handle. This symmetry ensures that during vibration, the center of mass <note>original: "centre of inertia"; the point where the total mass of the object is balanced</note> remains stationary—specifically, it remains still in the direction that the prongs are moving.

Tuning is achieved in the following ways. To make the pitch higher, the effective mass <note>original: "equivalent inertia"</note> of the system must be reduced. This is done by filing down the ends of the prongs, either by making them thinner or by actually shortening them. 

On the other hand, to lower the pitch, the thickness of the prongs near the bend may be reduced. This effect weakens the "spring" force of the metal while leaving the mass practically unchanged. Alternatively, the mass can be increased (a method preferred for temporary adjustments) by loading the ends of the prongs with wax or other materials. Large forks are sometimes equipped with movable weights that slide along the prongs and can be secured in any position with screws. As these weights move toward the ends—where the movement is fastest—the effective mass of the system increases. In this way, a wide range of pitches can be obtained from a single fork. The number of vibrations per second for different positions of the weights can be marked directly on the prongs.

The relationship between the pitch and the size of tuning forks is remarkably simple. In a later chapter, it will be proved that, provided the material and the shape remain the same, the period of vibration varies directly with the linear dimensions. For example, if the dimensions of a tuning fork are doubled, its pitch drops by an octave.

**58.** The sound produced by a tuning fork is almost a pure tone. Immediately after a fork is struck, high-pitched tones may indeed be heard, which correspond to other modes of vibration that will be discussed later. However, these fade away quickly. Even while they are audible, they do not blend with the fundamental tone of the fork, partly because of their very high pitch and partly because they do not belong to its harmonic series <note>original: "harmonic scale"; a series of frequencies that are whole-number multiples of the lowest frequency</note>. In the forks examined by the physicist Helmholtz, the first of these overtones had a frequency between 5.8 and 6.6 times higher than that of the fundamental tone.

Tuning forks are now generally supplied with resonance cases,

# ONE DEGREE OF FREEDOM

The effect of these methods is to greatly increase the volume and purity of the sound, according to principles that will be explained later in this book. In order to activate the forks, a violin or cello bow, well-coated with rosin <note>a sticky resin used to create friction between the bow hair and the instrument</note>, is drawn across the prongs in the direction that they vibrate. The sound produced this way will last for a minute or more.

**59.** Tuning forks are invaluable as standards for pitch. The pitch of organ pipes changes rapidly with the temperature and the pressure of the air <note>original: "wind"</note>; the pitch of strings changes with their tension, which can never be kept constant for very long. However, a tuning fork that is kept clean and not subjected to extreme changes in temperature or magnetism <note>original: "magnetization"</note> preserves its pitch with great accuracy.

[But one should not assume that the vibrations of a fork are entirely unaffected by temperature. According to the observations of McLeod and Clarke¹ <margin>¹ *Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society*, 1880, p. 12.</margin> the frequency <term>frequency</term><note>the number of vibrations per second, which determines the pitch of the note</note> decreases by 0.00011 of its total value for every degree Celsius that the temperature rises.]

Using "beats" <note>the pulsing sound heard when two notes of slightly different pitches are played together</note>, a standard tuning fork can be copied with very high precision. The number of beats heard in one second is equal to the difference between the frequencies of the two tones producing them. Therefore, if the beats can be made so slow that each one takes half a minute, the frequencies of the two forks differ by only one-thirtieth of a vibration per second. Even greater precision could be achieved using the optical method developed by Jules Antoine Lissajous <note>a French physicist who used mirrors and light beams to visualize sound vibrations</note>.

Because very slow beats are difficult to observe—due to the uncertainty of whether a dip in volume is caused by interference or by the vibrations naturally dying away—the researcher Johann Scheibler adopted a modified plan. He took a fork with a pitch slightly different from the standard one (it does not matter if it is higher or lower, but for this example, we will say lower) and counted the number of beats produced when they were sounded together. About four beats per second is the most ideal rate to count, and these can be monitored for perhaps a minute. The fork that needs to be adjusted is then tuned to a pitch slightly higher than this secondary <note>original: "auxiliary"</note> fork. It is adjusted until it produces exactly the same number of beats with the secondary fork as the standard did. In this way, a copy as exact as possible is guaranteed. To make counting the beats easier, Scheibler used pendulums whose swinging speed <note>original: "periods of vibration"</note> could be adjusted to match the rhythm.

[The choice between using slow or quick beats depends on the specific situation. It is sometimes mistakenly thought that quick beats are better because they allow for greater...]

59.] ...relative accuracy of counting. But a little consideration shows <note>original: "shews"</note> that in a comparison of frequencies, we are concerned not with the *relative* accuracy, but with the *absolute* accuracy of the counting. If we miscount the beats in a minute by one, it results in the exact same error in the final result, whether the total number of beats is 60 or 240.

When the sounds are pure tones and are well sustained, it is advisable to use beats much slower than four per second. By choosing a suitable position, it is often possible to make the volume <note>original: "intensities"</note> at the ear equal; when this happens, the phase of silence—which corresponds to the canceling out <note>original: "antagonism"</note> of equal and opposite vibrations—is extremely well-marked. Taking advantage of this, we may determine slow beats with very great accuracy by observing the time that elapses between these repetitions of silence. In favorable cases, the total number of beats during the observation period may be fixed to within one-tenth or one-twentieth of a single beat—a degree of accuracy that is impossible when the beats are fast. In this way, beats with periods exceeding 30 seconds may be utilized with excellent effect¹.]

**60.** The method of beats was also employed by Scheibler <note>Johann Heinrich Scheibler (1777–1837), a German silk manufacturer who invented the tonometer to precisely measure pitch</note> to determine the absolute pitch of his standards. Two tuning forks were tuned to an octave, and a number of others were prepared to bridge the gap <note>original: "bridge over the interval"</note> by steps so small that each fork produced a number of beats with its immediate neighbors in the series that could be easily counted. 

The difference in frequency for each step was observed with all possible accuracy. Their sum—being the total difference of frequencies for the interval of the octave—was equal to the frequency of the fork that formed the starting point at the bottom of the series <note>In an octave, the higher note has exactly twice the frequency of the lower note (a 2:1 ratio). Therefore, the difference between them ($2x - x$) equals the frequency of the lower note ($x$)</note>. From this, the pitch of the other forks in the series could be deduced.

If consecutive forks produce four beats per second, 65 forks in total would be required to bridge the interval from *c'* (256 Hz) to *c''* (512 Hz). Because of this, the method is tedious <note>original: "laborious"</note>; however, it is probably the most accurate method for the original determination of pitch, as it is liable to no errors except those that care and repetition will eliminate. It may be observed that the essential factor is the measurement of the *difference* of frequencies for two notes whose *ratio* of frequencies is independently known. If we could be sure of its accuracy, the interval of the fifth, fourth, or even the major third, might—

The frequency of large tuning forks can be determined by having them trace a harmonic curve on smoked paper, which is usually mounted on the surface of a revolving drum. The number of waves produced per second provides the frequency.

In many cases, the use of intermittent illumination (described in **§ 42**) provides a convenient way to determine an unknown frequency.

**61.** A series of forks covering an octave at small intervals is very useful for determining the frequency of any musical note; this set is called Scheibler’s Tonometer <note>Johann Scheibler’s tonometer typically consisted of 52 forks spanning a single octave, used as a high-precision reference for pitch</note>. It can also be used to tune a note to any desired pitch. In either case, the frequency of the note is determined by the number of beats <note>beats: an interference pattern between two sounds of slightly different frequencies, perceived as a periodic variation in volume</note> it produces when sounded with the forks closest to it in pitch (one above and one below).

For tuning pianos or organs, a set of twelve forks can be used to provide the notes of the chromatic scale in equal temperament <note>equal temperament: a system of tuning where every pair of adjacent notes has an identical frequency ratio, allowing music to be played in any key</note> or any other desired system. The corresponding notes are adjusted to unison, and the remaining notes are then tuned in octaves. However, it is better to prepare the forks so that they vibrate four times per second slower than the intended pitch. Each note is then tuned slightly higher than its corresponding fork until, when sounded together, they produce exactly four beats per second. It will be

# SCHEIBLER'S TONOMETER
