In the ordinary practice of tuners, $a'$ <note>a': the note A above middle C, currently standardized at 440 Hz, though standards varied in the 19th century</note> is taken from a tuning fork, and the other notes are determined by estimating fifths <note>fifths: a musical interval encompassing five notes of a scale; in acoustics, a "true" or "perfect" fifth has a frequency ratio of 3:2</note>. It will be remembered that twelve true fifths are slightly higher than seven octaves, so that in the equal temperament system <note>equal temperament: a tuning system where the octave is divided into twelve equal semitones, allowing music to be played in any key with the same intervals, though it slightly compromises the purity of individual intervals like fifths</note>, each fifth is tuned a little flat. The tuner proceeds upward from $a'$ by successive fifths, coming down an octave after about every alternate step in order to remain in nearly the same part of the scale. Twelve fifths should bring him back to $a$. If this is not the case, the work must be readjusted until all twelve fifths are too flat by nearly the same small amount, as far as can be judged. The inevitable error is then impartially distributed and rendered as unnoticeable as possible. The octaves, of course, are all tuned perfectly. The following numbers indicate the order in which the notes may be taken:

->*a# b c' c'# d' d'# e' f' f'# g' g'# a' a'# b' c'' c''# d'' d''# e''*<-
->**13 5 16 8 19 11 3 14 6 17 9 1 12 4 15 7 18 10 2**<-

In practice, equal temperament is only approximately attained; but this is perhaps not of much consequence, considering that the system aimed at is itself by no means perfect.

Violins and other instruments of that class are tuned by true fifths from $a'$.

**62.** To illustrate forced vibration <note>forced vibration: the motion of a system caused by an external, periodic force, causing the system to vibrate at the frequency of the force rather than its own natural frequency</note>, let us consider the case of a pendulum whose point of support is subject to a small horizontal harmonic motion <note>harmonic motion: a type of periodic motion where the restoring force is proportional to the displacement from equilibrium, like a swinging pendulum or a vibrating string</note>. $Q$ is the bob attached by a fine wire to a movable point $P$. $OP$ = $x_0$, $PQ$ = $l$, and $x$ is the horizontal coordinate of $Q$. Since the vibrations are assumed to be small, the vertical motion may be neglected, and the tension of the wire equated to the weight of $Q$. Hence, for the horizontal motion, $\ddot{x} + \kappa\dot{x} + \frac{g}{l} (x - x_0) = 0$.

<image-desc>FIG 14. A diagram showing a pendulum system. A horizontal line serves as the axis for the point of support P. A fixed origin O is on the line. The point P moves horizontally along this line (distance $x_0$). A pendulum bob Q hangs from P by a string of length $l$. The horizontal position of the bob Q is marked as $x$.</image-desc>

Now $x_0 \propto \cos pt$; so that by setting $g \div l = n^2$, our equation takes the form already discussed, namely:

If *p* is equal to *n*, the motion is limited only by friction. The assumed horizontal harmonic motion for *P* can be achieved by using a second pendulum of massive construction, which carries *P* along with its motion. An efficient arrangement is shown in the figure.

->*FIG 15.*<-

<image-desc>A line diagram labeled FIG 15 showing a complex pendulum system. A horizontal line at the top represents a beam with two rings, A and B. Wires descend from these rings, crossing each other and passing through rings C and D on a tilted stout bar. This bar has weights E and F at its ends. From a point P on this bar, a second pendulum PQ hangs vertically, ending in a bob Q.</image-desc>

*A* and *B* are iron rings screwed into a beam or another firm support; *C* and *D* are similar rings attached to a stout bar. This bar carries heavy, equal weights *E* and *F* attached near its ends, and is supported in a horizontal position at right angles to the beam by a wire passing through the four rings in the manner shown. When the pendulum is made to vibrate, a point in the rod midway between *C* and *D* performs a harmonic motion <note>harmonic motion: a type of periodic motion where the restoring force is proportional to the displacement, like a swing moving back and forth</note> in a direction parallel to *CD*. This point can serve as the point of attachment for another pendulum, *PQ*. 

If the weights *E* and *F* are very large compared to *Q*, the upper pendulum swings very nearly at its own natural frequency <note>original: "proper period"</note> and induces a forced vibration <note>forced vibration: when an oscillating system is driven by an external periodic force rather than just its own weight and length</note> in *Q* at that same frequency. When the length of *PQ* is adjusted so that the natural periods of the two pendulums are nearly the same, *Q* will be thrown into violent motion, even if the vibration of *P* has only a very small amplitude <note>amplitude: the maximum distance a pendulum swings from its center point</note>. In this case, the difference in phase <note>phase: the relative timing between two vibrating objects</note> is about a quarter of a cycle, meaning the upper pendulum is ahead by that amount. If the two periods are very different, the vibrations either match or are completely opposite in phase, according to equations (4) and (5) in section 46.

**63.** A very good example of a forced vibration is provided by a tuning fork influenced by an intermittent electric current with a frequency <note>original: "period"</note> nearly equal to its own.

->*FIG. 16.*<-

<image-desc>A technical diagram labeled FIG. 16 showing a tuning fork mounted horizontally on a base. Between the prongs of the fork (labeled A and B) is an electromagnet (labeled E) with an armature (labeled D and F). Below the main diagram is a detail view of the iron core E, showing its "Siemens armature" shape.</image-desc>

*ACB* is the tuning fork; *E* is a small electromagnet, made by winding insulated wire onto an iron core shaped like the one shown in *E* (similar to what is known as a "Siemens armature" <note>Siemens armature: an early type of H-shaped iron core used in electrical devices to concentrate magnetic flux</note>), and mounted between the prongs of the fork. When an intermittent current is sent through the wire, a periodic force acts on the fork. This force cannot be described by a simple circular function <note>circular function: a trigonometric function like a sine or cosine wave</note>; instead, it can be expanded using Fourier’s theorem <note>Fourier’s theorem: a mathematical method for breaking down complex periodic waves into a series of simple sine and cosine waves</note> into a series of such functions with periods of $\tau$, $\frac{1}{2}\tau$, $\frac{1}{3}\tau$, and so on. If any of these waves have enough amplitude and are nearly isochronous <note>isochronous: having the same frequency or timing</note> with the fork, the fork will begin to vibrate; otherwise, the effect is negligible. In the following explanation, we will assume that it is the full period $\tau$ that nearly matches the fork's timing, so we can treat the series representing the periodic force as being reduced to its first, most important term.

To achieve the strongest vibration, the fork must be carefully tuned—using a small sliding weight or some wax—until its natural frequency (ignoring friction) matches that of the driving force. This is best achieved through experimentation. As the frequencies get closer and the fork starts from rest, the driving force and the fork's natural vibration will have similar amplitudes and frequencies. As noted previously (§ 48), this produces *beats* <note>beats: an interference pattern between two sounds of slightly different frequencies, perceived as a periodic pulse in volume</note> at the start of the motion. The slower these beats are, the more accurate the adjustment. The motion only reaches its steady, permanent state after the initial free vibration has had time to die down. Because the vibrations of a well-made and properly mounted tuning fork experience very little damping <note>damping: the gradual loss of energy in an oscillation, usually caused by friction or air resistance</note>, even a tiny deviation from perfect synchronization causes a significant drop in the intensity of the resonance.

The slowness of these beats serves as a measure of how accurately the adjustment has been made. It is only after the free vibration has had time to fade away that the motion takes on its permanent, steady character. The vibrations of a tuning fork that is properly constructed and mounted are subject to very little damping. Consequently, even a very slight deviation from perfect isochronism causes a noticeable decrease in the intensity of the <term>resonance</term>.

# ONE DEGREE OF FREEDOM

To verify the relationships predicted by theory between the phase of a vibration and the force causing it, a modified experimental setup is required.

In this arrangement, two similar electromagnets act on two similar tuning forks. Both magnets are included in the same electrical circuit and are excited by the same intermittent current. Under these conditions, it is clear that both systems will be driven into similar vibrations because they are acted upon by equal forces. This similarity applies to both their **phase** <note>phase: the specific point in a cycle of a back-and-forth motion</note> and their **amplitude** <note>amplitude: the maximum distance the fork moves from its resting position</note>. 

Let us suppose now that the vibrations occur in directions perpendicular to one another and are visually combined using one of <term>Lissajous' methods</term> <note>Lissajous' methods: techniques used to visualize the intersection of two perpendicular oscillations, creating patterns that reveal the relationship between their frequencies and phases</note>. The resulting visual figure is necessarily a straight line. 

Starting from the case where the amplitudes are at their maximum—namely, when the natural periods of both forks are the same as that of the force—let one of the forks be put slightly out of tune. It must be remembered that, regardless of their natural periods, both forks will continue to vibrate in perfect unison with the driving force, and therefore in unison with each other. 

The principal effect of the difference in their natural periods is to destroy the **synchronism of phase**. The straight line, which previously represented the combined vibration, becomes an ellipse. This ellipse remains perfectly steady as long as the forks are not touched. Originally, both forks are a quarter-period behind the force. When the pitch of one is slightly lowered, its vibration falls even further behind the force, and at the same time, its amplitude diminishes. Let the difference of phase between the two forks be represented by $\epsilon'$, and the ratio of the amplitudes of vibration be $a : a_0$. Then, according to equation (6) in section 46:

-> $a = a_0 \cos \epsilon'$. <-

# FORK INTERRUPTER

It appears that a significant shift in **phase** <note>phase: the specific timing or point in a cycle of a back-and-forth motion</note> in either direction can be achieved without greatly reducing the **amplitude** <note>amplitude: the maximum distance a vibration moves from its resting position; its "strength"</note>. When one fork is vibrating at its peak, the other can be adjusted so its phase differs by as much as 60 degrees without losing more than half its amplitude. Alternatively, the phase can differ by as much as 45 degrees without losing more than half its energy. By setting one fork to vibrate 45 degrees ahead and the other 45 degrees behind the phase required for maximum **resonance** <note>resonance: when an object vibrates at its natural frequency due to an external force</note>, we achieve a phase difference of 90 degrees while keeping the amplitudes equal. In this case, the <term>Lissajous' figure</term> <note>Lissajous' figure: a complex curve representing the intersection of two perpendicular oscillations</note> becomes a circle.

An intermittent electric current can also be used to regulate the speed of a rotating object. The *phonic wheel*, invented independently by M. La Cour and by the author of this book¹, is very useful in scientific studies of sound. It can take various forms, but its essential feature is an electromagnet powered by an intermittent current. The magnetic circuit of this magnet is nearly completed by one or more soft iron **armatures** <note>armature: a piece of iron that is moved or acted upon by a magnetic field</note> mounted on the wheel and arranged symmetrically around its edge. 

If, as the wheel turns, the point where the armature passes closest to the magnet matches the middle of the pulse of electrical excitation, the electromagnetic forces pulling the armature forward and those resisting its retreat balance each other out. However, if the wheel lags slightly behind, the forces pulling it forward gain an advantage over those resisting its movement away from the magnet; overall, the magnetic forces then encourage the rotation. Similarly, if the timing (phase) of the wheel is ahead of that specific point, forces are triggered that slow the motion down. Through a self-adjusting process, the rotation settles into a timing where the driving forces exactly balance the resistance. 

When the wheel rotates with little friction and the electrical components are moderately powerful, an outside motor might not be needed to drive it. In this case, of course, the moment the armature passes closest to the magnet must *follow* the peak of the magnetization pulse. If an independent motor is used (which is sometimes advisable), the moment of closest passage can either come before or after the pulse.

In some cases, the oscillations of the movement—the way the wheel hunts back and forth around its ideal timing—are very persistent and interfere with how the instrument is used. A remedy can be found by using a ring containing water or mercury that rotates centered—

**64.** The intermittent current is best produced using a fork interrupter invented by Helmholtz. This device can consist of a tuning fork and an electromagnet mounted as previously described. One wire from the magnet is connected to one terminal of the battery, and the other wire is connected to a mercury cup. The battery's other terminal is connected to a second mercury cup. A U-shaped "rider" made of insulated wire is carried by the lower prong of the fork, positioned just over the cups. It is set at such a height that as the fork vibrates, the circuit is alternately opened and closed as one end of the rider moves in and out of the mercury. The other end of the rider may be kept permanently immersed in the mercury. By using the repeating (periodic) force created this way, the energy lost to friction is restored, and the vibrations of the fork are permanently maintained. To make a second fork vibrate through "forced vibration," its own electromagnet can be included in the same circuit, or in a separate circuit that is interrupted by another rider dipping into mercury cups¹.

The <note>original: *modus operandi*</note> way this self-acting instrument works is often misunderstood. If the force pushing the fork only depended on its physical position—that is, whether the circuit was open or closed—the work done as the prong moved in one direction would be canceled out when it returned. Consequently, after one full cycle, there would be no extra energy left to compensate for the effects of friction. Any explanation that does not account for the delay (retardation) of the electric current is entirely incorrect. This delay is caused by two things: inconsistent contact and **self-induction** <note>self-induction: a property of a circuit where a change in current creates an opposing electromagnetic force, delaying the flow of electricity</note>. When the tip of the rider first touches the mercury, the electrical contact is imperfect, probably on account of...

In Helmholtz's interrupter, a horseshoe-shaped electromagnet that wraps around the fork is used, but I prefer the current arrangement, at least for low-pitched forks. In some cases, more power is gained by using a horseshoe magnet that acts on a soft iron <term>armature</term> <note>armature: a piece of iron moved by a magnetic field</note> attached horizontally to the upper prong. I have usually found that a single **Smee cell** <note>Smee cell: an early type of electrical battery popular in the mid-19th century</note> provides enough power.

On the other hand, when leaving the mercury, the contact is prolonged because the liquid in the cup sticks to the coated <note>original: amalgamated</note> wire. For both of these reasons, the current is delayed <note>original: retarded</note> compared to what would be expected based simply on the physical position of the fork. But even if the circuit's resistance depended only on the fork's position, the current would still be delayed by its <term>self-induction</term> <note>self-induction: the property of an electrical circuit where a change in current creates an electromagnetic force that resists that very change</note>. However perfect the contact may be, a stable current cannot be generated until a short amount of time has passed, just as in basic physics, a specific velocity cannot be instantly forced upon a resting object. Whatever the cause of this delay¹, the result is that the fork gains more work as the wire <note>original: rider</note> leaves the mercury than it loses when entering it. This creates a surplus of energy to counteract friction.

If the magnetic force depended only on the fork’s position, the timing <note>original: phase</note> of its primary vibration <note>original: first harmonic component</note> would be 180º ahead of the fork’s own movement. The delay we mentioned reduces this lead. If the timing difference is reduced to 90º, the force acts in the most effective way, and the greatest possible vibration is produced.

It is important to note that (except in the case just mentioned), the actual pitch of the interrupter differs slightly from the fork’s natural pitch, according to the rule described in equation (5) of **§ 46**, where $\epsilon$ <note>original: epsilon</note> represents the specific timing difference caused by the nature of the contacts and the amount of self-induction. If the pulsing current is used to drive a second fork, the maximum vibration is achieved when the second fork’s frequency matches the modified frequency of the interrupter, rather than its natural frequency.

The shift of a tuning-fork interrupter from its natural pitch is very small in practice; however, the fact that such a shift is possible is surprising at first. The explanation (in the case of a small current delay) is that during the half of the motion where the prongs are furthest apart, the electromagnet helps the fork’s own natural springiness <note>original: recovering power due to rigidity</note>, which naturally raises the pitch. ## 65.
The general phenomenon of **resonance**, although it cannot be fully explained as a system with only "one degree of freedom," <note>one degree of freedom: a system whose motion can be described by a single variable, like the swing of a simple pendulum</note> is mostly based on these same general principles. When a **forced vibration** is triggered in one part of a system, all other parts are also affected; a vibration with the same timing <note>original: period</note> is created, and its size <note>original: amplitude</note> depends on how the entire system is structured.

However, we often focus our interest on the vibration of a separate part that is only loosely connected to the rest of the system. In such a case, as long as the vibration does not become too large, that part behaves very much like a system with one degree of freedom acted upon by a force. This force can be treated as *fixed* (given), regardless of the part's own natural timing. Therefore, the vibration follows the laws we have already studied. In cases where the timing of the force nearly matches the natural timing of the object—which is what we usually mean by **resonance**—the size of the vibration can become very large. In other cases, the vibration might be so small that it is hardly noticed. The level of precision needed in matching these timings to achieve resonance depends on the amount of **damping** <note>damping: the reduction in the size of vibrations caused by friction or energy loss</note> the system experiences.

Among objects that resonate without needing extremely precise tuning are stretched membranes <note>such as drumheads</note> and strings attached to sounding boards, as seen in the **pianoforte** <note>piano</note> and the violin. When the correct note is played nearby, these objects are made to vibrate in a very noticeable way. You can try this experiment by singing a note into a piano after first lifting the corresponding **damper** <note>damper: the felt pad that stops a piano string from vibrating</note>; the string will start to vibrate in response to your voice. Or, if you pluck one of the strings for a specific note (like a harp string) with your finger, the other strings for that same note will also start vibrating. You can prove this immediately by touching the first string to stop it; you will hear the others continue to ring.

The phenomenon of resonance is, however, most striking in cases where a very accurate match in timing is necessary to produce the full effect. Tuning forks mounted on **resonance boxes** <note>resonance box: a hollow wooden box designed to amplify the sound of a tuning fork</note> are a famous example of this. When they are perfectly in **unison** (the same pitch), the vibration of one fork will be picked up by another across the width of a room. However, even the slightest change in pitch...

It is found that a difference in timing that produces just one "beat" per second makes a massive difference in the result. When the forks are perfectly tuned and placed close together, the vibration can be passed back and forth between them several times by muffling <note>original: damping</note> them one after the other with a touch of the finger.

Examples of the powerful effects of **isochronism** <note>isochronism: when two or more processes, like the swing of a pendulum or the vibration of a string, happen in the same amount of time</note> are likely familiar to everyone. These effects are often important in many fields outside of acoustics. For example, few things are more dangerous for a ship than to lie in the **trough of the sea** <note>trough: the lowest point between two waves</note> while under the influence of waves whose timing nearly matches the ship's own natural rocking motion <note>original: rolling</note>.

### 65 a.
It has already been explained (§ 30) how the layering <note>original: superposition</note> of two vibrations with the same size <note>original: amplitude</note> and nearly the same frequency creates a combined result where the sound rises and falls in "beats." If we represent the two parts as $\cos 2\pi n_1 t$ and $\cos 2\pi n_2 t$, the combined result is:

->2 cos $\pi (n_1 - n_2) t$ . cos $\pi (n_1 + n_2) t$ .................(1);<-

This can be viewed as a vibration with a frequency of $\frac{1}{2} (n_1 + n_2)$ and a size <note>original: amplitude</note> of $2 \cos \pi (n_1 - n_2) t$. When the size passes through zero, it changes its sign (positive to negative), which is the same as the timing shifting by 180 degrees <note>original: change of phase of 180°</note>—at least if we usually think of size as always being positive. This shift in timing <note>original: change of phase</note> is easily seen in drawings made by machines that combine vibrations, and it is a very important feature. If a force of this nature acts on a system whose natural frequency is the average of the two ($\frac{1}{2} (n_1 + n_2)$), the effect is relatively small. If the system starts at rest, the repeated pushes at first work together, but after a while, the later pushes start to cancel out the effects of the earlier ones. The strongest reaction would come from forces at the original frequencies ($n_1$ and $n_2$), rather than from a force at the average frequency.

However, a very different result occurs if—as in some experiments by Professor A. M. Mayer¹—a steady sound is made intermittent by periodically placing an obstacle in its way. In this case, the timing <note>original: phase</note> resumes after each silence without being reversed. If a force like this acts on a system with the same natural timing <note>original: isochronous system</note>, the effect is indeed less than if there were no interruptions; but as all the...

When impulses <note>original: "impulses," referring here to physical pushes or electrical signals</note> operate in the same direction without any opposition, the response is powerful. One kind of pulsing <note>original: intermittent</note> vibration or force is represented by:

->2 (1 + cos 2$\pi$*mt*) cos 2$\pi$*nt*....................(2),<-

In this equation, *n* is the frequency of the vibration, and *m* is the frequency of the interruption <note>original: intermittence</note>¹. The size <note>original: amplitude</note> of the vibration is always positive here, and it varies between the values of 0 and 4. By using standard trigonometric transformations, equation (2) can be rewritten in this form:

->2 cos 2$\pi$*nt* + cos 2$\pi$ (*n* + *m*) *t* + cos 2$\pi$ (*n* $-$ *m*) *t*......(3);<-

This shows that the pulsing vibration in question is equal to three simple vibrations with frequencies of *n*, *n* + *m*, and *n* $-$ *m*. This provides the explanation for the "secondary sounds" <note>In modern physics, these are called sidebands—additional frequencies produced when a signal is modulated.</note> observed by the physicist Mayer.

The form shown in equation (2) is, of course, only one specific case. Another case, in which the volume <note>original: intensity</note> of the pulsing sound rises more suddenly to its maximum, is given by:

->4 cos⁴ $\pi$*mt* cos 2$\pi$*nt* ............................(4),<-

which may be transformed into:

->$\frac{3}{2}$ cos 2$\pi$*nt* + cos 2$\pi$ (*n* + *m*) *t* + cos 2$\pi$ (*n* $-$ *m*) *t*<-
->+ $\frac{1}{4}$ cos 2$\pi$ (*n* + 2*m*) *t* + $\frac{1}{4}$ cos 2$\pi$ (*n* $-$ 2*m*) *t*........(5).<-

In this instance, there are *four* secondary sounds. The frequencies of the two new tones differ from the primary sound by twice as much as the previous ones did.

The theory of pulsing vibrations is well illustrated by electrically driven tuning forks. A fork "interrupter" with a frequency of 128 produced a periodic electrical current; by passing this through an electromagnet, a second fork of the same pitch could be made to vibrate. The action of this current on the second fork could be made pulsing <note>original: intermittent</note> by short-circuiting the electromagnet. This was done using another interrupter with a frequency of 4, worked by an independent current from a Smee cell <note>Smee cell: an early form of battery consisting of silver and zinc plates in sulfuric acid.</note>. To power the main current, a Grove cell <note>Grove cell: a powerful early battery using zinc and platinum electrodes.</note> was used. When the contact of the second interrupter was permanently broken—so that the main current passed continuously through the electromagnet—the fork was, naturally, most powerfully affected when it was tuned to 128. Scarcely any response could be seen when the pitch was changed to 124 or 132. But if the second interrupter were allowed to operate, so as to—

<header>INTERMITTENT VIBRATIONS.</header>

...to make the periodic current flowing through the electromagnet intermittent <note>original: "intermittent," meaning starting and stopping at regular intervals</note>, then the fork would respond powerfully when tuned to 124 or 132 as well as when tuned to 128, but not when tuned to intermediate pitches, such as 126 or 130.

It is easy to understand how this intermittence creates a sensitivity that would not otherwise exist. When a tuning fork with a frequency of 124 starts from rest under the influence of a force with a frequency of 128, the impulses initially work together. However, after 1/8 of a second, the new impulses begin to oppose the earlier ones. After 1/4 of a second, another series of impulses begins, and their effect aligns with the first set, and so on. Thus, if all these impulses are allowed to act continuously, the resulting effect is negligible <note>original: "trifling"</note>; but if every other series is blocked, a large vibration builds up <note>original: "accumulates"</note>.

->Fig. 16 a.<-

<image-desc>A technical line drawing of an electrical circuit connected to a tuning fork apparatus. On the left is a battery and a contact breaker mechanism; on the right, a tuning fork is mounted with electrical connections to its tines and an electromagnet positioned between them.</image-desc>

The most general expression for a vibration of frequency *n*, where the amplitude <note>the "height" or strength of the wave</note> and phase <note>the specific point in the cycle of the wave</note> vary slowly with a frequency *m*, is:

> { $A_0 + A_1 \cos 2\pi mt + A_2 \cos 4\pi mt + A_3 \cos 6\pi mt + \dots$
> { $+ B_1 \sin 2\pi mt + B_2 \sin 4\pi mt + B_3 \sin 6\pi mt + \dots$ } $\cos 2\pi nt$
> $+$ { $C_0 + C_1 \cos 2\pi mt + C_2 \cos 4\pi mt + C_3 \cos 6\pi mt + \dots$
> { $+ D_1 \sin 2\pi mt + D_2 \sin 4\pi mt + D_3 \sin 6\pi mt + \dots$ } $\sin 2\pi nt$
> ......(6);

This formula applies both to the case of "beats" (for example, if only $A_1$ has a fixed value) and to the kind of intermittence caused when an obstacle is placed in the way. Therefore, in all cases, the vibration in question is equivalent to a combination of simple vibrations <note>In modern physics, these are called pure tones or sine waves.</note> with frequencies of *n*, *n + m*, *n - m*, *n + 2m*, *n - 2m*, and so on.

It is important to emphasize here that a "simple vibration" implies that it continues *forever* <note>original: "infinite continuance"</note>; it does not allow for changes in phase or amplitude. To assume—as is sometimes done in theories about light <note>original: "optical speculations"</note>—that a series of simple waves can start at a specific moment <note>original: "epoch"</note>, continue for a certain time (perhaps involving a large number of cycles), and eventually stop, is a contradiction in terms.

**66.** The solution of the equation for free vibration <term>free vibration: the motion of a system when it is displaced and then left to move on its own without external forces</term>, namely:
->$\ddot{u} + \kappa\dot{u} + n^2u = 0$ .............................. (1).<-
<note>In this equation, $u$ is the displacement, $\dot{u}$ (u-dot) is the velocity, and $\ddot{u}$ (u-double-dot) is the acceleration. The symbol $\kappa$ (kappa) represents resistance or friction, and $n$ relates to the system's natural frequency.</note>

This solution may be expressed in another form by defining the arbitrary constants of integration <term>constants of integration: fixed numbers in a formula that are determined by the starting state of the system</term> $A$ and $\alpha$ in terms of the initial values of $u$ and $\dot{u}$. We can denote these starting values as $u_0$ (initial displacement) and $\dot{u}_0$ (initial velocity). We immediately obtain:
->$u = e^{-\frac{1}{2}\kappa t} \left\{ \dot{u}_0 \frac{\sin n't}{n'} + u_0 \left( \cos n't + \frac{\kappa}{2n'} \sin n't \right) \right\}$ ...... (2),<-
where ->$n' = \sqrt{n^2 - \frac{1}{4}\kappa^2}$.<-

If there is no friction <note>original: "friction," meaning resistance or damping that slows the motion</note>, then $\kappa = 0$, and the formula simplifies to:
->$u = \dot{u}_0 \frac{\sin nt}{n} + u_0 \cos nt$..............................(3).<-

These results can be used to find the solution for the complete equation:
->$\ddot{u} + \kappa\dot{u} + n^2u = U$ .............................. (4),<-
where $U$ is a specific function of time representing an external force. From equation (2), we see that if a small change in velocity $\delta\dot{u}$ <note>the symbol $\delta$ (delta) indicates a very small change</note> is introduced at time $t'$, its effect at a later time $t$ is:
->$u = \delta\dot{u} e^{-\frac{1}{2}\kappa(t-t')} \frac{\sin n'(t-t')}{n'}$.<-

The force $U$ generates a velocity of $Udt'$ over a very short time interval $dt'$. The resulting effect at time $t$ will therefore be:
->$u = \frac{1}{n'} Udt' e^{-\frac{1}{2}\kappa(t-t')} \sin n'(t-t')$,<-
and thus the solution for equation (4) will be the sum of all these effects (the integral):
->$u = \frac{1}{n'} \int^t e^{-\frac{1}{2}\kappa(t-t')} \sin n'(t-t') \ U \ dt'$ ............ (5).<-

If there is no friction, we simply have:
->$u = \frac{1}{n} \int^t \sin n(t-t') \ U \ dt'$ ........................ (6),<-
where $U$ is the force acting at time $t'$.

The starting point (lower limit) of these integrals <term>integrals: a mathematical way to calculate the total accumulated effect of a changing force over time</term> is currently flexible, but it will generally be convenient to set it to zero.

Assuming this, $u$ (displacement) and $\dot{u}$ (velocity) as given by equation (6) are zero when $t = 0$. The complete solution, accounting for both the initial state and the external force, is:
$u = e^{-\frac{1}{2}\kappa t} \left\{ \dot{u}_0 \frac{\sin n't}{n'} + u_0 \left( \cos n't + \frac{\kappa}{2n'} \sin n't \right) \right\}$
->$+ \frac{1}{n'} \int_0^t e^{-\frac{1}{2}\kappa(t-t')} \sin n'(t-t') \ U \ dt'$ ...... (7).<-

Or, if there is no friction:
-> $u = \dot{u}_0 \frac{\sin nt}{n} + u_0 \cos nt + \frac{1}{n} \int_0^t \sin n (t - t') U dt' \dots\dots\dots (8).$ <-

When the time ($t$) is large enough, the secondary parts of the formula <term>complementary terms: the parts of a mathematical solution that represent the system's natural response to a disturbance, which usually fade away over time</term> tend to disappear because of the factor $e^{-\frac{1}{2}\kappa t}$, and they can then be ignored.

**66 a.** In section 66, we limited the discussion to the cases of greatest importance to the study of sound—that is, we assumed that $n'$ is a "real" number, which happens when $n^2$ is positive and the friction ($\kappa$) is not too high. However, a more general look at the problem of free vibrations is also interesting. Regardless of the values of $n^2$ and $\kappa$, the solution for the motion can be expressed as:
-> $u = Ae^{\mu_1 t} + Be^{\mu_2 t} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (1),$ <-
where $\mu_1$ and $\mu_2$ are the roots of:
-> $\mu^2 + \kappa\mu + n^2 = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (2).$ <-

The case already discussed is the one where the values of $\mu$ are imaginary <term>imaginary numbers: numbers that, when squared, result in a negative value; in physics, these usually indicate that a system is oscillating or vibrating back and forth</term>. In that case, the motion is oscillatory, with an extent of swing <term>amplitude: the maximum distance an object moves from its resting position during a vibration</term> that decreases if friction ($\kappa$) is positive, but increases if friction is negative.

However, if $n^2$ is positive but less than $\frac{1}{4}\kappa^2$, or if $n^2$ is negative, then $n'$ becomes imaginary, which means $\mu$ becomes a real number. The motion described by equation (1) is then non-oscillatory—it does not swing back and forth—and whether it increases or diminishes over time depends on whether $\mu$ is positive or negative. From the solution of equation (2), namely <note>original: "viz.", short for the Latin "videlicet"</note>:
-> $\mu = -\frac{1}{2}\kappa \pm \frac{1}{2} \sqrt{(\kappa^2 - 4n^2)} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (3),$ <-
it is clear that if $n^2$ is positive (and less than $\frac{1}{4}\kappa^2$), both values of $\mu$ will have the same sign, and that sign will be the opposite of the sign of the friction ($\kappa$). Therefore, if $\kappa$ is positive, both parts of the equation diminish over time, so the system—no matter how it is disturbed—eventually settles back into a state of rest. If, on the contrary, $\kappa$ is negative, the motion increases without limit.

We still need to consider the case where $n^2$ is negative. In this situation, the real values of $\mu$ have opposite signs (one positive and one negative). It is possible to start the system from a moved position in such a way that it slowly returns toward rest <term>asymptotically: approaching a value or condition closer and closer but never quite reaching it</term> in its original equilibrium position. However, unless there is a very specific relationship between the starting displacement and the starting velocity, the motion will tend to increase forever. Under these circumstances, the resting state must be regarded as **unstable**. In this sense, true stability requires that both $n^2$ and $\kappa$ be positive.

**67.** For most purposes in acoustics, it is sufficient to treat the vibrations of the systems we deal with as being infinitely small, or at least very similar to infinitely small vibrations. This limitation is the basis of the important laws of <term>isochronism</term> <note>the property where the time it takes for one vibration to occur remains the same regardless of its size or "amplitude"</note> for free vibrations, and the persistence of the period for forced vibrations. However, there are secondary but significant phenomena that depend fundamentally on the square and higher powers of the motion. We will, therefore, spend the rest of this chapter discussing the motion of a system with one degree of freedom where the motion is large enough that these squares and higher powers cannot be completely ignored.

The approximate formulas for the <term>kinetic energy</term> <note>energy of motion</note> and <term>potential energy</term> <note>stored energy based on position or state</note> will take the following form:
-> $T = \frac{1}{2} (m_0 + m_1 u) \dot{u}^2, \quad V = \frac{1}{2} (\mu_0 + \mu_1 u) u^2.$ <-
If we find the rate of change of the sum of $T$ and $V$ with respect to time, we find the following equation of motion:
-> $m_0 \ddot{u} + \mu_0 u + m_1 u \ddot{u} + \frac{1}{2} m_1 \dot{u}^2 + \frac{3}{2} \mu_1 u^2 = \text{External Force},$ <-
This can be solved using the method of successive approximation <note>a mathematical technique where one starts with a simple guess and refines it through repeated steps to reach a more accurate solution</note>. To keep things simple, we will consider the case where $m_1 = 0$, an assumption that does not change the core of the problem. In this case, the <term>inertia</term> <note>the tendency of the system to resist changes in its state of motion</note> of the system is constant, while the <term>restoring force</term> <note>original: "force of restitution"; the force that pulls the system back toward its equilibrium position</note> is a complex function of the displacement. It is partly proportional to the displacement itself and partly to its square—making it unsymmetrical relative to the starting position of equilibrium. Thus, for free vibrations, our equation is:
-> $\ddot{u} + n^2 u + \alpha u^2 = 0 \dotfill (1),$ <-
with the approximate solution:
-> $u = A \cos nt \dotfill (2),$ <-
where $A$—the <term>amplitude</term> <note>the maximum distance the system moves from its resting position during a vibration</note>—is treated as a small value.

By substituting the value of $u$ from equation (2) into the last term of equation (1), we find:
-> $\ddot{u} + n^2 u = - \alpha \frac{A^2}{2} (1 + \cos 2nt),$ <-

From this, we can find a second approximation for the value of $u$:

->$$u = A \cos nt - \frac{\alpha A^2}{2n^2} + \frac{\alpha A^2}{6n^2} \cos 2nt \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(3);$$<-

This shows that the <term>proper tone</term> <note>natural frequency or fundamental frequency</note> ($n$) of the system is accompanied by its <term>octave</term> <note>a frequency exactly double that of the fundamental tone</note> ($2n$). The relative importance of this octave increases as the <term>amplitude of vibration</term> <note>the maximum extent of a vibration or oscillation, measured from the position of equilibrium</note> grows larger. A trained ear can usually hear the octave in the sound of a <term>tuning-fork</term> <note>a metal tool that produces a fixed pitch when struck</note> when it is forced to vibrate strongly using a bow. With the help of specific equipment, which will be explained later, the existence of this octave can be demonstrated to anyone. 

By following this same method, the approximation can be taken even further; however, we will now move on to the case of a system in which the <term>recovering power</term> <note>restoring force; the force that pulls a displaced system back toward its center</note> is symmetrical relative to the position of <term>equilibrium</term> <note>the state of rest or balance where all acting forces cancel each other out</note>. In this case, the <term>equation of motion</term> <note>a mathematical formula describing how a system changes over time</note> is approximately:

->$$\ddot{u} + n^2u + \beta u^3 = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (4),$$<-

This can be understood as referring to the vibrations of a heavy <term>pendulum</term> <note>a weight hung from a fixed point so that it can swing freely</note> or a weight carried at the end of a straight spring.

If we take $u = A \cos nt$ as our first approximation (assuming $\beta = 0$) and substitute it into the term multiplied by $\beta$, we get:

->$$\ddot{u} + n^2u = - \frac{\beta A^3}{4} \cos 3nt - \frac{3\beta A^3}{4} \cos nt.$$<-

Based on the last term of this equation, we would obtain a solution containing a term in the form $t \sin nt$, which grows infinitely as time ($t$) increases. Just as in a similar case in <term>Lunar Theory</term> <note>the mathematical study of the Moon's motion and its perturbations</note>, this indicates that our assumed first approximation is not actually an approximation at all—or at least, it does not *continue* to be one. 

However, if we start with $u = A \cos mt$ using a suitable value for $m$, we will find that the solution can be completed using only <term>periodic terms</term> <note>mathematical terms that repeat at regular intervals</note>. In fact, it is obvious beforehand that we are only entitled to assume that the motion is approximately <term>simple harmonic</term> <note>a regular, repeating back-and-forth motion like a pure tone</note>, with a period that is *approximately* the same as if $\beta = 0$. Even a brief examination is enough to show that the term involving $u^3$ not only might, but *must affect* the period. At the same time, it is clear that any solution in which the period is assumed wrongly—no matter by how little—must eventually fail to represent the motion with any accuracy.

Therefore, we take the following for our approximate equation:

->$$\ddot{u} + n^2u = - \frac{3\beta A^3}{4} \cos mt - \frac{\beta A^3}{4} \cos 3mt \dots\dots\dots (5),$$<-

the solution to this equation will be:
-> $u = A \cos mt + \frac{\beta A^3}{4} \frac{\cos 3mt}{9m^2 - n^2} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (6),$ <-

as long as $m$ is chosen so as to satisfy:
-> $A (-m^2 + n^2) = - \frac{3\beta A^3}{4},$ <-

or
-> $m^2 = n^2 + \frac{3\beta A^2}{4} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (7).$ <-

The term containing $\beta$ <note>the coefficient representing the cubic non-linearity in the restoring force</note> thus produces two effects. It alters the <term>pitch</term> <note>the perceived frequency of the sound</note> of the fundamental vibration, and it introduces the *twelfth* <note>original: "twelfth"; the third harmonic, which sounds an octave plus a perfect fifth above the fundamental tone</note> as a necessary accompaniment. The alteration of pitch is, in most cases, exceedingly small—since it depends on the square of the <term>amplitude</term> <note>the maximum extent of the vibration</note>—but it is not entirely unnoticeable. <term>Tuning-forks</term> <note>metal instruments used as a standard of pitch</note> generally rise slightly, though very little, in pitch as the vibration dies away. It should be noted that the same slight dependence of pitch on amplitude occurs when the <term>force of restitution</term> <note>restoring force; the force pulling the object back to center</note> is in the form $n^2 u + \alpha u^2$, as can be seen by continuing the approximation of the solution for equation (1) one step further than equation (3). The result in that case is:
-> $m^2 = n^2 - \frac{5\alpha^2 A^2}{6n^2} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (8)^1.$ <-

The difference between $m^2$ and $n^2$ is of the same order regarding the amplitude ($A$) in both cases. However, there is one distinction worth noting: in equation (8), $m^2$ is always less than $n^2$, while in equation (7), the effect (whether to raise or lower the pitch) depends on whether the sign of $\beta$ is positive or negative. Nevertheless, in most cases of the unsymmetrical class, the change of pitch would depend partly on a term in the form $\alpha u^2$ and partly on another in the form $\beta u^3$, resulting in:
-> $m^2 = n^2 - \frac{5\alpha^2 A^2}{6n^2} + \frac{3\beta A^2}{4} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (9)^1.$ <-

[In all cases where the <term>period</term> <note>the time it takes for one complete cycle of vibration</note> depends upon amplitude, it is necessarily an *even function* <note>a mathematical property where changing the sign of the input (amplitude) does not change the result</note> of that amplitude; changing the sign of the amplitude is merely equivalent to altering the <term>phase</term> <note>the starting point or position in the cycle of vibration</note> by 180°.]

# TERMS OF THE SECOND ORDER.

The equation of motion is:
->$\ddot{u} + n^2u = -\alpha u^2 + E \cos pt + F \cos (qt - \epsilon) \dots\dots (1).$<-

To find a first approximation, we neglect the term containing $\alpha$ <note>the coefficient representing the non-linear part of the restoring force</note>. Thus:
->$u = e \cos pt + f \cos (qt - \epsilon) \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (2),$<-
where
->$e = \frac{E}{n^2 - p^2}, \quad f = \frac{F}{n^2 - q^2} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (3).$<-

Substituting this result back into the term multiplied by $\alpha$, we get:
->$\ddot{u} + n^2u = E \cos pt + F \cos (qt - \epsilon)$<-
->$-\alpha \left[ \frac{e^2 + f^2}{2} + \frac{e^2}{2} \cos 2pt + \frac{f^2}{2} \cos 2(qt - \epsilon) + ef \cos \{(p - q)t + \epsilon\} \right.$<-
->$\left. + ef \cos \{(p + q)t - \epsilon\} \right],$<-

from which we derive a second approximation for $u$:
->$u = e \cos pt + f \cos (qt - \epsilon) - \frac{\alpha(e^2 + f^2)}{2n^2} - \frac{\alpha e^2}{2(n^2 - 4p^2)} \cos 2pt$<-
->$- \frac{\alpha f^2}{2(n^2 - 4q^2)} \cos 2(qt - \epsilon) - \frac{\alpha ef}{n^2 - (p - q)^2} \cos \{(p - q)t + \epsilon\}$<-
->$- \frac{\alpha ef}{n^2 - (p + q)^2} \cos \{(p + q)t - \epsilon\} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (4).$<-

The additional terms represent vibrations with frequencies that are respectively the doubles ($2p, 2q$) and the sum ($p+q$) and difference ($p-q$) of the primary frequencies. For the latter two, the <term>amplitudes</term> <note>the maximum displacement or "loudness" of the wave</note> are proportional to the product of the original amplitudes ($ef$). This shows that these derived tones increase in relative importance as the intensity of their parent tones increases.

### 68$a$.
If an isolated vibrating system is subject to internal <term>dissipative influences</term> <note>forces like friction or resistance that cause energy to be lost as heat</note>, the vibrations cannot last forever, since they depend on an initial store of energy that is gradually exhausted. In order for the motion to be maintained, the vibrating body must be connected to a source of energy. We have already considered cases of this kind under the heading of **forced vibrations**, where the system is subject to forces whose amplitude and phase are prescribed, regardless of how the system itself behaves. Such forces may originate from a revolving mechanism (such as <term>electric alternators</term> <note>early terminology for alternating current generators</note>) regulated to move at a uniform speed. But more frequently, the forces under consideration depend upon the vibrations of other systems,

# ONE DEGREE OF FREEDOM.

...and this leads to the question of how vibrations are to be maintained. A good example of this is the case already discussed (sections 63 and 65) regarding a tuning fork whose vibrations are maintained electrically by currents controlled by a fork interrupter. As previously noted, the operation of the interrupter depends on the magnetic forces acting upon it being out of phase <note>original: "differing in phase"; meaning the forces are not perfectly synchronized</note> with the vibrations of the fork itself. 

For our purposes, we can group the interrupter with almost all acoustic and musical instruments capable of producing a sustained sound. Examples include vibrations maintained by wind (such as organ pipes, harmonium reeds, and <term>aeolian harps</term> <note>stringed instruments played by the wind</note>), by heat (like <term>singing flames</term> <note>sounds produced by a flame inside a tube</note> and <term>Rijke's tubes</term> <note>tubes that produce sound when heat is applied to a mesh inside</note>), by friction (violin strings or rubbing the rim of a crystal glass), and the slower vibrations of clock pendulums and watch balance-wheels.

When determining if a specific force is suitable for maintaining or encouraging a vibration, it is often helpful to view those forces as a series of impulses. For instance, consider a small, horizontal, positive impulse acting on the weight <note>the "bob"</note> of a swinging pendulum. The result depends, of course, on the phase of the vibration at the exact moment the impulse is applied. If the weight is already moving in the positive direction at that moment, the vibration is boosted. This effect is strongest when the positive motion is at its peak—that is, when the impulse occurs exactly as the weight passes through its center equilibrium position. 

Clock designers aim for this condition when creating an <term>escapement</term> <note>the mechanism that transfers energy to the timekeeping element</note>; at this point, the force is most effective at sustaining the vibration while causing the least amount of disturbance to the timing <note>the "period"</note>. Naturally, if the impulse occurs half a cycle earlier or later, it will dampen the vibration instead of boosting it, though it still will not change the timing. Similarly, if the impulse happens at the point of maximum swing <note>original: "elongation"</note>, it will affect the timing of the pendulum but will neither increase nor decrease the strength of the vibration.

In most cases, the force acting on a vibrating system from an external energy source can be treated as <term>harmonic</term> <note>periodic and oscillating, like a sine wave</note>. This force can be split into two parts: one proportional to the displacement $u$ (or the acceleration $\ddot{u}$), and the second proportional to the velocity $\dot{u}$. Including these forces does not change the basic structure of the equation of vibration:

->$\ddot{u} + \kappa\dot{u} + n^2u = 0$...........................(1).<-

It highlights that applying an impulse as a system passes through its equilibrium position is the most efficient way to maintain vibration without disturbing the timing.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the mathematical analysis of how vibrations are sustained or "maintained" over time. While the previous page discussed the impact of timed impulses (like a person pushing a swing), this page focuses on the mathematical equations that determine whether a vibration will fade away, grow uncontrollably, or reach a stable, steady state.</meta>

->### MAINTENANCE OF VIBRATIONS.<-

In the first part of the equation (which is proportional to $u$), the pitch is modified; in the second part, the <term>coefficient of decay</term> <note>the mathematical value representing how quickly the vibration loses energy and fades</note> is determined. If the adjusted $\kappa$ remains positive, the vibrations will gradually die down. However, if the effect of the forces involved is to make $\kappa$ negative, the vibrations will instead tend to increase. According to equation (1), the only case in which a steady vibration is possible is when the complete value of $\kappa$ is zero. If this condition is met, a vibration of any size (<term>amplitude</term>) is permanently maintained.

When $\kappa$ is negative—meaning small vibrations tend to grow—they eventually reach a point where the approximate equations are no longer accurate. We can get an idea of what happens then by adding a term to equation (1) that is proportional to a higher power of the velocity. Let us consider:

->$\ddot{u} + \kappa\dot{u} + \kappa'\dot{u}^3 + n^2u = 0$ ........................(2),<-

in which $\kappa$ and $\kappa'$ are assumed to be small quantities. The approximate solution of equation (2) is:

->$u = A \sin nt + \frac{\kappa' n A^3}{32} \cos 3nt$ ........................(3),<-

in which the amplitude $A$ is given by:

->$\kappa + \frac{3}{4} \kappa' n^2 A^2 = 0$ ........................(4).<-

From equation (4), we see that no steady vibration is possible unless $\kappa$ and $\kappa'$ have opposite signs (one positive and one negative). If $\kappa$ and $\kappa'$ are both positive, the vibration always dies down. If $\kappa$ and $\kappa'$ are both negative, the vibration (according to equation 2) increases without limit. If $\kappa$ is negative and $\kappa'$ is positive, the vibration becomes steady and reaches the amplitude determined by equation (4). A smaller vibration will increase until it reaches this point, and a larger vibration will decrease until it settles there. On the other hand, if $\kappa$ is positive while $\kappa'$ is negative, the steady vibration that is theoretically possible is unstable; any slight change from the amplitude given by equation (4) will tend to increase further <note>original footnote: On Maintained Vibrations, *Philosophical Magazine*, April, 1883</note>.

*...the direction of motion of the point of attachment being parallel to the length of the string.* The effect of this motion is to make the tension of the string change at regular intervals (periodically). At first glance, there is nothing that should cause the string to move away from its straight, resting position (<term>equilibrium</term>). It is known, however, that under these circumstances, the equilibrium may become unstable. The string may then establish a state of steady and strong vibration, with a cycle twice as long as that of the tuning fork.

As a simpler example of a system with only one <term>degree of freedom</term> <note>a single way or direction in which a system can move</note>, we can look at a pendulum made of a soft iron bar that swings on sharp pivots called knife-edges. An electromagnet bar is placed vertically and symmetrically underneath it. An electric current is passed through this magnet, but it is made intermittent by a switch (an interrupter) that operates at twice the frequency of the pendulum. This magnetic force does not directly push the pendulum away from its resting position. Instead, it produces the same effect as if the force of gravity were changing its intensity at regular intervals.

A similar result occurs if we cause the pendulum's support point to move up and down in a vertical path. If we represent this motion with the formula $\eta = \beta \sin 2pt$, the effect is the same as if gravity were varied by the term $4p^2\beta \sin 2pt$.

Of the same nature are the "crispations" <note>original: "crispations"; refers to the pattern of standing waves or ripples</note> observed by Michael Faraday <note>Michael Faraday (1791–1867), a pioneer in the study of electromagnetism and physics</note> and others on the surface of water that is vibrating vertically. Faraday concluded through experiments that there were two complete vibrations of the support for every one complete vibration of the liquid surface.

In the following investigation <note>original: *Phil. Mag.*, April, 1883; referring to the *Philosophical Magazine*</note>, regarding the case of one degree of freedom, we will start by assuming that a steady vibration is already occurring. We will then inquire into the conditions under which such a state of things is possible.

If the restoring force (the "springiness" that pulls an object back to center) of an object capable of vibrating is subjected to an imposed periodic change, the <term>differential equation</term> <note>a mathematical equation that describes how a physical quantity, like position, changes over time</note> takes this form:

->$\ddot{u} + \kappa\dot{u} + (n^2 - 2\alpha \sin 2pt) u = 0$ ................(1),<-

in which $\kappa$ <note>the coefficient representing resistance or friction</note> and $\alpha$ <note>the amount of variation in the restoring force</note> are assumed to be small. A similar equation would apply roughly if the object's effective mass were changing periodically. The motion described by the solution to equation (1) can only be regular when it maintains perfect timing...

# MAINTENANCE OF VIBRATIONS.
<sig>6—2</sig>

...with the variations imposed. It becomes clear that the necessary conditions cannot be strictly satisfied by any simple <term>harmonic vibration</term> <note>a smooth, repetitive oscillation like that of a pendulum</note>, but we may assume:

->*u* = *A*₁ sin *pt* + *B*₁ cos *pt*<-
->+ *A*₃ sin 3*pt* + *B*₃ cos 3*pt* + *A*₅ sin 5*pt* + .........(2),<-

in which it is not necessary to provide for sines and cosines of even multiples of *pt*. If this assumption is justifiable, the solution in (2) must <term>converge</term> <note>approach a definite limit or value</note>. Substituting this into the <term>differential equation</term> <note>a mathematical equation that relates a function with its derivatives, used here to describe the physics of motion</note> and setting the <term>coefficients</term> of sin *pt*, cos *pt*, etc., to zero, we find:

->*A*₁ (*n*² − *p*²) − *κpB*₁ − *αB*₁ + *αB*₃ = 0,<-
->*B*₁ (*n*² − *p*²) + *κpA*₁ − *αA*₁ − *αA*₃ = 0;<-
->*A*₃ (*n*² − 9*p*²) − 3*κpB*₃ − *αB*₁ + *αB*₅ = 0,<-
->*B*₃ (*n*² − 9*p*²) + 3*κpA*₃ + *αA*₁ − *αA*₅ = 0;<-
->*A*₅ (*n*² − 25*p*²) − 5*κpB*₅ − *αB*₃ + *αB*₇ = 0,<-
->*B*₅ (*n*² − 25*p*²) + 5*κpA*₅ + *αA*₃ − *αA*₇ = 0;<-
->............................................................<-

These equations show that *A*₃ and *B*₃ are of the order *α* <note>meaning they are proportional in size to the variable α</note> relative to *A*₁ and *B*₁; that *A*₅ and *B*₅ are of the same order relative to *A*₃ and *B*₃, and so on. If we ignore *A*₃ and *B*₃ in the first pair of equations, we find as a first <term>approximation</term>:

->*A*₁ (*n*² − *p*²) − (*κp* + *α*) *B*₁ = 0,<-
->*A*₁ (*κp* − *α*) + (*n*² − *p*²) *B*₁ = 0;<-

from which it follows:

->$\frac{B_1}{A_1} = \frac{n^2 - p^2}{\kappa p + \alpha} = \frac{\alpha - \kappa p}{n^2 - p^2} = \frac{\sqrt{(\alpha - \kappa p)}}{\sqrt{(\alpha + \kappa p)}}$ ........................(3),<-

and

->(*n*² − *p*²)² = *α*² − *κ*²*p*² ...........................(4).<-

Thus, if *α* is given, the value of *p* required for a regular motion is specific; and with *p* set to this value, the regular motion is:

->*u* = *P* sin (*pt* + *ε*),<-

in which *ε*—being equal to tan⁻¹ (*B*₁/*A*₁)—is also specific. On the other hand, as is immediately obvious from the linear nature of the original equation, there is nothing to limit the <term>amplitude</term> <note>original: "amplitude"; the maximum extent of a vibration or oscillation, measured from the position of equilibrium</note> of the vibration.

These characteristics remain consistent no matter how far the approximation is carried. If *A*₂ₘ₊₁ and *B*₂ₘ₊₁ can be ignored, the first *m* pairs of equations determine the ratios of all the coefficients while leaving the absolute magnitude undecided. Furthermore, they provide an equation linking *p* and *α*, which determines the <term>pitch</term> <note>the frequency or rate of the vibration</note>.

# ONE DEGREE OF FREEDOM.

For the second <term>approximation</term> <note>a calculation that is close but not exact, used to simplify complex equations</note>, the second pair of equations gives:
-> $A_3 = \frac{\alpha B_1}{n^2 - 9p^2} , \quad B_3 = - \frac{\alpha A_1}{n^2 - 9p^2} ,$ <-
from which:
-> $u = P \sin (pt + \epsilon) + \frac{\alpha P}{9p^2 - n^2} \cos (3pt + \epsilon) \dots \dots \dots (5),$ <-
and from the first pair:
-> $\tan \epsilon = \{ n^2 - p^2 - \frac{\alpha^2}{n^2 - 9p^2} \} \div (\alpha + \kappa p) \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (6),$ <-
while $p$ is determined by:
-> $\{ n^2 - p^2 - \frac{\alpha^2}{n^2 - 9p^2} \}^2 = \alpha^2 - \kappa^2 p^2 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (7).$ <-

Returning to the first approximation, we see from **(4)** that the solution is possible only under the condition that $\alpha$ is not less than $\kappa p$. If $\alpha = \kappa p$, then $p = n$; that is, the imposed variation in the "spring" <note>the restoring force, such as the tension in a string or the stiffness of a rod</note> must be exactly twice as fast as the natural <term>vibration</term> <note>the back-and-forth motion</note> of the body would be if there were no <term>friction</term> <note>resistance to motion</note>. From **(3)**, it appears that in this case $\epsilon = 0$, which indicates that the spring is at its minimum one-eighth of a cycle *after* the body has passed its position of <term>equilibrium</term> <note>the central point where the body naturally rests</note>, and at its maximum one-eighth of a cycle *before* it passes that point. Under these circumstances, the greatest possible amount of energy is transferred to the system; in this specific case, it is just enough to balance the loss by <term>dissipation</term> <note>the loss of energy, usually as heat, due to friction or resistance</term>, and the adjustment is clearly independent of the <term>amplitude</term> <note>the maximum distance the body moves from its resting position</note>.

If $\alpha$ is less than $\kappa p$, enough energy cannot be transferred to maintain the motion, regardless of the <term>phase-relation</term> <note>the timing of the forced variation relative to the body's motion</note>; but if $\alpha$ is greater than $\kappa p$, the balance between supplied energy and dissipated energy may be reached by changing the phase enough to reduce the energy supplied to the required amount. This change of phase can happen equally in either direction; but if $\epsilon$ is positive, we must have:
-> $p^2 = n^2 - \sqrt{(\alpha^2 - \kappa^2 p^2)};$ <-
while if $\epsilon$ is negative:
-> $p^2 = n^2 + \sqrt{(\alpha^2 - \kappa^2 p^2)}.$ <-

If $\alpha$ is much greater than $\kappa p$, then $\epsilon = \pm \frac{1}{4} \pi$, which indicates that when the system passes through its position of equilibrium, the spring is at its maximum or at its minimum.

# ABSOLUTE PITCH.

The conditions for steady vibration must be absolutely rigorous, though they will be subject to some modification in practice; otherwise, the experiment could not succeed. In most cases, $n^2$ <note>In this context, $n$ likely represents the natural frequency or a constant related to the system's restoring force</note> is to a certain extent a function of <term>amplitude</term> <note>the maximum extent of a vibration, measured from the equilibrium position</note>. Therefore, if $n^2$ has very nearly the required value, complete coincidence can be achieved by assuming an amplitude of a large and specific amount without other alterations in the conditions of the system.

The reader who wishes to pursue this subject further is referred to a paper by the author, "On the Maintenance of Vibrations by Forces of Double Frequency, and on the Propagation of Waves through a Medium endowed with a Periodic Structure,"¹ in which the analysis of Mr. Hill² is applied to the present problem.

## **68 c.**

The determination of absolute pitch by means of the <term>siren</term> <note>an instrument for measuring the frequency of sound by passing air through a rotating perforated disk</note> has already been mentioned (§ 17). In all probability, first-rate results might be obtained by this method if proper provision, with the aid of a <term>phonic wheel</term> <note>a motor that synchronizes its rotation with the frequency of an electric current, often used to maintain constant speed</note> for example, were made for uniform speed. In recent years, several experimenters have obtained excellent results by various methods, but a brief notice of these is all that our limits will allow.

One of the most direct determinations is that of Mr. Koenig³, to whom the scientific world has long been indebted for the construction of much excellent apparatus. This depends upon a special instrument consisting of a tuning fork that makes 64 complete vibrations per second, with the motion being maintained by a clock movement acting upon an <term>escapement</term> <note>a mechanism in a clock that controls the transfer of energy to the timekeeping element</note>. A dial is provided, marking ordinary time, which serves to record the number of vibrations executed. The performance of the fork is tested by a comparison between the instrument and any <term>chronometer</term> <note>a highly accurate timekeeping device</note> known to be keeping good time. The standard tuning fork of 256 complete vibrations was compared with that of the instrument by observing the <term>Lissajous figure</term> <note>a complex curve produced by combining two perpendicular vibrations, used to compare their frequencies</note> appropriate to the double <term>octave</term> <note>a series of eight notes where the higher frequency is exactly double the lower</note>.

Mr. Koenig has also investigated the influence of <term>resonators</term> <note>hollow chambers designed to vibrate at a specific frequency to amplify or analyze sound</note> upon the pitch of tuning forks. Thus, without a resonator, a fork of 256 complete vibrations sounded in a satisfactory manner for about 90 seconds. A resonator of adjustable pitch was then brought into proximity, and the pitch, originally much <term>graver</term> <note>original: "graver"; meaning lower in frequency or pitch</note> than that of the...

The pitch of the fork was gradually raised. Even when the <term>resonator</term> <note>a hollow chamber designed to vibrate at a specific frequency to amplify sound</note> was still a <term>minor third</term> <note>a musical interval spanning three semitones</note> below the fork, a slight decrease in the duration of the vibratory movement was observed. At the same time, there was an increase in frequency of about 0.005 Hz. As the natural note of the resonator approached closer to that of the fork, this decrease in vibration time and increase in frequency became more pronounced until they were very nearly in <term>unison</term> <note>vibrating at exactly the same frequency</note>. 

However, at the exact moment unison was established, the alteration of pitch suddenly disappeared, and the frequency became exactly the same as it was without the resonator. At this same moment, the sound was powerfully reinforced; but this extreme intensity fell off rapidly, and the vibration died away after 8 or 10 seconds. When the pitch of the resonator was raised a little further, the sound of the fork began to change in the opposite direction; it was now as much too <term>low</term> <note>original: "grave"</note> as it had been too <term>high</term> <note>original: "acute"</note> before reaching unison. This displacement then decreased by degrees as the pitch of the resonator was raised further, and the duration of the vibrations gradually recovered its original value of about 90 seconds. The maximum disturbance in frequency observed by Koenig was 0.035 complete vibrations. For the explanation of these effects, see § 117.

The temperature coefficient found by <term>Koenig</term> <note>Karl Rudolph Koenig (1832–1901), a physicist famous for his acoustic instruments</note> is 0.000112. This means that the pitch of a 256 Hz fork falls by 0.0286 Hz for each degree Celsius that the temperature rises.

In my own determinations of <term>absolute pitch</term>¹ <note>the exact frequency of a sound in vibrations per second, rather than its relative position on a musical scale</note>, I used an electrically maintained <term>interrupter fork</term> <note>a tuning fork that acts as a switch in an electrical circuit to keep itself and other components vibrating</note>. For example, an interrupter fork with a frequency of 32 Hz was used to drive a dependent fork with a pitch of 128 Hz. When the apparatus is in good working order, there is a fixed relationship between the two frequencies, with the higher one being precisely four times the frequency of the lower one. The higher frequency is, of course, easily compared with a standard 128 Hz fork—whose accuracy is being tested—by using <term>beats</term> <note>the pulsing sound heard when two tones of slightly different frequencies interfere</note> or optical methods. It then remains only to determine the frequency of the interrupter fork itself.

For this purpose, the interrupter is compared with the pendulum of a standard clock whose rate of timekeeping is known. This comparison may be done directly, or by using a <term>phonic wheel</term> <note>an electromagnetic motor that rotates at a speed synchronized with the pulses of an electric current</note> (§ 63). In either case, the clock's pendulum is equipped with a small silvered bead that reflects a concentrated beam of light from a lamp. Immediately in front of the pendulum is a screen with a narrow vertical slit cut into it. The bright point of light...

# ABSOLUTE PITCH.

The light reflected by the bead is seen intermittently, either by looking over the prong of the <term>interrupter</term> <note>a device used to break an electrical circuit or light path at regular intervals</note> or through a hole in the disc of the <term>phonic wheel</term> <note>an early synchronous motor that rotates at a speed governed by the frequency of an electrical signal</note>. In the first case, there are 32 views per second, but in the latter, this number is reduced by the intervention of the wheel. In the experiments referred to, the wheel was arranged so that one revolution corresponded to four complete vibrations of the interrupter, and there were thus 8 views of the pendulum per second, instead of 32. Any deviation of the period of the pendulum from a precise multiple of the period of intermittence shows itself as a cycle of changes in the appearance of the flash of light; an observation of the duration of this cycle provides the data for a precise comparison of frequencies.

The calculation of the results is very simple. Assuming in the first instance that the clock is correct, let *a* be the number of cycles per second (perhaps $\frac{1}{40}$) between the wheel and the clock. Since the period of a cycle is the time required for the wheel to gain, or lose, one revolution compared to the clock, the frequency of revolution is $8 \pm a$. The frequency of the <term>auxiliary fork</term> <note>a secondary tuning fork used as a reference point in the measurement process</note> is precisely 16 times as great—that is, $128 \pm 16a$. If *b* is the number of <term>beats</term> <note>the interference pattern between two sounds of slightly different frequencies, perceived as a periodic variation in volume</note> per second between the auxiliary fork and the standard, the frequency of the latter is:

-> $128 \pm 16a \pm b$. <-

An error in the mean rate of the clock is readily allowed for; but care is required to ascertain that the actual rate at the time of observation does not differ appreciably from the mean rate. To be quite safe, it would be necessary to repeat the determinations at intervals over the whole time required to <term>rate the clock</term> <note>to determine the clock's accuracy by comparing it to an absolute standard, such as the movement of the stars</note> by observation of the stars. In this case, it would probably be convenient to attach a counting apparatus to the phonic wheel.

In the method of M'Leod and Clarke,¹ time (given by a clock) is recorded automatically upon the revolving drum of a <term>chronograph</term> <note>an instrument for recording time intervals with great accuracy</note>, which is maintained in uniform rotation by a suitable governor. The circumference of the drum is marked with a <term>grating</term> <note>a set of parallel, equally spaced lines</note> of equidistant lines parallel to the axis, and the comparison between the drum and the standard fork is effected by observation of the wavy pattern seen when the revolving grating is looked at past the edges of the vibrating prongs. These observers made a special investigation as to the effect of <term>bowing</term> <note>using a violin bow to set a tuning fork into vibration</note> a fork upon previously existing vibrations. Their conclusion is that, in the case of unloaded forks, no sensible change of <term>phase</term> <note>the specific point in the cycle of a periodic motion or wave</note> occurs.

In the chronographic method of Professor A. M. Mayer,¹ the <term>tuning fork</term> being investigated is fitted with a triangular fragment of thin sheet metal weighing only one milligram. This point actually traces its vibrations as a <term>sine wave</term> <note>original: curve of sines; a smooth, periodic mathematical curve representing a single frequency</note> upon paper coated with soot <note>original: smoked paper</note>. The time is recorded by small electric discharges from an induction device <note>original: induction apparatus</note>, controlled by a clock, which are delivered from the same *tracing point*. Although the disturbance caused by the tracing point appears to be very small, it is doubtful whether this method could compete in accuracy with those described previously, where the comparison with the standard is optical or acoustical. On the other hand, it has the advantage of not requiring the drum to rotate at a perfectly uniform speed, and the equipment is easily adapted to determine small intervals of time in the manner originally proposed by Thomas Young.²

**68d.** The methods described so far for determining absolute pitch (with the exception of Scheibler’s) may be considered somewhat mechanical in nature, and they mostly depend on specialized equipment. It is possible, however, to determine pitch with fair accuracy using no other appliances than a common <term>harmonium</term> <note>a keyboard instrument that produces sound by blowing air through thin metal strips called reeds</note> and a watch. As this process is instructive regarding the theory of overtones, I will give a short account of it here.³

The fundamental principle is that the absolute frequencies of two musical notes can be deduced from the *interval* between them—that is, the ratio of their frequencies—and the number of <term>beats</term> <note>the pulse-like "throbbing" heard when two notes of slightly different pitches are played together</note> they produce in a given time when sounded together. For example, if $x$ and $y$ denote the frequencies of two notes whose interval is an <term>equal temperament</term> <note>a system of tuning where the octave is divided into twelve equal steps</note> major third, we know that $y = 1.25992x$. At the same time, the number of beats heard per second (depending on how much the third deviates from perfect <term>intonation</term> <note>original: true intonation; the mathematically "pure" pitch of an interval</note>) is $4y - 5x$. In the case of harmonium notes, which are rich in <term>overtones</term> <note>higher-frequency tones that ring out along with the main pitch, determining the instrument's sound quality</note>, these beats are easily counted. Thus, we obtain two equations from which the values of $x$ and $y$ are immediately found.

Of course, in practice, the accuracy of an equal temperament third could not be taken for granted. However, the difficulty arising from this would be easily overcome by including in the counting all three—
