# ABSOLUTE PITCH.

...major thirds which together make up an octave. Suppose, for example, that the frequencies of c, e, g#, and c' are respectively $x, y, z,$ and $2x$, and that the beats per second between $x$ and $y$ are $a$, between $y$ and $z$ are $b$, and between $z$ and $2x$ are $c$. Then:

-> $4y - 5x = a, \quad 4z - 5y = b, \quad 8x - 5z = c,$ <-

from which we can determine:

-> $x = \frac{1}{3} (25a + 20b + 16c),$ <-
-> $y = \frac{1}{3} (32a + 25b + 20c),$ <-
-> $z = \frac{1}{3} (40a + 32b + 25c).$ <-

In the above statements, the octave c—c' is assumed to be perfectly in tune for the sake of simplicity. The actual error could easily be accounted for if required; but in practice, it is not necessary to use the higher c' at all, since the third set of beats can be counted equally well between g# and the original c.

The main objection to the method in the form described above is that it assumes the notes remain absolutely constant—for example, that the frequency of $y$ remains the same whether it is being sounded alongside $x$ or alongside $z$. This condition is very poorly met by the notes of a <term>harmonium</term> <note>a keyboard instrument that produces sound by blowing air through thin metal strips called reeds</note>.

In order to apply the basic principle successfully, it is necessary to be able to check the accuracy of the interval that is supposed to be known at the same time that the beats are being counted. If the interval is a <term>major tone</term> <note>a specific musical interval defined by the frequency ratio of 9:8</note>, its accuracy is proven by the absence of beats between the ninth <term>component</term> <note>original: component; today typically called a harmonic or partial</note> of the lower note and the eighth of the higher note. Counting the beats between the tenth component of the lower and the ninth of the higher note provides the remaining data needed to determine the absolute pitch.

The <term>equal temperament</term> <note>the standard modern tuning system where an octave is divided into twelve equal steps</note> whole tone (1.12246) is between the <term>minor tone</term> (1.11111) and the <term>major tone</term> (1.12500), but it is much closer to the latter. Viewed as an imperfect major tone, it produces slow beats; viewed as an imperfect minor tone, it produces fast beats. Both sets of beats can be heard at the same time, and when counted (by two observers), they provide the means for calculating the absolute pitch of both notes. If $x$ and $y$ are the frequencies of the two notes, and $a$ and $b$ are the frequencies of the slow and fast beats respectively:

-> $9x - 8y = a, \quad 9y - 10x = b,$ <-

from which it follows that:

-> $x = 9a + 8b, \quad y = 10a + 9b.$ <-

# VIBRATING SYSTEMS IN GENERAL. [70.

...the static <note>original: "statical"</note> part of the subject. By the Principle of Virtual Work <note>original: "Virtual Velocities," a term used historically for what we now call the Principle of Virtual Work, which relates forces and displacements in a state of equilibrium.</note>, if we calculate the coordinates $\psi_1$, $\psi_2$, etc., from the state of equilibrium, the potential energy of any other arrangement will be a homogeneous quadratic function of the coordinates, provided that the displacement is sufficiently small. This quantity is called $V$, and it represents the work that may be gained in passing from the actual state to the equilibrium state. We may write:

-> $V = \frac{1}{2}c_{11}\psi_1^2 + \frac{1}{2}c_{22}\psi_2^2 + \dots + c_{12}\psi_1\psi_2 + c_{23}\psi_2\psi_3 + \dots \dots (1).$ <-

Since we assume that the equilibrium is completely stable, the quantities $c_{11}$, $c_{22}$, $c_{12}$, etc., must be such that $V$ is positive for all real values of the coordinates.

**71.** If the system is moved from its initial equilibrium state by the action of applied forces, the new arrangement may be found from the Principle of Virtual Work. If the work done by the applied forces during a hypothetical <note>original: "hypothetical," often referred to as a "virtual" displacement in modern physics.</note> displacement $\delta\psi_1$, $\delta\psi_2$, etc., is:

-> $\Psi_1\delta\psi_1 + \Psi_2\delta\psi_2 + \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (1),$ <-

this expression must be equivalent to $\delta V$ (the change in potential energy). Since the coordinate variations $\delta\psi_1$, $\delta\psi_2$, etc., are independent, the new position of equilibrium is determined by:

-> $\frac{dV}{d\psi_1} = \Psi_1, \quad \frac{dV}{d\psi_2} = \Psi_2, \text{ etc.} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (2),$ <-

or, using equation (1) from section 70:

-> $\left. \begin{aligned} c_{11}\psi_1 + c_{12}\psi_2 + c_{13}\psi_3 + \dots \dots = \Psi_1 \\ c_{21}\psi_1 + c_{22}\psi_2 + c_{23}\psi_3 + \dots \dots = \Psi_2 \\ \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \end{aligned} \right\} \dots \dots \dots \dots (3),$ <-

where there is no difference in value between $c_{rs}$ and $c_{sr}$ <note>This indicates the coefficients are symmetric, a standard property in these types of physical systems.</note>.

From these equations, the coordinates may be determined in terms of the forces. If $\nabla$ is the determinant:

-> $\nabla = \begin{vmatrix} c_{11}, & c_{12}, & c_{13}, & \dots \\ c_{21}, & c_{22}, & c_{23}, & \dots \\ c_{31}, & c_{32}, & c_{33}, & \dots \\ \dots & \dots & \dots & \dots \end{vmatrix} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (4),$ <-

the solution of equation (3) may be written as:

-> $\left. \begin{aligned} \nabla \cdot \psi_1 = \frac{d\nabla}{dc_{11}} \Psi_1 + \frac{d\nabla}{dc_{12}} \Psi_2 + \dots \dots \\ \nabla \cdot \psi_2 = \frac{d\nabla}{dc_{21}} \Psi_1 + \frac{d\nabla}{dc_{22}} \Psi_2 + \dots \dots \\ \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \end{aligned} \right\} \dots \dots \dots \dots (5).$ <-

# RECIPROCAL RELATION.

These equations determine $\psi_1$, $\psi_2$, etc. <note>original: "&c."</note> uniquely, since $\nabla$ <note>original: "$\nabla$" refers to the determinant of the coefficients of the potential energy function. **72.** If $\psi_1, \dots \Psi_1, \dots$ and $\psi_1', \dots \Psi_1', \dots$ are two sets of displacements and their corresponding forces, we have the following reciprocal relation:

->$\Psi_1\psi_1' + \Psi_2\psi_2' + \dots = \Psi_1'\psi_1 + \Psi_2'\psi_2 + \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (1),$<-

This can be seen by substituting the values of the forces, where each side of equation (1) takes the form:

->$c_{11}\psi_1\psi_1' + c_{22}\psi_2\psi_2' + \dots \dots$<-
->$\dots + c_{12} (\psi_2\psi_1' + \psi_2'\psi_1) + c_{23} (\psi_3\psi_2' + \psi_3'\psi_2) + \dots \dots$<-

Suppose in equation (1) that all the forces vanish except for $\Psi_2$ and $\Psi_1'$; then:

->$\Psi_2\psi_2' = \Psi_1'\psi_1 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (2).$<-

If the forces $\Psi_2$ and $\Psi_1'$ are of the same kind, we may suppose them to be equal. We then recognize that a force of any type acting alone produces a displacement of a second type equal to the displacement of the first type caused by an equal force of the second type. For example, if $A$ and $B$ are two points on a rod supported horizontally in any manner, the vertical deflection at $A$ when a weight $W$ is attached at $B$ is the same as the deflection at $B$ when $W$ is applied at $A^1$.

->$2V = \Psi_1\psi_1 + \Psi_2\psi_2 + \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (2).$<-

From equations (3) and (4), we may derive two important theorems relating to the value of $V$ (potential energy) for a system subjected to specific displacements and to specific forces, respectively.

**74.** The first theorem states that if specific displacements (which are not enough on their own to determine the entire configuration <note>original: "configuration" — the specific shape or position of all parts of a system</note>) are produced in a system by forces of corresponding types, the resulting value of $V$ for the system in equilibrium is as small as it can possibly be under those given displacement conditions. Furthermore, the value of $V$ for any other configuration exceeds this minimum by the potential energy of the configuration that represents the difference between the two. 

The only difficulty in the above statement consists in understanding what is meant by "forces of corresponding types." Suppose, for example, that the system is a stretched string and a specific point $P$ must be subjected to a required displacement. The "force of corresponding type" in this case is a force applied at point $P$ itself. Generally, the forces used to create the proposed displacement must be those that would perform no work on the system if that specific displacement were *not* made.

By a suitable choice of coordinates, the given displacement conditions may be expressed by assigning specific values to the first $r$ coordinates $\psi_1, \psi_2, ... \psi_r$. The conditions regarding the forces will then be represented by making the forces of the remaining types $\Psi_{r+1}, \Psi_{r+2}$, etc. <note>original: "&c."</note> equal zero. If $\psi + \Delta \psi$ refers to any other configuration of the system, and $\Psi + \Delta \Psi$ are the corresponding forces, we assume that $\Delta \psi_1, \Delta \psi_2$, etc., as far as $\Delta \psi_r$, all equal zero. Thus, for the first $r$ subscripts <note>original: "suffixes"</note>, $\Delta \psi$ vanishes, and for the remaining

# STATICAL THEOREMS.

<meta>catchword 74.] at top left</meta>

For the components of the forces where the displacements are not specified <note>original: "suffixes Ψ vanishes"</note>, the values are zero. Accordingly, the sum of the forces multiplied by the change in displacements ($\Sigma \Psi \cdot \Delta \psi$) is zero, and therefore the sum of the change in forces multiplied by the displacements ($\Sigma \Delta \Psi \cdot \psi$) is also zero. From this, we find:

-> $2 \Delta V = \Sigma \Delta \Psi \cdot \Delta \psi$................................(1), <-

This proves that if the specified displacements are made in any way other than the one naturally required for equilibrium, the potential energy is increased by the energy required for the difference between the two configurations.

By using this theorem, we can track the effect on potential energy ($V$) of any reduction in the stiffness of a system that is subject to specific displacement conditions. If we consider the original equilibrium configuration after the stiffness has been reduced, the value of $V$ for that configuration is, by definition, less than it was before. As we have just seen, there will be an even further decrease in the value of $V$ when the system reaches its new equilibrium under these altered conditions of reduced stiffness. Therefore, we conclude that a decrease in the potential energy function (as defined by the system's coordinates) also results in a decrease in the actual value of $V$ when a system is subjected to fixed displacements. It should be understood that in certain specific cases, this decrease might be zero $^1$.

For example, if a point $P$ on a bar clamped at both ends is moved sideways <note term="laterally">sideways or away from the center line</note> by a specific small amount by an applied force, the potential energy of that deformation will be reduced by any reduction in the stiffness of the bar, no matter how local that reduction may be.

**75.** The second theorem relates to a system displaced by *given forces*. It asserts that, in this case, the value of $V$ at equilibrium is greater than it would be in any other configuration where the system could be held at rest under those same forces by the use of simple constraints <note term="constraints">physical restrictions or supports that limit the movement of a system</note>. We will show <note>original: "shew"</note> that the removal of constraints increases the value of $V$.

The coordinates of the system may be chosen so that the conditions of the constraints are expressed as:

-> $\psi_1 = 0, \quad \psi_2 = 0, \dots \dots \psi_r = 0$....................(1). <-

We must then prove that when the forces $\Psi_{r+1}, \Psi_{r+2},$ and so on are fixed, the value of $V$ is at its minimum when these conditions (1) are met. If we represent the second configuration as we did before (using $\psi_1 + \Delta \psi_1$, etc.), we see that for the parts of the system up to $r$, the displacement ($\psi$) is zero, and for the parts higher than $r$, the change in force ($\Delta \Psi$) is zero. Therefore:

-> $\Sigma \psi \cdot \Delta \Psi = \Sigma \Delta \psi \cdot \Psi = 0,$ <-

**76.** We now pass to the investigation of the initial motion of a system which starts from rest under the operation of given impulses <note term="impulses">In mechanics, an impulse is a large force acting over an infinitesimally short period of time, such as a sudden blow or impact.</note>. The motion acquired in this way is independent of any potential energy which the system may possess when actually displaced, since, by the nature of impulses, we are concerned only with the initial configuration itself. The initial motion is also independent of any forces of a finite kind <note term="finite forces">Continuous forces like gravity or spring tension, as opposed to instantaneous impulses.</note>, whether they are impressed on the system from the outside or are caused by viscosity <note term="viscosity">Internal friction or resistance within the system.</note>.

If $P, Q, R$ are the component impulses, parallel to the axes, acting on a particle $m$ whose rectangular coordinates <note>original: "co-ordinates"</note> are $x, y, z$, we have by D'Alembert's Principle <note term="D'Alembert's Principle">A fundamental law of mechanics that allows the treatment of a dynamic system as a static system in equilibrium by considering the "inertial forces" alongside the applied forces.</note>:
-> $\Sigma m (\dot{x} \delta x + \dot{y} \delta y + \dot{z} \delta z) = \Sigma (P \delta x + Q \delta y + R \delta z)$......(1), <-
where $\dot{x}, \dot{y}, \dot{z}$ denote the velocities acquired by the particle because of the impulses, and $\delta x, \delta y, \delta z$ correspond to any arbitrary displacement of the system that does not violate the connection of its parts. It is required to transform equation (1) into an equation expressed by independent generalized coordinates.

For the first side of the equation:
$\Sigma m (\dot{x} \delta x + \dot{y} \delta y + \dot{z} \delta z) = \delta \psi_1 \Sigma m \left( \dot{x} \frac{dx}{d\psi_1} + \dot{y} \frac{dy}{d\psi_1} + \dot{z} \frac{dz}{d\psi_1} \right)$
->$ + \delta \psi_2 \Sigma m \left( \dot{x} \frac{dx}{d\psi_2} + \dot{y} \frac{dy}{d\psi_2} + \dot{z} \frac{dz}{d\psi_2} \right) + \text{etc.} $<-
->$ = \delta \psi_1 \Sigma m \left( \dot{x} \frac{d\dot{x}}{d\dot{\psi}_1} + \dot{y} \frac{d\dot{y}}{d\dot{\psi}_1} + \dot{z} \frac{d\dot{z}}{d\dot{\psi}_1} \right) + \text{etc.} $<-
->$ = \delta \psi_1 \cdot \frac{1}{2} \Sigma m \frac{d}{d\dot{\psi}_1} (\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2 + \dot{z}^2) + \text{etc.} $<-
->$ = \delta \psi_1 \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}_1} + \delta \psi_2 \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}_2} + ....................................(2), $<-
where $T$, the kinetic energy of the system, is supposed to be expressed as a function of $\dot{\psi}_1, \dot{\psi}_2, \text{etc.}$

On the other side of the equation,

$\Sigma (P\delta x + Q\delta y + R\delta z) = \delta\psi_1 \Sigma m \left( P \frac{dx}{d\psi_1} + Q \frac{dy}{d\psi_1} + R \frac{dz}{d\psi_1} \right) + \dots\dots$
$= \xi_1 \delta\psi_1 + \xi_2 \delta\psi_2 + \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (3),$

if we let $\Sigma m \left( P \frac{dx}{d\psi_1} + Q \frac{dy}{d\psi_1} + R \frac{dz}{d\psi_1} \right) = \xi_1$, and so on.

The transformed equation is therefore:

$\left( \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}_1} - \xi_1 \right) \delta\psi_1 + \left( \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}_2} - \xi_2 \right) \delta\psi_2 + \dots = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (4),$

where $\delta\psi_1, \delta\psi_2$, etc., are now completely independent. Hence, to determine the motion, we have:

$\frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}_1} = \xi_1, \quad \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}_2} = \xi_2, \text{ etc.} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (5),$

where $\xi_1, \xi_2$, etc., may be considered as the generalized components of impulse <note term="generalized components of impulse">These represent the effect of external sudden forces (impulses) expressed in terms of the system's coordinates rather than simple spatial directions.</note>.

**77.** Since $T$ <note>$T$ represents Kinetic Energy.</note> is a homogeneous quadratic function <note term="homogeneous quadratic function">A mathematical expression where every term is of the second degree (e.g., involves the square of a velocity or the product of two different velocities).</note> of the generalized coordinates <note>original: "co-ordinates"</note>, we may take:

$T = \frac{1}{2}a_{11}\dot{\psi}_1^2 + \frac{1}{2}a_{22}\dot{\psi}_2^2 + \dots\dots + a_{12}\dot{\psi}_1\dot{\psi}_2 + a_{23}\dot{\psi}_2\dot{\psi}_3 + \dots\dots (1),$

from which:

$\left. \begin{aligned} \xi_1 = \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}_1} = a_{11}\dot{\psi}_1 + a_{12}\dot{\psi}_2 + a_{13}\dot{\psi}_3 + \dots\dots \\ \xi_2 = \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}_2} = a_{21}\dot{\psi}_1 + a_{22}\dot{\psi}_2 + a_{23}\dot{\psi}_3 + \dots\dots \\ \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (2),$

where there is no difference in value between $a_{rs}$ and $a_{sr}$ <note>This indicates the coefficients are symmetric.</note>.
Again, by the nature of $T$:

$2T = \dot{\psi}_1 \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}_1} + \dot{\psi}_2 \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}_2} + \dots\dots = \xi_1\dot{\psi}_1 + \xi_2\dot{\psi}_2 + \dots\dots (3).$

The theory of initial motion is closely analogous to that of the displacement of a system from a state of stable equilibrium by steadily applied forces. In the present theory, the initial kinetic energy $T$ has the same relationship to the velocities and impulses as potential energy $V$ has to displacements and forces in the theory of equilibrium. In one respect, the theory of initial motions is the more complete, because $T$ is exactly a homogeneous quadratic function of the variables, while $V$ is generally only approximately so.

<page-num>98</page-num>
<header>VIBRATING SYSTEMS IN GENERAL. [77.</header>

If $\dot{\psi}_1, \dot{\psi}_2, \dots, \xi_1, \xi_2, \dots$ denote one set of velocities and impulses for a system started from rest, and $\dot{\psi}_1', \dot{\psi}_2', \dots, \xi_1', \xi_2', \dots$ denote a second set, we can prove the following reciprocal relation, as previously shown in section 72:
->$\xi_1' \dot{\psi}_1 + \xi_2' \dot{\psi}_2 + \dots = \xi_1 \dot{\psi}_1' + \xi_2 \dot{\psi}_2' + \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (4)^1.$<-

This theorem has an interesting application in fluid motion. It is established—and will be proven later in this work—that when a frictionless, incompressible liquid starts from rest, its motion is such that its component velocities at any point are the corresponding <term>derivatives</term> <note>original: "differential coefficients"</note> of a certain function called the <term>velocity-potential</term> <note term="velocity-potential">A mathematical function used in fluid dynamics where the velocity of the fluid at any point is determined by the rate of change (gradient) of the function at that point.</note>. Suppose the fluid is set in motion by a specific, arbitrary change in the shape of the surface $S$ of a closed space within it. The resulting motion is determined by the velocities perpendicular to the parts of $S$ (the normal velocities). Since these velocities are shared by the fluid in contact with the surface, they are denoted by $du/dn$, where $u$ represents the velocity-potential. Physically, this $u$ represents the <term>impulsive pressure</term> <note term="impulsive pressure">A sudden, very high pressure applied over a very short time, which causes an immediate change in the fluid's velocity.</note>. 

Therefore, according to the theorem, if $v$ is the velocity-potential of a second motion corresponding to another set of arbitrary surface velocities $dv/dn$, then:
->$\iint u \frac{dv}{dn} dS = \iint v \frac{du}{dn} dS \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (5),$<-
—an equation that follows directly from Green's theorem <note term="Green's theorem">A fundamental theorem in vector calculus that relates a line integral around a simple closed curve to a double integral over the plane region it surrounds; here it relates surface properties to the volume within.</note>, provided that any other objects in the fluid besides surface $S$ are fixed solids. This current method, however, allows us to apply the theorem much more broadly. For instance, the immersed solids do not have to be fixed; they could be free, either entirely or in part, to move in response to the fluid pressures.

**78.** One specific case of this general theorem deserves special attention. In the first motion, let:
->$\dot{\psi}_1 = A, \quad \dot{\psi}_2 = 0, \quad \xi_3 = \xi_4 = \xi_5 \dots \dots = 0;$<-
and in the second motion, let:
->$\dot{\psi}_1' = 0, \quad \dot{\psi}_2' = A, \quad \xi_3' = \xi_4' = \xi_5' \dots \dots = 0.$<-
Then:
->$\xi_1' = \xi_2 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (1).$<-

In plain language: if we apply a specific impulse to give a certain velocity to one coordinate <note>original: "co-ordinate"</note>, the impulse required at a second coordinate to keep it from changing is the same as the impulse that would be required for the first coordinate if that same velocity were applied to the second.

<meta>This page continues the mathematical analysis of reciprocal relations in dynamic systems, moving from theoretical fluid motion to practical examples in mechanics and electromagnetism, leading into Thomson's (Lord Kelvin's) theorem on minimum kinetic energy.</meta>

<page-num>99</page-num>
<header>KELVIN'S THEOREM.</header>
<sig>7—2</sig>

As a simple example, consider the case of two spheres, *A* and *B*, submerged in a liquid, with their centers free to move along certain lines. If *A* is set in motion with a specific velocity, *B* will naturally begin to move as well. The theorem asserts that the <term>impulse</term> <note term="impulse">The total force applied over a very short time that changes an object's momentum; in fluid dynamics, this often relates to the pressure required to initiate or stop motion.</note> required to prevent the motion of *B* is the same as if the roles of *A* and *B* were swapped. This holds true even if there are other rigid bodies, such as *C*, *D*, etc., in the fluid, whether they are fixed in place or free to move in any way.

The case of electric currents influencing each other through <term>induction</term> <note term="induction">The process where a changing magnetic field from one electrical circuit creates an electromotive force (voltage) in a nearby circuit.</note> is exactly similar. Suppose there are two circuits, *A* and *B*, in the neighborhood of which there may be any number of other wire circuits or solid conductors. If a unit of current is suddenly created in circuit *A*, the electromotive impulse induced in *B* is the same as the impulse that would have been induced in *A* if the current had been forcibly created in *B*.

**79.** The motion of a system in which specific arbitrary velocities are produced by the necessary impulses possesses a remarkable property discovered by <term>Thomson</term> <note>William Thomson (1824–1907), later known as Lord Kelvin, a Scottish-Irish physicist who formulated many of the foundational laws of thermodynamics and electromagnetism.</note>. The conditions are that the velocities $\dot{\psi}_1, \dot{\psi}_2, \dot{\psi}_3, \dots \dot{\psi}_r$ are given, while the impulses $\xi_{r+1}, \xi_{r+2}, \dots$ are zero. Let $\dot{\psi}_1, \dot{\psi}_2, \dots \xi_1, \xi_2, \text{etc.}$ correspond to the actual motion; and let

->$\dot{\psi}_1 + \Delta\dot{\psi}_1, \dot{\psi}_2 + \Delta\dot{\psi}_2, \dots \xi_1 + \Delta\xi_1, \xi_2 + \Delta\xi_2, \dots$<-

correspond to another possible motion that satisfies the same velocity conditions. For each variable, either the change in velocity ($\Delta\dot{\psi}$) or the impulse ($\xi$) is zero. Now, for the kinetic energy of this alternative motion:

->$2 (T + \Delta T) = (\xi_1 + \Delta\xi_1) (\dot{\psi}_1 + \Delta\dot{\psi}_1) + \dots$<-
->$= 2T + \xi_1 \Delta\dot{\psi}_1 + \xi_2 \Delta\dot{\psi}_2 + \dots$<-
->$+ \Delta\xi_1 \cdot \dot{\psi}_1 + \Delta\xi_2 \cdot \dot{\psi}_2 + \dots + \Delta\xi_1 \Delta\dot{\psi}_1 + \Delta\xi_2 \Delta\dot{\psi}_2 + \dots$<-

However, according to the reciprocal relation (equation 4) of section 77:

->$\xi_1 \Delta\dot{\psi}_1 + \dots = \Delta\xi_1 \cdot \dot{\psi}_1 + \dots,$<-

of which the first part is zero by our hypothesis; so that:

->$2\Delta T = \Delta\xi_1 \Delta\dot{\psi}_1 + \Delta\xi_2 \Delta\dot{\psi}_2 + \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (1),$<-

showing that the energy of the alternative motion exceeds that of the actual motion. Specifically, it exceeds it by the energy of the motion that would have to be combined with the actual motion to produce the alternative one. Thus, the motion actually induced in the system has less energy than any other motion satisfying the same velocity conditions. In a later chapter, we will use this property to find an upper limit to the energy of a system set in motion with prescribed velocities.

<summary>This page explains Kelvin's (Thomson's) theorem, demonstrating that the actual motion of a system under specific velocity constraints minimizes kinetic energy compared to other possible motions. It provides physical examples in fluid dynamics and electromagnetic induction to illustrate reciprocal relationships between impulses and velocities.</summary>
<keywords>Kelvin's Theorem, William Thomson, kinetic energy, electromagnetic induction, fluid dynamics, impulses, reciprocal relation, minimum energy principle</keywords>

<page-num>100</page-num>
<header>VIBRATING SYSTEMS IN GENERAL. [79.</header>

If any reduction is made in the <term>inertia</term> <note term="inertia">The resistance of any physical object to any change in its velocity.</note> of any part of a system, the motion that occurs under specific velocity conditions will generally change. The value of $T$ (kinetic energy) will necessarily be less than it was before; for there would be a decrease even if the motion remained unchanged, and therefore even more so <note>original: "a fortiori"</note> when the motion is such that it makes $T$ an absolute minimum. Conversely, any increase in the inertia increases the initial value of $T$.

This theorem is similar to the one in § 74. The equivalent for initial motions of the theorem in § 75—which relates to the potential energy of a system moved by specific forces—is known as **Bertrand’s theorem**. It may be stated as follows: If a system starts from rest under the influence of given impulses, the kinetic energy of the actual motion is greater than the kinetic energy of any other motion the system might have been forced to take using simple constraints. The difference is equal to the kinetic energy of the difference between those two motions¹.

[The theorems of **Kelvin** and **Bertrand** represent different sides of the same truth. Let us suppose that the prescribed impulse is entirely of the first type $\xi_1$. Then $T = \frac{1}{2} \xi_1 \dot{\psi}_1$, whether the motion is free or subjected to any constraint. Furthermore, under any given set of constraints, $\dot{\psi}_1$ is proportional to $\xi_1$, and the ratio $\xi_1 : \dot{\psi}_1$ may be viewed as the <term>moment of inertia</term> <note term="moment of inertia">In this context, it refers to the "effective mass" or resistance to acceleration in a specific direction or coordinate.</note>; so that:
-> $T = \frac{1}{2} \xi_1 \dot{\psi}_1 = \frac{1}{2} m \dot{\psi}_1^2 = \frac{1}{2} \xi_1^2 / m$. <-

Kelvin's theorem asserts that introducing a constraint can only increase the value of $T$ when the velocity $\dot{\psi}_1$ is fixed. Therefore, whether $\dot{\psi}_1$ is fixed or not, the constraint can only increase the ratio of $2T$ to $\dot{\psi}_1^2$ or of the impulse $\xi_1$ to the velocity $\dot{\psi}_1$. Both theorems are included in the statement that the moment of inertia is increased by the introduction of a constraint.]

### 80. We will not spend any more time on the mechanics of a system subject to impulses. Instead, we will move on to investigate **Lagrange's equations** for continuous motion. We shall assume that the connections binding the parts of the system together do not change over time; any cases of "forced motion" we consider will be shown <note>original: "shewn"</note> specifically to be within the scope of this investigation.

By **D'Alembert's Principle** <note term="D'Alembert's Principle">A principle that allows the laws of static equilibrium to be applied to a moving system by including "inertial forces."</note> in combination with that of **Virtual Velocities** <note term="Virtual Velocities">Also known as the principle of virtual work; it analyzes the equilibrium of a system by imagining tiny, hypothetical displacements.</note>,
-> $\Sigma m (\ddot{x} \delta x + \ddot{y} \delta y + \ddot{z} \delta z) = \Sigma (X \delta x + Y \delta y + Z \delta z) \dots \dots (1)$, <-

# LAGRANGE'S EQUATIONS.

In this context, $\delta x$, $\delta y$, and $\delta z$ denote a displacement of the system of the most general kind possible without violating the constraints <note>original: "connections of its parts"</note> of its parts. Since the displacements of the individual particles of the system are mutually related, $\delta x, \dots$ are not independent. The goal now is to transform these into other variables, $\psi_1, \psi_2, \dots$, which shall be independent. We have

->$\ddot{x} \delta x = \frac{d}{dt} (\dot{x} \delta x) - \frac{1}{2} \delta \dot{x}^2,$<-

so that

->$\Sigma m (\ddot{x} \delta x + \ddot{y} \delta y + \ddot{z} \delta z) = \frac{d}{dt} . \Sigma m (\dot{x} \delta x + \dot{y} \delta y + \dot{z} \delta z) - \delta T.$<-

But (referring back to § 76) we have already found that

->$\Sigma m (\dot{x} \delta x + \dot{y} \delta y + \dot{z} \delta z) = \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}_1} \delta \psi_1 + \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}_2} \delta \psi_2 + \dots,$<-

while

->$\delta T = \frac{dT}{d\psi_1} \delta \psi_1 + \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}_1} \delta \dot{\psi}_1 + \dots,$<-

if $T$ (kinetic energy) is expressed as a quadratic function of $\dot{\psi}_1, \dot{\psi}_2, \dots$, whose coefficients are generally functions of $\psi_1, \psi_2, \dots$. Also

->$\frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}_1} \delta \psi_1 \right) = \frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}_1} \right) . \delta \psi_1 + \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}_1} \delta \dot{\psi}_1,$<-

because <note>original: "inasmuch as"</note>

->$\frac{d}{dt} \delta \psi_1 = \delta \frac{d}{dt} \psi_1.$<-

Accordingly,

$\Sigma m (\ddot{x} \delta x + \ddot{y} \delta y + \ddot{z} \delta z) = \left\{ \frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}_1} \right) - \frac{dT}{d\psi_1} \right\} \delta \psi_1$
->$+ \left\{ \frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}_2} \right) - \frac{dT}{d\psi_2} \right\} \delta \psi_2 + \dots \dots \dots (2).$<-

Thus, if the transformation of the right-hand side <note>original: "second side"</note> of equation (1) is

->$\Sigma (X \delta x + Y \delta y + Z \delta z) = \Psi_1 \delta \psi_1 + \Psi_2 \delta \psi_2 + \dots \dots \dots (3),$<-

we have **equations of motion** of the form

->$\frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}} \right) - \frac{dT}{d\psi} = \Psi \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (4).$<-

Since $\Psi \delta \psi$ denotes the work done on the system during a displacement $\delta \psi$, $\Psi$ may be regarded as the <term>generalized component of force</term> <note term="generalized component of force">The force corresponding to a specific generalized coordinate, such that the product of the force and the coordinate change equals work.</note>.

In the case of a <term>conservative system</term> <note term="conservative system">A system where the total mechanical energy is conserved, and forces can be derived from a potential energy function.</note>, it is convenient to separate from $\Psi$ those parts which depend only on the configuration—

configuration of the system. Thus, if $V$ denotes the potential energy, we may write:

->$\frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}} \right) - \frac{dT}{d\psi} + \frac{dV}{d\psi} = \Psi$........................ (5),<-

where $\Psi$ is now limited to the forces acting on the system which are not already accounted for in the term $dV/d\psi$.

**81.** There is also another group of forces that is often helpful to identify separately, namely those arising from friction or viscosity <note>internal friction within a fluid or solid</note>. If we suppose that each particle of the system is retarded by forces proportional to its component velocities, the effect will be shown in the fundamental equation (1) of § 80 by adding the following terms to the left-hand side:

->$\Sigma (\kappa_x \dot{x} \delta x + \kappa_y \dot{y} \delta y + \kappa_z \dot{z} \delta z)$,<-

where $\kappa_x$, $\kappa_y$, and $\kappa_z$ are coefficients independent of the velocities, but possibly dependent on the configuration <note>the physical arrangement or shape</note> of the system. The transformation to the independent coordinates $\psi_1, \psi_2$, etc., is carried out in a similar manner to that of

->$\Sigma m (\ddot{x} \delta x + \ddot{y} \delta y + \ddot{z} \delta z)$<-

considered above (§ 80), and gives:

->$\frac{dF}{d\dot{\psi}_1} \delta\psi_1 + \frac{dF}{d\dot{\psi}_2} \delta\psi_2 + \dots$ ........................ (1),<-

where

->$F = \frac{1}{2} \Sigma (\kappa_x \dot{x}^2 + \kappa_y \dot{y}^2 + \kappa_z \dot{z}^2)$<-
->$= \frac{1}{2} b_{11} \dot{\psi}_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} b_{22} \dot{\psi}_2^2 + \dots + b_{12} \dot{\psi}_1 \dot{\psi}_2 + b_{23} \dot{\psi}_2 \dot{\psi}_3 + \dots (2).$<-

One can see that $F$ is like $T$ (kinetic energy), a homogeneous quadratic function of the velocities, and is positive for all real values of the variables. It represents half the rate at which energy is dissipated <note>original: "dissipated"; energy lost from the system, usually as heat</note>.

The analysis above refers to retarding forces proportional to the absolute velocities; however, it is equally important to consider those that depend on the *relative* velocities of the parts of the system. Fortunately, this can be done without any added complexity. For example, if a force acts on the particle $x_1$ proportional to $(\dot{x}_1 - \dot{x}_2)$, there will be at the same moment an equal and opposite force acting on the particle $x_2$. The additional terms in the fundamental equation will take the form:

->$\kappa_x (\dot{x}_1 - \dot{x}_2) \delta x_1 + \kappa_x (\dot{x}_2 - \dot{x}_1) \delta x_2$,<-

which may be written:

->$\kappa_x (\dot{x}_1 - \dot{x}_2) \delta (x_1 - x_2) = \delta\psi_1 \frac{d}{d\dot{\psi}_1} \{ \frac{1}{2} \kappa_x (\dot{x}_1 - \dot{x}_2)^2 \} + \dots,$<-

# THE DISSIPATION FUNCTION.

...and so on for any number of pairs of particles that influence each other. The only effect is the addition of new terms to $F$, which still appears in the form shown in equation (2)¹. We shall see shortly that the existence of the function $F$, which may be called the **Dissipation Function**, implies certain relationships among the coefficients of the generalized equations of vibration; these relationships lead to important consequences².

The equations of motion may now be written in the form:

->$\frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}} \right) - \frac{dT}{d\psi} + \frac{dF}{d\dot{\psi}} + \frac{dV}{d\psi} = \Psi$ ................. (3).<-

**82.** We may now introduce the condition that the motion takes place very close to a state <note>original: "configuration"</note> of thoroughly stable equilibrium. In this case, $T$ <note>kinetic energy</note> and $F$ <note>the dissipation function</note> are homogeneous quadratic functions of the velocities, with coefficients that are to be treated as constants. $V$ <note>potential energy</note> is a similar function of the coordinates themselves, provided that (as we assume to be the case) the starting point <note>original: "origin"</note> of each coordinate is chosen to correspond with the state of equilibrium. Moreover, all three functions are essentially positive. Since terms in the form $dT/d\psi$ are of the second order of small quantities <note>meaning they are so small they can be ignored in these linear approximations</note>, the equations of motion become linear, taking the form:

->$\frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}} \right) + \frac{dF}{d\dot{\psi}} + \frac{dV}{d\psi} = \Psi$ ................. (1),<-

where $\Psi$ includes all forces acting on the system that are not already accounted for by the derivatives of $F$ and $V$.

The three quadratic functions will be expressed as follows:

->$\left. \begin{aligned} T &= \frac{1}{2} a_{11} \dot{\psi}_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} a_{22} \dot{\psi}_2^2 + \dots + a_{12} \dot{\psi}_1 \dot{\psi}_2 + \dots \\ F &= \frac{1}{2} b_{11} \dot{\psi}_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} b_{22} \dot{\psi}_2^2 + \dots + b_{12} \dot{\psi}_1 \dot{\psi}_2 + \dots \\ V &= \frac{1}{2} c_{11} \psi_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} c_{22} \psi_2^2 + \dots + c_{12} \psi_1 \psi_2 + \dots \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots (2),$<-

where the coefficients $a, b,$ and $c$ are constants.

From equation (1), we can, of course, return to previous results by assuming that either $F$ and $V$, or $F$ and $T$, disappear <note>original: "vanish"</note>.

# VIBRATING SYSTEMS IN GENERAL.

Equations for electricity <note>original: "tricity"; likely a transcription error for "electricity" in the OCR</note> may be obtained by omitting $T$ <note>kinetic energy or inductance</note> and $V$ <note>potential energy or capacitance</note> while retaining $F$ <note>the dissipation function or resistance</note>, but it is unnecessary to pursue that subject here.

If we substitute the values of $T$, $F$, and $V$, and write $D$ for the rate of change over time ($d/dt$), we obtain a system of equations which may be written in the following form:

->$\left. \begin{aligned} e_{11}\psi_1 + e_{12}\psi_2 + e_{13}\psi_3 + \dots &= \Psi_1 \\ e_{21}\psi_1 + e_{22}\psi_2 + e_{23}\psi_3 + \dots &= \Psi_2 \\ e_{31}\psi_1 + e_{32}\psi_2 + e_{33}\psi_3 + \dots &= \Psi_3 \\ \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(3).$<-

where $e_{rs}$ denotes the quadratic operator <term>a mathematical expression representing the combined effects of mass, friction, and stiffness</term>:

->$e_{rs} = a_{rs}D^2 + b_{rs}D + c_{rs} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(4).$<-

It must be particularly noted that since

->$a_{rs} = a_{sr}, \quad b_{rs} = b_{sr}, \quad c_{rs} = c_{sr},$<-

it follows that

->$e_{rs} = e_{sr} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(5).$<-

[The theory of *motional forces*—that is, forces proportional to the velocities—was further developed in the second edition of Thomson and Tait’s *Natural Philosophy* (1879) <note>a foundational physics textbook by William Thomson (Lord Kelvin) and Peter Guthrie Tait</note>. In the most general case, the equations may be written:

->$\left. \begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}_1} \right) + \frac{dV}{d\psi_1} + b_{11}\dot{\psi}_1 + (b_{12} + \beta_{12}) \dot{\psi}_2 + (b_{13} + \beta_{13}) \dot{\psi}_3 + \dots &= \Psi_1 \\ \frac{d}{dt} \left( \frac{dT}{d\dot{\psi}_2} \right) + \frac{dV}{d\psi_2} + (b_{21} - \beta_{21}) \dot{\psi}_1 + b_{22}\dot{\psi}_2 + (b_{23} - \beta_{23}) \dot{\psi}_3 + \dots &= \Psi_2 \end{aligned} \right\} (6),$<-

where

->$b_{rs} = b_{sr}, \quad \beta_{rs} = \beta_{sr} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(7).$<-

Among these, the terms with the $b$ coefficients can be derived from the dissipation function:

->$F = \frac{1}{2}b_{11}\dot{\psi}_1^2 + \frac{1}{2}b_{22}\dot{\psi}_2^2 + \dots + b_{12}\dot{\psi}_1\dot{\psi}_2 + \dots$<-

The terms in $\beta$, on the other hand, do not represent dissipation; these are called the gyrostatic terms <term>forces that depend on velocity but do not drain energy from the system, common in rotating bodies</term>.

If we multiply the first of equations (6) by $\dot{\psi}_1$, the second by $\dot{\psi}_2$, and so on, and then add them together, we obtain:

->$\frac{d(T + V)}{dt} + 2F = \Psi_1\dot{\psi}_1 + \Psi_2\dot{\psi}_2 + \dots \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(8).$<-

In this equation, the first term represents the rate at which energy is being stored in the system; $2F$ is the rate of dissipation; and the two together account for the work done on the system by the external forces.]

# COEXISTENCE OF SMALL MOTIONS.

**83.** Before proceeding further, we may draw an important inference from the linear nature <note>original: "linearity"</note> of our equations. If two different motions, denoted by $\psi_1, \psi_2, \dots$ and $\psi'_1, \psi'_2, \dots$, are possible when they correspond respectively to two sets of forces ($\Psi_1, \Psi_2, \dots$ and $\Psi'_1, \Psi'_2, \dots$), then the combined motion ($\psi_1 + \psi'_1, \psi_2 + \psi'_2, \dots$) must also be possible in conjunction with the combined forces ($\Psi_1 + \Psi'_1, \Psi_2 + \Psi'_2, \dots$). As a specific case, when there are no external <term>impressed</term> forces, the superposition of any two natural vibrations also constitutes a natural vibration. This is the celebrated principle of the **Coexistence of Small Motions**, first clearly stated by Daniel Bernoulli <note>Daniel Bernoulli (1700–1782) was a Swiss mathematician and physicist who founded the field of hydrodynamics and pioneered the study of vibrating strings.</note>. It should be understood that the truth of this principle generally depends on the validity of the assumption that the motion is so small that its square may be neglected.

[Furthermore, if a system is under the influence of constant forces ($\Psi_1$, etc.) which shift it into a new position of equilibrium <term>a state of rest or balance</term>, the vibrations that may occur around the new position are the same as those which might have previously occurred around the original position.]

**84.** To investigate "free vibrations" <note>vibrations that occur naturally without an ongoing external force</note>, we must set $\Psi_1, \Psi_2, \dots$ equal to zero. We will begin with a system where no frictional forces act; for such a system, the coefficients $e_{rs}$, etc., are *even* functions of the symbol $D$ <note>meaning the equations remain the same whether time moves forward or backward, as there is no energy loss to friction</note>. We have:

->$\left. \begin{aligned} e_{11}\psi_1 + e_{12}\psi_2 + \dots = 0 \\ e_{21}\psi_1 + e_{22}\psi_2 + \dots = 0 \\ \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(1).$<-

From these equations—of which there are as many ($m$) as the system has degrees of freedom <term>the number of independent ways the system can move</term>—let all but one of the variables be eliminated. The result, which takes the same form regardless of which coordinate is kept, may be written as:

->$\nabla \psi = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(2),$<-

where $\nabla$ denotes the determinant <term>a mathematical value calculated from a square matrix of numbers</term>:

->$\begin{vmatrix} e_{11}, & e_{12}, & e_{13}, \dots \\ e_{21}, & e_{22}, & e_{23}, \dots \\ e_{31}, & e_{32}, & e_{33}, \dots \\ \dots & \dots & \dots \end{vmatrix} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(3),$<-

In a system without friction, this is an even function of $D$ of the degree $2m$. Let $\pm \lambda_1, \pm \lambda_2, \dots, \pm \lambda_m$ be the roots <term>the values that solve the equation</term> of $\nabla = 0$ when considered as an equation in $D$. Then, according to the theory of differential equations, the most general value of $\psi$ is:

->$\psi = A e^{\lambda_1 t} + A' e^{-\lambda_1 t} + B e^{\lambda_2 t} + B' e^{-\lambda_2 t} + \dots\dots\dots(4).$<-

# VIBRATING SYSTEMS IN GENERAL.

where the $2m$ quantities $A, A', B, B'$, and so on, are arbitrary constants. This form applies to each of the coordinates, but the constants in the various expressions are not independent of one another. In fact, if a specific <term>particular</term> solution is
->$\psi_1 = A_1 \epsilon^{\lambda_1 t}, \psi_2 = A_2 \epsilon^{\lambda_1 t}, \text{etc.},$<-
the ratios $A_1 : A_2 : A_3 \dots$ are completely determined by the following equations:
->$\left. \begin{aligned} e_{11} A_1 + e_{12} A_2 + e_{13} A_3 + \dots \dots = 0 \\ e_{21} A_1 + e_{22} A_2 + e_{23} A_3 + \dots \dots = 0 \\ \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \end{aligned} \right\} \dots \dots \dots (5),$<-
where, in each of the coefficients (such as $e_{rs}$), $\lambda_1$ is substituted for $D$. Equations (5) are necessarily consistent <note>original: "compatible"</note>, because $\lambda_1$ is a root of the determinant <note>The symbol $\nabla$ here refers to the characteristic determinant of the system's equations.</note> $\nabla = 0$. The ratios $A'_1 : A'_2 : A'_3 \dots$ corresponding to the root $-\lambda_1$ are identical to the ratios $A_1 : A_2 : A_3 \dots$. However, for the other pairs of roots such as $\lambda_2, -\lambda_2$, and so on, there are different sets of ratios.

### 85.
The nature of the system with which we are dealing imposes an important restriction on the possible values of $\lambda$. If $\lambda_1$ were a real number, then either $\lambda_1$ or $-\lambda_1$ would be positive. This would lead to a specific solution where the coordinates—and consequently the kinetic energy represented by
->$\lambda_1^2 \{ \frac{1}{2} a_{11} A_1^2 + \dots a_{12} A_1 A_2 + \dots \} \epsilon^{\pm 2 \lambda_1 t},$<-
would increase infinitely <note>original: "without limit"</note>. Such a motion is clearly impossible for a **conservative system**, where the total energy must always equal the sum of the potential and kinetic energies it possessed <note>original: "was animated with"</note> at the start. We cannot avoid this conclusion by choosing a negative $\lambda_1$, because we are just as free to trace the motion backward in time as forward. It is as certain that the motion never *was* infinite, as that it never *will be*. This same argument also rules out the possibility of $\lambda$ having a complex value.

We can conclude that all the values of $\lambda$ are purely **imaginary** <note>In mathematics, an imaginary number is one that, when squared, gives a negative result. In physics, this indicates a stable, repeating vibration rather than a growth or decay.</note>, which corresponds to real, negative values for $\lambda^2$. Mathematically <note>original: "Analytically"</note>, the fact that the roots of $\nabla = 0$ (viewed as an equation for $D^2$) are all real and negative must result from the relationships between the coefficients $a_{11}, a_{12}, \dots, c_{11}, c_{12}, \dots$. This is because, for all real values of the variables, the kinetic energy ($T$) and potential energy ($V$) are always positive. The case of a system with two **degrees of freedom** <note>original: "degrees of liberty"</note> will be explored in detail later.

# NORMAL COORDINATES

**86.** The form of the solution can now be effectively changed by substituting $in_1$ for $\lambda_1$, and so on (where $i = \sqrt{-1}$ <note>The imaginary unit, used here to convert exponential growth or decay into oscillating wave motion.</note>), and adopting new arbitrary constants. Thus:

$\left. \begin{aligned} \psi_1 = A_1 \cos (n_1 t - \alpha) + B_1 \cos (n_2 t - \beta) + C_1 \cos (n_3 t - \gamma) + \dots \\ \psi_2 = A_2 \cos (n_1 t - \alpha) + B_2 \cos (n_2 t - \beta) + C_2 \cos (n_3 t - \gamma) + \dots \\ \psi_3 = A_3 \cos (n_1 t - \alpha) + B_3 \cos (n_2 t - \beta) + C_3 \cos (n_3 t - \gamma) + \dots \end{aligned} \right\} \dots (1),$
..................................................................................................................

In this expression, $n_1^2, n_2^2$, and so on, are the $m$ roots of the equation of the $m^{th}$ degree in $n^2$, which is found by substituting $-n^2$ for $D^2$ in the determinant equation $\nabla = 0$. For every value of $n$, the ratios $A_1 : A_2 : A_3 \dots$ are fixed <note>original: "determinate"</note> and real.

This provides the complete solution for the problem of the free vibrations of a <term>conservative system</term> <note>A system where the total mechanical energy is conserved and no energy is lost to friction or heat.</note>. We can see that the total motion can be broken down into $m$ <term>normal harmonic vibrations</term>, which generally have different periods, each acting completely independently of the others. If the motion resulting from the initial disturbance is such that it simplifies into just one of these modes (for example, $n_1$), we have:

->$\psi_1 = A_1 \cos (n_1 t - \alpha), \quad \psi_2 = A_2 \cos (n_1 t - \alpha), \text{ etc. } \dots \dots (2),$<-

where the ratios $A_1 : A_2 : A_3 \dots$ depend on the physical makeup of the system, and only the overall <term>amplitude</term> <note>The maximum extent of a vibration or oscillation, measured from the position of equilibrium.</note> and <term>phase</term> <note>The specific point in the cycle of a periodic motion.</note> are arbitrary. The various coordinates are always in similar (or opposite) phases of vibration, and the entire system reaches its configuration of equilibrium at the same moment.

Here we see the mechanical reason why <term>harmonic vibrations</term> are so prominent. If the motion is small enough, the differential equations become linear with constant coefficients. Circular functions (such as sine and cosine) and exponential functions are the only types that maintain their form <note>original: "retain their type"</note> when differentiated.

**87.** The $m$ periods of vibration, determined by the equation $\nabla = 0$, are inherent properties <note>original: "quantities intrinsic"</note> of the system. They must result in the same values regardless of which coordinates are chosen to define the configuration. However, there is one coordinate system that is especially useful: the one where each normal mode of vibration is defined by all coordinates except one becoming zero.

In the first type of vibration, the original coordinates $\psi_1, \psi_2$, and so on, have fixed ratios. Let the variable that determines the absolute values be $\phi_1$, so that in this mode, every coordinate is a known multiple of $\phi_1$. Similarly, in the second mode, every coordinate can be seen as a known multiple of a second variable $\phi_2$, and so forth. By a suitable determination...

# VIBRATING SYSTEMS IN GENERAL.

...determination of the *m* quantities $\phi_1$, $\phi_2$, etc., any configuration of the system may be represented as a combination of the *m* configurations of these types. Thus, the quantities $\phi$ themselves may be viewed as coordinates defining the configuration of the system. They are called the *normal coordinates*$^1$.

When expressed in terms of these normal coordinates, the <term>kinetic energy</term> <note>Represented by the symbol *T*.</note> and <term>potential energy</term> <note>Represented by the symbol *V*.</note> are reduced to sums of squares. It is easy to see that if cross-product terms were also present, the resulting equations of vibration would not be satisfied by setting any $m - 1$ coordinates to zero while leaving the remaining one as a finite value.

We could have started with this transformation by assuming from algebra that any two <term>homogeneous quadratic functions</term> <note>Mathematical expressions where every term is of the second degree, like $x^2$ or $xy$.</note> can be reduced to sums of squares through linear transformations. Thus:

$$\left. \begin{aligned} T &= \frac{1}{2}a_1\dot{\phi}_1^2 + \frac{1}{2}a_2\dot{\phi}_2^2 + ... \\ V &= \frac{1}{2}c_1\phi_1^2 + \frac{1}{2}c_2\phi_2^2 + ... \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(1),$$

where the coefficients (where double <term>suffixes</term> <note>original: "suffixes"; modern: "subscripts"</note> are no longer required) are necessarily positive.

Lagrange’s equations now become:

$$a_1\ddot{\phi}_1 + c_1\phi_1 = 0, \quad a_2\ddot{\phi}_2 + c_2\phi_2 = 0, \text{ etc.} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(2),$$

the solution of which is:

$$\phi_1 = A \cos (n_1t - \alpha), \quad \phi_2 = B \cos (n_2t - \beta), \text{ etc.} \dots\dots(3),$$

where *A*, *B*..., $\alpha$, $\beta$... are arbitrary constants, and:

$$n_1^2 = c_1 \div a_1, \quad n_2^2 = c_2 \div a_2, \text{ etc.} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(4).$$

[The vibrations expressed by the various normal coordinates are completely independent of one another. The energy of the entire motion is simply the sum of the parts corresponding to the several normal vibrations taken separately. In fact, according to equation (1):

$$T + V = \frac{1}{2}c_1A_1^2 + \frac{1}{2}c_2A_2^2 + \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(5).$$

By the nature of the physical system, the coefficients *a* must be positive. However, if the <term>equilibrium</term> is unstable, some of the coefficients *c* may be negative. For any negative *c*, the frequency *n* becomes <term>imaginary</term> <note>In physics, an imaginary frequency indicates that instead of oscillating like a wave, the system's displacement will grow or decay exponentially.</note>, and the circular functions of time (sines and cosines) are replaced by exponential functions.

In any motion proportional to $e^{\lambda t}$, the disturbance is multiplied by the same factor over equal intervals of time. The degree of instability may be considered as being measured by $\lambda$. If there is more than one...

In an unstable mode, the relative importance of different terms is largely determined by their corresponding values of $\lambda$. Thus, if:
->$\psi = Ae^{\lambda_1 t} + Be^{\lambda_2 t}$,<-
where $\lambda_1 > \lambda_2$, then regardless of the initial ratio between $A$ and $B$, the first term eventually becomes dominant. This is because $Ae^{\lambda_1 t} : Be^{\lambda_2 t} = (A/B) e^{(\lambda_1 - \lambda_2) t}$.

In general, when an unstable equilibrium is disturbed by an <term>infinitesimal</term> <note>An infinitely small amount.</note> amount, the system will move away from equilibrium according to the mode that is *most* unstable—namely, the one where $\lambda$ is greatest. In a later chapter, we will see interesting applications of this principle.

Reducing the system to <term>normal coordinates</term> <note>A coordinate system where each coordinate corresponds to a single natural mode of vibration.</note> allows us to easily see what happens when two of the values for $n^2$ are equal. It is clear that the form of the equation does not change. The <term>spherical pendulum</term> <note>A pendulum free to swing in any direction around a fixed point, like a weight on a string.</note> serves as a simple example of these "equal roots." It is remarkable that both <term>Lagrange</term> <note>Joseph-Louis Lagrange (1736–1813), a mathematician who made major contributions to mechanics.</note> and <term>Laplace</term> <note>Pierre-Simon Laplace (1749–1827), known for his work on celestial mechanics.</note> mistakenly thought that having equal roots necessarily required terms that include $t$ as a factor <gloss>1</gloss>. The analytical theory for the general case, where the coordinates are not normal, has been discussed by Somoff <gloss>2</gloss> and by Routh <gloss>3</gloss>.

**88.** Interpreting the <term>equations of motion</term> <note>The mathematical formulas describing how a system changes over time.</note> leads to a very important theorem, which can be stated as follows <gloss>4</gloss>: **The period of a <term>conservative system</term> <note>A system where total energy is conserved, with no loss to friction or heat.</note> vibrating in a <term>constrained</term> <note>A system where certain movements are restricted.</note> type about a position of stable equilibrium is <term>stationary in value</term> <note>In this context, "stationary" means the period reaches a maximum or minimum, so small changes in the way the system vibrates do not significantly change the time it takes to complete a cycle.</note> when the vibration is in a normal mode.** We could prove this using the original vibration equations, but it is more convenient to use normal coordinates. The constraint, which we can assume restricts the system to only one <term>degree of freedom</term> <note>The number of independent ways a system can move.</note>, is represented by setting the quantities of $\phi$ in specific ratios.

->$\phi_1 = A_1 \theta, \enspace \phi_2 = A_2 \theta, \enspace \text{etc.} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(1)$,<-

The theorem now allows us to assert that the removal of a constraint, and the consequent change in the type of vibration, can only affect the period by a very small amount <note>original: "a quantity of the second order"; in mathematics, this indicates that the error is proportional to the square of a small change, making the difference negligible.</note>. Therefore, in the limit, the free period cannot be shorter than it was before the change. By mathematical integration, we can infer that a finite increase of mass must lengthen the period of every vibration that involves the motion of the part affected, and that in no case can the period be diminished. However, in order to see how the two sets of periods correspond, it may be necessary to imagine the alterations being made in small steps. Conversely, the effect of removing part of the mass of a vibrating system must be to shorten the periods of all the free vibrations.

In like manner, we may prove that if the system undergoes a change where the potential energy of a given configuration is diminished while the kinetic energy of a given motion remains unaltered, the periods of the free vibrations are all increased, and vice versa. This proposition may sometimes be used for tracing the effects of a constraint; for if we suppose that the potential energy of any configuration violating the condition of constraint gradually increases, we shall approach a state of things in which the condition is observed with any desired degree of completeness. During each step of this process, every free vibration becomes (in general) more rapid, and a number of the free periods (equal to the degrees of freedom <note>original: "degrees of liberty"</note> lost) become infinitely small.

The same practical result may be reached without altering the potential energy by supposing that the kinetic energy of any motion violating the condition increases without limit. In this case, one or more periods become infinitely large, but the finite periods are ultimately the same as those arrived at when the potential energy is increased—even though in one case the periods have been increasing throughout, and in the other diminishing. This example shows the necessity of making the alterations by steps; otherwise, we would not understand the correspondence between the two sets of periods. Further illustrations will be given under the section regarding two degrees of freedom.

**89.** There is another important point to consider regarding the period of a system vibrating in an arbitrary mode <note>original: "type"; in this context, "type" refers to the specific shape or pattern of the vibration</note>. It appears from equation (2) in Section 88 that the period of vibration for any hypothetical mode is always between the longest and shortest natural periods of the system. In the case of systems like strings and plates, which are treated as being capable of continuous deformation, there is no "shortest" natural period (as they can theoretically vibrate at infinitely high frequencies). However, we can still assert that the period calculated from any hypothetical mode cannot exceed the period belonging to the gravest <note>original: "gravest"; this refers to the fundamental or lowest-frequency mode, which has the longest period</note> normal mode. Therefore, when the goal is to estimate the longest natural period of a system using calculations based on an assumed mode, we know beforehand <note>original: "a priori"</note> that the result will be slightly too small.

In choosing a hypothetical mode, one must use good judgment; the goal is to get as close to the truth as possible without making the math too complicated. For example, the vibration mode for a string with a very heavy weight at one point might be modeled after the extreme case of an infinite load, where the two parts of the string would be perfectly straight. As an example of this kind of calculation—where the actual result is already known—we will look at a uniform string of length $l$ stretched with tension $T_1$, and determine what the period would be based on certain assumptions about the mode of vibration.

Setting the center of the string as the starting point (the origin of $x$), let the curve of vibration on the positive side be:

-> $y = \cos pt \left\{ 1 - \left( \frac{2x}{l} \right)^n \right\}$ ........................(1), <-

and on the negative side, let it be the mirror image of this across the $y$-axis, where $n$ is no less than one. This formula satisfies the condition that the displacement ($y$) becomes zero at the ends of the string ($x = \pm \frac{1}{2}l$). We now need to create the expressions for kinetic energy ($T$) and potential energy ($V$); it will be enough to consider only the positive half of the string. Thus, where $\rho$ represents the mass per unit length <note>original: "longitudinal density"</note>:

-> $T = \frac{1}{2} \int_0^{\frac{1}{2}l} \rho \dot{y}^2 dx = \frac{\rho n^2 l p^2 \sin^2 pt}{2(n + 1)(2n + 1)},$ <-

and

-> $V = \frac{1}{2} T_1 \int_0^{\frac{1}{2}l} \left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right)^2 dx = \frac{n^2 T_1 \cos^2 pt}{(2n - 1)l}.$ <-

->$p^2 = \frac{10 \ T_1}{\rho l^2}$.<-

->$p^2 = 9.8990 \ \frac{T_1}{\rho l^2}$.<-

In this case, the period is only slightly too short, with a ratio of:
->$\pi : \sqrt{9.8990} = 0.99851 : 1$.<-

As we can see, there is a lot of flexibility in choosing a vibration pattern <note>original: "type"</note>. Even the extreme assumption <note>original: "violent supposition"</note> that the string vibrates as two straight segments meeting at an angle results in an error of less than ten percent. Furthermore, no matter what shape we assume, the calculated period will never be longer than the actual truth.

This involves comparing the system in question to a simpler one that is easier to analyze, then calculating corrections based on the assumption that the difference between the two systems is small. # VIBRATING SYSTEMS IN GENERAL. [90.]

The study of simple systems is of great importance, especially because it is impossible in practice to actually realize the simple forms about which we can most easily reason.

Suppose we thoroughly understand the vibrations of a simple system and wish to investigate those of a system derived from it by introducing small variations in the mechanical functions <note>original: "mechanical functions"; here referring to the kinetic and potential energy of the system</note>. If $\phi_1, \phi_2, \text{etc.}$ are the normal coordinates <note>original: "normal co-ordinates"; specific variables that allow each mode of vibration to be analyzed independently</note> of the original system, then:
-> $T = \frac{1}{2} a_1 \dot{\phi}_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} a_2 \dot{\phi}_2^2 + \dots,$ <-
-> $V = \frac{1}{2} c_1 \phi_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} c_2 \phi_2^2 + \dots,$ <-
And for the modified system, referred to the same coordinates (which are now only approximately normal):
$\left. \begin{aligned} T + \delta T &= \frac{1}{2} (a_1 + \delta a_{11}) \dot{\phi}_1^2 + \dots + \delta a_{12} \dot{\phi}_1 \dot{\phi}_2 + \dots \\ V + \delta V &= \frac{1}{2} (c_1 + \delta c_{11}) \phi_1^2 + \dots + \delta c_{12} \phi_1 \phi_2 + \dots \end{aligned} \right\} \dots \dots (1),$
In this equation, $\delta a_{11}, \delta a_{12}, \delta c_{11}, \delta c_{12}, \text{etc.}$ are to be considered small quantities. In certain cases, new coordinates may appear, but if they do, their coefficients must be small. From equation (1), we obtain the Lagrangian equations of motion:
$\left. \begin{aligned} (a_1 + \delta a_{11} D^2 + c_1 + \delta c_{11}) \phi_1 + (\delta a_{12} D^2 + \delta c_{12}) \phi_2 & \\ + (\delta a_{13} D^2 + \delta c_{13}) \phi_3 + \dots &= 0 \\ (\delta a_{21} D^2 + \delta c_{21}) \phi_1 + (a_2 + \delta a_{22} D^2 + c_2 + \delta c_{22}) \phi_2 & \\ + (\delta a_{23} D^2 + \delta c_{23}) \phi_3 + \dots &= 0 \end{aligned} \right\} \dots \dots (2).$
......................................................................................................................................................

In the original system, the fundamental modes <note>original: "types"</note> of vibration are those that correspond to the variation of only a single coordinate at a time. Let us focus our attention on one of them—for instance, a variation of $\phi_r$—while all the remaining coordinates remain at zero. 

A change in the system will generally result in an alteration of these fundamental or normal modes; however, under the circumstances we are considering, the alteration is small. The new normal mode is expressed by the simultaneous <note>original: "synchronous"</note> variation of the other coordinates in addition to $\phi_r$, but the ratio of any other coordinate $\phi_s$ to $\phi_r$ is small. When these ratios are known, the normal mode of the altered system will be determined.

Since the entire motion is simple harmonic, we may assume that each coordinate varies according to $\cos p_r t$ and substitute $-p_r^2$ for $D^2$ in the differential equations. In the $s^{\text{th}}$ equation, $\phi_s$ appears with the finite coefficient:
-> $-a_s p_r^2 - \delta a_{ss} p_r^2 + c_s + \delta c_{ss}.$ <-

<summary>This page introduces a general mathematical method for calculating how small physical changes to a vibrating system affect its normal modes and frequencies using Lagrangian equations.</summary>
<keywords>vibrating systems, mechanical functions, normal coordinates, Lagrangian equations, simple harmonic motion, differential equations, perturbation theory</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the mathematical analysis of how small changes in a system's physical properties (like mass or stiffness) affect its natural frequencies and modes of vibration. It specifically derives the "second-order" corrections that occur when the shape of the vibration itself changes.</meta>

# APPROXIMATELY SIMPLE SYSTEMS.
<sig>8—2</sig>
<meta>catchword: 90.]</meta>

The coefficient of $\phi_s$ is
->$-\delta a_{rs} p_r^2 + \delta c_{rs}.$<-

The other terms are to be neglected in a first approximation, since both the coordinate (relative to $\phi_r$) and its coefficient are small quantities. Hence
->$\phi_s : \phi_r = - \frac{\delta c_{rs} - p_r^2 \delta a_{rs}}{c_s - p_r^2 a_s} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (3).$<-

Now
->$- a_s p_s^2 + c_s = 0,$<-

and thus
->$\phi_s : \phi_r = \frac{p_r^2 \delta a_{rs} - \delta c_{rs}}{a_s (p_s^2 - p_r^2)} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (4),$<-

which is the required result.

If only the kinetic energy <note>the energy of motion</note> undergoes variation,
->$\phi_s : \phi_r = \frac{p_r^2}{p_s^2 - p_r^2} \frac{\delta a_{rs}}{a_s} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (5).$<-

The corrected value of the period <note>here referring to the frequency factor $p^2$</note> is determined by the $r$th equation of (2), which has not been used so far. We may write it as:
->$\phi_r \{ - p_r^2 a_r - p_r^2 \delta a_{rr} + c_r + \delta c_{rr} \} + \Sigma \phi_s (- p_r^2 \delta a_{rs} + \delta c_{rs}) = 0.$<-

Substituting for the ratio $\phi_s : \phi_r$ from equation (4), we get
->$p_r^2 = \frac{c_r + \delta c_{rr}}{a_r + \delta a_{rr}} - \Sigma \frac{(\delta c_{rs} - p_r^2 \delta a_{rs})^2}{a_s a_r (p_s^2 - p_r^2)} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (6).$<-

The first term gives the value of $p_r^2$ calculated without accounting for the change in the mode's shape <note>original: "change of type"; this refers to how the spatial pattern of the vibration shifts when the system is altered</note>. This is sufficient, as we have already proven, when the square of the alteration to the system can be ignored. The terms included under the summation symbol $\Sigma$ (where the sum includes all values of $s$ other than $r$) provide the correction due to the change in the mode's shape and are of the second order <note>meaning these effects are much smaller, proportional to the square of the initial change</note>. Since $a_s$ and $a_r$ are positive, the sign of any term depends on the sign of $p_s^2 - p_r^2$. 

If $p_s^2 > p_r^2$—that is, if mode $s$ is higher-pitched <note>original: "more acute"</note> than mode $r$—the correction is negative, which makes the calculated note lower <note>original: "graver"</note> than before. However, if mode $s$ is the lower note, the correction raises the note. If $r$ refers to the lowest <note>original: "gravest"</note> mode of the system, the entire correction is negative; and if $r$ refers to the highest <note>original: "acutest"</note> mode, the entire correction is positive, as we have already seen by another method.

**91.** As an example of how to use these formulas, we may take the case of a stretched string, whose density per unit length <note>original: "longitudinal density"</note> $\rho$ is not perfectly constant. If $x$ is measured from one end, and $y$

If we let $y$ represent the transverse <term>sideways</term> displacement, the configuration of the string at any time $t$ can be expressed by the following series:

-> $y = \phi_1 \sin \frac{\pi x}{l} + \phi_2 \sin \frac{2\pi x}{l} + \phi_3 \sin \frac{3\pi x}{l} + \dots \dots \dots (1),$ <-

where $l$ is the length of the string. Here, $\phi_1, \phi_2, \dots$ are the normal coordinates <term>independent variables that describe the motion of each specific harmonic</term> for a case where the density $\rho$ is constant. Although in this specific problem the density $\rho$ is not strictly constant, the configuration of the system can still be expressed using these same quantities. Since the potential energy <note>the energy stored in the string due to its tension and displacement</note> of any configuration is the same as if the density were constant, the variation in potential energy $\delta V$ is zero. For the kinetic energy <note>the energy of motion</note> we have:

-> $T + \delta T = \frac{1}{2} \int_0^l \rho \left( \dot{\phi}_1 \sin \frac{\pi x}{l} + \dot{\phi}_2 \sin \frac{2\pi x}{l} + \dots \right)^2 dx$ <-

-> $= \frac{1}{2} \dot{\phi}_1^2 \int_0^l \rho \sin^2 \frac{\pi x}{l} dx + \frac{1}{2} \dot{\phi}_2^2 \int_0^l \rho \sin^2 \frac{2\pi x}{l} dx + \dots$ <-

-> $+ \dot{\phi}_1 \dot{\phi}_2 \int_0^l \rho \sin \frac{\pi x}{l} \sin \frac{2\pi x}{l} dx + \dots$ <-

If the density $\rho$ were constant, the products of the different velocities would disappear, because $\phi_1, \phi_2, \text{etc.}$, are, on that assumption, the normal coordinates. In this case, however, the integral coefficients—though not actually vanishing <note>original: "evanescent"</note>—are small quantities. Let the density be defined as $\rho = \rho_0 + \delta \rho$ <note>where $\rho_0$ is the baseline density and $\delta \rho$ is a small variation</note>; then, using our previous notation:

-> $a_r = \frac{1}{2} l \rho_0, \quad \delta a_{rr} = \int_0^l \delta \rho \sin^2 \frac{r\pi x}{l} dx, \quad \delta a_{rs} = \int_0^l \delta \rho \sin \frac{r\pi x}{l} \sin \frac{s\pi x}{l} dx.$ <-

Thus, the mode of vibration <note>original: "type of vibration"; the specific spatial pattern of the string's movement</note> is expressed by:

-> $\phi_s : \phi_r = \frac{p_r^2}{p_s^2 - p_r^2} \cdot \frac{2}{l \rho_0} \int_0^l \delta \rho \sin \frac{r\pi x}{l} \sin \frac{s\pi x}{l} dx;$ <-

or, since the ratio of the squared frequencies is $p_r^2 : p_s^2 = r^2 : s^2$,

-> $\phi_s : \phi_r = \frac{r^2}{s^2 - r^2} \int_0^l \frac{2 \delta \rho}{l \rho_0} \sin \frac{r\pi x}{l} \sin \frac{s\pi x}{l} dx \dots \dots \dots (2).$ <-

Let us apply this result to calculate the displacement of the nodal point <term>a stationary point on a vibrating string</term> of the second mode ($r = 2$), which would be exactly in the middle if the string were uniform. In the vicinity of this point, if we set $x = \frac{1}{2} l + \delta x$, the approximate value of $y$ is:

-> $y = \phi_1 \sin \frac{\pi}{2} + \phi_2 \sin \frac{2\pi}{2} + \phi_3 \sin \frac{3\pi}{2} + \dots$ <-

-> $+ \delta x \left\{ \frac{\pi}{l} \phi_1 \cos \frac{\pi}{2} + \frac{2\pi}{l} \phi_2 \cos \frac{2\pi}{2} + \dots \right\}$ <-

-> $= \phi_1 - \phi_3 + \phi_5 - \dots + \frac{\pi}{l} \delta x \{ - 2\phi_2 + 2\phi_4 + \dots \}.$ <-

Therefore, when the displacement $y = 0$ <note>This indicates the position of a node, where the string does not move.</note>, we find that:

->$\delta x = \frac{l}{2\pi\phi_2} \{ \phi_1 - \phi_3 + \phi_5 - \dots \} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (3)$<-

approximately, where:

->$\phi_s : \phi_2 = \frac{4}{s^2 - 4} \int_0^l \frac{2\delta\rho}{l\rho_0} \sin \frac{2\pi x}{l} \sin \frac{s\pi x}{l} dx \dots\dots\dots (4).$<-

To show how these formulas are applied, we can imagine that the irregularity consists of a small load with a mass of $\rho_0\lambda$ located at the point $x = \frac{1}{4}l$ <note>one-quarter of the way along the string</note>, though this result could be found much more easily through a direct calculation. From this, we have:

->$\delta x = \frac{2\lambda}{\pi\sqrt{2}} \left\{ \frac{2}{1^2 - 4} - \frac{2}{3^2 - 4} - \frac{2}{5^2 - 4} + \frac{2}{7^2 - 4} + \dots\dots\dots \right\},$<-

from which the value of the shift $\delta x$ can be calculated by approximation. The actual value of $\delta x$, however, is very simple. The series inside the brackets can be rewritten as:

->$-\left\{ 1 + \frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{5} - \frac{1}{7} + \frac{1}{9} + \frac{1}{11} - \text{etc.} \right\},$<-

which is equal to:

->$-\int_0^1 \frac{1 + x^2}{1 + x^4} dx.$<-

The value of this definite integral is:

->$\pi \div 4 \sin \frac{\pi}{4}^1,$<-

and thus:

->$\delta x = -\frac{2\lambda}{\pi\sqrt{2}} \cdot \frac{\pi\sqrt{2}}{4} = -\frac{\lambda}{2},$<-

This can also be easily proven by setting the periods of vibration <term>the time it takes for one full back-and-forth motion</term> of the two parts of the string equal to each other. In that case, the period of the loaded part is calculated approximately by assuming that the shape of the vibration <note>original: "type"</note> remains unchanged.

As an example of using formula (6) in Section 90 to find the period, we can consider the case of a string carrying a small load of mass $\rho_0\lambda$ at its exact middle point. In this case, we have:

->$a_r = \frac{1}{2}l\rho_0, \quad \delta a_{rr} = \rho_0\lambda \sin^2 \frac{r\pi}{2}, \quad \delta a_{rs} = \rho_0\lambda \sin \frac{r\pi}{2} \sin \frac{s\pi}{2},$<-

and therefore, if $P_r$ is the value when $\lambda = 0$ <note>the frequency when there is no extra load</note>, we find that when $r$ is an even number, $p_r = P_r$. When $r$ is an odd number, the formula becomes:

->$p_r^2 = P_r^2 \left\{ \frac{1}{1 + 2\lambda/l} - \sum \frac{4r^2}{s^2 - r^2} \frac{\lambda^2}{l^2} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (5),$<-

**92.** The theory of vibrations clarifies how arbitrary functions can be expanded into series of other specific types of functions. The best-known example of such expansions is the one generally named after Fourier <note>Jean-Baptiste Joseph Fourier (1768–1830), who showed that any periodic wave can be broken down into simple sine waves.</note>, in which an arbitrary periodic function is resolved into a series of harmonics, whose periods are whole-number fractions <note>original: "submultiples"</note> of the original function's period. It is well known that the main difficulty of this subject is proving that such an expansion is actually *possible*; if we assume it is possible, determining the coefficients <note>the numerical values that multiply each term in the series</note> is easy enough. What I wish to draw attention to now is that in this case, and in a vast variety of similar cases, we can infer that the expansion is possible based on physical considerations.

To illustrate this <note>original: "To fix our ideas"</note>, let us consider the small vibrations of a uniform string stretched between two fixed points. We know from general theory that any motion, no matter what it is, can be analyzed into a series of component motions. Each of these components is represented by a harmonic function of time and is capable of existing on its own. If we can identify these "normal modes" <note>original: "normal types"; these are the natural ways a system oscillates, like the fundamental tone and overtones of a guitar string</note>, we will be able to represent the most general vibration possible by combining them, assigning to each an arbitrary amplitude <term>the maximum extent of a vibration</term> and phase <term>the specific point in the cycle of a wave at a given time</term>.
