->**NORMAL FUNCTIONS**<-

If we assume that a motion is harmonic in relation to time, the type of vibration is determined by an equation of the form

->$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + k^2y = 0,$<-

from which it follows that the normal functions <note>The basic shapes or modes in which a system naturally vibrates.</note> are

->$y = \sin \frac{\pi x}{l}, \quad y = \sin \frac{2\pi x}{l}, \quad y = \sin \frac{3\pi x}{l}, \text{ etc.}$<-

We can conclude that the most general position the string can take can be represented by a series of the form

->$A_1 \sin \frac{\pi x}{l} + A_2 \sin \frac{2\pi x}{l} + A_3 \sin \frac{3\pi x}{l} + \dots \dots,$<-

which is a specific case of Fourier's theorem <note>A mathematical principle stating that complex periodic wave patterns can be broken down into a sum of simple sine waves.</note>. There would be no difficulty in proving this theorem in its most general form.

Up to this point, the string has been assumed to be uniform. However, we only need to introduce a variable density, or even a single weight <note>original: "load"</note> at any point on the string, to completely change the expansion that is predicted by the dynamical theory. There is no need to linger on this subject here, as we will see further examples in the chapters on the vibrations of specific systems, such as bars, membranes, and enclosed volumes <note>original: "confined masses"</note> of air.

**92 a.** In Section 88, we provided a formula for the vibration frequency used when specific constraints are applied, leaving the original system with only one degree of freedom. It is also interesting to trace the effect of less restrictive constraints, such as those expressed by linear relationships among the normal coordinates, where the number of constraints is at least two fewer than the original degrees of freedom. Thus, we may suppose that

->$\left. \begin{aligned} f_1\phi_1 + f_2\phi_2 + f_3\phi_3 + \dots = 0 \\ g_1\phi_1 + g_2\phi_2 + g_3\phi_3 + \dots = 0 \\ h_1\phi_1 + h_2\phi_2 + h_3\phi_3 + \dots = 0 \\ \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \end{aligned} \right\} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (1).$<-

If the number of equations ($r$) is one less than the number of degrees of freedom, the ratios $\phi_1 : \phi_2 : \phi_3 \dots$ are fully determined, and the case becomes that of a single remaining degree of freedom discussed in Section 88.

This problem may be treated in more than one way, but the...

# VIBRATING SYSTEMS IN GENERAL.

The most helpful way to proceed is to trace the effect of adding terms to the kinetic energy ($T$) and potential energy ($V$). We will assume that equations (1) in Section 87 are altered to:

-> $T = \frac{1}{2}a_1\dot{\phi}_1^2 + \frac{1}{2}a_2\dot{\phi}_2^2 + \dots + \frac{1}{2}\alpha (f_1\dot{\phi}_1 + f_2\dot{\phi}_2 + \dots)^2 \dots\dots\dots(2),$ <-
-> $V = \frac{1}{2}c_1\phi_1^2 + \frac{1}{2}c_2\phi_2^2 + \dots + \frac{1}{2}\gamma (f_1\phi_1 + f_2\phi_2 + \dots)^2 \dots\dots\dots(3),$ <-

and that $F$ (the dissipation function <note>A function representing energy lost to friction or damping.</note>), which did not exist before, is now:

-> $F = \frac{1}{2}\beta (f_1\dot{\phi}_1 + f_2\dot{\phi}_2 + \dots)^2 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(4).$ <-

The connection with the proposed problem will be understood by assuming, for instance, that $\alpha = 0$ and $\beta = 0$, while $\gamma$ is infinite. According to equation (3), the potential energy of any displacement that violates the condition:

-> $f_1\phi_1 + f_2\phi_2 + \dots = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(5)$ <-

is then infinite. This is essentially the same as imposing the constraint <note>A restriction on the possible movements of a system.</note> represented by equation (5).

Lagrange's equations <note>A set of fundamental equations used to describe the dynamics of a mechanical system.</note>, with $\lambda$ substituted for the operator $D$, now become:

> $(a_1\lambda^2 + c_1) \phi_1 + f_1 (\alpha\lambda^2 + \beta\lambda + \gamma) (f_1\phi_1 + f_2\phi_2 + \dots) = 0$
> $(a_2\lambda^2 + c_2) \phi_2 + f_2 (\alpha\lambda^2 + \beta\lambda + \gamma) (f_1\phi_1 + f_2\phi_2 + \dots) = 0$ } ...(6).

If we multiply the first of these by $f_1/(a_1\lambda^2 + c_1)$, the second by $f_2/(a_2\lambda^2 + c_2)$, and so on, and add the results together, the common factor $(f_1\phi_1 + f_2\phi_2 + \dots)$ will divide out, and the determinant <note>In this context, the equation that determines the possible frequencies of the system.</note> takes the form:

-> $\frac{f_1^2}{a_1\lambda^2 + c_1} + \frac{f_2^2}{a_2\lambda^2 + c_2} + \dots\dots\dots + \frac{1}{\alpha\lambda^2 + \beta\lambda + \gamma} = 0 \dots\dots (7).$ <-

If any one of the quantities $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ becomes infinite while the others remain finite, the effect is equivalent to the imposition of the constraint (5), and the result may be written:

-> $\Sigma f^2/(a\lambda^2 + c) = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(8)^1.$ <-

When expanded, this equation is of degree $(m - 1)$ in $\lambda^2$, showing that one degree of freedom <note>One of the independent ways in which a system can move or vibrate.</note> has been lost.

If we set $\beta = 0$, equation (7) is an equation of the $m$-th degree in $\lambda^2$, and the coefficients $\alpha, \gamma$ enter the equation in the same way as $a_1, c_1; a_2, c_2; \text{etc.}$

To refer more directly to the case of vibrations around a point of stable equilibrium, we will write $p^2$ for $-\lambda^2$. The values of $p^2$ belonging to the original, unaltered system, namely <note>original: "viz."</note> $n_1^2, n_2^2, \dots$, are given as before by:

-> $c_1 - a_1n_1^2 = 0, \quad c_2 - a_2n_2^2 = 0, \text{ etc.,} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (9);$ <-

and we will also write:

-> $\gamma - \alpha\nu^2 = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(10).$ <-

<meta>This page continues the mathematical analysis of how adding constraints or changing energy parameters (specifically kinetic energy $T$ and potential energy $V$) influences the natural frequencies of a vibrating system.</meta>

<page-num>121</page-num>
# ONE CONSTRAINT.

In this context, $\nu^2$ refers to the proposed additions to the kinetic energy ($T$) and potential energy ($V$), treated as if they belong to an independent vibrator <note>A separate system or component capable of oscillation.</note>. Let us assume the order of magnitude of these quantities is:

-> $n_1^2, n_2^2, \dots \dots \dots n_r^2, \nu^2, n_{r+1}^2, \dots \dots \dots n_m^2 \dots \dots \dots \dots$ (11). <-

We will see that there is a root <note>In this mathematical context, a "root" represents a value for $p^2$, which relates to the natural frequency of the system.</note> of equation (7) between each consecutive pair of the quantities listed in (11).

Our equation may be written as:

-> $f_1^2 (\gamma - a p^2) (c_2 - a_2 p^2) (c_3 - a_3 p^2) \dots \dots$ <-
-> $+ f_2^2 (\gamma - a p^2) (c_1 - a_1 p^2) (c_3 - a_3 p^2) \dots \dots$ <-
-> $+ \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots$ <-
-> $+ (c_1 - a_1 p^2) (c_2 - a_2 p^2) \dots \dots \dots \dots = 0 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots$ (12). <-

When $p^2$ matches any of the quantities in (11), all but one of the terms in equation (12) disappear (vanish), and the mathematical sign (positive or negative) of the expression is the same as that of the term which remains. When $p^2 < n_1^2$, all the terms are positive, meaning there is no root less than $n_1^2$. When $p^2 = n_1^2$, expression (12) simplifies to the positive quantity:

-> $f_1^2 (\gamma - a n_1^2) (c_2 - a_2 n_1^2) (c_3 - a_3 n_1^2) \dots \dots$ <-

When $p^2$ rises to $n_2^2$, equation (12) becomes:

-> $f_2^2 (\gamma - a n_2^2) (c_1 - a_1 n_2^2) (c_3 - a_3 n_2^2) \dots \dots$ ; <-

and this result is *negative*, because the factor $(c_1 - a_1 n_2^2)$ is now negative. Therefore, there is a root of (12) located between $n_1^2$ and $n_2^2$. When $p^2 = n_3^2$, the expression is positive again, and thus there is a root between $n_2^2$ and $n_3^2$. This argument can be continued, and it proves that there is a root of (12) between any two consecutive values of the $(m + 1)$ quantities listed in (11). 

The $m$ roots of equation (12) are now accounted for, and none are greater than $n_m^2$. If we compare the values of the roots before and after the change, we see that the effect is to cause a shift which is, in every case, toward $\nu^2$.$^1$ Viewed in absolute terms, the shift is in one direction for those roots greater than $\nu^2$ and in the opposite direction for those that are less than $\nu^2$. Consequently, the interval from $n_r^2$ to $n_{r+1}^2$, where $\nu^2$ lies, contains *two* roots after the change—one on either side of $\nu^2$.

If $\nu^2$ is less than any of the $n^2$ quantities (which occurs when $\gamma = 0$), one root lies between $\nu^2$ and $n_1^2$, one between $n_1^2$ and $n_2^2$, and so on. In this case, every root is lowered <term>depressed: in this context, reduced in value or frequency</term>. On the other hand, if $\nu^2 > n_m^2$, every root is increased. This occurs if $\alpha = 0$ (see § 88).

---
$^1$ **It should be understood that in specific cases, this movement may be zero.**

<summary>This page provides a mathematical proof for how the natural frequencies (roots) of a vibrating system shift when a constraint is added. It demonstrates that the new roots are interleaved between the original frequencies and a specific value determined by the added energy parameters.</summary>

### VIBRATING SYSTEMS IN GENERAL.

The results reached so far are, of course, independent of the specific mathematical framework of "normal coordinates" <note>A set of coordinates chosen so that each one corresponds to a single natural mode of vibration.</note> used in this investigation. If a vibrator ($\nu^2$) with a single degree of freedom <note>A component that can only move in one specific way, such as a simple pendulum.</note> is attached to any part of a system ($n_1^2, n_2^2 \dots \dots$), the effect is to shift all the values $n_r^2, \dots$ toward the value of $\nu^2$. 

Let us now suppose that a second change is made to the vibrator, where $\alpha$ becomes $\alpha + \alpha'$ and $\gamma$ becomes $\gamma + \gamma'$. Every root <note>Every solution for the frequency in the system's governing equation.</note> of the determinantal equation moves toward $\nu'^2$, where $\gamma' - \alpha' \nu'^2 = 0$. If we assume that $\nu'^2 = \nu^2$, the movements in all cases go in the same directions as before. Returning now to the original system, and assuming that $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ grow from zero to their actual values in such a way that $\nu^2$ remains constant, we see that during this process the roots move toward closer agreement with $\nu^2$ without ever reversing direction (regression).

As $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ become infinite, one root of equation (12) moves to match $\nu^2$, while the remaining ($m - 1$) roots—which correspond to the constrained system <note>A system where a specific movement has been restricted or fixed.</note>—are given by:

->$\Sigma f^2 / (c - a p^2) = 0 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (13),$<-

and these are independent of the value of $\nu^2$.

Specific cases are found by assuming either $\nu^2 = 0$ or $\nu^2 = \infty$. It makes no difference to the remaining vibrations whether the constraint is achieved by making the kinetic energy of any motion infinite (effectively adding an infinite mass) or by making the potential energy of any displacement infinite (making it perfectly rigid). In the first case, one vibration becomes infinitely slow; in the second case, one becomes infinitely fast. However the constraint is reached, the ($m - 1$) frequencies of vibration of the constrained system *separate*$^1$ the $m$ frequencies of the original system.

Any number of examples of this theorem may be easily created. Consider the case of a uniform stretched string, held at both ends and vibrating transversely <note>Vibrating side-to-side, perpendicular to the length of the string.</note>. This is the original system. Now, introduce a constraint by holding a point still that divides the length in a ratio of (for example) $3 : 2$. The two parts now vibrate independently, and the frequencies for each part form an arithmetic progression <note>A sequence of numbers where the difference between each consecutive term is constant.</note>. If the frequencies proper to the undivided string are $1, 2, 3, 4 \dots \dots$, then the frequencies for the parts are:

In its general form, it appears to be credited to Routh <note>Edward John Routh (1831–1907), an English mathematician famous for his work on the stability of systems.</note>.

$\frac{s}{l} (1, 2, 3, \dots)$ and $\frac{s}{l'} (1, 2, 3, \dots)$. The beginning of each series is shown in the accompanying diagram;

It will be seen that between any consecutive numbers in the first row, a number can be found *either* in the second *or* in the third row. In the case of 5 and 10, we have an extreme condition; but the slightest displacement of the point at which the constraint <note>A restriction that limits the movement of a system, such as pinning a vibrating string at a specific point.</note> is applied will shift one of the fives, tens, etc., to the left and the other to the right.

These coincidences may be avoided by dividing the string incommensurably <note>Dividing a length into parts that have no common measure, resulting in an irrational ratio.</note>. Thus, if $x$ is an irrational number <note>original: "incommensurable number"</note> less than one, exactly one value from the series $m/x$ or $m/(1 - x)$ (where $m$ is a whole number) can be found which will lie between any given consecutive integers, and only one such value can be found.

Again, let us suppose that a system is described by coordinates which are not "normal" (see § 84), and let a constraint represented by the equation $\psi_1 = 0$ be imposed. The determinant <note>A mathematical value used to solve systems of linear equations; here it represents the characteristic equation of the vibrating system.</note> of the modified system is formed from that of the original system by erasing the first row and the first column. It may be called $\nabla_1$, and from this, a new determinant $\nabla_2$ may be formed in the same manner, and so on. These determinants form a series of functions of $p^2$ that regularly decrease in degree <note>The highest power of the variable in the polynomial equation.</note>; and we conclude that the roots <note>The specific values of $p^2$ that solve the equation, representing the natural frequencies.</note> of each separate the roots of the one immediately preceding it$^1$.

It may be noted that while, for the sake of simplicity, we have assumed that the equilibrium of the original system was perfectly stable—as was the vibration connected to it—these restrictions can easily be set aside. In any case, the series of positive and negative quantities, $n_1^2, n_2^2, \dots$ and $\nu^2$, may be arranged in numerical order, and the effect of the vibrator is to cause a movement of every value of $p^2$ in the direction of $\nu^2$.

and the addition to the potential energy $V$ <note>$V$ represents the potential energy of the system, which accounts for the forces acting to restore it to equilibrium.</note>
->$\frac{1}{2}\gamma_f (f_1\phi_1 + f_2\phi_2 + ...)^2 + \frac{1}{2}\gamma_g (g_1\phi_1 + g_2\phi_2 + ...)^2 + ......(15).$<-
If we define
->$a_f\lambda^2 + \gamma_f = F', \quad a_g\lambda^2 + \gamma_g = G', \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(16),$<-
and so on, Lagrange's equations <note>A set of fundamental equations in classical mechanics used to describe the motion of a system based on its energy.</note> become:
->$(a_1\lambda^2 + c_1) \phi_1 + F'f_1 (f_1\phi_1 + f_2\phi_2 + \dots)$<-
->$+ G'g_1 (g_1\phi_1 + g_2\phi_2 + \dots) + H'h_1 (h_1\phi_1 + h_2\phi_2 + \dots) + \dots = 0 \dots(17),$<-
->$(a_2\lambda^2 + c_2) \phi_2 + F'f_2 (f_1\phi_1 + f_2\phi_2 + \dots)$<-
->$+ G'g_2 (g_1\phi_1 + g_2\phi_2 + \dots) + H'h_2 (h_1\phi_1 + h_2\phi_2 + \dots) + \dots = 0 \dots(18),$<-
and so forth. The number of equations is equal to the number ($m$) of coordinates <note>The independent variables, such as $\phi_1$ and $\phi_2$, that define the position or state of the system.</note> $\phi_1, \phi_2 \dots$. We assume the number of additions ($r$), which correspond to the letters $f, g, h, \dots$, is less than $m$.

From the $m$ equations above, let us form $r$ new equations as follows. For the first, multiply equation (17) by $f_1/(a_1\lambda^2 + c_1)$, multiply (18) by $f_2/(a_2\lambda^2 + c_2)$, and so on, then add all the results together. For the second equation, proceed in the same way using the multipliers $g_1/(a_1\lambda^2 + c_1)$, $g_2/(a_2\lambda^2 + c_2)$, etc. For the third equation, use $h$ instead of $g$, and continue this pattern. In this way, we obtain $r$ equations which may be written as:
->$F' (f_1\phi_1 + f_2\phi_2 + \dots) \{1/F' + F_1^2 + F_2^2 + F_3^2 + \dots\}$<-
->$+ G' (g_1\phi_1 + g_2\phi_2 + \dots) \{F_1G_1 + F_2G_2 + \dots\}$<-
->$+ H' (h_1\phi_1 + h_2\phi_2 + \dots) \{F_1H_1 + F_2H_2 + \dots\} + \dots\dots = 0 \dots(19),$<-
->$F' (f_1\phi_1 + f_2\phi_2 + \dots) \{G_1F_1 + G_2F_2 + \dots\}$<-
->$+ G' (g_1\phi_1 + g_2\phi_2 + \dots) \{1/G' + G_1^2 + G_2^2 + \dots\}$<-
->$+ H' (h_1\phi_1 + h_2\phi_2 + \dots) \{G_1H_1 + G_2H_2 + \dots\} + \dots\dots = 0 \dots(20),$<-
and so on, where for the sake of brevity:
<image-desc>A system of three equations grouped by a right curly brace, labeled (21). The equations define shorthand terms for variables F squared, G squared, and FG products as ratios involving lambda squared and constants.</image-desc>
> $F_1^2 = f_1^2/(a_1\lambda^2 + c_1), \quad F_2^2 = f_2^2/(a_2\lambda^2 + c_2), \text{ etc.},$
> $G_1^2 = g_1^2/(a_1\lambda^2 + c_1), \quad G_2^2 = g_2^2/(a_2\lambda^2 + c_2), \text{ etc.},$ $\Biggr\} \dots\dots(21).$
> $F_1G_1 = f_1g_1/(a_1\lambda^2 + c_1), \text{ etc.}$

The determinantal equation <note>An equation used to find the natural frequencies (eigenvalues) of the system by setting the determinant of the system's matrix to zero.</note> of the $r$th order is therefore:
<image-desc>A determinant of a 3x3 matrix (with ellipses indicating higher orders) set equal to zero, labeled (22). The elements consist of reciprocal terms and summations of F, G, and H products.</image-desc>
$$\begin{vmatrix} 1/F' + \Sigma F^2, & \Sigma FG, & \Sigma FH, \dots \\ \Sigma FG, & 1/G' + \Sigma G^2, & \Sigma GH, \\ \Sigma FH, & \Sigma GH, & 1/H' + \Sigma H^2, \dots \\ \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots \end{vmatrix} = 0 \dots\dots(22).$$

# SEVERAL CONSTRAINTS.

If, for example, there are two additions to $T$ <note>$T$ represents the kinetic energy of the system.</note> and $V$ <note>$V$ represents the potential energy of the system.</note> of the kind previously described, the equation is:

->$\frac{1}{FG'} + \frac{\Sigma F^2}{G'} + \frac{\Sigma G^2}{F} + \Sigma F^2 . \Sigma G^2 - \{\Sigma FG\}^2 = 0$ .........(23),<-

and in this context:

->$(F_1^2 + F_2^2 + ...) (G_1^2 + G_2^2 + ...) - (F_1 G_1 + F_2 G_2 + ...)^2$<-
->$= \Sigma \Sigma (F_1 G_2 - F_2 G_1)^2$ .........(24).<-

Equation (23) is generally of the $m$-th degree in $\lambda^2$ <note>The variable $\lambda$ relates to the frequency of the vibration.</note>, and it determines the frequencies of vibration. In the extreme case where $F'$ and $G'$ are made infinite, the system is subject to the two constraints:

->$\left. \begin{array}{r} f_1 \phi_1 + f_2 \phi_2 + ... = 0 \\ g_1 \phi_1 + g_2 \phi_2 + ... = 0 \end{array} \right\}$ .........(25),<-

and the equation <gloss>1</gloss> giving the $(m - 2)$ remaining <note>original: "outstanding"</note> roots is:

->$\frac{(f_1 g_2 - f_2 g_1)^2}{(a_1 \lambda^2 + c_1) (a_2 \lambda^2 + c_2)} + \frac{(f_1 g_3 - f_3 g_1)^2}{(a_1 \lambda^2 + c_1) (a_3 \lambda^2 + c_3)} + ...... = 0$ ......(26).<-

In general, if the system is subject to $r$ constraints (1), the determinantal equation <note>A mathematical equation used to find the characteristic values (like frequencies) of a system.</note> is:

->$\begin{vmatrix} \Sigma FF, & \Sigma FG, & \Sigma FH, ... \\ \Sigma FG, & \Sigma GG, & \Sigma GH, ... \\ \Sigma FH, & \Sigma GH, & \Sigma HH, ... \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \end{vmatrix} = 0$ ......... (27).<-

If $r$ is less than $m$ <note>$m$ is the number of degrees of freedom, or independent ways the system can move.</note>, this determinant can be decomposed <gloss>2</gloss> into a sum of squares of determinants of the same order ($r$). Thus, if there are three constraints, the first of these squares is:

->$\begin{vmatrix} F_1 & F_2 & F_3 \\ G_1 & G_2 & G_3 \\ H_1 & H_2 & H_3 \end{vmatrix}^2$ ...........................(28),<-

and the others are found by including every combination of the $m$ suffixes <note>Subscript numbers or letters used to identify specific components.</note> taken three at a time. To return to the original notation, we simply need to replace the capital letters $F, G, ...$ in (28) with $f, g, ...$, and introduce the denominator:

->$(a_1 \lambda^2 + c_1) (a_2 \lambda^2 + c_2) (a_3 \lambda^2 + c_3).$<-

The determinantal equation for a system originally having $m$ degrees of freedom and subjected to $r$ constraints is thus found. Its form...

### VIBRATING SYSTEMS IN GENERAL. [92 a.

This result is largely determined by the consideration that it must remain unaffected by swapping either the letters or the subscripts. It could also have been foreseen that the equation would become invalid <note>original: "nugatory"</note> if two of the conditions of constraint coincided. If $r = m - 1$ <note>$r$ is the number of constraints and $m$ is the number of degrees of freedom. When $r = m - 1$, only one degree of freedom remains.</note>, the system is reduced to one degree of freedom, and the equation is:

$$\begin{vmatrix} f_2 & f_3 & f_4 \dots \\ g_2 & g_3 & g_4 \dots \\ h_2 & h_3 & h_4 \dots \\ \dots & \dots & \dots \end{vmatrix}^2 (a_1\lambda^2 + c_1) + \begin{vmatrix} f_1 & f_3 & f_4 \dots \\ g_1 & g_3 & g_4 \dots \\ h_1 & h_3 & h_4 \dots \\ \dots & \dots & \dots \end{vmatrix}^2 (a_2\lambda^2 + c_2) + \dots = 0 \dots \dots (29),$$

which agrees with section 88.

There are theories, parallel to those mentioned above, for systems in which kinetic energy ($T$) and the dissipation function ($F$), or potential energy ($V$) and the dissipation function ($F$), are the only significant <note>original: "sensible"</note> factors. In these cases, if the functions are naturally positive, the normal motions are proportional to exponential functions of time, such as $e^{-t/\tau}$. The quantities $\tau_1, \tau_2, \dots$ are called the <term>time-constants</term>, or <term>persistences</term>, of the motions. These represent the time required for the motions to decay <note>original: "subside"</note> by a ratio of $e : 1$ <note>$e$ is the mathematical constant approximately equal to 2.718; this is the standard rate of exponential decay.</note>. The new persistences, after a constraint is introduced, will fall between the original values.

The best illustrations of this theory are electrical, where the motions are not restricted to being small. Suppose (to use an electromagnetic example) that a coil is introduced into one branch of a network of conductors. This coil has a persistence (when closed upon itself) equal to $\tau'$, while the original persistences of the network are $\tau_1, \tau_2, \dots$. In all cases, the new persistences will lie closer to $\tau'$, and they will separate the values of $\tau', \tau_1, \tau_2, \dots$. If $\tau'$ is made infinite—such as by increasing the self-induction of the additional coil without limit—or if it is made to vanish—such as by breaking the electrical contact in that branch—the result is a constraint. In these cases, the new values of the persistences will fall between the former ones.

**93.** Finding the coefficients to fit arbitrary initial conditions can always be easily achieved by using the fundamental property of the <term>normal functions</term> <note>Normal functions, or eigenfunctions, describe the natural shapes or patterns in which a system like a string or drumhead prefers to vibrate.</note>. It may be helpful to outline the process here for systems such as strings, bars, membranes, and plates, where there is only one dependent variable $\zeta$ <note>$\zeta$ (zeta) typically represents the displacement or movement of the system from its resting position.</note> to consider. If $u_1, u_2 \dots$ are the normal functions, and $\phi_1, \phi_2 \dots$ are the corresponding coordinates:

$$\zeta = \phi_1 u_1 + \phi_2 u_2 + \phi_3 u_3 + \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (1).$$

### INITIAL CONDITIONS.

The equations of free motion <note>The movement of a physical system when no external forces are acting upon it.</note> are:

->$\ddot{\phi}_1 + n_1^2 \phi_1 = 0, \quad \ddot{\phi}_2 + n_2^2 \phi_2 = 0, \text{ and so on} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(2),$<-

of which the solutions are:

->$\left. \begin{aligned} \phi_1 &= A_1 \sin n_1 t + B_1 \cos n_1 t \\ \phi_2 &= A_2 \sin n_2 t + B_2 \cos n_2 t \\ &\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(3).$<-

The initial values of displacement ($\zeta$) and velocity ($\dot{\zeta}$) at the start of the motion are therefore:

->$\left. \begin{aligned} \zeta_0 &= B_1 u_1 + B_2 u_2 + B_3 u_3 + \dots \\ \dot{\zeta}_0 &= n_1 A_1 u_1 + n_2 A_2 u_2 + n_3 A_3 u_3 + \dots \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(4),$<-

and the problem is to determine the constants $A_1, A_2, \dots$ and $B_1, B_2 \dots$ so that they correspond with the arbitrary starting values of $\zeta_0$ and $\dot{\zeta}_0$.

If we let $\rho \, dx$ represent the mass of the infinitesimal element $dx$, we have from equation (1):

->$T = \frac{1}{2} \int \rho \dot{\zeta}^2 dx$<-
->$= \frac{1}{2} \dot{\phi}_1^2 \int \rho \, u_1^2 dx + \frac{1}{2} \dot{\phi}_2^2 \int \rho \, u_2^2 dx + \dots + \dot{\phi}_1 \dot{\phi}_2 \int \rho u_1 u_2 dx + \dots$<-

However, the expression for kinetic energy ($T$) when written in terms of the <term>generalized velocities</term> <note>The rate of change of coordinates that define the configuration of a system.</note> ($\dot{\phi}_1, \dot{\phi}_2, \text{ etc.}$) cannot include the products of these velocities. Therefore, every integral in the following form must equal zero:

->$\int \rho u_r u_s dx = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(5).$<-

Consequently, to determine the constant $B_r$, we only need to multiply the first of the equations in (4) by $\rho u_r$ and integrate across the entire system. By doing this, we obtain:

->$B_r \int \rho \, u_r^2 dx = \int \rho \, u_r \zeta_0 dx \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(6).$<-

In a similar way:

->$n_r A_r \int \rho \, u_r^2 dx = \int \rho \, u_r \dot{\zeta}_0 dx \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(7).$<-

This process remains exactly the same whether the element $dx$ represents a line, an area, or a volume.

The <term>conjugate property</term> <note>Also known as orthogonality; it means that different modes of vibration do not interfere with one another's energy.</note> expressed by equation (5) depends on the fact that the functions $u$ are "normal" modes. As soon as this is established by solving a differential equation or by some other method, we may assume the conjugate property is true without further proof. However, the property itself is most intimately connected with the fundamental <term>variational equation of motion</term> <note>A principle used to derive the equations of motion for a system by considering small variations in its path or state.</note> discussed in section 94.

**94.** If $V$ is the potential energy of deformation, $\zeta$ is the displacement, and $\rho$ is the density of the element $dx$ (whether that element represents a line, area, or volume), the equation of <term>virtual velocities</term> <note>A principle in mechanics stating that for a system in equilibrium, the total work done by all forces during a small, hypothetical displacement is zero.</note> immediately gives:

->$\delta V + \int \rho \ddot{\zeta} \delta \zeta dx = 0 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (1).$<-

In this equation, $\delta V$ is a symmetrical function of $\zeta$ and $\delta \zeta$, which can be easily proven from the expression for $V$ when written in terms of <term>generalized coordinates</term> <note>A set of independent variables used to uniquely describe the configuration of a physical system.</note>. In fact, if:
->$V = \frac{1}{2} c_{11} \psi_1^2 + \dots + c_{12} \psi_1 \psi_2 + \dots,$<-
then
->$\delta V = c_{11} \psi_1 \delta \psi_1 + c_{22} \psi_2 \delta \psi_2 + \dots$<-
->$+ c_{12} (\psi_1 \delta \psi_2 + \psi_2 \delta \psi_1) + \dots.$<-

Now, suppose that $\zeta$ refers to the motion associated with a <term>normal function</term> <note>In this context, a "normal function" (or eigenfunction) describes the shape of a specific mode of vibration where every part of the system moves with the same frequency.</note> $u_r$, so that $\ddot{\zeta} + n_r^2 \zeta = 0$, while $\delta \zeta$ is identified with another normal function $u_s$. Then:

->$\delta V = n_r^2 \int \rho u_r u_s dx.$<-

Likewise, if we suppose—as we are equally entitled to do—that $\zeta$ varies as $u_s$ and $\delta \zeta$ as $u_r$, we obtain the same value for $\delta V$:

->$\delta V = n_s^2 \int \rho u_r u_s dx;$<-

and therefore,
->$(n_r^2 - n_s^2) \int \rho u_r u_s dx = 0 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (2),$<-

From this, the <term>conjugate property</term> <note>original: "conjugate property". This refers to the orthogonality of the vibrational modes, meaning different modes of vibration do not interfere with one another's energy.</note> follows, provided that the motions represented by $u_r$ and $u_s$ have different periods.

A good example of the connection between these two methods of treatment can be found in the chapter on the transverse vibrations of bars.

If a velocity of any type is given to a system at rest, and then, after a small interval of time, the opposite velocity is given, the ultimate effect will be to start the system without velocity, but with a displacement of the corresponding type. <margin>95.</margin> To derive the motion that depends on <term>initial displacements</term> <note>The positions of the parts of a system at the exact moment it begins to move (time = 0).</note> from the motion that depends on the <term>initial velocities</term> <note>The speeds at which the parts of a system are moving at the exact moment observations begin.</note>, it is only necessary to differentiate with respect to time and to replace the arbitrary constants (or functions) that represent the initial velocities with those that represent the corresponding initial displacements.

of which the first term may be obtained from the second by <term>Stokes' rule</term> <note>original: "Stokes' rule"; A mathematical principle formulated by George Gabriel Stokes stating that the solution for a system starting with an initial displacement can be found by differentiating the solution for a system starting with an initial velocity.</note>.

**98.** The complete independence of the normal coordinates leads to an interesting theorem regarding the relationship between the subsequent motion and the initial disturbance. For if the forces acting upon the system are of such a character that they perform no work on the displacement indicated by $\delta \phi_1$, then $\Phi_1 = 0$. No such forces, regardless of how long they continue, can produce any effect on the motion $\phi_1$. If the motion exists, these forces cannot destroy it; if it does not exist, they cannot generate it. 

The most important application of this theorem occurs when the forces applied to the system act at a <term>node</term> <note>original: "node"; a point in a vibrating system that remains stationary during a particular mode of vibration</note> of the normal component $\phi_1$—that is, at a point which the specific component vibration in question does not tend to set in motion. Two extreme cases of such forces should be specifically noted: 

1. When the force is an impulse, starting the system from rest.
2. When the force has acted so long that the system is again at rest under its influence in a disturbed position. 

As soon as the force ceases, natural vibrations begin, and in the absence of friction, they would continue for an indefinite time. We can infer that, whatever their character may be in other respects, they contain no component of the type $\phi_1$. This conclusion is limited to cases where $T, F, \text{and } V$ <note>original: "$T, F, V$"; these represent the kinetic energy, the dissipation function (friction), and the potential energy of the system respectively</note> allow for simultaneous reduction, which includes, of course, the case where there is no friction.

**99.** The formulas cited in § 97 are applicable to any kind of force, but it will often happen that we have to deal only with the effects of <term>impressed forces</term> <note>external forces applied to a system from the outside</note> of the harmonic type. In these cases, we may more effectively employ the specific formulas designated for such forces. 

When using normal coordinates, we must first calculate the forces $\Phi_1, \Phi_2, \text{etc.}$ corresponding to each period, and from there determine the values of the coordinates themselves. If among the natural periods (calculated without accounting for friction) there are any that nearly match the period of an impressed force, the corresponding component vibrations will be unusually large—unless, of course, the force itself is greatly diminished during the initial analysis. Suppose, for example, that a transverse force of a harmonic type and a given period acts at a single point of a stretched string. Generally, all the normal modes of vibration will be excited, though not in their own natural periods, but...

<margin>99.</margin> in the period of the applied force; however, any normal component that has a <term>node</term> <note>original: "node"; a point in a vibrating system that remains stationary during a specific mode of vibration.</note> at the point where the force is applied will not be activated. The strength of each component depends on two factors: (1) the position of its nodes relative to the point where the force is applied, and (2) how closely its own natural period matches the period of the applied force. It is important to remember that when responding to a simple harmonic force, the system will generally vibrate in *all* of its possible modes, although in specific cases it may be enough to focus on only one mode of primary importance.

**100.** When the timing of the applied forces is very long compared to the natural vibration periods of the system, an "equilibrium theory" is sometimes sufficient. However, in such cases, the solution can usually be found more easily without using normal coordinates. Daniel Bernoulli’s <note>Daniel Bernoulli (1700–1782) was a Swiss mathematician who developed an early "equilibrium theory" of the tides in 1740.</note> theory of the tides is an example of this; it operates on the assumption that the natural vibration periods of the Earth's oceans are very short compared to the cycles of the forces acting upon them. If this were true, the water's <term>inertia</term> <note>original: "inertia"; the tendency of an object to resist changes in its state of rest or motion.</note> could be ignored. In reality, this assumption is only a very rough approximation, and we are consequently still unsure about many important points regarding the tides. The primary tidal forces have a <term>semi-diurnal</term> <note>original: "semi-diurnal"; occurring twice daily. The main lunar tide occurs roughly every 12.4 hours.</note> period, which is not long enough compared to the natural periods of the water to allow us to ignore inertia. However, if the Earth's rotation were much slower, the equilibrium theory of the tides might have been adequate.

A modified equilibrium theory is sometimes useful when the period of the applied force is long enough compared to *most* of the natural periods of a system, but not compared to one or two of them. It will be sufficient to look at a case where there is no friction. In the equation

-> $a\ddot{\phi} + c\phi = \Phi$, or $\ddot{\phi} + n^2\phi = \Phi/a$, <-

suppose that the applied force varies as $\cos pt$. Then

-> $\phi = \Phi \div a(n^2 - p^2) \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (1).$ <-

The equilibrium theory ignores $p^2$ in comparison with $n^2$, and assumes

-> $\phi = \Phi \div an^2 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (2).$ <-

Suppose now that this approach is justifiable, except for one specific <term>normal coordinate</term> <note>original: "normal co-ordinate"; a mathematical way of describing a complex vibration as a set of independent, simpler movements.</note>, $\phi_1$. In this case, we only need to add the difference between the actual value of $\phi_1$ and the value assumed by the equilibrium theory to our result: namely,

->$\phi_1 = \frac{\Phi_1}{a_1 (n_1^2 - p^2)} - \frac{\Phi_1}{a_1 n_1^2} = \frac{p^2}{n_1^2 - p^2} \cdot \frac{\Phi_1}{a} \dots\dots\dots\dots(3).$<-

We should also consider the opposite extreme case. If the forced vibrations are extremely rapid, they may become almost independent of the <term>potential energy</term> <note>original: "potential energy"; the stored energy in a system based on its position or configuration, such as a stretched spring.</note> of the system. Rather than ignoring $p^2$ relative to $n^2$, we ignore $n^2$ relative to $p^2$, which gives:

->$\phi = - \Phi \div ap^2 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(4).$<-

If there are one or two coordinates where this treatment does not work, we can take the result—calculated on the assumption that the potential energy ($V$) is completely negligible—and add corrections for those specific coordinates.

**101.** Before moving on to the general theory of vibrations in systems subject to <term>dissipation</term> <note>original: "dissipation"; the process where energy is lost from a vibrating system, typically through friction or heat.</note>, it is useful to highlight some unique features of the free vibrations of continuous systems that are triggered by a force applied at a single point. Using the assumptions and notation from Section 93, the configuration of the system at any given time is determined by:

->$\zeta = \phi_1 u_1 + \phi_2 u_2 + \phi_3 u_3 + \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(1),$<-

where the normal coordinates satisfy equations of the form:

->$a_r \ddot{\phi}_r + c_r \phi_r = \Phi_r \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(2).$<-

Now, suppose the system is held at rest by a force applied at point $Q$. We determine the value of $\Phi_r$ by considering that $\Phi_r \delta \phi_r$ represents the work done on the system by the <term>impressed forces</term> <note>original: "impressed forces"; external forces applied to a system.</note> during a hypothetical <term>displacement</term> <note>original: "displacement"; the distance an object has moved from its resting position.</note> $\delta \zeta = \delta \phi_r u_r$. That is:

->$\delta \phi_r \int Z u_r dx;$<-

thus,

->$\Phi_r = \int Z u_r dx = u_r (Q) \int Z dx;$<-

so that initially, according to equation (2):

->$c_r \phi_r = u_r (Q) \int Z dx \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(3).$<-

### SPECIAL INITIAL CONDITIONS.

If the system is released from this configuration at $t = 0$, we have at any subsequent time $t$:

->$\phi_r = \cos n_r t \frac{u_r(Q) \int Z dx}{c_r} = \cos n_r t \frac{u_r(Q) \int Z dx}{n_r^2 \int \rho u_r^2 dx} \dots \dots \dots (4),$<-

and at the point $P$:

->$\zeta = \Sigma \cos n_r t \frac{u_r(P) u_r(Q) \int Z dx}{n_r^2 \int \rho u_r^2 dx} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (5).$<-

At specific points $u_r(P)$ and $u_r(Q)$ vanish, but generally the expression

->$u_r(P) u_r(Q) \div \int \rho u_r^2 dx$<-

neither <term>converges</term> <note>original: "converges"; in mathematics, this refers to a series of numbers getting closer and closer to a specific finite value.</note> nor diverges as $r$ increases. The series for $\zeta$ <note>$\zeta$ (zeta) represents the displacement or movement of the system at point P.</note> therefore converges at the rate of $n_r^{-2}$.

Next, suppose that the system is started by an <term>impulse</term> <note>original: "impulse"; a sudden force applied over a very short interval of time, like a hammer strike.</note> from the configuration of <term>equilibrium</term> <note>original: "equilibrium"; the state where the system is at rest and all forces are balanced.</note>. In this case, the initial state is:

->$a_r \dot{\phi}_r = \int \Phi_r dt = u_r(Q) \int Z_1 dx,$<-

from which we find at time $t$:

->$\phi_r = \frac{\sin n_r t}{a_r n_r} \cdot u_r(Q) \cdot \int Z_1 dx = \frac{\sin n_r t \cdot u_r(Q)}{n_r \int \rho u_r^2 dx} \int Z_1 dx \dots \dots (6).$<-

This gives:

->$\zeta = \Sigma \sin n_r t \frac{u_r(P) u_r(Q) \int Z_1 dx}{n_r \int \rho u_r^2 dx} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (7),$<-

showing <note>original: "shewing"</note> that in this case, the series converges at the rate of $n_r^{-1}$, which is more slowly than in the previous case.

In both cases, it may be observed that the value of $\zeta$ is symmetrical with respect to points $P$ and $Q$. This proves that the displacement at point $P$ at time $t$ when the force or impulse is applied at $Q$ is the same as the displacement would be at $Q$ if the force or impulse had been applied at $P$. This is an example of a very general <term>reciprocal theorem</term> <note>original: "reciprocal theorem"; a fundamental principle in physics stating that the relationship between a cause (force) and an effect (displacement) is interchangeable between two points in a linear system.</note>, which we shall consider in detail presently.

As a third case, we can assume the body starts from rest after being deformed by a force spread evenly over its length, area, or volume. We find that:

->$\zeta = \Sigma \cos n_r t \frac{u_r(P) . Z . \int u_r dx}{n_r^2 \int \rho u_r^2 dx}$ ........................(8).<-

The mathematical series for $\zeta$ <note>$\zeta$ (zeta) represents the displacement or movement of the system at point P.</note> will <term>converge</term> <note>original: "be more convergent"; in mathematics, this means the later terms in the sum become small more quickly, making the total value easier to calculate.</note> more quickly than when the force is focused on a single point.

In exactly the same way, we can treat the case of a continuous body whose motion is subject to <term>dissipation</term> <note>original: "dissipation"; the loss of energy, usually through friction or heat.</note>, provided that the three <term>mechanical functions</term> <note>original: "mechanical functions"; here, $T$ represents kinetic energy, $V$ potential energy, and $F$ the dissipation function.</note> $T$, $F$, and $V$ can be simplified at the same time. However, it is not necessary to write down the formulas here.

## 102.

If the three mechanical functions $T$, $F$, and $V$ of any system cannot be simplified together, the natural vibrations (as has already been observed) are more complex in their character. However, when the dissipation is small, the method of simplification is still useful. This class of cases is important in itself and serves as a good introduction to the more general theory. We assume then that $T$ and $V$ are expressed as sums of squares:

->$\left. \begin{aligned} T &= \frac{1}{2} a_1 \dot{\phi}_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} a_2 \dot{\phi}_2^2 + \dots \\ V &= \frac{1}{2} c_1 \phi_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} c_2 \phi_2^2 + \dots \end{aligned} \right\}$ ........................(1),<-

while $F$ still appears in a more general form:

->$F = \frac{1}{2} b_{11} \dot{\phi}_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} b_{22} \dot{\phi}_2^2 + \dots + b_{12} \dot{\phi}_1 \dot{\phi}_2 + \dots$ ............(2).<-

The <term>equations of motion</term> <note>original: "equations of motion"; the mathematical descriptions of how the system changes over time based on the forces acting upon it.</note> are accordingly:

->$\left. \begin{aligned} a_1 \ddot{\phi}_1 + b_{11} \dot{\phi}_1 + b_{12} \dot{\phi}_2 + b_{13} \dot{\phi}_3 + \dots + c_1 \phi_1 &= 0 \\ a_2 \ddot{\phi}_2 + b_{21} \dot{\phi}_1 + b_{22} \dot{\phi}_2 + b_{23} \dot{\phi}_3 + \dots + c_2 \phi_2 &= 0 \\ \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \end{aligned} \right\}$ ............(3),<-

in which the <term>coefficients</term> <note>original: "coefficients"; the constant values, such as $b_{11}$ or $b_{12}$, that multiply the variables in an equation.</note> $b_{11}$, $b_{12}$, etc., are to be treated as small. If there were no <term>friction</term> <note>original: "friction"; resistance to motion that slows down the system.</note>, the system of equations above would be satisfied by assuming that one <term>coordinate</term> <note>original: "co-ordinate"; a variable, such as $\phi$, used to specify the position or state of the system.</note> $\phi_r$ changes appropriately while the other coordinates remain at zero. In the actual case, there will be a corresponding solution in which the value of any other coordinate $\phi_s$ will be very small compared to $\phi_r$.

Therefore, if we ignore the very smallest terms (those of the "second order"), the $r^{\text{th}}$ equation becomes:

->$a_r \ddot{\phi}_r + b_{rr} \dot{\phi}_r + c_r \phi_r = 0$ ........................(4).<-

# SMALL DISSIPATIVE FORCES <note>original: "dissipative forces"; forces like friction or air resistance that cause a system to lose energy, usually as heat.</note>

<margin>102.</margin>

From this, we infer that $\phi_r$ <note>$\phi_r$ (phi) represents a specific coordinate or mode of vibration.</note> varies approximately as if there were no change in the pattern of vibration due to friction. If $\phi_r$ varies according to $e^{p_r t}$ <note>This mathematical expression describes a vibration that gradually dies out over time ($t$).</note>, we determine $p_r$ using the following equation:

-> $a_r p_r^2 + b_{rr} p_r + c_r = 0$ ........................ (5). <-

The roots <note>The solutions to the equation.</note> of this equation are complex numbers, but the real part is small compared to the imaginary part. [The nature of the motion represented by equation (5) has already been discussed (Section 45). The rate at which the vibrations die down is proportional to $b_{rr}$ <note>$b_{rr}$ represents the coefficient of resistance.</note>, and the period—if we still use that term—is approximately the same as if there were no energy loss.]

From the $s^{\text{th}}$ equation, if we assume that all the coordinates vary according to $e^{p_r t}$, we get:

-> $(p_r^2 a_s + c_s) \phi_s + b_{rs} p_r \phi_r = 0$, <-

omitting terms of the second order; from which we find:

-> $\phi_s : \phi_r = - \frac{b_{rs} p_r}{p_r^2 a_s + c_s} = \frac{b_{rs} p_r}{a_s (p_s^2 - p_r^2)}$ .........(6). <-

This equation determines approximately how the pattern of vibration is altered. Since the main part of $p_r$ is <term>imaginary</term> <note>In the mathematics of physics, the "imaginary" part of a number often represents the frequency of an oscillation, while the "real" part represents how fast it fades away.</note>, we see that the coordinates $\phi_s$ are approximately in the same phase, but that *that phase differs by a quarter-period from the phase of* $\phi_r$. Therefore, when the resistance function $F$ cannot be simplified into a basic sum of squares, the character of the elementary modes of vibration is less simple than it would be otherwise, and the various parts of the system no longer reach their peak displacement at the same time.

We proved above that when friction is small, the value of $p_r$ may be calculated approximately without accounting for the change in the vibration pattern. However, by using equation (6), we can obtain an even closer approximation that includes the squares of the small quantities. The $r^{\text{th}}$ equation (3) gives:

-> $a_r p_r^2 + c_r + b_{rr} p_r + \Sigma \frac{p_r^2 b_{rs}^2}{a_s (p_s^2 - p_r^2)} = 0$ ................ (7). <-
<note>$\Sigma$ (Sigma) is the Greek letter used to indicate a mathematical sum.</note>

Because the primary part of the terms included under the sum ($\Sigma$) is a real number, the correction has no effect on the real part of $p_r$, which is the part that determines the rate of decay.

**102 *a*.** Following an analogy with electricity, we may conveniently describe the forces expressed by $F$ as forces of resistance. In Section 102, we have seen that if the resistances are small, the timing of the cycles (the periods) is independent of them. We may therefore extend to this case...

# VIBRATING SYSTEMS IN GENERAL. [102 a.

We can apply the theorems regarding how adding to kinetic energy ($T$) and potential energy ($V$) affects the periods of vibration, which have already been proven for systems without resistance.

By equation (5) in Section 102, if the resisting forces are increased, the rates at which all standard patterns of vibration die out <note>original: "rates of subsidence"</note> generally increase along with them. However, in specific cases, it may happen that the rate at which a vibration fades remains unchanged.

It is natural to ask whether this conclusion is limited only to *small* resistances, as at first glance it seems likely to hold true generally. An argument sufficient to decide this question can be based on a specific example. Imagine a system formed by attaching two weights at any points along a stretched string vibrating side-to-side. If we ignore the mass of the string itself, there are two <term>degrees of freedom</term> <note>The number of independent ways a system can move.</note> and two vibration periods corresponding to two <term>normal modes</term> <note>The natural patterns in which a system prefers to vibrate.</note>. In each of these modes, both weights generally vibrate. 

Now, suppose a resisting force is introduced that slows down the motion of *one* of the weights, and this force gradually increases. At first, the effect is to cause both types of vibration to die out at an increasing rate, but eventually, the rule changes. When the resistance becomes infinite, it acts as a <term>constraint</term> <note>A physical limit that prevents motion; here, it holds the weight perfectly still.</note>, holding the weight it acts upon completely at rest. Because that weight is no longer moving, the remaining vibration is unaffected by that resistance and maintains itself indefinitely. Thus, the rate at which one of the vibration patterns dies out has decreased until it vanished <note>original: "evanescence"</note>, despite a continual increase in the resisting forces ($F$). This case is, of course, enough to disprove the suggested general rule.

**103.** We now return to the consideration of the general equations from Section 84.

->$\left. \begin{aligned} e_{11}\psi_1 + e_{12}\psi_2 + \dots &= \Psi_1 \\ e_{21}\psi_1 + e_{22}\psi_2 + \dots &= \Psi_2, \text{etc.} \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(1),$<-

where

->$e_{rs} = a_{rs}D^2 + b_{rs}D + c_{rs} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(2).$<-
<note>In this equation, $D$ represents the rate of change over time. $a$ represents mass/inertia, $b$ represents resistance/friction, and $c$ represents stiffness/elasticity.</note>

For free vibrations, the forces ($\Psi_1, \text{etc.}$) vanish. If $\nabla$ <note>The symbol $\nabla$ (nabla) here represents the determinant, a mathematical value used to solve systems of simultaneous equations.</note> is the determinant:

# GENERAL EQUATIONS.

The result of removing all but one of the coordinates from equation (1) is:
->$\nabla \psi = 0$..........................................(4).<-

Because the <term>differential operator</term> $\nabla$ <note>A mathematical symbol representing a sequence of operations like differentiation.</note> now contains odd powers of the rate of change $D$, the $2m$ roots of the equation $\nabla = 0$ no longer appear in equal pairs of positive and negative numbers. Instead, they contain both a real part and an <term>imaginary part</term> <note>A component of a complex number involving the square root of -1.</note>. However, the complete solution (the integral) may still be written as:
->$\psi = A e^{\mu_1 t} + A' e^{\mu_1' t} + B e^{\mu_2 t} + B' e^{\mu_2' t} + \dots$............(5),<-
where the pairs of <term>conjugate roots</term> <note>Complex numbers that come in pairs, such as $a + bi$ and $a - bi$.</note> are $\mu_1, \mu_1'$; $\mu_2, \mu_2'$; etc. Corresponding to each root, there is a particular solution such as:
->$\psi_1 = A_1 e^{\mu t}, \quad \psi_2 = A_2 e^{\mu t}, \quad \psi_3 = A_3 e^{\mu t}, \text{ etc.},$<-
in which the ratios $A_1 : A_2 : A_3 \dots$ are determined by the equations of motion, and only the absolute value remains flexible. In this case, however (where $\nabla$ contains odd powers of $D$), these ratios are generally not real numbers. Therefore, the changes in the coordinates $\psi_1, \psi_2, \text{ etc.}$ do not happen at exactly the same time—they are not **synchronous in phase**. If we write the root as $\mu_1 = \alpha_1 + i\beta_1$ and $\mu_1' = \alpha_1 - i\beta_1$, we see that none of the values for $\alpha$ (the real part) can be positive. If they were, the energy of the motion would increase over time, which we know is impossible in a system with resistance.

**103 $a$.** The general argument (from Sections 85 and 103) regarding how energy considerations affect the roots of the <term>determinantal equation</term> <note>The characteristic equation used to find the natural frequencies of a system.</note> (found in Thomson and Tait's *Natural Philosophy*, 1st edition 1867) has been expressed in a more mathematical form by Edward Routh$^1$. His investigation relates to the most general form of the equation where the symmetry relations described in Section 82:
->$a_{rs} = a_{sr}, \quad b_{rs} = b_{sr}, \quad c_{rs} = c_{sr}$ ...................(1),<-
are not assumed to be true. But for the sake of being brief, and because it is sufficient for almost all acoustical problems, these relations will be assumed to hold here.

We will need to consider two solutions corresponding to two roots, $\mu$ and $\nu$, of the equation. For the first root, we have:
->$\psi_1 = M_1 e^{\mu t}, \quad \psi_2 = M_2 e^{\mu t}, \quad \psi_3 = M_3 e^{\mu t}, \text{ etc.} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (2),$<-
and for the second root:
->$\psi_1 = N_1 e^{\nu t}, \quad \psi_2 = N_2 e^{\nu t}, \quad \psi_3 = N_3 e^{\nu t}, \text{ etc.} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (3).$<-
In either of these solutions, for example solution (2), the ratios:
->$M_1 : M_2 : M_3 : \dots \dots$<-

## VIBRATING SYSTEMS IN GENERAL.

The ratios of the coordinates are fixed once $\mu$ has been chosen. These ratios are real when $\mu$ is real; however, when $\mu$ is a complex number ($\alpha \pm i\beta$), the ratios take the form $P \pm iQ$.

If we now substitute the values of $\psi$ from equation (2) <note>Referring to the general solution for displacement over time mentioned on the previous page.</note> into the equations of motion, we obtain:

> $(a_{11}\mu^2 + b_{11}\mu + c_{11}) M_1 + (a_{12}\mu^2 + b_{12}\mu + c_{12}) M_2 + \dots = 0$
>
> $(a_{12}\mu^2 + b_{12}\mu + c_{12}) M_1 + (a_{22}\mu^2 + b_{22}\mu + c_{22}) M_2 + \dots = 0$
>
> $\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots$
<note>The three lines above represent a system of linear equations, grouped together as equation (4).</note>

The first result is obtained by multiplying these equations in order by $M_1$, $M_2$, etc., and then adding them together. This can be written as:

-> $A\mu^2 + B\mu + C = 0, \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots$ (5), <-

where

-> $A = \frac{1}{2}a_{11}M_1^2 + \frac{1}{2}a_{22}M_2^2 + a_{12}M_1M_2 + \dots\dots\dots\dots$ (6), <-
-> $B = \frac{1}{2}b_{11}M_1^2 + \frac{1}{2}b_{22}M_2^2 + b_{12}M_1M_2 + \dots\dots\dots\dots$ (7), <-
-> $C = \frac{1}{2}c_{11}M_1^2 + \frac{1}{2}c_{22}M_2^2 + c_{12}M_1M_2 + \dots\dots\dots\dots$ (8). <-

It will be observed that the functions $A, B$, and $C$ are the same as those we previously identified as $T$ (kinetic energy), $F$ (the dissipation function), and $V$ (potential energy), respectively. However, this change in notation is useful to remind us that, for now, we have placed no restrictions on the mathematical nature of these <term>quadratic functions</term> <note>Functions where the variables are squared or multiplied by each other, typically representing energy in physical systems.</note>.

The following conclusions from equation (5) are drawn by <term>Routh</term> <note>Edward John Routh (1831–1907), an English mathematician famous for his work on the stability of mechanical systems.</note>:

($\alpha$) If $A, B$, and $C$ are either zero or <term>one-signed functions</term> <note>Functions that always yield a result with the same sign (all positive or all negative).</note> of the same sign, the <term>fundamental determinant</term> <note>The characteristic equation used to solve for the system's natural frequencies and stability.</note> cannot have a real positive root. This is because if $\mu$ were real, the coefficients $M_1, M_2, \dots$ would also be real. Consequently, we would be claiming that the sum of three positive quantities is equal to zero, which is impossible.

($\beta$) If there are no <term>forces of resistance</term> <note>Damping or friction that removes energy from the system.</note>—meaning the term $B$ is absent—and if $A$ and $C$ are one-signed and share the same sign, the fundamental determinant cannot have any real root, whether positive or negative.

($\gamma$) If $A, B$, and $C$ are all one-signed functions, but the sign of $B$ is the opposite of $A$ and $C$, the fundamental determinant cannot have a real negative root.

The second equation is obtained from equation (4) in the same manner as before, except that the multipliers used are $N_1, N_2, \dots$, which correspond to a different root, $\nu$. The result may be written as:

-> $A(\mu, \nu)\mu^2 + B(\mu, \nu)\mu + C(\mu, \nu) = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots$(9), <-

where

-> $2A(\mu, \nu) = a_{11}M_1N_1 + a_{22}M_2N_2 + \dots\dots$ <-
-> $+ a_{12}(M_1N_2 + M_2N_1) + \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots$(10). <-

### ROUTH'S THEOREMS.

Using similar assumptions for $B(\mu, \nu)$ and $C(\mu, \nu)$, we find that $A(\mu, \nu)$ is a symmetrical function of the $M$ and $N$ values <note>The $M$ and $N$ values represent the relative amplitudes of the coordinates for the different modes of vibration associated with roots $\mu$ and $\nu$.</note>, so that:

-> $A(\mu, \nu) = A(\nu, \mu)$ ........................(11). <-

It should be noted that according to this notation, $A(\mu, \mu)$ is the same as the function $A$ in equation (6) on the previous page.

In a similar way, we can show that:
-> $A(\mu, \nu) \nu^2 + B(\mu, \nu) \nu + C(\mu, \nu) = 0$ ....................(12), <-
showing that both $\mu$ and $\nu$ are roots of the quadratic equation whose coefficients are $A(\mu, \nu), B(\mu, \nu),$ and $C(\mu, \nu)$. Accordingly:
-> $\mu + \nu = - \frac{B(\mu, \nu)}{A(\mu, \nu)}, \quad \mu\nu = \frac{C(\mu, \nu)}{A(\mu, \nu)}$ ....................(13). <-

We will now assume that $\mu$ and $\nu$ are two conjugate complex roots <note>original: "conjugate complex roots"; these are pairs of numbers in the form $\alpha + i\beta$ and $\alpha - i\beta$, where $i$ is the imaginary unit $\sqrt{-1}$.</note>, so that:
-> $\mu = \alpha + i\beta, \quad \nu = \alpha - i\beta,$ <-
where $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are real numbers. Under these circumstances, if $M_1, M_2, \dots$ are represented as $P_1 + iQ_1, P_2 + iQ_2, \dots$, then $N_1, N_2, \dots$ will be $P_1 - iQ_1, P_2 - iQ_2, \dots$, where the $P$ and $Q$ values are real. Thus, by equation (10):
-> $2A(\mu, \nu) = a_{11}(P_1^2 + Q_1^2) + a_{22}(P_2^2 + Q_2^2) + \dots \dots$ <-
-> $+ 2a_{12}(P_1P_2 + Q_1Q_2) + \dots \dots$ <-
-> $= 2A(P) + 2A(Q)$ ........................(14). <-

In equation (14), $A(P)$ and $A(Q)$ are functions of real variables, similar to equation (6). From equation (13), we now find:
-> $2\alpha = - \frac{B(P) + B(Q)}{A(P) + A(Q)}$ ........................(15), <-
-> $\alpha^2 + \beta^2 = \frac{C(P) + C(Q)}{A(P) + A(Q)}$ ........................(16). <-

From these results, Routh deduces the following conclusions:

($\delta$) If $A$ and $B$ are "one-signed" <note>original: "one-signed"; in modern terms, "definite," meaning the function always returns a value with the same sign (always positive or always negative) regardless of the input variables.</note> and have the same sign (regardless of whether $C$ is a one-signed function or not), then the real part $\alpha$ of every complex root <note>original: "imaginary root"; here meaning a root with an imaginary component.</note> must be negative and cannot be zero. However, if $B$ (the dissipation or damping function) is absent, then the real part of every complex root is zero. <note>This implies that if there is no damping, the oscillations neither grow nor decay over time.</note>

($\epsilon$) If $A$ and $C$ are one-signed but have opposite signs, then regardless of the nature of $B$, there can be no complex roots. <note>This indicates that the system will likely experience pure exponential growth or decay rather than oscillating.</note>

It may be noted that if $B$ does not occur, and if $\mu^2$ and $\nu^2$ are different roots of the determinant, it follows from equations (9) and (12) that:
-> $A(\mu, \nu) = C(\mu, \nu) = 0$........................(17). <-

# VIBRATING SYSTEMS IN GENERAL. [103 a.

When the number of degrees of freedom <note>Degrees of freedom refer to the number of independent ways a system can move.</note> is finite, the fundamental determinant <note>The fundamental determinant is the mathematical expression used to find the characteristic equation of the system.</note> may be expanded in powers of $\mu$, giving an equation $f(\mu) = 0$ of degree $2m$. The condition for stability is that all the real roots and the real parts of all the complex roots should be negative. If, as is common, complex quantities $x + iy$ are represented by points with coordinates $x, y$, the condition is that all points representing roots should lie to the left of the $y$-axis. The application of Cauchy's rule <note>original: "Cauchy's rule"; a mathematical theorem used to determine the number of roots of a function within a certain boundary or contour.</note> regarding the number of roots within any contour, by taking an infinite semi-circle on the positive side of the $y$-axis as the contour, is discussed very fully by Routh$^1$. He has presented the results in forms convenient for practical application to particular cases.

## **103 b.**
The theorems of § 103 $a$ do not exhaust all that general mechanical principles would lead us to expect regarding the character of the roots of the fundamental determinant, and it may be beneficial to pursue the question a little further. We will suppose throughout that $A$ is one-signed <note>original: "one-signed"; meaning the value remains either entirely positive or entirely negative, regardless of the variables (positive definite).</note> and positive.

If $B$ and $C$ are both one-signed and positive, we see that the equilibrium is thoroughly stable; for from equation ($\alpha$) it follows that there can be no positive root, and from equation ($\delta$) that no complex root can have a positive real part.

In like manner, the equations of § 103 $a$ are sufficient for the case where $C$ is one-signed and positive, and $B$ is one-signed and negative. By equation (5), every real root is positive, as is the real part of every complex root according to equation (15). Hence, the equilibrium is unstable in *every mode*.

When $C$ is one-signed and negative, all the roots are real (see $\delta$); but equation (5) does not tell us whether they are positive or negative. When $B = 0$, we know (§ 87) that the roots occur in pairs of equal numerical value but with opposite signs. In this case, therefore, there are $m$ positive and $m$ negative roots. We will prove that this state of things cannot be disturbed by $B$. For if the determinant is expanded, the coefficient of $\mu^{2m}$ is the discriminant <note>The discriminant is a specific value calculated from the coefficients of a polynomial that provides information about the roots.</note> of $A$, and the coefficient of $\mu^0$ (the constant term) is the discriminant of $C$. By our assumption, neither of these quantities is zero, and thus no root of the equation can be anything other than finite. Hence, as $B$ increases from zero to its actual magnitude as a function of the variables, no root of the equation can change sign, and accordingly, there remain $m$

In the case of a real root, the values of *M*₁, *M*₂, ... are real. This means the motion is such as might occur under a constraint that reduces the system to a single degree of freedom <note>Degrees of freedom refer to the number of independent ways a system can move.</note>. But if this constraint were actually applied, there would be *two* corresponding values for $\mu$, which are the values provided by equation (5). Generally, only one of these applies to the problem at hand. Otherwise, it would be possible to define *m* types of constraint, where any one of them would be consistent with any of the 2*m* roots. However, this can only happen when the *three* functions *A*, *B*, and *C* can all be simplified into sums of squares at the same time (see § 97).

When *B* = 0, there are *m* modes of motion, and two roots for each mode. In this specific application, where *C* is one-signed <note>original: "one-signed"; meaning the function consistently yields values of only one sign—in this case, always negative.</note> and negative, each of the *m* modes for *B* = 0 produces one positive and one negative root. The positive root indicates instability. Even though the negative root describes a motion that fades away completely, the quality of instability is considered to belong to the mode as a whole, and all *m* modes are said to be unstable. However, when *B* is a finite value, there are generally 2*m* distinct modes, with one root corresponding to each. Of these 2*m* modes, *m* are unstable, while the remaining *m* modes must be considered stable. Overall, however, the equilibrium is unstable; the influence of *B*—even when it is positive—is not enough to prevent <note>original: "obviate"; to remove or avoid a difficulty.</note> the instability caused by the nature of *C*.

We should not dwell much longer on our discussion of unstable systems, but there is one theorem regarding real roots that is too fundamental to be skipped. It may be viewed as an extension of the theorem discussed in § 88.

The value of $\mu$ corresponding to a specific constraint *M*₁ : *M*₂ : ... is one of the roots of equation (5). It follows from equation (4) that the value of $\mu$ is stationary <note>original: "stationary value"; a point in a mathematical function where the rate of change is zero, often representing a peak, valley, or balance point.</note> when the applied constraint matches one of the modes of free motion. The effect of small changes in *A*, *B*, and *C* may therefore be calculated from equation (5) without needing to account for the resulting change in the type of motion.

This latter condition requires that the roots of equation (5)—one of which is positive and one negative—must move either both toward zero or both away from zero. ### VIBRATING SYSTEMS IN GENERAL.

By examining whether we use the positive or the negative root of equation (5)—which is the root of the determinant <note>In linear algebra, a determinant is a scalar value that provides information about a matrix of coefficients, used here to find the system's natural frequencies.</note>—we can conclude that the change in question causes the root to move further away from zero.

In the same way, if *A* <note>Likely representing inertia or mass.</note> increases while *B* <note>Likely representing friction or damping.</note> and *C* <note>Likely representing stiffness or potential energy.</note> remain unchanged, the movement of the root, whether it is positive or negative, is inevitably toward zero.

Furthermore, if *A* and *C* are held constant while *B* increases mathematically as a function of the variables, the movement of the determinant's root must be in the positive direction.

Therefore, a mathematical increase in *B* increases the stability (or decreases the instability) in every mode of vibration. On the other hand, a numerical increase in *C* or a decrease in *A* promotes the stability of the stable modes and increases the instability of the unstable modes.

We can do little more than briefly mention the theorem regarding the effect of a single constraint <note>A physical restriction that limits the ways a system can move.</note> upon a system where *C* is consistently negative <note>original: "one-signed and negative."</note>. Regardless of the nature of *B*, the (*m* - 1) positive roots of the determinant—calculated for the system after the constraint is applied—will fall between the original *m* positive roots. A similar rule applies to the negative roots. 

Based on this, we can form a general conclusion similar to that found in Section 92a. Consider an independent vibrator with one degree of freedom <note>The number of independent ways a system can move.</note> where *C* is positive, and let the roots of its frequency equation be $\nu_1$ <note>The Greek letter nu.</note> and $\nu_2$, where one is negative and one is positive. If we treat this vibrator as part of the larger system, we have (2*m* + 2) roots in total. The effect of applying a constraint to connect these two parts of the system will be to reduce the (2*m* + 2) roots back down to 2*m*. Of these, the *m* positive roots will fall between the (*m* + 1) quantities made up of the original *m* positive roots plus the new positive root $\nu_2$. The same principle holds for the negative roots. The effect of adding the vibrator to the original system is thus to cause the positive roots to move toward $\nu_2$ and the negative roots to move toward $\nu_1$. This conclusion accounts for all previous statements regarding how changes in *A*, *B*, and *C* affect the values of the roots.

We have now said enough regarding the free vibrations of a system in general. Any further explanation required will be provided by the discussion of systems with two degrees of freedom in Section 112, and by the study of vibrating strings and other specific objects that we will soon examine. # FORCED VIBRATIONS.

We consider the equations (1) from § 103, with the goal of further investigating the nature of *forced vibrations* <note>Vibrations maintained by an external, periodic force, rather than the system's own natural internal energy.</note>.

**104** To eliminate all coordinates from the equations except for one ($\psi_1$), apply the minor determinants <note>A minor determinant is the value of a smaller matrix created by deleting one or more rows and columns from a larger square matrix; they are used here to solve systems of linear equations.</note> in sequence:
->$\frac{d\nabla}{de_{11}}, \frac{d\nabla}{de_{21}}, \frac{d\nabla}{de_{31}},$ etc.,<-
and add the results together. Do the same for the other coordinates. We thus obtain the following as the equivalent of the original system of equations:

$$\left. \begin{aligned} \nabla \psi_1 = \frac{d\nabla}{de_{11}} \Psi_1 + \frac{d\nabla}{de_{21}} \Psi_2 + \frac{d\nabla}{de_{31}} \Psi_3 + \dots \\ \nabla \psi_2 = \frac{d\nabla}{de_{12}} \Psi_1 + \frac{d\nabla}{de_{22}} \Psi_2 + \frac{d\nabla}{de_{32}} \Psi_3 + \dots \\ \nabla \psi_3 = \frac{d\nabla}{de_{13}} \Psi_1 + \frac{d\nabla}{de_{23}} \Psi_2 + \frac{d\nabla}{de_{33}} \Psi_3 + \dots \\ \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots (1),$$

In these equations, the differentiations of $\nabla$ are to be performed without assuming the equality existing between $e_{rs}$ and $e_{sr}$ <note>The author is treating the matrix elements as independent variables during the differentiation process before applying the symmetry of the physical system.</note>.

The forces $\Psi_1, \Psi_2,$ etc., may be any forces at all, provided they do not produce such a large displacement or motion that the squares of the small quantities become significant. If, as is often the case, the forces acting on the system are composed of two parts—one constant with respect to time and the other periodic—it is convenient to mentally separate the two types of effects produced. The effect caused by the constant forces is exactly the same as if they acted alone, and is found by solving a statical problem. Therefore, it will generally be sufficient to assume the forces are periodic. The effects of any constant forces, such as gravity, merely change the configuration around which the actual vibrations are performed. We may thus, without any real loss of generality, limit ourselves to periodic forces, and therefore—by Fourier's theorem <note>A mathematical principle stating that any periodic function can be represented as a sum of simple sine and cosine waves.</note>—to harmonic forces.

We could, therefore, use trigonometric functions <note>original: "circular functions"</note> of time to represent $\Psi_1,$ etc.; but, as we will frequently notice throughout this work, it is usually more convenient to use an imaginary exponential function, such as $Ee^{ipt}$, where $E$ is a constant that may be a complex number. # VIBRATING SYSTEMS IN GENERAL.

Once a corresponding symbolic solution <note>A "symbolic solution" refers to the method of using complex exponentials (like $e^{ipt}$) to represent oscillating systems, simplifying calculus into algebra.</note> is obtained, its real and imaginary parts may be separated; these parts belong respectively to the real and imaginary components of the data. In this way, the analysis becomes much more brief, since differentiation and changes in phase are expressed merely by modifying the complex coefficient without changing the form of the function. We therefore write:

->$\Psi_1 = E_1 e^{ipt}, \quad \Psi_2 = E_2 e^{ipt}, \text{ etc.}$<-

The minor determinants of the type $\frac{d\nabla}{de_{rs}}$ are polynomial functions <note>original: "rational integral functions"</note> of the operator $D$, and act on $\Psi_1$, etc., according to the rule:

->$f(D) e^{ipt} = f(ip) e^{ipt} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (2).$<-

Our equations therefore take the form:

->$\nabla \psi_1 = A_1 e^{ipt}, \quad \nabla \psi_2 = A_2 e^{ipt}, \text{ etc.} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (3),$<-

where $A_1, A_2,$ etc., are certain complex constants. And the symbolic solutions are:

->$\psi_1 = A_1 \nabla^{-1} e^{ipt}, \text{ etc.},$<-

or by equation (2),

->$\psi_1 = A_1 \frac{e^{ipt}}{\nabla(ip)}, \text{ etc.} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (4),$<-

where $\nabla(ip)$ denotes the result of substituting $ip$ for $D$ in $\nabla$.

Consider first the case of a system without friction. $\nabla$ and its derivatives are then *even* functions of $D$, so that $\nabla(ip)$ is real. By discarding the imaginary part of the solution and writing $R_1 e^{i\theta_1}$ for $A_1$, etc., we have:

->$\psi_1 = \frac{R_1}{\nabla(ip)} \cos(pt + \theta_1), \text{ etc.} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (5).$<-

If we assume that the forces $\Psi_1,$ etc. (in the case of more than one generalized component <note>A "generalized component" of force refers to the force associated with a specific coordinate in a complex system.</note>), all have the same phase, they may be expressed by:

->$E_1 \cos(pt + \alpha), \quad E_2 \cos(pt + \alpha), \text{ etc.};$<-

and then, as is easily seen, the coordinates themselves agree in phase with the forces:

->$\psi_1 = \frac{R_1}{\nabla(ip)} \cos(pt + \alpha) \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (6).$<-

The amplitudes of the vibrations depend, among other things, on the magnitude of $\nabla(ip)$. Now, if the period of the forces...

# FORCED VIBRATIONS.

If the frequency of the force happens to be the same as one of the natural frequencies belonging to the free vibrations, then $\nabla (ip) = 0$, and the amplitude of the vibration becomes infinite. This is, of course, the exact case where it is essential to consider the role of friction, from which no physical system is truly exempt.

If there is friction, the expression $\nabla (ip)$ is complex; however, it may be divided into two parts—one real and the other purely imaginary—where the latter depends entirely on the friction. Thus, if we set:
->$\nabla (ip) = \nabla_1 (ip) + ip \nabla_2 (ip) \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (7),$<-
$\nabla_1$ and $\nabla_2$ are even functions <note>An "even function" is one where the variable (here $ip$) only appears in even powers, meaning the result remains real even when the input is imaginary.</note> of $ip$, and are therefore real. If, as before, $A_1 = R_1 e^{i\theta_1}$, our solution takes the following form:
->$\psi_1 = \frac{R_1 e^{i\theta_1} e^{i\gamma} e^{ipt}}{\{\nabla_1 (ip)^2 + p^2 \nabla_2 (ip)^2\}^{\frac{1}{2}}},$<-
or, by discarding the imaginary part,
->$\psi_1 = \frac{R_1 \cos (pt + \theta_1 + \gamma)}{\{\nabla_1 (ip)^2 + p^2 \nabla_2 (ip)^2\}^{\frac{1}{2}}} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (8),$<-
where
->$\tan \gamma = - \frac{p \nabla_2 (ip)}{\nabla_1 (ip)} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (9).$<-

We have stated that $\nabla_2 (ip)$ depends entirely on friction; however, it is not true, on the other hand, that $\nabla_1 (ip)$ is exactly the same as it would have been if there were no friction. Nevertheless, this is approximately the case if the friction is small, because any part of $\nabla (ip)$ that depends on the first power of the coefficients of friction is necessarily imaginary. Whenever there is a coincidence between the period <note>The "period" refers to the time it takes for one full vibration; a coincidence of periods is what we now commonly call resonance.</note> of the force and that of one of the free vibrations, $\nabla_1 (ip)$ vanishes, and we find that $\tan \gamma = - \infty$. Therefore:
->$\psi_1 = \frac{R_1 \sin (pt + \theta_1)}{p \nabla_2 (ip)} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (10),$<-
This indicates a vibration with a large amplitude, limited only by the friction.

Assuming that friction is small, the angle $\theta$ is generally small, and so is $\gamma$, except in cases where the periods are approximately equal. With certain exceptions, therefore, the resulting motion has nearly the same (or opposite) phase as the force that excites it.

When a force expressed by a harmonic term <note>A "harmonic term" refers to a force that follows a smooth, repetitive sine or cosine wave pattern.</note> acts on a system, the resulting motion is everywhere harmonic and retains the original period, provided always that the squares of the displacements—
