If the force is not a harmonic function of time, the types of vibration in different parts of the system are generally different from each other and from the force itself. Harmonic functions are therefore the only ones that keep their "type" (their wave shape and frequency) unchanged. As was noted in the Introduction, this is a strong reason to expect that they correspond to simple tones <note>A "simple tone" refers to a pure sound wave, like a sine wave, consisting of a single frequency.</note>.

**105.** We now turn to a slightly different kind of forced vibration. Instead of using given forces as we have done so far, we will now look at cases where specific, unavoidable <term>inexorable: movements that must occur exactly as specified, regardless of the other forces in the system</term> motions are prescribed.

If we assume that the coordinates $\psi_1, \psi_2, \dots \psi_r$ are given functions of time, while the forces of the remaining types $\Psi_{r+1}, \Psi_{r+2}, \dots \Psi_m$ are zero, the equations of motion divide themselves into two groups:

$$\left. \begin{aligned} e_{11} \psi_1 + e_{12} \psi_2 + \dots + e_{1m} \psi_m &= \Psi_1 \\ e_{21} \psi_1 + e_{22} \psi_2 + \dots + e_{2m} \psi_m &= \Psi_2 \\ \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \\ e_{r1} \psi_1 + e_{r2} \psi_2 + \dots + e_{rm} \psi_m &= \Psi_r \end{aligned} \right\} \dots \dots \dots \dots (1);$$

and

$$\left. \begin{aligned} e_{r+1, 1} \psi_1 + e_{r+1, 2} \dots + e_{r+1, m} \psi_m &= 0 \\ \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \\ e_{m1} \quad \psi_1 + e_{m2} \quad \psi_2 + \dots + e_{mm} \quad \psi_m &= 0 \end{aligned} \right\} \dots \dots \dots \dots (2).$$

In each of the $m - r$ equations in the second group, the first $r$ terms are known, explicit functions of time. They have the same effect as known forces acting on the system. Therefore, the equations in this group are sufficient to determine the unknown quantities. After that, if necessary, the forces required to maintain the prescribed motion can be determined from the first group. It is obvious that there is no fundamental difference between these two classes of forced vibration problems.

**106.** When a system has no friction and performs simple harmonic vibrations because certain coordinates are forced to change, it has a specific characteristic similar to those discussed in sections 74 and 79. Let:
$$\psi_1 = A_1 \cos pt, \quad \psi_2 = A_2 \cos pt, \text{ etc.}$$

# INEXORABLE MOTIONS.

In this context, the quantities **A₁... Aᵣ** <note>These represent the amplitudes of the prescribed or "inexorable" motions.</note> are regarded as given, while the remaining ones are arbitrary. From the expressions for **T** (kinetic energy) and **V** (potential energy) in § 82, we have:

**2 (T + V) = ½ (c₁₁ + p² a₁₁) A₁² + ... + (c₁₂ + p² a₁₂) A₁ A₂ + ...**
->**+ { ½ (c₁₁ - p² a₁₁) A₁² + ... + (c₁₂ - p² a₁₂) A₁ A₂ + ... } cos 2pt,**<-

From this, we can see that the equations of motion express a specific condition: the variable part of the total energy **T + V**, which we will call **E**, is proportional to:
->**½ (c₁₁ - p² a₁₁) A₁² + ... + (c₁₂ - p² a₁₂) A₁ A₂ + ... ...... (1)**<-
This value **E** must be stationary for all variations of the arbitrary quantities **Aᵣ₊₁ ... Aₘ**. Let **p'²** be the value of **p²** <note>p² is the square of the angular frequency.</note> that is natural to the system when it vibrates under the specific constraints defined by the ratios:
->**A₁ : A₂ ... Aᵣ : Aᵣ₊₁ : ... Aₘ ;**<-
then
**p'² = { ½ c₁₁ A₁² + ... + c₁₂ A₁ A₂ + ... } ÷ { ½ a₁₁ A₁² + ... + a₁₂ A₁ A₂ + ... },**
so that
->**E = (p'² - p²) { ½ a₁₁ A₁² + ... + a₁₂ A₁ A₂ + ... } ......... (2).**<-

From this, we see that if **p²** is definitely less than **p'²**—meaning the prescribed period of vibration is longer than any of the natural periods of the system under those partial constraints—then **E** is necessarily positive. In this case, the stationary value (and there can be only one) is an absolute minimum.

For a similar reason, if the prescribed period is *shorter* than any of the natural periods of the partially constrained system, **E** is an absolute maximum algebraically, but an absolute minimum arithmetically <note>This means while the number might be a large negative value (an algebraic maximum), its magnitude or distance from zero is as small as possible.</note>. However, when **p²** falls within the range of possible natural values for **p'²**, **E** may be positive or negative, and the actual value is not necessarily the greatest or least possible. Whenever a natural vibration is consistent with the imposed conditions, the system will assume that vibration. In that specific case, the variable part of the total energy **T + V** is zero.

For convenience, we have analyzed the two great classes of forced vibrations and free vibrations separately. In reality, there is nothing to prevent them from occurring at the same time. After enough time has passed, however, the free vibrations always disappear due to friction, no matter how small that friction may be. A case with absolutely no friction is a purely theoretical ideal.

There is one caution, however, which is worth mentioning regarding cases where specific motions are forced on the system. Suppose, as before, that the coordinates **ψ₁, ψ₂, ... ψᵣ** are given. Then the free vibrations, whose existence or non-existence...

# VIBRATING SYSTEMS IN GENERAL. [106.

The specific nature of the motion does not matter as far as the forced motion is concerned. It should be understood that this motion is what the system is capable of when the coordinates $\psi_1 \dots \psi_r$ <note>$\psi$ (psi) represents the displacement or position of a part of the system.</note> are not permitted to vary from zero. To prevent them from moving, forces of the corresponding types must be introduced. Therefore, from one perspective, the motion in question can be seen as a forced vibration. However, these applied forces act simply as a constraint, and their effect is the same as limiting the system's freedom of motion.

**106 a.** The principles from the previous sections show that if $\psi_1, \psi_2 \dots \psi_r$ are given harmonic functions of time, such as $A_1 \cos pt$, $A_2 \cos pt, \dots$, and the forces of the other types are zero, then the motion is completely determined. The only exception occurs if the frequency $p$ is chosen to match one of the natural frequencies of the system when $\psi_1, \psi_2 \dots \psi_r$ are held at zero.

As an example, consider a membrane <note>A thin, flexible sheet, like a drumhead.</note> capable of vibrating transversely <note>Vibrating up and down, perpendicular to the surface.</note>. If the displacement $\psi$ at every point along the boundary is given (and is proportional to $\cos pt$), then the movement in the interior of the membrane is generally determined. However, an exception occurs if $p$ matches one of the natural frequencies the membrane would have if its boundary were held perfectly still. This problem is discussed by Pierre Duhem <note>original: *Cours de Physique Mathématique*, Tome Second, p. 190, Paris, 1891; "Course on Mathematical Physics, Volume Two."</note> based on a specialized analytical study by Hermann Schwarz. We can see that this is simply a specific instance of a much broader general theorem.

A similar result can be stated for an elastic solid where the motion of its surface (proportional to $\cos pt$) is specified at every point. Of course, the motion at the boundary does not need to be fully specified. For example, in a mass of air, we might specify only the motion normal <note>Perpendicular to the surface.</note> to a closed surface. The internal motion is then determined, unless the chosen frequency is one of the natural frequencies of the air mass when the surface is made rigid and unyielding.

**107.** Very remarkable reciprocal relations <note>These are "tit-for-tat" physical laws: if a force at point A causes a certain motion at point B, then the same force at point B will cause the same motion at point A.</note> exist between the forces and motions of different types. These can be seen as extensions of similar theorems for systems where only potential energy ($V$) or kinetic energy ($T$) is considered (see § 72 and §§ 77, 78). If we assume that all component forces are zero except for two—$\Psi_1$ and $\Psi_2$—we obtain from § 104:

$$\left. \begin{aligned} \nabla \psi_1 = \frac{d\nabla}{de_{11}} \Psi_1 + \frac{d\nabla}{de_{21}} \Psi_2 \\ \nabla \psi_2 = \frac{d\nabla}{de_{12}} \Psi_1 + \frac{d\nabla}{de_{22}} \Psi_2 \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (1).$$

# RECIPROCAL THEOREM.

<meta>107.]</meta>

We now consider two cases of motion for the same system: first, when force $\Psi_2$ is zero, and secondly (using prime marks) when force $\Psi_1'$ is zero. If $\Psi_2 = 0$,

->$\psi_2 = \nabla^{-1} \frac{d\nabla}{de_{12}} \Psi_1$ ............................ (2).<-

Similarly, if $\Psi_1' = 0$,

->$\psi_1' = \nabla^{-1} \frac{d\nabla}{de_{21}} \Psi_2'$ ............................ (3).<-

In these equations, the determinant $\nabla$ <note>$\nabla$ (nabla) here represents a characteristic determinant of the system's equations of motion.</note> and its derivatives <note>original: "differential coefficients"</note> are polynomial functions <note>original: "rational integral functions"</note> of the differential operator $D$. Because $e_{rs} = e_{sr}$ in every case <note>This symmetry is a fundamental property of the physical constants representing the system's stiffness, mass, and friction.</note>, $\nabla$ is a symmetrical determinant, and therefore:

->$\frac{d\nabla}{de_{rs}} = \frac{d\nabla}{de_{sr}}$ ............................ (4).<-

Hence, we see that if a force $\Psi_1$ acts on the system, the coordinate $\psi_2$ relates to it in the same way as the coordinate $\psi_1'$ relates to the force $\Psi_2'$, assuming this second force acts alone.

In addition to the motion discussed here, there may be free vibrations <note>Vibrations that continue naturally without an ongoing external force.</note> caused by a disturbance that existed before the current forces (included in $\Psi$) began. However, these vibrations are themselves the result of forces that acted previously. No matter how small the energy loss <note>original: "dissipation"</note> may be, there must be an interval of time after which free vibrations die out, and beyond which it is unnecessary to go when accounting for the forces that have acted on a system. Therefore, if we include forces from far enough in the past within $\Psi$, there are no independent vibrations to consider. In this way, the theorem may be extended to cases which might not at first glance appear to fit its scope. 

Suppose, for example, that the system is at rest in its position of equilibrium and then begins to be acted upon by a force of the first type. This force gradually increases in magnitude from zero to a finite value $\Psi_1$, at which point it stops increasing. If at a specific moment <note>original: "epoch of time"</note> the force is suddenly removed and remains zero ever after, free vibrations of the system will begin and continue until they are stopped by friction. At any time $t$ after that moment, the coordinate $\psi_2$ has a value (dependent on $t$) that is proportional to $\Psi_1$. The theorem allows us to assert that this value $\psi_2$ bears the same relation to $\Psi_1$ as $\psi_1'$ would at the same moment have borne to $\Psi_2'$, if the original cause of the vibrations had been a force of the second type in-

In these applications of our theorem, we obtain results relating to free vibrations <note>Vibrations that continue naturally after the external force has stopped.</note>, seen as the remaining effect of forces whose actual operation may have ended long before.

**108.** In an important class of cases, the forces $\Psi_1$ and $\Psi_2'$ are harmonic <note>Harmonic forces vary over time like a smooth wave (a sine or cosine curve).</note> and have the same period. We may represent them by $A_1 e^{ipt}$ and $A_2' e^{ipt}$, where $A_1$ and $A_2'$ may be assumed to be real numbers if the forces are in the same phase <note>In the same "phase" means they reach their peak values at the same time.</note> at the moments compared. The results may then be written as:

->$\left. \begin{aligned} \psi_2 &= A_1 \frac{d \log \nabla (ip)}{de_{12}} e^{ipt} \\ \psi_1' &= A_2' \frac{d \log \nabla (ip)}{de_{21}} e^{ipt} \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(1),$<-

where $ip$ is substituted for the differential operator $D$. Thus:

-> $A_2' \psi_2 = A_1 \psi_1' \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (2).$ <-

Since the ratio $A_1 : A_2'$ is by definition <note>original: "by hypothesis"</note> real, the same is true of the ratio $\psi_1' : \psi_2$; this means that the motions represented by those symbols are in the same phase. Converting these to real-valued quantities, we may state the theorem this way:

*If a force $\Psi_1 = A_1 \cos pt$, acting on the system, gives rise to the motion $\psi_2 = \theta A_1 \cos (pt - \epsilon)$; then a force $\Psi_2' = A_2' \cos pt$ will produce the motion $\psi_1' = \theta A_2' \cos (pt - \epsilon)$.*

If there is no friction, the phase lag $\epsilon$ will be zero.

If the magnitudes of the forces are equal ($A_1 = A_2'$), then the resulting displacements will be equal ($\psi_1' = \psi_2$). However, it must be remembered that the forces $\Psi_1$ and $\Psi_2'$ are not necessarily directly comparable, just as the coordinates of corresponding types may differ; for example, one might represent a linear displacement <note>Movement in a straight line.</note> and another an angular displacement <note>Rotation around an axis.</note>.

The reciprocal theorem may be stated in several ways, but before proceeding to these, we will provide another analysis that does not require a knowledge of determinants <note>A mathematical tool used to solve systems of linear equations.</note>.

# RECIPROCAL THEOREM.

Regarding the forces and their corresponding displacements, the equations of motion (from § 103) give:

->$\Psi_1 \psi_1' + \Psi_2 \psi_2' + \dots = \psi_1' (e_{11} \psi_1 + e_{12} \psi_2 + e_{13} \psi_3 + \dots)$<-
->$+ \psi_2' (e_{21} \psi_1 + e_{22} \psi_2 + e_{23} \psi_3 + \dots) + \dots$<-

Now, if all the forces vary according to the expression $e^{ipt}$ <note>This mathematical term represents a harmonic or wave-like motion over time.</note>, the effect of a symbolic operator such as $e_{rs}$ on any of the quantities of $\psi$ is simply to multiply that quantity by a constant found by substituting $ip$ for $D$ in $e_{rs}$. Assuming this substitution is made, and considering the relationships $e_{rs} = e_{sr}$, we can write:

->$\Psi_1 \psi_1' + \Psi_2 \psi_2' + \dots = e_{11} \psi_1 \psi_1' + e_{22} \psi_2 \psi_2' + \dots$<-
->$+ e_{12} (\psi_1' \psi_2 + \psi_2' \psi_1) + \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (3).$<-

Therefore, due to symmetry:

->$\Psi_1 \psi_1' + \Psi_2 \psi_2' + \dots = \Psi_1' \psi_1 + \Psi_2' \psi_2 + \dots \dots \dots (4),$<-

which expresses the reciprocal relationship.

**109.** In the applications we are about to explore, we will assume throughout that all types of forces except for two (which we may designate as the first and second) are zero. Thus:

->$\Psi_1 \psi_1' + \Psi_2 \psi_2' = \Psi_1' \psi_1 + \Psi_2' \psi_2 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (1).$<-

The results of this equation can be shown in three different ways. In the first, we suppose that:

->$\Psi_2 = 0, \quad \Psi_1' = 0,$<-

which results in:

->$\psi_2 : \Psi_1 = \psi_1' : \Psi_2' \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (2),$<-

showing <note>original: "shewing"</note>, as before, that the relationship of $\psi_2$ to $\Psi_1$ in the first case (when $\Psi_2 = 0$) is the same as the relationship of $\psi_1'$ to $\Psi_2'$ in the second case (when $\Psi_1' = 0$). This identity of relationship extends to both the phase and the amplitude <note>Phase refers to the timing of the vibration, while amplitude refers to the maximum extent or "strength" of the vibration.</note>.

A few examples may help clarify this law, as its broad nature might otherwise seem vague.

If $P$ and $Q$ are two points on a horizontal bar supported in any way (for example, with one end clamped and the other free), a specific harmonic transverse force <note>A force that acts perpendicular to the length of the bar and repeats in a regular wave-like pattern.</note> applied at point $P$ will produce, at any moment, the same vertical deflection at point $Q$ as would have been produced at $P$ if the force had been applied at $Q$ instead.

If we consider angular displacements <note>A measurement of how much an object has rotated, rather than how far it has moved in a straight line.</note> instead of linear ones, the

# VIBRATING SYSTEMS IN GENERAL.

The theorem is as follows: a given <term>harmonic couple</term> <note>a pair of equal and opposite forces that causes a periodic rotation</note> at point $P$ will produce the same **rotation** at point $Q$ as that same couple at $Q$ would produce at $P$.

Or, if one displacement is linear and the other is angular, the result may be stated this way: suppose for the first case that a harmonic couple acts at $P$, and for the second case that a vertical force with the same period and phase acts at $Q$. Then, the linear displacement at $Q$ in the first case has the same phase at every moment as the rotatory displacement at $P$ in the second case. Furthermore, the amplitudes of the two displacements are related such that the maximum couple at $P$ would do the same work while acting through the maximum rotation at $P$ (caused by the force at $Q$) as the maximum force at $Q$ would do while acting through the maximum displacement at $Q$ (caused by the couple at $P$). In this instance, the statement is more complicated, as the forces—being of different kinds—cannot be considered equal.

If we assume the period of the forces is extremely long, the temporary position of the system tends to match the position it would hold if kept at rest by the forces acting at that time; thus, the <term>equilibrium theory</term> <note>the study of systems in a state of balance where all acting forces cancel each other out</note> becomes applicable. Our theorem then simplifies to the statical one proved in section 72.

As a second example, suppose that in an air-filled space—which is either entirely or partially enclosed by solid boundaries—there are two spheres, $A$ and $B$, whose centers have one degree of freedom. A periodic force acting on $A$ will produce the same motion in $B$ as if the parts were swapped. This remains true regardless of any membranes, strings, tuning forks on resonance boxes, or other bodies capable of vibrating that might be nearby.

Alternatively, if $A$ and $B$ represent two points on a solid elastic body of any shape, a force parallel to the $OX$ axis acting at $A$ will produce the same motion at point $B$ parallel to the $OY$ axis as an equal force parallel to $OY$ acting at $B$ would produce at point $A$ parallel to $OX$.

Or again, let $A$ and $B$ be two points in an air-filled space with obstacles of any kind located between them. A sound starting at $A$ is perceived at $B$ with the same intensity as an identical sound starting at $B$ would be perceived at $A$.¹ The obstacle, for instance, might consist of a rigid...

# APPLICATIONS.

...a wall pierced with one or more holes. This example corresponds to the optical law stating that if any combination of reflecting or refracting surfaces allows one point to be seen from a second, the second point can also be seen from the first. In <term>acoustics</term> <note>the branch of physics concerned with the properties of sound</note>, sound shadows are usually only partial because the wave-length of sound is significant compared to the dimensions of ordinary obstacles; therefore, this reciprocal relationship is of considerable interest.

A further example may be taken from electricity. Suppose there are two circuits of insulated wire, *A* and *B*, and nearby is any combination of wire circuits or solid conductors connected to <term>condensers</term> <note>now commonly called capacitors; devices used to store electrical energy</note>. A periodic <term>electromotive force</term> <note>often abbreviated as EMF; the electrical action produced by a non-electrical source, like a battery, which creates a voltage</note> in circuit *A* will produce the same current in *B* as would be induced in *A* if the electromotive force were operated in *B*.

Our last example will be taken from the theory of the conduction and radiation of heat, using <term>Newton’s law of cooling</term> <note>the principle that the rate of heat loss of a body is proportional to the difference in temperatures between the body and its surroundings</note> as a basis. The temperature at any point *A* of a conducting and radiating system caused by a steady (or harmonic) source of heat at *B* is the same as the temperature at *B* would be if an equal source were placed at *A*. Moreover, if at any time the source at *B* is removed, the entire subsequent progression of temperature at *A* will be the same as it would be at *B* if the positions of *B* and *A* were interchanged.

**110.** The second way of stating the reciprocal theorem is arrived at by taking the first equation from § 109 and setting certain variables to zero:
->$\Psi_1 = 0, \quad \Psi_2' = 0;$<-
from which we get
->$\Psi_1 \Psi_1' = \Psi_2' \Psi_2 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (1),$<-
or
->$\Psi_1 : \Psi_2 = \Psi_2' : \Psi_1' \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (2),$<-
showing that the relation of $\Psi_1$ to $\Psi_2$ in the first case, when $\psi_1 = 0$, is the same as the relation of $\Psi_2'$ to $\psi_1'$ in the second case, when $\psi_2' = 0$.

Thus, in the example of the rod, if point *P* is held at rest while a specific vibration is applied to *Q* (by a force applied there), the reaction force at *P* is the same in both <term>amplitude</term> <note>the maximum extent of a vibration or oscillation, measured from the position of equilibrium</note> and <term>phase</term> <note>the stage in a cycle of a periodic motion or wave</note> as it would be at *Q* if that point were held at rest and the same vibration were applied to *P*.

Similarly, if *A* and *B* are two electric circuits near any number of other circuits, *C*, *D*, etc., whether they are closed loops or end...

### VIBRATING SYSTEMS IN GENERAL. [110.]

If there are capacitors <note>original: "condensers"</note> and a specific periodic current is triggered in circuit *A* by the necessary electromotive force, the induced electromotive force in *B* is the same as it would be in *A* if the parts of *A* and *B* were interchanged.

The third form of the statement is obtained by substituting values into equation (1) of Section 109:
->$\Psi_1 = 0, \quad \psi_2' = 0;$<-
from which we get
->$\Psi_1' \psi_1 + \Psi_2' \psi_2 = 0$ ........................ (3),<-
or
->$\psi_1 : \psi_2 = - \Psi_2' : \Psi_1'$ ........................ (4),<-
proving that the ratio of displacement $\psi_1$ to $\psi_2$ in the first case (when force $\Psi_2$ acts alone) is the negative of the ratio of force $\Psi_2'$ to $\Psi_1'$ in the second case (when the forces are balanced to keep the displacement $\psi_2'$ equal to zero).

Thus, if point *P* of a rod is held at rest while a periodic force acts at point *Q*, the reaction <note>the counter-force required to keep the point stationary</note> at *P* bears the same numerical ratio to the force at *Q* as the displacement <note>movement from the equilibrium position</note> at *Q* would bear to the displacement at *P* if the rod were caused to vibrate by a force applied at *P*.

**111.** The reciprocal theorem has been proved for all systems in which the frictional forces can be represented by the function *F* <note>the dissipation function, which mathematically describes how energy is lost to friction</note>, but it can be further and significantly generalized. We have indeed proved the existence of the function *F* for many cases where motion is resisted by forces proportional to the absolute or relative velocities. However, there are other sources of dissipation <note>the process by which energy, such as motion, is transformed into heat</note> that do not fall under this category; for example, the dissipation caused by the conduction or radiation of heat. 

Now, while it is true that in these cases the forces are not always in a constant ratio to the velocities or displacements for *all possible motions*, they are necessarily periodic in any actual case of periodic motion ($\tau$) <note>$\tau$ (tau) represents the period, or the time it takes for one full cycle of the vibration</note>. Therefore, whatever their phase, they can be expressed as a sum of two terms: one proportional to the displacement (absolute or relative) and the other proportional to the velocity of the part of the system affected. If the coefficients remain the same—not necessarily for every possible motion, but for *all motions of the period* $\tau$—then the function *F* exists in the only sense required for our current purpose. In fact, since the theorem is concerned exclusively with motions of period $\tau$, it does not matter whether the functions *T* (kinetic energy), *F* (dissipation), and *V* (potential energy) depend on $\tau$ or not. Thus extended, the theorem is:

->RECIPROCAL THEOREM.<-

...perhaps sufficiently general to cover the whole field of dissipative forces <note>forces, like friction or air resistance, that cause a system to lose energy</note>.

It is important to remember that the Principle of Reciprocity is limited to systems which vibrate about a configuration of **equilibrium**, and is therefore not to be applied without reservation to such a problem as that presented by the transmission of sound waves <note>original: "sonorous waves"</note> through the atmosphere when disturbed by wind. The vibrations must also be of such a character that the square of the motion can be neglected throughout <note>this refers to "linear" vibrations, where the movements are small enough that the math remains simple</note>; otherwise our proof would not be valid. Other apparent exceptions depend on a misunderstanding of the principle itself. Care must be taken to observe a proper correspondence between the forces and displacements; the rule is that the product of the force and the displacement must represent **work done**. Thus, couples <note>pairs of equal and opposite forces that cause rotation; torque</note> correspond to rotations, pressures correspond to increases in volume, and so on.

<margin>111 a.</margin>**111 *a*.** The substance of the preceding sections is taken from a paper by the author¹, in which the action of dissipative forces appears to have been included for the first time. Reciprocal theorems of a special character, which excluded energy loss <note>original: "dissipation"</note>, had been previously given by other writers. One, by von Helmholtz, has already been quoted. Reference may also be made to the reciprocal theorem of Betti², relating to a uniform isotropic <note>having the same physical properties in all directions</note> elastic solid, upon which body forces and surface forces act. Lamb³ has shown that these results, and more recent ones by von Helmholtz⁴, may be deduced from a very general equation established by Lagrange in *Analytical Mechanics* <note>original Latin/French title: *Mécanique Analytique*</note>.

**111 *b*.** In many cases of practical interest, the external force to which a system responds with harmonic vibration is applied at a single point. This may be called the **driving-point**, and it becomes important to estimate how the system reacts back upon it. When only *T* and *F* are significant, or only *F* and *V* <note>In this context, *T* represents kinetic energy, *V* represents potential energy, and *F* represents the dissipation function (energy lost to friction)</note>, certain general conclusions may be stated, of which an example will be given here. For further details, reference should be made to a paper by the author⁵.

Consider a system that lacks potential energy <note>energy stored due to position, such as in a compressed spring</note>, in which the coordinate $\psi_1$ is moved by a harmonic force <note>a force that pulses rhythmically like a pendulum</note> $\Psi_1$, which is proportional to $e^{ipt}$ <note>a mathematical expression representing wave-like motion over time at a specific frequency</note>. The other coordinates may be chosen however we like, but it is very convenient to choose them so that no product of them appears in the expressions for $T$ <note>kinetic energy</note> and $F$ <note>the dissipation function, which represents energy lost to friction or resistance</note>. In fact, these would be the "normal coordinates" of the system, assuming that $\psi_1$ is held at zero by a specific force. The expressions for $T$ and $F$ thus take the following forms:

-> $T = \frac{1}{2} a_{11} \dot{\psi}_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} a_{22} \dot{\psi}_2^2 + \frac{1}{2} a_{33} \dot{\psi}_3^2 + \dots$ <-
-> $+ a_{12} \dot{\psi}_1 \dot{\psi}_2 + a_{13} \dot{\psi}_1 \dot{\psi}_3 + a_{14} \dot{\psi}_1 \dot{\psi}_4 + \dots \dots \dots \dots (1).$ <-
-> $F = \frac{1}{2} b_{11} \dot{\psi}_1^2 + \frac{1}{2} b_{22} \dot{\psi}_2^2 + \frac{1}{2} b_{33} \dot{\psi}_3^2 + \dots$ <-
-> $+ b_{12} \dot{\psi}_1 \dot{\psi}_2 + b_{13} \dot{\psi}_1 \dot{\psi}_3 + b_{14} \dot{\psi}_1 \dot{\psi}_4 + \dots \dots \dots \dots (2).$ <-
<note>In these equations, the "dot" over the symbol (like $\dot{\psi}_1$) represents velocity, or the rate of change over time.</note>

The equations for a force $\Psi_1$, proportional to $e^{ipt}$, are accordingly:

-> $(ipa_{11} + b_{11}) \dot{\psi}_1 + (ipa_{12} + b_{12}) \dot{\psi}_2 + (ipa_{13} + b_{13}) \dot{\psi}_3 + \dots = \Psi_1,$ <-
-> $(ipa_{12} + b_{12}) \dot{\psi}_1 + (ipa_{22} + b_{22}) \dot{\psi}_2 = 0,$ <-
-> $(ipa_{13} + b_{13}) \dot{\psi}_1 + (ipa_{33} + b_{33}) \dot{\psi}_3 = 0,$ <-
-> $\dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots$ <-

By using the second and following equations, the velocities $\dot{\psi}_2, \dot{\psi}_3, \dots$ can be expressed in terms of $\dot{\psi}_1$. Introducing these values into the first equation, we get:

-> $\Psi_1 / \dot{\psi}_1 = ipa_{11} + b_{11} - \frac{(ipa_{12} + b_{12})^2}{ipa_{22} + b_{22}} - \frac{(ipa_{13} + b_{13})^2}{ipa_{33} + b_{33}} - \dots \dots \dots \dots (3).$ <-

The ratio $\Psi_1 / \dot{\psi}_1$ <note>force divided by velocity</note> is a complex quantity <note>a number with both "real" and "imaginary" parts</note>, of which the real part corresponds to the work done by the force in a complete period and dissipated <note>lost as heat or friction</note> in the system. By an extension of electrical language, we may call it the *resistance* of the system and denote it by the letter $R'$. The other part of the ratio is "imaginary" <note>involving $i$, the square root of -1</note>. If we denote it by $ipL' \dot{\psi}_1$, or $L' \ddot{\psi}_1$, $L'$ will represent the **moment of inertia** <note>resistance to changes in rotation</note> or, in electrical theory, **self-induction**. We therefore write:

-> $\Psi_1 = (R' + ipL') \dot{\psi}_1 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (4);$ <-

And the values of $R'$ and $L'$ are to be calculated by separating the real and the imaginary parts of the right-hand member of equation (3). In this way we get:

-> $R' = b_{11} - \Sigma \frac{b_{12}^2}{b_{22}} + p^2 \Sigma \frac{(a_{12}b_{22} - a_{22}b_{12})^2}{b_{22} (b_{22}^2 + p^2 a_{22}^2)} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (5).$ <-

This is the value of the resistance as determined by the structure of the system and by the frequency of the imposed...

As can be seen most easily by looking at its reciprocal <note>the mathematical inverse</note>, this value increases steadily as $p^2$ increases from zero to infinity. We can conclude that as the frequency of vibration increases, the value of the effective resistance $R'$ increases steadily along with it. If the frequency $p$ is either very large or very small, equation (8) becomes equivalent to $2T/\dot{\psi}_1^2$ <note>$T$ represents the kinetic energy of the system</note>.

For a simple example, consider the problem of the reaction upon a primary electrical circuit caused by the currents generated in a neighboring secondary circuit. Using standard electrical notation, we represent the coefficients of self-induction <note>the property where a change in current induces a voltage in the same circuit</note> as $L$ and $N$, and the coefficient of mutual induction <note>where a change in current in one circuit induces a voltage in a nearby circuit</note> as $M$, so that:

-> $T = \frac{1}{2}L\dot{\psi}_1^2 + M\dot{\psi}_1\dot{\psi}_2 + \frac{1}{2}N\dot{\psi}_2^2,$ <-

and the resistances are represented by $R$ and $S$. Thus:

-> $a_{11} = L, \quad a_{12} = M, \quad a_{22} = N;$ <-
-> $b_{11} = R, \quad b_{12} = 0, \quad b_{22} = S;$ <-

**112.** In Chapter III, we considered the vibrations of a system with one <term>degree of freedom</term> <note>a system that can be described by a single variable, like a simple pendulum</note>. The remainder of this chapter will be devoted to some details of the case where there are two degrees of freedom.

If $x$ and $y$ denote the two coordinates, the expressions for $T$ <note>Kinetic Energy</note> and $V$ <note>Potential Energy</note> are of the form:
-> $\left. \begin{aligned} 2T &= L\dot{x}^2 + 2M\dot{x}\dot{y} + N\dot{y}^2 \\ 2V &= Ax^2 + 2Bxy + Cy^2 \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (1);$ <-
so that, in the absence of friction, the <term>equations of motion</term> <note>the mathematical equations describing how the system changes over time</note> are:
-> $\left. \begin{aligned} L\ddot{x} + M\ddot{y} + Ax + By &= X \\ M\ddot{x} + N\ddot{y} + Bx + Cy &= Y \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (2).$ <-

When there are no <term>impressed forces</term> <note>external forces applied to the system</note>, we have for the natural vibrations:
-> $\left. \begin{aligned} (LD^2 + A)x + (MD^2 + B)y &= 0 \\ (MD^2 + B)x + (ND^2 + C)y &= 0 \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (3),$ <-
$D$ being the symbol for differentiation <note>the derivative operator $d/dt$</note> with respect to time.

If a solution of (3) is $x = le^{\lambda t}$, $y = me^{\lambda t}$, then $\lambda^2$ is one of the roots of:
-> $(L\lambda^2 + A)(N\lambda^2 + C) - (M\lambda^2 + B)^2 = 0 \dots\dots\dots (4),$ <-
or
-> $\lambda^4 (LN - M^2) + \lambda^2 (LC + NA - 2MB) + AC - B^2 = 0 \dots\dots (5).$ <-

The constants $L, M, N; A, B, C,$ are not entirely arbitrary. Since $T$ and $V$ must always be positive values, the following inequalities must be satisfied:
-> $LN > M^2, AC > B^2 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (6).$ <-

Moreover, $L, N, A,$ and $C$ must themselves be positive.

# ROOTS OF DETERMINANTAL EQUATION.

<sig>11</sig>

We will now examine the effect of these restrictions on the **roots** <note>original: "roots"; the values of $\lambda$ that satisfy the equation, representing frequencies of vibration</note> of equation (5).

In the first place, the three coefficients in the equation are positive. For the first and third coefficients, this is obvious from equation (6). The coefficient of $\lambda^2$ is:

->$= (\sqrt{LC} - \sqrt{NA})^2 + 2\sqrt{LNAC} - 2MB,$<-

in which, as seen from equation (6), $\sqrt{LNAC}$ is necessarily greater than $MB$. From this, we conclude that the values of $\lambda^2$, if they are real, are both negative.

Next, we must prove that the roots are, in fact, real. The condition to be satisfied is that the following quantity must not be negative:

->$(LC + NA - 2MB)^2 - 4(LN - M^2)(AC - B^2).$<-

After simplification <note>original: "reduction"</note>, this can be written in the following form:

->$4(\sqrt{LN} \cdot B - \sqrt{AC} \cdot M)^2$<-
->$+ (\sqrt{LC} - \sqrt{NA})^2 \{(\sqrt{LC} - \sqrt{NA})^2 + 4(\sqrt{LNAC} - MB)\},$<-

which shows that the condition is satisfied, since $\sqrt{LNAC} - MB$ is positive. This provides the analytical proof that the values of $\lambda^2$ are both real and negative. This fact might have been anticipated even without mathematical analysis, based on the physical nature of the system whose vibrations these values represent.

The two values of $\lambda^2$ are different, unless both of these conditions are met:

->$\left. \begin{aligned} \sqrt{LN} \cdot B - \sqrt{AC} \cdot M = 0 \\ \sqrt{LC} - \sqrt{NA} = 0 \end{aligned} \right\},$<-

which requires that:

->$L : M : N = A : B : C \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(7).$<-

The common **spherical pendulum** <note>a pendulum that can swing in any direction, like a weight on a string, tracing a path on the surface of a sphere</note> is an example of this specific case.

By applying a suitable force $Y$, the **coordinate** <note>original: "co-ordinate"; a variable used to describe the position of the system</note> $y$ can be prevented from changing. The system then loses one **degree of freedom** <note>the independent ways in which a system can move</note>, and the period of vibration for the remaining degree is generally different from either of the periods possible before the force $Y$ was introduced. Suppose that the types of motions obtained by alternately preventing the variation of $y$ and then $x$ are $e^{\mu_1 it}$ and $e^{\mu_2 it}$ respectively. Then $\mu_1^2$ and $\mu_2^2$ are the roots of the equation:

->$(L\lambda^2 + A)(N\lambda^2 + C) = 0,$<-

<meta>This page continues the mathematical proof regarding the frequencies of vibrating systems with two degrees of freedom. It establishes that when a system is constrained, its new frequency of vibration will always fall outside the range defined by its two original natural frequencies.</meta>

<page-num>162 [112.]</page-num>
<header>VIBRATING SYSTEMS IN GENERAL.</header>

This is obtained from equation (4) by removing $M$ and $B$. Hence, equation (4) may itself be written in the form:

->$LN (\lambda^2 - \mu_1^2) (\lambda^2 - \mu_2^2) = (M\lambda^2 + B)^2$ ............(8),<-

which shows <note>original: "shews"</note> at once that neither of the roots of $\lambda^2$ can fall between the values of $\mu_1^2$ and $\mu_2^2$. A more detailed examination will prove that one of the roots is greater than both the quantities $\mu_1^2$ and $\mu_2^2$, while the other is less than both. For if we set:

->$f(\lambda^2) = LN (\lambda^2 - \mu_1^2) (\lambda^2 - \mu_2^2) - (M\lambda^2 + B)^2$,<-

we see that when $\lambda^2$ is very small, $f$ is positive ($AC - B^2$); as $\lambda^2$ decreases (mathematically) toward $\mu_1^2$, $f$ changes sign and becomes negative. Therefore, a root exists between 0 and $\mu_1^2$; and by similar reasoning, another root exists between $\mu_2^2$ and $-\infty$. We conclude that the frequencies <note>original: "tones"</note> obtained by subjecting the system to the two kinds of constraint in question are both intermediate in pitch between the frequencies produced by the natural vibrations of the system. In specific cases where $\mu_1^2$ and $\mu_2^2$ are equal, then:

->$\lambda^2 = \frac{\sqrt{LN} \mu^2 \pm B}{\sqrt{LN} \mp M} = \frac{-\sqrt{AC} \pm B}{\sqrt{LN} \mp M}$ ............(9).<-

This proposition may be generalized. *Any kind of constraint which leaves the system still possessing one degree of freedom <note>degree of freedom: the number of independent ways a system can move</note> may be regarded as the imposition of an enforced relationship between the coordinates, such as:*

->$ax + \beta y = 0$...........................(10).<-

Now if $ax + \beta y$, and any other balanced linear function of $x$ and $y$, are taken as new variables, the same argument proves that the single period of vibration possible to the system after the constraint is introduced is intermediate in value between the two periods in which the natural vibrations were previously performed. Conversely, the two periods that become possible when a constraint is removed lie one on each side of the original period.

If the values of $\lambda^2$ are equal—which can only happen when:

->$L : M : N = A : B : C$,<-

the introduction of a constraint has no effect on the period; for instance, restricting a spherical pendulum <note>A pendulum that can swing in any direction, not just a single plane</note> to one vertical plane.

### 113. As a simple example of a system with two degrees of freedom, we may take a stretched string of length $l$, which itself has no <note>The text continues on the next page, likely discussing a weightless string with attached masses</note>

<header>FREE VIBRATIONS.</header>
<sig>11—2</sig>
<meta>catchword: 113. at top left refers to section number</meta>

[113.] ...inertia, but carrying two equal masses $m$ at distances $a$ and $b$ from one end (Fig. 17). Let the tension be $T_1$.

->Fig. 17.<-

---

If $x$ and $y$ denote the displacements,
-> $2T = m (\dot{x}^2 + \dot{y}^2)$, <-
-> $2V = T_1 \left\{ \frac{x^2}{a} + \frac{(x - y)^2}{b - a} + \frac{y^2}{l - b} \right\}$. <-

Since the kinetic energy ($T$) and potential energy ($V$) are not in the same mathematical form, it follows that the two periods of vibration are unequal in every case.

If the loads are symmetrically attached, the nature of the two component vibrations is clear. In the first vibration, which will have the longer period, the two masses move together so that $x$ and $y$ remain equal throughout the vibration. In the second, $x$ and $y$ are equal in magnitude but opposite in direction <note>original: "numerically equal, but opposed in sign"</note>. The midpoint of the string then remains stationary <note>original: "at rest"</note>, and the two masses are always located on a straight line passing through that midpoint. In the first case $x - y = 0$, and in the second $x + y = 0$; thus, $x - y$ and $x + y$ are the new variables that must be used <note>original: "assumed"</note> in order to simplify the functions $T$ and $V$ simultaneously into a sum of squares <note>sum of squares: a mathematical technique used to decouple the equations of motion, allowing each mode of vibration to be solved independently</note>.

For example, if the masses are attached so that they divide the string into three equal parts:

$\left. \begin{aligned} 2T &= \frac{m}{2} \{(\dot{x} + \dot{y})^2 + (\dot{x} - \dot{y})^2\} \\ 2V &= \frac{3T_1}{2l} \{(x + y)^2 + 3(x - y)^2\} \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots(1),$

from which we obtain the complete solution:

$\left. \begin{aligned} x + y &= A \cos \left( \sqrt{\frac{3T_1}{lm}} \cdot t + \alpha \right) \\ x - y &= B \cos \left( \sqrt{\frac{9T_1}{lm}} \cdot t + \beta \right) \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots(2),$

where, as usual, the constants $A, \alpha, B, \beta$ are to be determined by the initial conditions <note>original: "initial circumstances"</note>.

### 114. When the two natural periods of a system are nearly equal, the phenomenon of intermittent vibration sometimes appears in a very curious manner. In order to illustrate this,

<page-num>164 [114.]</page-num>

# VIBRATING SYSTEMS IN GENERAL.

To better understand this, we can return to the example of a string loaded with two equal masses, placed at distances from its ends equal to one-fourth of its total length. If the middle point of the string were perfectly fixed, the two identical systems on either side of it would be completely independent; or, if we viewed the whole thing as one system, the two periods of vibration would be exactly equal. Now, however, we will suppose that instead of being perfectly fixed, the middle point is attached to springs or other mechanisms that have no inertia <note>original: "destitute of inertia," meaning the mechanism is massless and does not add to the system's momentum</note>, so that it is capable of yielding *slightly*. The requirement that the mechanism has no inertia is to avoid adding a third degree of freedom <note>degree of freedom: an independent way in which a physical system can move</note> to the system.

From the symmetry of the setup, it is clear that the fundamental vibrations of the system are those represented by $x + y$ and $x - y$. Their periods are slightly different because, due to the yielding of the center, the potential energy of a displacement where $x$ and $y$ move in the same direction is less than the potential energy of a displacement where $x$ and $y$ move in opposite directions. However, the kinetic energies (the energy of motion) are the same for both types of vibration. In the solution:

->$\left. \begin{aligned} x + y &= A \cos (n_1 t + \alpha) \\ x - y &= B \cos (n_2 t + \beta) \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(1),$<-

we must therefore consider $n_1$ and $n_2$ <note>These variables represent the angular frequencies of the two modes of vibration</note> to be nearly, but not quite, equal. Now let us suppose that at the beginning (when $t=0$), the position $x$ and its velocity $\dot{x}$ are both zero. The conditions are:

->$\left. \begin{aligned} A \cos \alpha + B \cos \beta &= 0 \\ n_1 A \sin \alpha + n_2 B \sin \beta &= 0 \end{aligned} \right\},$<-

which give approximately:

->$A + B = 0, \quad \alpha = \beta.$<-

Thus:

->$\left. \begin{aligned} x &= A \sin \frac{n_2 - n_1}{2} t \enspace \sin \left( \frac{n_1 + n_2}{2} t + \alpha \right) \\ y &= A \cos \frac{n_2 - n_1}{2} t \enspace \cos \left( \frac{n_1 + n_2}{2} t + \alpha \right) \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots(2).$<-

Here, the value of the coordinate $x$ is expressed approximately by a harmonic term <note>a mathematical expression describing a simple back-and-forth motion</note>. Its amplitude <note>the maximum extent of a vibration</note>, being proportional to $\sin \frac{1}{2} (n_2 - n_1) t$, is a slowly varying harmonic function of time. The vibrations of the coordinates are therefore intermittent; they are adjusted so that the amplitude of one vanishes at the exact moment the other reaches its maximum.

This phenomenon can be beautifully shown using a tuning fork of very low pitch, heavily weighted at the ends and firmly held by

# VIBRATING SYSTEMS IN GENERAL.

It is $\tau_1$ <note>$\tau$ represents a time constant or period of vibration.</note> that increases indefinitely, and $\tau_2$ that approaches a finite limit.

We will now consider **forced vibrations**.

### 116.
The general equations for a system of two degrees of freedom <note>Degrees of freedom: the number of independent ways a system can move.</note> including friction are:

$$\left. \begin{matrix} (LD^2 + \alpha D + A)x + (MD^2 + \beta D + B)y = X \\ (MD^2 + \beta D + B)x + (ND^2 + \gamma D + C)y = Y \end{matrix} \right\} \dots\dots\dots(1).$$

In the following discussion, we will assume that $Y = 0$, and that $X = e^{ipt}$ <note>This represents a periodic driving force using complex exponential notation.</note>. The solution for $y$ is:

$$y = - \frac{(B - p^2M + i\beta p) e^{ipt}}{(A - p^2L + i\alpha p)(C - p^2N + i\gamma p) - (B - p^2M + i\beta p)^2} \dots(2).$$

If the connection between $x$ and $y$ is "loose" <note>This refers to "weak coupling," where the two parts of the system don't influence each other very strongly.</note>, the constants $M, \beta$, and $B$ are small. Consequently, the term $(B - p^2M + i\beta p)^2$ in the denominator can generally be ignored. When this is allowed, the coordinate $y$ behaves as if $x$ were fixed in place, and a force $Y$ had been applied with a magnitude that does not depend on $N, \gamma$, and $C$. 

However, if there is an approximate resonance <note>original: "isochronism"; the state of having the same period or frequency.</note> between the external force and one of the motions that would occur if $x$ or $y$ were held at zero, then either $(A - p^2L + i\alpha p)$ or $(C - p^2N + i\gamma p)$ will be small. In that case, the term in the denominator representing the <term>mutual influence</term> (coupling) between the parts must be kept, as it is no longer negligible. Consequently, the solution becomes more complex.

Symmetry shows that if we had assumed $X = 0$ and $Y = e^{ipt}$, we would have found the same value for $x$ as we have now found for $y$. This is the **Reciprocal Theorem** <note>The Reciprocal Theorem states that the response of a system at one point due to a force at another is the same as the response at the second point if the force were applied at the first.</note> of section 108 applied to a system capable of two independent motions. A string with two attached loads serves as a helpful example of this principle.

### 117.
Thus far, we have discussed an applied force. Next, we will assume that the motion of one coordinate ($x = e^{ipt}$) is specifically prescribed (forced), while $Y = 0$. For simplicity, we will limit ourselves to the case where there is no mutual friction ($\beta = 0$). The value of $y$ is:

$$y = - \frac{(B - Mp^2) e^{ipt}}{C - Np^2 + i\gamma p} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (1).$$

Let us now investigate how this motion reacts back on $x$. We find:

$$(MD^2 + B)y = - \frac{(B - Mp^2)^2 e^{ipt}}{C - Np^2 + i\gamma p} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(2).$$

# REACTION OF A DEPENDENT SYSTEM.

<margin>117.</margin>

If the real and imaginary parts of the coefficient of $e^{ipt}$ <note>The term $e^{ipt}$ represents a periodic or oscillating force.</note> are respectively $A'$ and $i\alpha'p$, we may write the equation as:

->$(MD^2 + B)y = A'x + \alpha'\dot{x}$ ........................(3),<-

and

->$A' = - \frac{(B - Mp^2)^2 (C - Np^2)}{(C - Np^2)^2 + \gamma^2 p^2}$ ........................(4),<-

->$\alpha' = \frac{(B - Mp^2)^2 \gamma}{(C - Np^2)^2 + \gamma^2 p^2}$ ........................(5).<-

It appears that the effect of the reaction of $y$ (in addition to what would be caused by holding $y = 0$) is represented by changing $A$ into $A + A'$, and $\alpha$ into $\alpha + \alpha'$, where $A'$ and $\alpha'$ have the values shown above. This reaction is therefore equivalent to an alteration in the coefficients of the "spring" <note>Spring constant, representing the stiffness or restorative force of the system.</note> and the "friction" <note>Damping coefficient, representing the resistance to motion.</note>. These alterations, however, are not constants; they are functions of the period of the motion being considered, the nature of which we will now examine.

Let $n$ be the value of $p$ corresponding to the natural frictionless period of $y$ (when $x$ is held at zero), so that $C - n^2 N = 0$. Then:

$$\left. \begin{aligned} A' &= (B - Mp^2)^2 \frac{N(p^2 - n^2)}{N^2(p^2 - n^2)^2 + \gamma^2 p^2} \\ \alpha' &= (B - Mp^2)^2 \frac{\gamma}{N^2(p^2 - n^2)^2 + \gamma^2 p^2} \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots(6).$$

In most cases that we deal with in practice, the friction $\gamma$ is small, and our interest is focused mainly on values of $p$ that do not differ much from $n$ <note>This refers to the state of resonance, where the driving frequency $p$ is close to the natural frequency $n$.</note>. Accordingly, we will ignore the variations of the positive factor $(B - Mp^2)^2$, and in the small term $\gamma^2 p^2$, we will substitute $p$ with its approximate value $n$. When $p$ is not nearly equal to $n$, this term is of no importance.

As might be expected from the general principle of work <note>The principle of conservation of energy; energy added to the system must be accounted for by work or heat.</note>, $\alpha'$ is always positive. Its maximum value occurs when $p$ is nearly equal to $n$, and it is then proportional to $1/\gamma n^2$, which varies *inversely* with $\gamma$. This might not be expected at first glance, for it seems like a <term>paradox</term> <note>A seemingly absurd or self-contradictory statement that may prove to be true.</note> that the greater the friction, the smaller its result. However, we must remember that $\gamma$ is only the *coefficient* of friction. When $\gamma$ is small, the maximum motion increases so much that the total work spent against friction is actually greater than if $\gamma$ were more substantial.

But the point of most interest is how $A'$ depends on $p$. If $p$ is less than $n$, $A'$ is negative. As $p$ passes through the value...

# MASS CONCENTRATED IN POINTS.

At the $m$ points of division, equal masses ($\mu$) are assumed to be concentrated. These represent the mass of the portions ($a$) of the string that they each bisect. The mass of each terminal portion of length $\frac{1}{2}a$ is assumed to be concentrated at the endpoints. Based on this understanding, we have:

->$(m + 1) \mu = \rho l$ .............................. (2).<-
<note>original: $\rho$ represents the linear density (mass per unit length) and $l$ the total length.</note>

We now proceed to investigate the vibrations of a string that has no mass of its own (it is <term>devoid of inertia</term> <note>original: "devoid of inertia" means the string itself is weightless and does not resist changes in motion; only the added masses do.</note>), but is loaded at each of $m$ points—spaced equally at a distance ($a$) from one another and from the ends—with a mass $\mu$.

If $\psi_1, \psi_2 \dots \psi_{m+2}$ represent the lateral displacements of the loaded points, including the starting and ending points, we have the following expressions for $T$ <note>Kinetic energy</note> and $V$ <note>Potential energy</note>:

->$T = \frac{1}{2} \mu \{ \dot{\psi}_1^2 + \dot{\psi}_2^2 + \dots + \dot{\psi}_{m+1}^2 + \dot{\psi}_{m+2}^2 \}$ ................. (3)<-
<note>The dots above the symbols ($\dot{\psi}$) represent the velocity of the displacement.</note>

->$V = \frac{T_1}{2a} \{ (\psi_2 - \psi_1)^2 + (\psi_3 - \psi_2)^2 + \dots + (\psi_{m+2} - \psi_{m+1})^2 \} \dots (4),<-
<note>original: $T_1$ represents the tension of the string.</note>

subject to the condition that the displacements at the ends, $\psi_1$ and $\psi_{m+2}$, <term>vanish</term> <note>original: "vanish" here means they equal zero because the ends of the string are fixed and cannot move.</note>. Using Lagrange's Method, these yield the $m$ equations of motion:

->$\left. \begin{aligned} B\psi_1 + A\psi_2 + B\psi_3 &= 0 \\ B\psi_2 + A\psi_3 + B\psi_4 &= 0 \\ B\psi_3 + A\psi_4 + B\psi_5 &= 0 \\ \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \\ B\psi_m + A\psi_{m+1} + B\psi_{m+2} &= 0 \end{aligned} \right\} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (5),$<-

where 

->$A = \mu D^2 + \frac{2T_1}{a}, \quad B = -\frac{T_1}{a}$ ........................ (6).<-
<note>original: $D^2$ is a differential operator representing the second derivative with respect to time.</note>

Assuming now that the vibration being studied is of a <term>normal type</term> <note>A "normal type" or normal mode is a pattern of motion in which all parts of the system move sinusoidally with the same frequency.</note>, we suppose that $\psi_1, \psi_2,$ etc., are all proportional to $\cos (nt - \epsilon)$, where $n$ is a value yet to be determined. In this case, $A$ and $B$ may be treated as constants by substituting $-n^2$ in place of $D^2$.

For the sake of brevity, if we set

->$C = A \div B = -2 + \frac{\mu a n^2}{T_1}$ ........................ (7),<-

the determinantal equation, which provides the values for $n^2$, takes the following form:

expressing $A_s$ in terms of the initial displacements.

This is based on two assumptions: (1) that the magnitude of the tension may be considered constant, and (2) that the square of the inclination <note>The angle or slope of the string's curve.</note> of any part of the string to its initial direction is small enough to be ignored. As before, $\rho$ denotes the <term>linear density</term> <note>The mass per unit of length.</note> at any point, and $T_1$ is the constant tension. # TRANSVERSE VIBRATIONS OF STRINGS.

Consider a string fixed at its two ends and acted upon by external <note>original: "impressed"</note> forces $Y \rho \, dx$ and $Z \rho \, dx$. According to **D'Alembert's Principle** <note>A fundamental rule in mechanics that allows us to treat a dynamic system (one in motion) as if it were in equilibrium by including "inertial forces" alongside external forces.</note>, these external forces form a balanced system when combined with the reactions against acceleration, $-\rho \, d^2y/dt^2$ and $-\rho \, d^2z/dt^2$. At any point $x$, the components of tension are

-> $T_1 \frac{dy}{dx}$, $T_1 \frac{dz}{dx}$, <-

if we assume the slopes ($dy/dx$ and $dz/dx$) are small enough that their squares can be ignored <note>This is a standard simplification in physics for strings that are not stretched or bent too violently.</note>. Thus, the forces acting on the tiny segment <note>original: "element"</note> $dx$ arising from the tension are

-> $T_1 \frac{d}{dx} \left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right) dx$, $T_1 \frac{d}{dx} \left( \frac{dz}{dx} \right) dx$. <-

From this, we derive the **equations of motion**:

> $\left. \begin{aligned} \frac{d^2y}{dt^2} &= \frac{T_1}{\rho} \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + Y \\ \frac{d^2z}{dt^2} &= \frac{T_1}{\rho} \frac{d^2z}{dx^2} + Z \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (1),$

which show that the vertical and horizontal movements ($y$ and $z$) are entirely independent of one another.

The student should compare these equations with the corresponding equations for discrete particles (using the method of **finite differences**) in Section 120. The latter may be written as:

-> $\mu \frac{d^2}{dt^2} \psi (x) = \frac{T_1}{a} \{ \psi (x - a) + \psi (x + a) - 2 \psi (x) \}$. <-

In the limit, as the distance $a$ between the mass points becomes infinitely small:

-> $\psi (x - a) + \psi (x + a) - 2 \psi (x) = \psi'' (x) a^2$, <-

while $\mu$ (the mass of the segment) equals $\rho a$. The equation eventually takes the form:

-> $\frac{d^2}{dt^2} \psi (x) = \frac{T_1}{\rho} \frac{d^2}{dx^2} \psi (x)$, <-

which matches Equation (1).

Similarly, the limiting forms of equations (3) and (4) from Section 120 are:

> $T = \frac{1}{2} \int \rho \left( \frac{dy}{dt} \right)^2 dx \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (2),$

> $V = \frac{1}{2} T_1 \int \left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right)^2 dx \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (3),$

where $T$ represents the **kinetic energy** and $V$ represents the **potential energy**. These can also be proven directly.

To prove the second point, we only need to observe that the potential energy in any given shape <note>original: "configuration"</note> is the work needed to stretch the string to that shape against the tension $T_1$. -> $V = T_1 \int (\frac{ds}{dx} - 1) dx$; <-

-> $\frac{ds}{dx} - 1 = \frac{1}{2} (\frac{dy}{dx})^2$. <-

**123.** In most of the applications we will encounter, the density $\rho$ is constant, there are no external <note>original: "impressed"</note> forces, and we can assume the motion occurs within a single plane. We may then conveniently write:

-> $\frac{T_1}{\rho} = a^2$ .................................... (1), <-

and the differential equation is expressed as:

-> $\frac{d^2y}{d(at)^2} = \frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ .................................... (2). <-

If we now assume that $y$ is proportional to $\cos mat$, our equation becomes:

-> $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} + m^2y = 0$ .................................... (3), <-

the most general solution for which is:

-> $y = (A \sin mx + C \cos mx) \cos mat$ ............ (4). <-

However, this is not the most general harmonic motion <note>A type of periodic motion or vibration where the restoring force is directly proportional to the displacement.</note> for the period in question. To find the latter, we must assume:

-> $y = y_1 \cos mat + y_2 \sin mat$ ..................... (5), <-

where $y_1$ and $y_2$ are functions of $x$, though not necessarily the same function. By substituting this into equation (2), it appears that both $y_1$ and $y_2$ are subject to equations in the form of equation (3), so that finally:

-> $\left. \begin{aligned} y = (A \sin mx + C \cos mx) \cos mat \\ + (B \sin mx + D \cos mx) \sin mat \end{aligned} \right\}$ ............ (6), <-

This expression contains four arbitrary constants <note>term: arbitrary constants; values that can be changed to fit specific physical conditions (like how the string is held or plucked) without changing the underlying mathematical law.</note>. **124.** The most simple as well as the most important problem connected with our present subject is the investigation of the free vibrations of a finite string of length $l$ held fast at both its ends. If we take the origin of $x$ at one end, the boundary conditions <note>original: "terminal conditions"</note> are that when $x = 0$, and when $x = l$, $y$ vanishes <note>Meaning the displacement $y$ is zero because the ends are fixed.</note> for all values of $t$. The first requires that in equation (6) of § 123
-> $C = 0, \quad D = 0$ ........................ (1); <-
and the second requires that
-> $\sin ml = 0$ ........................ (2), <-
or that $ml = s\pi$, where $s$ is an integer. We learn that the only harmonic vibrations possible are such as make
-> $m = \frac{s\pi}{l}$ ........................ (3), <-
and then
-> $y = \sin \frac{s\pi x}{l} \left( A \cos \frac{s\pi at}{l} + B \sin \frac{s\pi at}{l} \right)$ ......... (4). <-

Now we know from first principles <note>original: "a priori"</note> that whatever the motion may be, it can be represented as a sum of simple harmonic vibrations, and we therefore conclude that the most general solution for a string, fixed at $0$ and $l$, is
-> $y = \sum_{s=1}^{s=\infty} \sin \frac{s\pi x}{l} \left( A_s \cos \frac{s\pi at}{l} + B_s \sin \frac{s\pi at}{l} \right)$ ....... (5). <-

The slowest vibration <note>This is the fundamental frequency or the lowest natural pitch of the string.</note> is that corresponding to $s = 1$. Its period ($\tau_1$) is given by
-> $\tau_1 = \frac{2l}{a} = 2l \sqrt{\frac{\rho}{T_1}}$ ........................ (6). <-

The other components have periods which are exact divisors <note>original: "aliquot parts"</note> of $\tau_1$:—
-> $\tau_s = \tau_1 \div s$ ........................ (7); <-

# FIXED EXTREMITIES.

<margin>124.</margin>

So that, as has been already stated, the whole motion is under all circumstances periodic in the time $\tau_1$ <note>The Greek letter tau ($\tau$) represents the period, or the time it takes for one complete cycle of vibration.</note>. The sound emitted constitutes in general a **musical note**, according to our definition of that term, whose pitch is fixed by $\tau_1$, the period of its lowest <note>original: "gravest"</note> component. It may happen, however, in special cases that the lowest vibration is absent, and yet the whole motion is not periodic in any shorter time. This condition occurs if $A_1^2 + B_1^2$ vanish, while, for example, $A_2^2 + B_2^2$ and $A_3^2 + B_3^2$ are finite. In such cases, the sound could hardly be called a note; but it usually happens in practice that, when the lowest tone is absent, some other takes its place as the fundamental tone, and the sound still constitutes a note in the ordinary sense, though, of course, of a higher pitch. A simple case is when all the odd components, beginning with the first, are missing. The whole motion is then periodic in the time $\frac{1}{2}\tau_1$, and if the second component is present, the sound presents nothing unusual.

The pitch of the note produced by a string (6), and the character of the fundamental vibration, were first investigated on mechanical principles by Brook Taylor in 1715; but it is to Daniel Bernoulli (1755) that we owe the general solution contained in (5). He obtained it, as we have done, by the synthesis of particular solutions, which is permissible according to his Principle of the Coexistence of Small Motions <note>This principle, now known as superposition, states that multiple waves can travel through the same medium independently, and their effects can be added together.</note>. In his time, the general application of the result reached in this way was open to question; in fact, it was the opinion of Leonhard Euler, and also, strangely enough, of Joseph-Louis Lagrange¹, that the series of sines in (5) was not capable of representing an <term>arbitrary function</term> <note>A function that can take any shape, not just a simple mathematical curve; this debate eventually led to the development of Fourier analysis.</note>; and Bernoulli's argument for the other side, based on the infinite number of available constants, was certainly inadequate².

Most of the laws embodied in Taylor's formula (6) had been discovered experimentally long before (1636) by Marin Mersenne. They may be stated thus:—

# TRANSVERSE VIBRATIONS OF STRINGS.

<margin>124.</margin>

(1) For a specific string under a specific tension, the vibration time varies directly with its length.

This is the fundamental principle of the **monochord** <note>A monochord is an ancient scientific and musical instrument consisting of a single string stretched over a soundboard, used to identify the mathematical relationships of musical intervals.</note>, and it appears to have been understood by the ancient Greeks¹.

(2) When the length of the string is fixed, the vibration time varies inversely as the square root of the tension.

(3) Strings of the same length and tension vibrate in times that are proportional to the square roots of their **linear density** <note>Linear density refers to the mass of the string per unit of length.</note>.

These important results can all be derived using the **method of dimensions** <note>The method of dimensions, or dimensional analysis, is a mathematical tool used in physics to find relationships between different physical quantities by examining their fundamental units like mass, length, and time.</note>, if we assume that the period of vibration ($\tau$) depends only on length ($l$), linear density ($\rho$), and tension ($T_1$).

For instance, if the units of length, time, and mass are represented by $[L]$, $[T]$, and $[M]$, the dimensions of these symbols are:

-> $l = [L]$, $\rho = [ML^{-1}]$, $T_1 = [MLT^{-2}]$, <-

Therefore (see section 52), the only combination of these variables capable of representing a unit of time is $T_1^{-\frac{1}{2}} \cdot \rho^{\frac{1}{2}} \cdot l$. The only part of the equation left to determine is the specific numerical factor.

**125.** **Mersenne’s laws** <note>Named after Marin Mersenne (1588–1648), these laws describe the relationship between the frequency of a vibrating string and its length, tension, and mass.</note> are demonstrated in all stringed instruments. In playing the violin, different notes are produced from the same string by shortening its effective length <note>by pressing the string against the fingerboard</note>. In tuning a violin or a piano, the pitch is adjusted while keeping the length constant by changing the tension; however, it must be remembered that the linear density ($\rho$) is not perfectly constant as the string stretches.

To achieve a specific pitch with a string made of a particular material, only one specific relationship must be maintained between the length, the thickness, and the tension. In practice, however, there is usually not much room for variation. Length is often limited by what is convenient for the instrument's size. Furthermore, shortening a string cannot always be corrected by making it thicker; if the tension is not increased in proportion to the thickness <note>original: "section"</note>, the string loses its flexibility. If the tension is increased, it does nothing to lower the pitch. This problem is solved for the lower strings of the piano and violin by wrapping them with a coil of fine wire. This adds **inertia** <note>In this context, inertia refers to the mass or weight of the string.</note> without making the string too stiff or sacrificing its flexibility.

***

¹ Aristotle "knew that a pipe or a string <note>original: "chord"</note> of double length produced a sound where the vibrations occupied twice as much time; and that the qualities of musical harmonies <note>original: "concords"</note> depended on the ratios of the times occupied by the vibrations of the individual sounds."—*Young's Lectures on Natural Philosophy*, Vol. I. p. 404.

# MERSENNE’S LAWS

For quantitative studies into the laws governing vibrating strings, the <term>sonometer</term> <note>A sonometer (also called a monochord) is a diagnostic tool used to measure the relationship between the frequency of a sound produced by a plucked string and the string's length, tension, and mass.</note> is used. By using a weight hanging over a pulley, a catgut string or a metallic wire is stretched across two bridges mounted on a **resonance case** <note>A hollow wooden box that amplifies the sound of the vibrating string.</note>. A moveable bridge, whose position is determined by a scale running parallel to the wire, allows the user to shorten the active portion of the wire to any desired length. The vibrations may be produced by plucking, as with a harp, or with a bow (well-supplied with resin), as with a violin.

If the moveable bridge is placed exactly halfway between the fixed bridges, the pitch is raised by an octave. When the string is reduced to one-third of its length, the note produced is a **twelfth** <note>In music, a twelfth is an interval spanning an octave and a perfect fifth.</note>.

By using the "law of lengths," <term>Marin Mersenne</term> <note>Marin Mersenne (1588–1648) was a French polymath often called the "father of acoustics" for his pioneering work in sound theory.</note> determined the frequencies of known musical notes for the first time. He adjusted the length of a string until its pitch matched a specific note on the musical scale. He then lengthened that same string—maintaining the same tension—until the vibrations became slow enough to be counted by the eye.

For experimental purposes, it is convenient to have two or more strings mounted side by side to vary their lengths, their masses, and the tensions to which they are subjected. For example, for two strings of equal length to produce the interval of an octave, their tensions must be at a ratio of 1:4 if their masses are the same. Alternatively, if the tensions are kept the same, their masses must be in the reciprocal ratio <note>Meaning the heavier string must have four times the mass of the lighter one to sound an octave lower.</note>.

The sonometer is very useful for the numerical determination of pitch. By varying the tension, a string is tuned to unison with a tuning fork (or another standard of known frequency). Then, by adjusting the moveable bridge, the specific length of the string is determined that vibrates in unison with whatever note is being measured. The "law of lengths" then provides the means to compare these frequencies mathematically.

Another application by <term>Johann Scheibler</term> <note>Johann Scheibler (1777–1837) was a German experimenter who developed precise methods for measuring pitch using tuning forks.</note> for determining absolute pitch is also important. The principle is the same as that explained in Chapter III, and the method depends on calculating the absolute pitch of two notes by knowing both the *ratio* and the *difference* of their frequencies. The lengths of the sonometer string are carefully measured when it is in unison with a tuning fork, and again when it produces four **beats** <note>"Beats" are the rhythmic pulsing heard when two sounds of slightly different frequencies interfere with one another.</note> per second with that fork. The ratio of the...

lengths is the inverse ratio of the frequencies, and the difference of the frequencies is four. From these data, the absolute pitch of the tuning fork can be calculated.

The pitch of a string can also be calculated using <term>Taylor’s formula</term> <note>A formula developed by Brook Taylor in 1713 to describe the frequency of a vibrating string based on its length, tension, and mass.</note> from the mechanical elements of the system, but great precautions are necessary to ensure accuracy. The tension is produced by a weight, whose mass (expressed with the same unit as $\rho$) may be called $P$; so that $T_1 = gP$, where $g = 32.2$ <note>The acceleration due to gravity, roughly 32.2 feet per second squared.</note>, if the units of length and time are the foot and the second. In order to ensure that the entire tension acts on the vibrating segment, no bridge must be placed in the way—a condition that can only be satisfied by suspending the string vertically. After the weight is attached, a portion of the string is isolated by clamping it firmly at two points, and the length is measured. The mass of the unit of length $\rho$ refers to the stretched state of the string. This may be found indirectly by observing the elongation (stretching) caused by a tension of the same magnitude as $T_1$, and calculating what would be produced by $T_1$ according to <term>Hooke’s law</term> <note>The principle that the extension of a spring or string is directy proportional to the force applied to it.</note>, and by weighing a known length of the string in its normal, unstretched state. After the clamps have been secured, great care is required to avoid fluctuations in temperature, which would seriously affect the tension. In this way, <term>Seebeck</term> <note>August Seebeck (1805–1849), a German physicist who specialized in acoustics and the perception of sound.</note> obtained very accurate results.

**126.** When a string vibrates in its <term>gravest normal mode</term> <note>The fundamental frequency, or the lowest possible frequency at which a string naturally vibrates.</note>, the displacement is at any moment proportional to $\sin (\pi x / l)$, increasing in value from either end toward the center; no point along the string remains permanently at rest. But it is different in the case of the higher <term>normal components</term> <note>Also known as overtones or harmonics.</note>. Thus, if the vibration is of the mode expressed by:

-> $y = \sin \frac{s \pi x}{l} \left( A_s \cos \frac{s \pi a t}{l} + B_s \sin \frac{s \pi a t}{l} \right),$ <-

the displacement is proportional to $\sin (s \pi x / l)$, which becomes zero at $s - 1$ points, dividing the string into $s$ equal parts. These points of no motion are called **nodes**, and they may obviously be touched or held fast without in any way disturbing the vibration. The production of "harmonics" by lightly touching the string at points of <term>aliquot division</term> <note>Dividing the string into exact fractions, such as halves, thirds, or quarters.</note> is a well-known technique of the violinist. All component modes are excluded which do not have a node at the point touched; so that, regarding pitch, the effect is the same as if the string were securely fastened there.

### NORMAL MODES.

**127.** The constants that appear in the general value of $y$ (from § 124) depend on the specific circumstances of the vibration and can be expressed in terms of the initial values of $y$ and $\dot{y}$ <note>$\dot{y}$ represents the initial velocity of the string at time zero.</note>.

Setting $t = 0$, we find:

-> $y_0 = \sum_{s=1}^{s=\infty} A_s \sin \frac{s\pi x}{l}; \quad \dot{y}_0 = \frac{\pi a}{l} \sum_{s=1}^{s=\infty} s B_s \sin \frac{s\pi x}{l} \dots \dots (1).$ <-

By multiplying by $\sin \frac{s\pi x}{l}$ and integrating from $0$ to $l$, we obtain:

-> $A_s = \frac{2}{l} \int_0^l y_0 \sin \frac{s\pi x}{l} dx; \quad B_s = \frac{2}{\pi a s} \int_0^l \dot{y}_0 \sin \frac{s\pi x}{l} dx \dots \dots (2).$ <-

These results exemplify **Stokes' law** <note>original: "Stokes' law"</note> <note>Named after Sir George Gabriel Stokes; in this context, it refers to a principle where the effects of initial displacement and initial velocity on a system can be mathematically related.</note> (see § 95). The part of $y$ that depends on the initial velocities is:

-> $y = \sum_{s=1}^{s=\infty} \frac{2}{\pi a s} \sin \frac{s\pi x}{l} \sin \frac{s\pi at}{l} \int_0^l \dot{y}_0 \sin \frac{s\pi x}{l} dx,$ <-

From this, the part depending on initial displacements can be determined by differentiating with respect to time and substituting $y_0$ for $\dot{y}_0$.

When the condition of the string at any single moment is completely known, these formulas allow us to calculate the motion for all future time. For example, suppose the string is initially at rest and is displaced so that it forms two sides of a triangle. In this case, $B_s = 0$ because there is no initial velocity; and:

-> Fig. 20. <-

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a horizontal line representing a string of length 'l'. The string is pulled upward at a point 'P' to a height 'gamma' (γ), creating a triangular shape. The distance from the left end 'A' to the point directly below 'P' is labeled 'b'.</image-desc>

-> $A_s = \frac{2\gamma}{l} \left\{ \int_0^b \frac{x}{b} \sin \frac{s\pi x}{l} dx + \int_b^l \frac{l - x}{l - b} \sin \frac{s\pi x}{l} dx \right\}$ <-

-> $= \frac{2\gamma l^2}{\pi^2 s^2 b (l - b)} \sin \frac{s\pi b}{l} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (3),$ <-

upon calculation <note>original: "on integration"</note>.

We can see that $A_s$ becomes zero if $\sin (s\pi b/l) = 0$. This means that the specific vibration component (harmonic) will not exist if there is a <term>node</term> <note>A point on a vibrating string that remains stationary during vibration.</note> of that component located at point $P$. A more comprehensive view of this subject will be provided by another method of solution to be given shortly.
