<meta>This page continues the discussion on the physics of vibrating bars, moving from general definitions to the specific mechanical constants like Young's modulus that govern longitudinal, lateral, and torsional movement.</meta>

# 149.] CLASSIFICATION OF VIBRATIONS.
<sig>16—2</sig>

In this case—namely, the resistance to bending—the resistance increases more rapidly than the thickness in that plane. Therefore, an increase in thickness is accompanied by a rise in pitch.

In the case of longitudinal and lateral vibrations, the mechanical constants involved are the density of the material and the value of Young’s modulus. For small extensions (or compressions), Hooke’s law—according to which tension varies in proportion to extension—holds good. If the extension (calculated as the actual length minus the natural length, divided by the natural length) is called $\epsilon$, we have $T = q\epsilon$. In this formula, $q$ is Young’s modulus and $T$ is the tension per unit area necessary to produce the extension $\epsilon$. Young’s modulus may therefore be defined as the force which would have to be applied to a bar of unit section in order to double its length, if Hooke’s law continued to hold true for such great extensions; its dimensions are accordingly those of a force divided by an area.

The torsional vibrations depend also on a second elastic constant, $\mu$, the interpretation of which will be considered in its proper place.

Although in theory the three classes of vibrations—depending respectively on resistance to extension, to torsion, and to <term>flexure</term><note>The act of bending.</note>—are quite distinct and independent of one another as long as the squares of the strains may be neglected, yet in actual experiments with bars which are neither uniform in material nor accurately cylindrical in shape, it is often found impossible to excite longitudinal or torsional vibrations without causing some measure of lateral motion. In bars of ordinary dimensions, the <term>lowest</term><note>original: "gravest"; referring to the lowest frequency or pitch.</note> lateral motion has a much lower pitch than the lowest longitudinal or torsional motion. Consequently, it will generally happen that the principal tone of either of the latter kinds agrees more or less perfectly in pitch with some <term>overtone</term><note>A higher frequency component of a sound, also known as a harmonic.</note> of the former kind. Under such circumstances, the regular modes of vibrations become unstable, and a small irregularity may produce a great effect. The difficulty of exciting purely longitudinal vibrations in a bar is similar to that of getting a string to vibrate in only one plane.

With this explanation, we may proceed to consider the three classes of vibrations independently, commencing with longitudinal vibrations. These will, in fact, raise no mathematical questions beyond those already resolved in the previous chapters.

<header>LONGITUDINAL VIBRATIONS OF BARS.</header>

**150.** When a rod is stretched by a force parallel to its length, the stretching is generally accompanied by lateral <term>contraction</term><note>The rod becomes thinner as it is pulled longer.</note> in such a way that the increase in volume is less than it would be if the displacement of every particle were only parallel to the axis. In the case of a short rod, or a particle situated near the cylindrical boundary, this lateral motion would be comparable in size to the longitudinal motion and could not be overlooked without risking significant error. However, where a rod is very long in proportion to the dimensions of its cross-section and is subject to stretching in one direction throughout, the longitudinal motion accumulates. Thus, in the case of ordinary rods vibrating longitudinally in the lower <note>original: "graver"</note> modes, the inertia of the lateral motion may be neglected. Furthermore, we shall see later how a correction may be introduced if necessary.

Let $x$ be the distance of a layer of particles composing any section from the resting <note>original: "equilibrium"</note> position of one end when the rod is unstretched (either by permanent tension or as the result of vibrations), and let $\xi$ be the displacement, so that the actual position is given by $x + \xi$. The resting and actual positions of a neighboring layer are $x + \delta x$ and $x + \delta x + \xi + \frac{d\xi}{dx} \delta x$, respectively. Therefore, the elongation is $d\xi/dx$, and thus, if $T$ is the tension per unit area acting across the section,

-> $T = q \frac{d\xi}{dx}$ .................................(1). <-

Now, consider the forces acting on the slice bounded by $x$ and $x + \delta x$. If the area of the section is $\omega$, the tension at $x$ is, by equation (1), $q \omega \ d\xi/dx$, acting in the negative direction. At $x + \delta x$, the tension is

-> $q \omega \left( \frac{d\xi}{dx} + \frac{d^2\xi}{dx^2} \delta x \right)$, <-

acting in the positive direction. Thus, the total force on the slice due to the action of the adjoining parts is

-> $q \omega \frac{d^2\xi}{dx^2} \delta x$. <-

The mass of this element is $\rho \omega \ \delta x$, where $\rho$ is the original density. Therefore, if $X$ is the accelerating force acting on it, the equation of equilibrium is

-> $X + \frac{q}{\rho} \frac{d^2\xi}{dx^2} = 0$ .................................(2). <-

<page-num>245</page-num>
<header>GENERAL DIFFERENTIAL EQUATION.</header>
<meta>150.]</meta>

In the following discussion, we will not need to consider the effect of an external <note>original: "impressed"</note> force. To find the equation of motion, we only have to replace $X$ with the reaction against acceleration, represented by $-\ddot{\xi}$. Thus, if $q : \rho = a^2$, we have:

->$\frac{d^2\xi}{dt^2} = a^2 \frac{d^2\xi}{dx^2} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (3).$<-

This equation takes the same form as the one used for the transverse displacements of a stretched string. It indicates that waves of any type will propagate undisturbed in both positive and negative directions. The velocity $a$ is relative to the *unstretched* state of the bar. The apparent velocity at which a disturbance moves through space will be greater, proportional to the ratio of the stretched and unstretched lengths of any part of the bar. This distinction is only significant <note>original: "material"</note> in the case of permanent tension.

**151.** To find the actual value for the velocity of propagation, we use:

->$a^2 = q : \rho = q\omega : \rho\omega,$<-

which is the ratio between the total tension required (according to Hooke's Law) to double the length of the bar and its longitudinal density. If the same bar were flexible and stretched with a total tension $T$, the velocity of wave propagation along it would be $\sqrt{(T : \rho\omega)}$. Therefore, for the velocity to be the same in both cases, $T$ would have to equal $q\omega$. In other words, the tension would need to be the amount theoretically required to double the bar's length. Because of this, the tones produced by longitudinally vibrating rods are very high compared to those obtainable from strings of a similar length.

In the case of steel, the value of $q$ <note>This constant is known today as Young's Modulus.</note> is approximately $22 \times 10^8$ grams-force per square centimeter. To express this in absolute units of force using the <term>C. G. S.</term>$^1$ system, we must multiply by $980$ <note>The acceleration due to gravity in cm/s².</note>. In this same system, the density of steel (which is the same as its specific gravity relative to water) is $7.8$. Therefore, for steel:

->$a = \sqrt{\frac{980 \times 22 \times 10^8}{7\cdot8}} = 530,000$<-

approximately. This shows <note>original: "shews"</note> that the velocity of sound in steel is about $530,000$ centimeters per second, or about $16$ times greater than...

***

$^1$ <term>Centimeter, Gram, Second</term>. This system was recommended by a Committee of the British Association. *British Association Report*, 1873.

It concludes with a sample calculation showing the velocity of sound in steel is approximately 530,000 cm/s.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the velocity of sound in solids, comparing different materials and introducing the mathematical conditions for vibrations in a bar with free ends.</meta>

<header>LONGITUDINAL VIBRATIONS OF BARS. [151.</header>

than the velocity of sound in air. In glass, the velocity is about the same as in steel.

It should be mentioned that, strictly speaking, the value of *q* <note>Young's modulus, a measure of a material's stiffness</note> determined by static experiments is not the one that should be used here. As with gases, which will be discussed in a later chapter, the rapid changes of state involved in the transmission of sound are accompanied by thermal effects. One result of this is an increase in the effective value of *q* beyond what is obtained from observations of stretching conducted at a constant temperature. However, the available data are not precise enough for this correction to be of any significance in the case of solids.

**152.** The solution of the general equation for the longitudinal vibrations of an infinite <note>original: "unlimited"</note> bar, namely

->$\xi = f(x - at) + F(x + at),$<-

is the same as the solution for a string and does not need to be considered further here.

When both ends of a bar are free, there is, of course, no permanent tension; at the ends themselves, there is also no temporary tension. The condition for a free end is therefore

->$\frac{d\xi}{dx} = 0$ ........................................(1).<-

To determine the normal modes of vibration, we must assume that $\xi$ <note>the displacement of a particle in the bar</note> varies as a harmonic function of time—specifically, $\cos nat$. Then, as a function of $x$, $\xi$ must satisfy

->$\frac{d^2\xi}{dx^2} + n^2\xi = 0$ ........................................(2),<-

of which the complete solution <note>original: "integral"</note> is

->$\xi = A \cos nx + B \sin nx$ ........................................(3),<-

where $A$ and $B$ are constants independent of $x$.

Now, since $d\xi/dx$ always equals zero <note>original: "vanishes"</note> when $x = 0$, we find that $B = 0$. Furthermore, since $d\xi/dx$ equals zero when $x = l$ (the natural length of the bar), it follows that $\sin nl = 0$. This shows that $n$ takes the form

->$n = \frac{i\pi}{l}$ ........................................(4),<-

where $i$ is an integer <note>original: "integral"</note>.

<page-num>247</page-num>
<header>BOTH ENDS FREE.</header>
<margin>152.]</margin>

Accordingly, the normal modes <note>the natural patterns of vibration</note> are given by equations of the form

->$\xi = A \cos \frac{i\pi x}{l} \cos \frac{i\pi at}{l} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (5),$<-

in which, of course, an arbitrary constant may be added to $t$, if desired.

The complete solution for a bar with both ends free is therefore expressed by

->$\xi = \sum_{i=0}^{i=\infty} \cos \frac{i\pi x}{l} \left\{ A_i \cos \frac{i\pi at}{l} + B_i \sin \frac{i\pi at}{l} \right\} \dots\dots (6),$<-

where $A_i$ and $B_i$ are arbitrary constants, which may be determined in the usual manner when the initial values of $\xi$ <note>displacement</note> and $\dot{\xi}$ <note>velocity</note> are given.

A value of $i = 0$ is allowed; it gives a term representing a displacement $\xi$ that is constant with respect to both space and time, which in fact only amounts to a change in the starting point <note>original: "alteration of the origin"</note>.

The period of the lowest <note>original: "gravest"</note> component in equation (6), corresponding to $i = 1$, is $2l/a$, which is the time taken by a disturbance to travel twice the length of the rod. The other tones, found by assigning whole-number <note>original: "integral"</note> values to $i$, form a complete harmonic scale; so that according to this theory, the note produced by a rod in longitudinal vibration would be musical in all cases.

In the lowest mode, the center of the rod (where $x = \frac{1}{2}l$) is a place of no motion, or a node; but the periodic stretching <note>original: "elongation"</note> or compression $d\xi/dx$ is at its maximum there.

**153.** The case of a bar with one end free and the other fixed may be derived from the general solution for a bar with both ends free and of twice the length. For whatever the initial state of the bar free at $x = 0$ and fixed at $x = l$ may be, such displacements and velocities can always be assigned to the sections of a bar extending from $0$ to $2l$ and free at both ends as shall make the motions of the parts from $0$ to $l$ identical in the two cases. It is only necessary to suppose that from $l$ to $2l$, the displacements and velocities are initially equal and opposite to those found in the portion from $0$ to $l$ at an equal distance from the center $x = l$. Under these circumstances, the center must remain at rest throughout the motion due to symmetry, and then the

The tones of the bar still belong to a harmonic scale, but the even tones (such as the octave of the fundamental, etc.) are missing <note>original: "wanting"</note>.

### 154.
When both ends of a bar are fixed, the conditions to be satisfied at the ends are that the value of $\xi$ <note>displacement</note> must be constant. At $x = 0$, we may suppose that $\xi = 0$. At $x = l$, $\xi$ is a small constant $\alpha$, which is zero if there is no permanent tension. Independent of the vibrations, we clearly <note>original: "evidently"</note> have $\xi = x \alpha \div l$, and we could obtain our result most simply by assuming this term immediately. However, it may be instructive to proceed using the general method.

Assuming that as a function of time $\xi$ varies as
-> $A \cos nat + B \sin nat$, <-
we see that as a function of $x$ it must satisfy
-> $\frac{d^2 \xi}{dx^2} + n^2 \xi = 0$, <-
for which the general solution is
-> $\xi = C \cos nx + D \sin nx \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(1).$ <-

But since $\xi$ equals zero when $x$ is zero <note>original: "vanishes with x"</note> for all values of $t$, then $C = 0$, and thus we may write
-> $\xi = \Sigma \sin nx \{A \cos nat + B \sin nat\}.$ <-

The condition at $x = l$ now gives
-> $\Sigma \sin nl \{A \cos nat + B \sin nat\} = \alpha,$ <-
from which it follows that for every finite admissible value of $n$
-> $\sin nl = 0, \text{ or } n = \frac{i\pi}{l}.$ <-

But for the zero value of $n$, we get
-> $A_0 \sin nl = \alpha,$ <-

->$\xi = A_0 \sin nx = a \frac{\sin nx}{\sin nl} = a \frac{x}{l}.$<-

The complete value of $\xi$ is therefore
->$\xi = a \frac{x}{l} + \sum_{i=1}^{i=\infty} \sin \frac{i\pi x}{l} \left\{ A_i \cos \frac{i\pi at}{l} + B_i \sin \frac{i\pi at}{l} \right\} \dots (2).$<-

The solution for the problem of the bar fixed at both ends, in the case where there is no permanent tension, could also be derived from the solution for a bar free at both ends simply by differentiating with respect to $x$. ->$\frac{d^2}{dt^2} \left( \frac{d\xi}{dx} \right) = a^2 \frac{d^2}{dx^2} \left( \frac{d\xi}{dx} \right),$<-
since $\xi$ satisfies

and at both ends $d\xi/dx$ becomes zero <note>original: "vanishes"</note>. Consequently, $d\xi/dx$ in this problem satisfies all the conditions required for $\xi$ in the case where both ends are fixed. The two series of tones are thus identical.

### 155.
The effect of a small load $M$ attached to any point of the rod is easily calculated approximately, as it is sufficient to assume the type of vibration remains unchanged (see § 88). We will take the case of a rod fixed at $x = 0$ and free at $x = l$. The kinetic energy is proportional to
->$\frac{1}{2} \int_0^l \rho \omega \sin^2 \frac{i\pi x}{2l} dx + \frac{1}{2} M \sin^2 \frac{i\pi x}{2l},$<-
or to
->$\frac{\rho \omega l}{4} \left( 1 + \frac{2M}{\rho \omega l} \sin^2 \frac{i\pi x}{2l} \right).$<-

<meta>This page continues the analysis of longitudinal vibrations in rods, focusing on how adding a mass (a "load") to the rod changes its natural frequencies and how waves behave when they encounter changes in the material.</meta>

<page-num>250</page-num>
<header>LONGITUDINAL VIBRATIONS OF BARS. [155.</header>

Since the potential energy is unchanged, we see by the principles of Chapter IV that the effect of a small load $M$ at a distance $x$ from the fixed end is to increase the period of the component tones in the ratio:
-> $1 : 1 + \frac{M}{\rho \omega l} \sin^2 \frac{i \pi x}{2l} \cdot$ <-

The small quantity $M : \rho \omega l$ <note>$\rho \omega l$ represents the total mass of the rod, where $\rho$ is density, $\omega$ is the cross-sectional area, and $l$ is the length.</note> is the ratio of the load to the total mass of the rod.

If the load is attached at the free end, then $\sin^2 (i \pi x / 2l) = 1$, and the effect is to lower <note>original: "depress"</note> the pitch of every tone by the same small interval. It should be remembered that $i$ is an odd <note>original: "uneven"</note> integer in this case.

If the point of attachment of $M$ is a node <note>A point of zero displacement in a standing wave.</note> of any component, the pitch of that component remains unchanged by the addition.

**156.** Another problem worth noting occurs when the load at the free end is large compared with the mass of the rod. In this case, we may assume the mode <note>original: "type"</note> of vibration to be a state of uniform extension along the entire length of the rod.

If $\xi$ is the displacement of the load $M$, the kinetic energy <note>The energy of motion.</note> is:
-> $T = \frac{1}{2} M \dot{\xi}^2 + \frac{1}{2} \dot{\xi}^2 \int_0^l \rho \omega \frac{x^2}{l^2} dx = \frac{1}{2} \dot{\xi}^2 (M + \frac{1}{3} \rho \omega l) \dots \dots \dots (1).$ <-

The tension corresponding to the displacement $\xi$ is $q \omega \xi / l$ <note>$q$ represents Young's modulus, a measure of the material's stiffness.</note>, and thus the potential energy <note>Stored energy due to the rod's elasticity.</note> of the displacement is:
-> $V = \frac{q \omega \xi^2}{2l} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (2).$ <-

The equation of motion is:
-> $(M + \frac{1}{3} \rho \omega l) \ddot{\xi} + \frac{q \omega}{l} \xi = 0,$ <-
and if $\xi \propto \cos pt$:
-> $p^2 = \frac{q \omega}{l} \div (M + \frac{1}{3} \rho \omega l) \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (3).$ <-

The correction due to the inertia <note>The resistance of the rod's mass to changes in motion.</note> of the rod is thus equivalent to adding one-third of the rod's mass to the load $M$.

<header>CORRECTION FOR LATERAL MOTION.</header>
<meta>156 a.] at top left</meta>

The problem of determining the reflection at the junction may be approached as in § 148 *a*. The conditions that must be satisfied at the junction are (i) the continuity of the displacement $\xi$, and (ii) the continuity of the tension, measured by $q \omega \, d\xi/dx$. If $\rho_1, \rho_2, \omega_1, \omega_2, a_1,$ and $a_2$ represent the volume densities, the cross-sections, and the wave velocities in the two wires, the ratio of the reflected amplitude to the incident amplitude is given by:

->$\frac{K}{H} = \frac{\rho_1 \omega_1 a_1 - \rho_2 \omega_2 a_2}{\rho_1 \omega_1 a_1 + \rho_2 \omega_2 a_2} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (1).$<-

The reflection vanishes, meaning the incident wave is transmitted through the junction without any loss, if:

->$\rho_1 \omega_1 a_1 = \rho_2 \omega_2 a_2 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (2).$<-

This result illustrates the difficulty encountered when trying to effectively transmit sound from air to metal, or from metal to air, in the mechanical telephone. For instance, the value of $\rho a$ <note>The product of density ($\rho$) and sound velocity ($a$) is known as acoustic impedance. A large mismatch in impedance causes most of the sound energy to reflect rather than pass through.</note> is about 100,000 times greater in steel than it is in air.

**157.** Our mathematical discussion of longitudinal vibrations <note>Vibrations where the particles move back and forth in the same direction that the wave travels.</note> may conclude with an estimate of the error involved in neglecting the inertia of the lateral (sideways) motion of the parts of the rod not located on the central axis. If the ratio of lateral contraction to longitudinal extension is denoted by $\mu$ <note>Today this is commonly called Poisson's ratio.</note>, the lateral displacement of a particle at a distance $r$ from the axis will be $\mu r \epsilon$ in a state of equilibrium, where $\epsilon$ is the extension. Although, strictly speaking, this relationship will be modified by the inertia of the lateral motion, for our current purpose we may assume it holds true (see § 88).

The constant $\mu$ is a numerical value lying between 0 and $\frac{1}{2}$. If $\mu$ were negative, a longitudinal tension (a pull) would produce a lateral swelling; if $\mu$ were greater than $\frac{1}{2}$, the lateral contraction would be great enough to outweigh the elongation, causing the total volume to decrease. This latter state would be inconsistent with physical stability, and the former is likely impossible in ordinary solids. At one time, it was assumed that $\mu$ was necessarily equal to $\frac{1}{4}$, which would mean there was only one independent elastic constant. However, experiments have since shown that $\mu$ is variable. For glass and brass, the physicist Wertheim found experimentally that $\mu = \frac{1}{3}$.

If $\eta$ represents the lateral displacement of a particle at distance $r$

<meta>This page continues the analysis of longitudinal vibrations in rods, focusing on how the lateral (sideways) expansion and contraction of a rod's thickness affects its vibration period and total kinetic energy.</meta>

from the axis, and if the section is circular, the kinetic energy due to the lateral motion is:

->$\delta T = \pi \rho \int_{0}^{l} \int_{0}^{r} \dot{\eta}^2 dx . r dr = \frac{\rho \omega \mu^2 r^2}{4} \cdot \int_{0}^{l} \left( \frac{d\dot{\xi}}{dx} \right)^2 dx.$<-

Thus, the total kinetic energy is:

->$T + \delta T = \frac{\rho \omega}{2} \int_{0}^{l} \dot{\xi}^2 dx + \frac{\rho \omega \mu^2 r^2}{4} \int_{0}^{l} \left( \frac{d\dot{\xi}}{dx} \right)^2 dx.$<-

In the case of a bar that is free at both ends, we have:

->$\xi \propto \cos \frac{i \pi x}{l}, \quad \frac{d\xi}{dx} \propto - \frac{i \pi}{l} \sin \frac{i \pi x}{l},$<-

and thus:

->$T + \delta T : T = 1 + \frac{i^2 \mu^2 \pi^2}{2} \frac{r^2}{l^2}.$<-

The effect of the inertia from the lateral motion is, therefore, to increase the period in the ratio:

->$1 : 1 + \frac{i^2 \mu^2 \pi^2}{4} \frac{r^2}{l^2}.$<-

This correction will be nearly imperceptible <note>original: "insensible"</note> for the lower frequency <note>original: "graver"</note> modes of bars with ordinary proportions of length to thickness.

[A more complete solution to the problem in this section was provided by Pochhammer$^1$, who applied the general equations for an elastic solid to the case of an infinitely long cylinder with a circular cross-section. The result for longitudinal vibrations, specifically regarding the term $r^2/l^2$, matches the calculation determined above. A similar investigation was also published by Chree$^2$, who also treated the more general case$^3$ in which the cylindrical cross-section is not restricted to being circular.]

**158.** Experiments on longitudinal vibrations may be performed using rods made of pine <note>original: "deal"</note> or glass. The vibrations are triggered by friction (as described in § 138), using a wet cloth for glass; however, for metal or wooden rods, it is necessary to use leather dusted with powdered rosin. "The longitudinal vibrations of a piano string may be triggered by gently rubbing it lengthwise with a piece of india-rubber, and those of a violin string by placing the bow obliquely across the string and moving it lengthwise, keeping the same point of the bow on the string. The resulting note is unpleasantly shrill in both cases."

<meta>This page transitions from the discussion of longitudinal vibrations to torsional vibrations. It notes that while longitudinal vibrations are minimally affected by changes in tension (unlike lateral vibrations), they can sometimes produce secondary sounds. The text then introduces torsional vibrations, which relate to a material's rigidity.</meta>

# TORSIONAL VIBRATIONS.

> "If a violin peg is turned to significantly change the pitch of the lateral <note>sideways</note> vibrations, the pitch of the longitudinal vibrations will change only slightly. This happens because, for lateral vibrations, the change in wave-transmission speed depends mainly on the change in tension, which is significant. However, for longitudinal vibrations, the change in wave speed depends on the change in extension <note>the stretching of the material</note>, which is relatively small $^1$."

In Savart’s experiments on longitudinal vibrations, a peculiar sound—which he called a *rough sound* <note>original: "son rauque"</note>—was occasionally observed. Its pitch was an octave below that of the longitudinal vibration. According to Terquem $^2$, this sound is caused by a transverse <note>sideways</note> vibration. Its appearance is due to a near-perfect match between its own timing <note>period</note> and that of the sub-octave of the longitudinal vibration (see section 68 *b*). If this view is correct, the phenomenon is a secondary effect <note>original: "of the second order"</note>, likely resulting from the fact that the longitudinal compression of a bar tends to cause it to bend or curve.

**159.** The second class of vibrations, called **torsional vibrations**, depend on the resistance a material offers to being twisted. These are generally of very little importance in this context. A solid or hollow cylindrical rod with a circular cross-section may be twisted by applying suitable forces at the ends so that each cross-section remains flat within its own plane. However, if the section is not circular, the effect of a twist is more complicated; the twist necessarily causes a warping <note>distortion</note> of the layers of matter that originally made up the flat sections. Although the effects of this warping could likely be determined for any specific case if necessary, we will limit ourselves here to rods with circular cross-sections, where there is no movement parallel to the axis of the rod.

The force that resists twisting depends on an elastic constant different from the modulus of elasticity (*q*), called **rigidity**. If we represent rigidity as *n*, the relationship between *q*, *n*, and the ratio of lateral contraction to longitudinal extension ($\mu$) <note>known today as Poisson's ratio</note> may be written as:

-> $n = \frac{q}{2(\mu + 1)} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(1)^3,$ <-

***

$^1$ **Donkin's *Acoustics*, p. 154.**
$^2$ **Annals of Chemistry <note>original: "Ann. de Chimie"</note>, LVII. 129—190.**
$^3$ **Thomson and Tait, § 683. It should be noted that this applies only to isotropic material <note>material that has the same physical properties in all directions</note>.**

<summary>This page explains why longitudinal vibrations are less sensitive to tension than lateral ones and introduces torsional vibrations, focusing on circular rods and the concept of rigidity.</summary>
<keywords>torsional vibrations, longitudinal vibrations, lateral vibrations, son rauque, Savart, Terquem, rigidity, elastic constant, isotropic material, Poisson's ratio</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the mathematical analysis of vibrations in bars, shifting focus to the relationship between the shear modulus and Young's modulus, and establishing the equations for torsional vibrations.</meta>

showing that $n$ <note>the shear modulus or rigidity</note> lies between $\frac{1}{3}q$ and $\frac{1}{2}q$ <note>$q$ is Young's modulus</note>. In the case where $\mu = \frac{1}{4}$ <note>$\mu$ is Poisson’s ratio, a measure of how much a material thins when stretched</note>, $n = \frac{2}{5}q$.

Let us now consider a rod in the form of a thin tube with a radius $r$ and thickness $dr$. Let $\theta$ represent the angular displacement of any section at a distance $x$ from the origin. The rate of twist at $x$ is represented by $d\theta/dx$, and the shear of the material composing the pipe is represented by $r \ d\theta/dx$. The opposing force per unit of area is $nr \ d\theta/dx$; and since the area of the cross-section is $2\pi r \ dr$, the torque <note>original: "moment"</note> around the axis is:

->$$2n\pi r^3 \ dr \frac{d\theta}{dx}.$$<-

Thus, the restoring force <note>original: "force of restitution"</note> acting on the slice $dx$ has the torque:

->$$2n\pi r^3 \ dr \ box \frac{d^2\theta}{dx^2}.$$<-

Now, the moment of inertia of the slice under consideration is $2\pi r \ dr \cdot dx \cdot \rho \cdot r^2$ <note>where $\rho$ is the density</note>, and therefore the equation of motion takes the form:

->$$\rho \frac{d^2\theta}{dt^2} = n \frac{d^2\theta}{dx^2} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (2).$$<-

Since this equation is independent of the radius $r$, the same rule applies to a cylinder of any thickness or to one that is solid throughout.

The speed of wave propagation is $\sqrt{(n/\rho)}$, and the entire theory is exactly similar to that of longitudinal vibrations. The condition for a free end is $d\theta/dx = 0$, and for a fixed end $\theta = 0$. If a permanent twist is considered, the condition is $\theta = \text{constant}$.

The speed of longitudinal vibrations relates to the speed of torsional vibrations in the ratio of $\sqrt{q} : \sqrt{n}$ or $\sqrt{(2 + 2\mu)} : 1$. The same ratio applies to the vibration frequencies for bars of equal length vibrating in corresponding modes under the same end conditions. If $\mu = \frac{1}{4}$, the ratio of frequencies would be:

->$$\sqrt{q} : \sqrt{n} = \sqrt{8} : \sqrt{3} = 1.63,$$<-

which corresponds to a musical interval slightly larger than a fifth.

In any case, the ratio of these frequencies must fall between:

->$\sqrt{2} : 1 = 1.414$, and $\sqrt{3} : 1 = 1.732$.<-

Longitudinal and torsional vibrations were first investigated by Chladni <note>Ernst Chladni (1756–1827), a physicist known as the father of acoustics</note>.

# CHAPTER 8.

->LATERAL VIBRATIONS OF BARS.<-

**160.** In this chapter, we will examine the <term>lateral vibrations</term> <note>side-to-side or transverse movements</note> of thin elastic rods that are straight in their natural state. After the study of strings, this class of vibrations is perhaps the most suited for both theoretical and experimental study. There is enough complexity here to highlight important points regarding general theory—points that a reader's familiarity with circular functions <note>trigonometric functions like sine and cosine</note> might otherwise lead them to overlook when applying them to strings. At the same time, the mathematical difficulties are not so great that they distract from the essential mathematical and physical principles.

Daniel Bernoulli <note>1700–1782; a Swiss mathematician who pioneered the study of fluid dynamics and vibration</note> seems to have been the first to tackle this problem. Euler, Riccati, Poisson, Cauchy, and more recently Strehlke, Lissajous, and A. Seebeck are among the primary researchers who have advanced our understanding of it.

**161.** The problem is divided into two parts, depending on whether a permanent <term>longitudinal tension</term> <note>a constant pull along the length of the rod</note> is present or absent. Considering permanent tension introduces additional complexity and is mainly interesting when applied to stretched strings, where the <term>stiffness</term> <note>resistance to bending</note>, though small, cannot be completely ignored. Therefore, our attention will be focused primarily on the two extreme cases: (1) when there is no permanent tension, and (2) when the tension is the primary factor in the vibration.

## LATERAL VIBRATIONS OF BARS. [161.

Regarding the cross-section of the rod, we will assume that one <term>principal axis</term> <note>the axis along which a shape is most or least resistant to bending</note> lies within the plane of vibration. This ensures that the bending at every point occurs in a direction of maximum, minimum, or constant <term>flexural rigidity</term> <note>the measure of how much a structure resists being bent</note>. For instance, the rod might be a <term>surface of revolution</term> <note>a shape formed by rotating a curve around an axis, like a cylinder or cone</note>, where every section is circular, even if the radius changes along its length.

Under these circumstances, the <term>potential energy</term> <note>stored energy</note> of the bending for each element of length is proportional to the square of the curvature. This value is multiplied by a quantity determined by the rod's material and the <term>moment of inertia</term> <note>a mathematical value representing how the mass of the cross-section is distributed relative to the center</note> of the cross-section about an axis passing through its center of gravity and perpendicular to the plane of bending. If $\omega$ is the area of the section, $\kappa^2 \omega$ is its moment of inertia, $q$ is Young's modulus <note>original: "q Young's modulus"; a measure of a material's stiffness</note>, $ds$ is the element of length, and $dV$ is the corresponding potential energy for a curvature $1 \div R$ of the axis of the rod, then:

-> $dV = \frac{1}{2} q \kappa^2 \omega \frac{ds}{R^2}$ ........................(1). <-

We can easily find this result by considering the stretching of the various fibers (or "filaments") that make up the bar. Let $\eta$ represent the distance from the central axis to a specific fiber (with a cross-section of $d\omega$) as projected onto the plane of bending. In this case, the length of the fiber is changed by the bending in the ratio:

-> $1 : 1 + \frac{\eta}{R},$ <-

where $R$ is the <term>radius of curvature</term> <note>the radius of the circle that best fits the curve of the rod at that point</note>. Thus, on the side of the axis where $\eta$ is positive—namely, on the *outer* side—a fiber is stretched, while on the other side of the axis, it is compressed.

Based on the definition of Young's modulus, the force required to produce this stretch ($\eta/R$) is $q \eta/R \cdot d\omega$. Therefore, the total <term>couple</term> <note>a system of forces that results in a turning effect or torque</note> resisting the bend is:

-> $\int q \frac{\eta}{R} \cdot \eta \cdot d\omega = \frac{q}{R} \kappa^2 \omega,$ <-

if $\omega$ is the area of the section and $\kappa$ is its <term>radius of gyration</term> <note>the distance from the axis at which the entire area could be concentrated to have the same moment of inertia</note> about a line through the axis and perpendicular to the plane of bending. The angle of bending for a segment of the axis of length $ds$ is $ds \div R$. Consequently, the work required to bend $ds$ to a curvature of $1 \div R$ is:

-> $\frac{1}{2} q \kappa^2 \omega \frac{ds}{R^2},$ <-

since the *average* value of the couple is exactly half of its *final* value.

### POTENTIAL ENERGY OF BENDING.

For the calculation method mentioned above, the reader should refer to works on the Theory of Elasticity. [The problem of lateral vibrations has been specifically addressed by Pochhammer¹ based on the general equations.]

For a circular cross-section, $\kappa$ is half of the radius.

It is clear from the start that the potential energy of the bending is proportional, all other things being equal <note>original: "cæteris paribus"</note>, to the square of the curvature. If we call the coefficient $B$, we can express this as:

->$$V = \frac{1}{2} \int B \frac{ds}{R^2},$$<-

or, given that the rod is approximately straight:

->$$V = \frac{1}{2} \int B \left( \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} \right)^2 dx \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (2),$$<-

In this equation, $y$ is the lateral displacement of the point on the rod's axis where the <term>abscissa</term> <note>the horizontal coordinate along the axis</note> $x$ is measured parallel to the rod's original, undisturbed position. In the case of a rod where the cross-sections are the same shape and oriented the same way throughout, $B$ is a constant and can be moved outside the integral sign.

The <term>kinetic energy</term> <note>energy of motion</note> of the moving rod is derived partly from the motion of <term>translation</term> <note>movement in a straight line without rotation</note> of its parts parallel to $y$, and partly from the rotation of those same parts around axes passing through their <term>centers of mass</term> <note>original: "centres of inertia"; the point where the mass of the object is balanced</note> perpendicular to the plane of vibration. The first part is expressed by:

->$$\frac{1}{2} \int \rho \omega \dot{y}^2 dx \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (3),$$<-

where $\rho$ represents the <term>volume-density</term> <note>mass per unit volume</note>. To express the second part, we only need to observe that the <term>angular displacement</term> <note>the angle through which an object moves</note> of the element $dx$ is $dy/dx$, and therefore its <term>angular velocity</term> <note>the speed of rotation</note> is $d^2y/dt\ dx$. The square of this value must be multiplied by half the <term>moment of inertia</term> of the element—specifically, by $\frac{1}{2} \kappa^2 \rho \omega\ dx$. We therefore obtain:

->$$T = \frac{1}{2} \int \rho \omega \dot{y}^2 dx + \frac{1}{2} \int \kappa^2 \rho \omega \left( \frac{d}{dt} \frac{dy}{dx} \right)^2 dx \dots\dots\dots\dots (4).$$<-

# LATERAL VIBRATIONS OF BARS. [162.]

**162.** To derive the <term>equation of motion</term> <note>the mathematical formula describing how the bar moves over time</note>, we can use the principle of <term>virtual velocities</term> <note>a fundamental method in mechanics used to derive equations of motion by considering small, hypothetical displacements</note>. For simplicity, if we restrict our analysis to a bar with a **uniform section** <note>a bar where the cross-sectional shape and area are constant along its entire length</note>, we have:

->$\delta V = B \int \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} \frac{d^2\delta y}{dx^2} dx$<-
->$= B \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} \frac{d\delta y}{dx} - B \frac{d^3y}{dx^3} \delta y + B \int \frac{d^4y}{dx^4} \delta y \ dx \dots\dots\dots(1),$<-

The terms outside the integral are to be evaluated at the boundaries (the ends of the bar). This expression includes only the **internal forces** resulting from the bending. In the following discussion, we will assume that no external forces are acting on the system—or specifically, no forces that perform work upon the system. A force of **constraint** <note>a force that limits the motion of the system, such as a fixed support</note>, such as the force required to keep a specific point of the bar stationary, does not need to be considered because it performs no work and thus cannot appear in the equation of virtual velocities.

The **virtual moment** of the <term>accelerations</term> <note>the rate at which the velocity of the bar's parts changes</note> is:

->$\int \rho\omega \frac{d^2y}{dt^2} \delta y \ dx + \int \rho\omega\kappa^2 \frac{d^2}{dt^2} \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) \delta \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) dx$<-
->$= \int \rho\omega \left(\frac{d^2y}{dt^2} - \kappa^2 \frac{d^4y}{dx^2 dt^2}\right) \delta y \ dx + \rho\omega\kappa^2 \delta y \frac{d^3y}{dt^2 dx} \dots\dots\dots(2).$<-

Therefore, the <term>variational equation of motion</term> <note>an equation derived using the calculus of variations to find the path of motion</note> is:

->$\int \left\{ B \frac{d^4y}{dx^4} + \rho\omega \left(\frac{d^2y}{dt^2} - \kappa^2 \frac{d^4y}{dx^2 dt^2}\right) \right\} \delta y \ dx$<-
->$+ B \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} \delta \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) + \left\{ \rho\omega\kappa^2 \frac{d^3y}{dt^2 dx} - B \frac{d^3y}{dx^3} \right\} \delta y = 0 \dots\dots\dots(3),$<-

In this equation, the terms outside the integral are to be evaluated at the boundaries. From this, we derive the general equation that must be satisfied at every point along the length of the bar:

->$B \frac{d^4y}{dx^4} + \rho\omega \left(\frac{d^2y}{dt^2} - \kappa^2 \frac{d^4y}{dx^2 dt^2}\right) = 0,$<-

while at each end:

->$B \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} \delta \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) + \left\{ \rho\omega\kappa^2 \frac{d^3y}{dt^2 dx} - B \frac{d^3y}{dx^3} \right\} \delta y = 0;$<-

Alternatively, if we substitute the value of $B$ (namely $q\kappa^2\omega$ <note>original: "viz. $q\kappa^2\omega$"</note>) and let $q/\rho = b^2$:

->$\frac{d^2y}{dt^2} + b^2\kappa^2 \frac{d^4y}{dx^4} - \kappa^2 \frac{d^4y}{dx^2 dt^2} = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(4),$<-

### TERMINAL CONDITIONS.

...and for each end:
-> $b^2 \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} \delta \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) + \left\{ \frac{d^3y}{dt^2 dx} - b^2 \frac{d^3y}{dx^3} \right\} \delta y = 0 \dots\dots\dots(5).$ <-

In these equations, $b$ represents the velocity of transmission of **longitudinal waves** <note>waves that travel in the same direction as the displacement of the medium, like sound waves in air</note>.

The condition (5) that must be satisfied at the ends of the rod takes different forms depending on the physical circumstances of each case. It is possible to imagine a <term>constraint</term> <note>a physical limitation on the rod's movement</note> where the ratio $\delta (dy/dx) : \delta y$ has a fixed, finite value. The second boundary condition would then be obtained from equation (5) by introducing this ratio. However, in all the cases we shall consider, there is either no constraint at all, or the constraint is such that either $\delta (dy/dx)$ or $\delta y$ vanishes (is zero). In those instances, the <term>boundary conditions</term> <note>the specific mathematical states at the very edges of the system</note> take the form:
-> $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} \delta \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) = 0, \quad \left\{ \frac{d^3y}{dt^2 dx} - b^2 \frac{d^3y}{dx^3} \right\} \delta y = 0 \dots\dots\dots(6).$ <-

We must now distinguish the special cases that may arise:

1.  **Free End:** If an end is free, both $\delta y$ and $\delta (dy/dx)$ are <term>arbitrary</term> <note>they can be any value</note>, and the conditions become:
-> $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 0, \quad \frac{d^3y}{dt^2 dx} - b^2 \frac{d^3y}{dx^3} = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(7),$ <-
The first of these can be seen as expressing that no <term>couple</term> <note>a pair of forces that would cause the end of the rod to rotate</note> acts at the free end, and the second expresses that no external force acts upon it.

2.  **Supported End:** If the direction at the end is free, but the end itself is constrained to remain at rest by the action of an applied force of the necessary magnitude—a case which, for lack of a better word, we say the rod is ***supported***—the conditions are:
-> $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 0, \quad \delta y = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(8),$ <-
by which equation (5) is satisfied.

3.  **Fixed-Direction End:** A third case arises when an extremity is constrained to maintain its direction by an applied <term>couple</term> of the necessary magnitude, but is otherwise free to take any position. In this case, we have:
-> $\delta \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) = 0, \quad \frac{d^3y}{dt^2 dx} - b^2 \frac{d^3y}{dx^3} = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(9).$ <-

# LATERAL VIBRATIONS OF BARS. [Section 162.]

Fourthly, the end <note>original: "extremity"</note> may be restricted both in its position and its direction, in which case the rod is said to be *clamped*. The conditions are clearly:

->$\delta \left(\frac{dy}{dx}\right) = 0, \quad \delta y = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (10).$<-

Of these four cases, the first and the last are the more important; we shall omit the third case from our consideration, as there are no experimental means by which that specific constraint could be achieved. Even with this simplification, a considerable variety of problems remain for discussion, as either end of the bar may be free, clamped, or supported. However, the complication arising from this is not as great as might have been expected. We shall find that different cases may be treated together, and that the solution for one case may sometimes be derived immediately from that of another.

In experimenting on the vibrations of bars, the condition for a clamped end may be achieved with the help of a **vise** <note>original: "vice"; a mechanical tool used to hold an object firmly in place</note> of massive construction. In the case of a free end, there is of course no difficulty regarding the end itself; but, when both ends are free, a question arises as to how the weight of the bar is to be supported. In order to interfere with the vibration as little as possible, the supports must be limited to the neighborhood of the **nodal points** <note>points along a vibrating body where the displacement is zero</note>. It is sometimes sufficient merely to lay the bar on bridges, or to pass a loop of string around the bar and draw it tight with screws attached to its ends. For more exact purposes, it would perhaps be preferable to carry the weight of the bar on a pin passing through a hole drilled through the middle of the thickness in the plane of vibration.

When an end is to be "supported," it may be pressed into contact with a fixed plate whose surface is perpendicular to the length of the bar.

## 163.

Before proceeding further, we shall introduce an assumption which will greatly simplify the mathematical analysis without seriously reducing the value of the solution. We shall assume that the terms depending on the **angular motion** <note>the rotation or tilting of the bar's cross-sections during vibration</note> of the sections of the bar may be neglected. This is equivalent to assuming that the **inertia** <note>the resistance of the object to changes in its state of motion</note> of each section is concentrated at its center. We shall later (Section 186) investigate a correction for this **rotational inertia** <note>original: "rotatory inertia"; the resistance of an object to changes in its rotation</note>...

<margin>Section 163.</margin> inertia, and we shall prove that under ordinary circumstances it is small. The equation of motion now becomes

->$\frac{d^2y}{dt^2} + \kappa^2 b^2 \frac{d^4y}{dx^4} = 0$ ........................(1),<-

and the boundary conditions for a free end

->$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 0, \quad \frac{d^3y}{dx^3} = 0$ ........................(2).<-

The next step, following the general plan, will be to assume a **harmonic form** <note>a mathematical function describing repetitive, periodic motion</note> for $y$. We may conveniently take

->$y = u \cos \left( \frac{\kappa b}{l^2} m^2 t \right)$ ........................(3),<-

where $l$ is the length of the bar and $m$ is a pure number <note>original: "abstract number"; a dimensionless value</note> whose value must be determined. Substituting this into equation (1), we obtain

->$\frac{d^4u}{dx^4} = \frac{m^4}{l^4} u$ ........................(4).<-

If $u = e^{pmx/l}$ is a solution, we see that $p$ is one of the **fourth roots of unity** <note>numbers that, when raised to the fourth power, equal 1</note>, namely <note>original Latin: "viz." (videlicet)</note>: $+1, -1, +i, -i$. Therefore, the complete solution is

->$u = A \cos m \frac{x}{l} + B \sin m \frac{x}{l} + C e^{mx/l} + D e^{-mx/l} \dots \dots \dots (4a),<-

containing four arbitrary constants.

[The simplest case occurs when the motion is strictly periodic with respect to $x$, and constants $C$ and $D$ are zero. If $\lambda$ is the wavelength and $\tau$ is the period of the vibration, we have

->$\frac{2\pi}{\lambda} = \frac{m}{l}, \quad \frac{2\pi}{\tau} = \kappa b \frac{m^2}{l^2},$<-

so that

->$\tau = \frac{\lambda^2}{2\pi \kappa b}$ ........................($4b$).]<-

In the case of a finite rod, we still must satisfy the four boundary conditions—two for each end. These determine the ratios between the constants ($A : B : C : D$) and also provide an equation that $m$ must satisfy. Consequently, only a series of specific values for $m$ are allowed <note>original: "admissible"</note>. For each value of $m$, the corresponding function $u$ is determined entirely, except for a constant multiplier. We will distinguish the different functions of $u$ belonging to the same system using **subscripts** <note>original: "suffixes"</note>.

# LATERAL VIBRATIONS OF BARS. [163.

The value of $y$ <note>the sideways displacement of the bar</note> at any time may be expanded in a series of the functions $u$ (§§ 92, 93). If $\phi_1, \phi_2$, etc., are the **normal coordinates** <note>independent variables that describe the state of a system in terms of its natural modes of vibration</note>, we have:

-> $y = \phi_1 u_1 + \phi_2 u_2 + \dots$ ........................(5), <-

and the **kinetic energy** ($T$) is expressed as:

-> $T = \frac{1}{2} \rho \omega \int (\dot{\phi}_1 u_1 + \dot{\phi}_2 u_2 + \dots)^2 dx$ <-

-> $= \frac{1}{2} \rho \omega \left\{ \dot{\phi}_1^2 \int u_1^2 dx + \dot{\phi}_2^2 \int u_2^2 dx + \dots \right\}$ .................(6). <-

We are fully justified in asserting at this stage that each integrated product of the functions **vanishes** <note>equals zero; this occurs because the vibration modes are "orthogonal," meaning they do not interfere with one another's energy</note>, and therefore the process in the following section should be regarded as a **verification**. It is, however, required in order to determine the value of the **integrated squares** <note>the integral of the square of the function, $\int u^2 dx$, which is necessary to calculate the total energy</note>.

**164.** Let $u_m$ and $u_{m'}$ denote two of the normal functions corresponding respectively to the values $m$ and $m'$. Then:

-> $\frac{d^4 u_m}{dx^4} = \frac{m^4}{l^4} u_m$, $\frac{d^4 u_{m'}}{dx^4} = \frac{m'^4}{l^4} u_{m'}$ ....................(1); <-

or, if prime symbols (dashes) indicate differentiation with respect to $(mx/l)$ and $(m'x/l)$:

-> $u_m'''' = u_m$, $u_{m'}'''' = u_{m'}$ ........................(2). <-

If we subtract these equations (1) after multiplying them by $u_{m'}$ and $u_m$ respectively, and then integrate over the length of the bar, we have:

-> $\frac{m'^4 - m^4}{l^4} \int u_m u_{m'} dx = \int \left( u_m \frac{d^4 u_{m'}}{dx^4} - u_{m'} \frac{d^4 u_m}{dx^4} \right) dx$ <-

-> $= u_m \frac{d^3 u_{m'}}{dx^3} - u_{m'} \frac{d^3 u_m}{dx^3} + \frac{du_{m'}}{dx} \frac{d^2 u_m}{dx^2} - \frac{du_m}{dx} \frac{d^2 u_{m'}}{dx^2} \dots \dots$ (3), <-

where the integrated terms are evaluated at the boundaries (the ends of the bar).

Now, whether the end in question is **clamped**, **supported**, or **free** <margin>The physical constraints at the ends of the bar.</margin>, each term vanishes because of one or the other of its conditions.

---

<note>Footnote 1</note> The reader should observe that the cases specified here are specific examples, and that the right-hand side of equation (3) vanishes provided that:

-> $u_m : \frac{d^3 u_m}{dx^3} = u_{m'} : \frac{d^3 u_{m'}}{dx^3}$, <-

and 

-> $\frac{du_m}{dx} : \frac{d^2 u_m}{dx^2} = \frac{du_{m'}}{dx} : \frac{d^2 u_{m'}}{dx^2}$. <-

These conditions include, for instance, the case of a rod whose end is pushed toward its position of equilibrium by a force proportional to the displacement, such as by a **spring without inertia** <note>a theoretical spring that has stiffness but no mass of its own</note>.

# CONJUGATE PROPERTY.

$$\int u_m u_{m'} dx = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(4),$$

provided that $m$ and $m'$ are different.

The careful reader will notice that in the process we have just followed, we have in fact followed the same steps used to prove the fundamental **differential equation** <note>an equation that relates a function to its derivatives, representing how a physical system changes</note> itself in § 162. The original **variational equation** <note>an equation used to find the state of a system that minimizes energy</note> is most directly connected to the **conjugate property** <note>also called orthogonality; a mathematical condition where two different modes of vibration do not interfere with each other's energy</note>. If we represent the displacement $y$ as $u$ and the change in displacement $\delta y$ as $v$, then the variation in **potential energy** ($V$) is:

$$\delta V = B \int \frac{d^2 u}{dx^2} \frac{d^2 v}{dx^2} dx,$$

and the equation in question is:

$$B \int \frac{d^2 u}{dx^2} \frac{d^2 v}{dx^2} dx + \rho \omega \int \ddot{u} v dx = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(5).$$

Suppose now that $u$ relates to a **normal component vibration** <note>a natural mode of vibration where every part of the system moves with the same frequency</note>, so that $\ddot{u} + n^2 u = 0$ <note>where $\ddot{u}$ is acceleration and $n$ is a constant related to frequency</note>; then:

$$n^2 \rho \omega \int u v dx = B \int \frac{d^2 u}{dx^2} \frac{d^2 v}{dx^2} dx.$$

By similar reasoning, if $v$ is a normal function and $u$ represents any displacement possible for the system:

$$n'^2 \rho \omega \int u v dx = B \int \frac{d^2 u}{dx^2} \frac{d^2 v}{dx^2} dx.$$

We conclude that if $u$ and $v$ are both normal functions that have *different periods* <note>vibrate at different frequencies</note>:

$$\int u v dx = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(6);$$

and this proof is evidently as direct and general as could be desired.

The reader may investigate the formula corresponding to equation (6) when the term representing **rotatory inertia** <note>the resistance of the bar's cross-sections to rotating as the bar bends</note> is retained.

By means of equation (6), we may verify that the allowed values of $n^2$ are real numbers. For if $n^2$ were a **complex number** <note>a number involving the square root of a negative number</note>, and $u = \alpha + i\beta$ were a normal function, then its **conjugate** $\alpha - i\beta$ would also be a normal function corresponding to the conjugate of $n^2$, and then the

If in equation (3) $m$ and $m'$ are the same, the equation becomes always true, and we cannot immediately determine the value of $\int u_m^2 dx$. We must set $m'$ equal to $m + \delta m$ and find the limiting form of the equation as $\delta m$ approaches zero. [It should be observed that the function $u_{m+\delta m}$ is not a natural mode (normal function) of the system; it is assumed to be derived from $u_m$ by varying $m$ in equation (4a) of § 163, while the coefficients $A, B, C,$ and $D$ are kept constant.] In this way we find:

$$\frac{4m^3}{l^4} \int u_m^2 dx = u \frac{d}{dm} \frac{d^3u}{dx^3} - \frac{du}{dm} \frac{d^3u}{dx^3} + \frac{d^2u}{dx^2} \frac{d}{dm} \frac{du}{dx} - \frac{du}{dx} \frac{d}{dm} \frac{d^2u}{dx^2},$$

the right-hand side being evaluated between the limits.

Since $\frac{du}{dx} = \frac{m}{l} u'$, and so on, and $\frac{du}{dm} = \frac{x}{l} u'$, and so on,
then:

$$\frac{4m^3}{l^4} \int u_m^2 dx = \frac{3m^2}{l^3} uu''' + \frac{m^3x}{l^4} uu'''' - \frac{m^3x}{l^4} u'u'''$$
$$+ \frac{m^2}{l^3} u'u'' + \frac{m^3x}{l^4} (u'')^2 - \frac{2m^2}{l^3} u'u'' - \frac{m^3x}{l^4} u'u''',$$

in which the fourth derivative $u'''' = u$, so that:

$$\frac{4m}{l} \int u_m^2 dx = 3uu''' + \frac{mx}{l} u^2 - \frac{2mx}{l} u'u''' - u'u'' + \frac{mx}{l} (u'')^2 \dots (7),$$

evaluated between the limits.

Now, whether an end is clamped, supported, or free,
$$uu''' = 0, \quad u'u'' = 0,$$
and therefore, if we place the origin of $x$ at one end of the rod,

$$\int_0^l u^2 dx = \left\{ \frac{x}{4} (u^2 - 2u'u''' + u''^2) \right\}_0^l$$
$$= \frac{1}{4} l (u^2 - 2u'u''' + u''^2)_{x=l} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (8).$$

The form of our integral is independent of the terminal condition <note>also known as a boundary condition; the physical constraints at the ends of the bar</note> at $x = 0$. If the end at $x = l$ is free, $u''$ and $u'''$ vanish <note>they become zero</note>, and accordingly:

$$\int_0^l u^2 dx = \frac{1}{4} l \ u^2(l) \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (9),$$

VALUES OF INTEGRATED SQUARES.

That is to say, for a rod with one end free, the mean value of $u^2$ <note>The variable $u$ represents the lateral displacement of the rod from its equilibrium position.</note> is one-fourth of the terminal value <note>The "terminal value" is the value at the very end of the rod.</note>, and this holds true whether the other end is clamped, supported, or free.

Again, if we suppose that the rod is clamped at $x = l$, then both $u$ and $u'$ <note>In modern notation, $u'$ and $u''$ represent the first and second derivatives of displacement with respect to the position $x$, representing the slope and bending of the rod.</note> vanish, and equation (8) gives:
->$\int_0^l u^2 dx = \frac{1}{4} l [u''(l)]^2.$<-

Since this must hold true regardless of the terminal condition at the other end, we see that for a rod where one end is fixed and the other is free:
->$\int_0^l u^2 dx = \frac{1}{4} l u^2 \text{ (at the free end)} = \frac{1}{4} l u''^2 \text{ (at the fixed end)},$<-
showing that in this case $u^2$ at the free end is the same as $u''^2$ at the clamped end.

The annexed table gives the values of four times the mean of $u^2$ for various cases.

| End Conditions | Value of $4 \times \text{mean } u^2$ |
| :--- | :--- |
| clamped, free......... | $u^2$ (at free end), or $u''^2$ (at clamped end) |
| free, free ............ | $u^2$ (at free end) |
| clamped, clamped ... | $u''^2$ (at clamped end) |
| supported, supported | $- 2u'u'''$ (at supported end) $= 2u'^2$ |
| supported, free ...... | $u^2$ (at free end), or $- 2u'u'''$ (at supported end) |
| supported, clamped | $u''^2$ (at clamped end), or $- 2u'u'''$ (at supported end) |

By introducing these values, the expression for $T$ <note>original: "T". In physics, $T$ usually represents the total kinetic energy of the system.</note> takes a simpler form. In the case, for example, of a clamped-free or a free-free rod:
->$T = \frac{\rho l \omega}{8} \{ \phi_1^2 u_1^2 (l) + \phi_2^2 u_2^2 (l) + \dots \} \dots \dots \dots (10),$<-
where the end $x = l$ is assumed to be free.

# LATERAL VIBRATIONS OF BARS. [Section 165]

Based on the derived functions, we are free to replace $u$ with $u'$ or $u''$. Thus:
$$\frac{4m}{l} \int_0^l u'^2 dx = 3u'u + \frac{mx}{l} u'^2 - 2 \frac{mx}{l} u''u - u''u''' + \frac{mx}{l} u'''^2$$
$$= 3uu' + \frac{mx}{l} u'^2 - u''u''' + \frac{mx}{l} u'''^2,$$
evaluated between the limits <note>The "limits" refer to the two ends of the rod, usually $x=0$ and $x=l$.</note>, because the term $u u''$ equals zero in all three cases.

For a free-free rod <note>A rod where both ends are entirely unconstrained.</note>:
$$\frac{4m}{l} \int_0^l u'^2 dx = 3 (uu')_l - 3 (uu')_0 + m (u'^2)_l$$
$$= 6 (uu')_l + m (u'^2)_l \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(1),$$
because, as we will see, the values of $u u'$ must be equal and opposite at the two ends. Regardless of whether $u$ is positive or negative at $x = l$, the product $u u'$ is positive.

For a rod which is clamped at $x = 0$ and free at $x = l$:
$$\frac{4m}{l} \int_0^l u'^2 dx = 3 (uu')_l + m u_l'^2 + (u'' u'''' )_0.$$

[We have already seen that $u_0'' = \pm u_l$; and it can be proved from the formulas in section 173 that:
$$- \frac{u_0'''}{u_l'} = \frac{u_0''}{u_l} = \frac{\cos m + \cosh m}{\sin m \sinh m},$$
so that:
$$\frac{(u'' u''')_0}{(u' u)_l} = - \frac{(\cos m + \cosh m)^2}{\sin^2 m \sinh^2 m} = - 1.]$$

Thus:
$$\frac{4m}{l} \int_0^l u'^2 dx = 2 (uu')_l + m u_l'^2 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(2),$$
a result that we will need to use later.

By applying the same equation to calculate the value of $\int u''^2 dx$, we find:
$$\frac{4m}{l} \int u''^2 dx = 3u''u' + \frac{mx}{l} u''^2 - 2 \frac{mx}{l} u'''u' - u'''u + \frac{mx}{l} u^2$$
$$= m (u''^2 - 2u' u''' + u^2)_l,$$
because the terms $u' u''$ and $u u'''$ equal zero.

**166.** We can now construct the expression for the potential energy $V$ in terms of the <term>normal coordinates</term> <note>original: "normal co-ordinates"; these are independent coordinates that simplify the description of complex vibrations into individual modes.</note>.

->$V = \frac{b^2 \kappa^2 \rho \omega}{2} \int \left\{ \phi_1 \frac{d^2 u_1}{dx^2} + \phi_2 \frac{d^2 u_2}{dx^2} + \dots \right\}^2 dx$<-

->$= \frac{b^2 \kappa^2 \rho \omega}{2} \left\{ \phi_1^2 \int \left( \frac{d^2 u_1}{dx^2} \right)^2 dx + \phi_2^2 \int \left( \frac{d^2 u_2}{dx^2} \right)^2 dx + \dots \right\}$<-

->$= \frac{b^2 \kappa^2 \rho \omega}{2 l^4} \left\{ m_1^4 \phi_1^2 \int u_1^2 dx + m_2^4 \phi_2^2 \int u_2^2 dx + \dots \right\}$.........(1).<-

If the functions $u$ are those specific to a rod that is free at the end $x = l$, this expression simplifies to:

->$V = \frac{b^2 \kappa^2 \rho \omega}{8 l^3} \left\{ m_1^4 [u_1(l)]^2 \phi_1^2 + m_2^4 [u_2(l)]^2 \phi_2^2 + \dots \right\}$.........(2).<-

In any case, the equations of motion take the following form:

->$\rho \omega \int u_1^2 dx \ \ddot{\phi}_1 + \frac{b^2 \kappa^2 \rho \omega}{l^4} m_1^4 \int u_1^2 dx \ \phi_1 = \Phi_1$.........(3),<-

and, since $\Phi_1 \delta \phi_1$ is by definition the work done by the <term>applied forces</term> <note>original: "impressed forces"</note> during the displacement variation $\delta \phi_1$:

->$\Phi_1 = \int Y u_1 \rho \omega dx$ ........................... (4),<-

where $Y \rho \omega dx$ represents the lateral force acting on the element of mass $\rho \omega dx$. If there are no applied forces, the equation simplifies to:

->$\ddot{\phi}_1 + \frac{b^2 \kappa^2 m_1^4}{l^4} \phi_1 = 0$ ........................... (5),<-

just as we would expect it to do.

# LATERAL VIBRATIONS OF BARS. [167.

**167.** The significance of reducing the integrals $\int u^2 dx$ to depend on the terminal values <note>The values at the ends (boundaries) of the rod.</note> of the function and its derivatives may be understood more clearly through the following argument. To illustrate the idea, consider a rod clamped at $x = 0$ and free at $x = l$, vibrating in the normal mode <note>A natural pattern of vibration where all parts of the system move at the same frequency.</note> expressed by $u$.

If a small addition $\Delta l$ is made to the rod at the free end, the form of $u$ (viewed as a function of $x$) changes. However, according to the general principle established in Chapter IV (§ 88) <note>This refers to Rayleigh's Principle, which states that a small change in the system's parameters results in a much smaller, second-order change in the natural frequency.</note>, we can calculate the period under these altered circumstances without accounting for the change in the vibration type, if we are satisfied with neglecting the square of that change. Because the rod is straight at the point where the addition is made, there is no change in the potential energy; therefore, the change in the period depends entirely on the variation of $T$ <note>Kinetic energy.</note>. This quantity is increased in the ratio:

->$\int_0^l u^2 dx : \int_0^{l+\Delta l} u^2 dx,$<-

->or $1 : 1 + \frac{u_l^2 \Delta l}{\int_0^l u^2 dx},$<-

which is also the ratio by which the square of the period is increased <note>original: "augmented"</note>. Now, as we will see shortly, the actual period varies as $l^2$, and therefore the change in the square of the period is in the ratio:

->$1 : 1 + 4\Delta l/l.$<-

A comparison of these two ratios shows that:

->$u_l^2 : \int u^2 dx = 4 : l.$<-

The reasoning above is not presented as a formal proof <note>original: "demonstration"</note>, but it serves at least to explain why the integral is capable of being reduced in this way. Other cases where such integrals occur may be treated similarly, but it would often require care to predict with certainty what amount of discontinuity in the varied type could be allowed without moving outside the range of the principle on which the argument depends. The reader may, if they wish, examine the case of a string in which a small piece is inserted in the middle.

### INITIAL CONDITIONS.

...types and then investigate the integral formulas <note>original: "formulæ"</note> by which the particular solutions can be combined to fit any arbitrary initial conditions. I have chosen to follow a different order to better demonstrate the general nature of this method, *which does not depend on knowing the normal functions* <note>Normal functions, or eigenfunctions, are the specific mathematical shapes a rod takes when vibrating at a natural frequency.</note>. Continuing with this plan, I will now investigate the relationship between the arbitrary constants <note>Values in an equation that stay the same for one specific setup but can change depending on how the vibration starts.</note> and the initial conditions, and solve one or two problems similar to those discussed regarding Strings <note>This refers to the earlier study of vibrating strings, such as those on a musical instrument.</note>.

The general value of $y$ <note>The displacement or "wiggle" of the rod from its center position.</note> can be written as:

-> $y = \left( A_1 \cos \frac{\kappa b}{l^2} m_1^2 t + B_1 \sin \frac{\kappa b}{l^2} m_1^2 t \right) u_1$ <-
-> $+ \left( A_2 \cos \frac{\kappa b}{l^2} m_2^2 t + B_2 \sin \frac{\kappa b}{l^2} m_2^2 t \right) u_2$ <-
-> $+ \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (1),$ <-

so that, at the start (when time $t = 0$):

-> $y_0 = A_1 u_1 + A_2 u_2 + \dots \quad \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (2),$ <-
-> $\dot{y}_0 = \frac{\kappa b}{l^2} \{ m_1^2 B_1 u_1 + m_2^2 B_2 u_2 + \dots \} \quad \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (3).$ <note>$\dot{y}_0$ represents the initial velocity of the rod.</note> <-

If we multiply equation (2) by $u_r$ and integrate across the length of the rod, we get:

-> $\int y_0 u_r dx = A_r \int u_r^2 dx \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (4),$ <-

and similarly from equation (3):

-> $\frac{l^2}{\kappa b} \int \dot{y}_0 u_r dx = m_r^2 B_r \int u_r^2 dx \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (5),$ <-

these formulas determine the arbitrary constants $A_r$ and $B_r$.

It should be noted that we do not need a mathematical proof to show that the expansion in equation (1) is possible. If *all* possible individual solutions are included, equation (1) must represent the most general vibration possible; therefore, it can be adjusted to represent any valid initial state.

Let us now assume that the rod is initially at rest in its position of equilibrium <note>The state where the rod is perfectly straight and under no external force.</note> and is set in motion by a strike that gives velocity to a small section of it. At the start—that is, the moment the rod is released—$y_0 = 0$, and the velocity $\dot{y}_0$ is only non-zero near a single point ($x = c$).

### LATERAL VIBRATIONS OF BARS. [168.]

From equation (4), it appears that the coefficients $A$ disappear <note>original: "vanish"; in mathematics, this means their value becomes zero.</note>, and from equation (5) we find that:

$$m_r^2 B_r \int u_r^2 dx = \frac{l^2}{\kappa b} u_r (c) \int \dot{y}_0 dx.$$

If we define the total momentum of the blow as $Y$ (where $Y = \int \dot{y}_0 \rho \omega dx$), we have:

$$B_r = \frac{l^2 Y}{\kappa b \rho \omega} \frac{u_r (c)}{m_r^2 \int u_r^2 dx} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(6),$$

and the final solution for the displacement $y$ is:

$$y = \frac{l^2 Y}{\kappa b \rho \omega} \left\{ \frac{u_1 (c) u_1 (x)}{m_1^2 \int u_1^2 dx} \sin \left( \frac{\kappa b}{l^2} m_1^2 t \right) + \dots \right.$$
$$\left. + \frac{u_r (c) u_r (x)}{m_r^2 \int u_r^2 dx} \sin \left( \frac{\kappa b}{l^2} m_r^2 t \right) + \dots\dots \right\} \dots\dots(7).$$

To apply this result to a rod that is free at the end where $x = l$, we can substitute:

$$\int u_r^2 dx \quad \text{with} \quad \frac{1}{4} l [u_r (l)]^2.$$

If the blow is applied at a node <note>A node is a point along a vibrating body that remains stationary during the vibration.</note> of one of the natural vibration patterns <note>original: "normal components"</note>, that specific pattern will be missing from the resulting motion. This current calculation is just a specific case of the investigation found in Section 101.

**169.** As another example, we can consider a bar that is initially at rest but bent <note>original: "deflected"</note> from its natural position by a sideways <note>original: "lateral"</note> force acting at the point $x = c$. In these circumstances, the coefficients $B$ disappear, and the others are determined by equation (4) in Section 168.

Now,

$$\int_0^l y_0 u_r dx = \frac{l^4}{m_r^4} \int_0^l y_0 \frac{d^4 u_r}{dx^4} dx,$$

and by using the method of integration by parts <note>A technique in calculus used to integrate the product of two functions.</note>:

$$\int_0^l y_0 \frac{d^4 u_r}{dx^4} dx = y_0 \frac{d^3 u_r}{dx^3} - \frac{dy_0}{dx} \frac{d^2 u_r}{dx^2}$$
$$+ \frac{d^2 y_0}{dx^2} \frac{du_r}{dx} - \frac{d^3 y_0}{dx^3} u_r + \int_0^l \frac{d^4 y_0}{dx^4} u_r dx,$$

In this equation, the terms outside the integral are to be evaluated between the boundary limits. Because of the physical setup, the initial shape $y_0$ satisfies the same boundary conditions <note>original: "terminal conditions"; these are the physical constraints at the ends of the bar, such as being fixed or free.</note> as the vibration function $u_r$. Consequently, all of these terms...

# SPECIAL CASES. [169.]

->$\rho \omega \ \kappa^2 b^2 \frac{d^4 y_0}{dx^4} = Y \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (1),$<-

and consequently,

->$\int_0^l y_0 u_r dx = \frac{l^4}{\rho \omega \kappa^2 b^2 m_r^4} \int_0^l Y u_r (x) dx.$<-

If we now assume that the initial displacement is caused by a force applied in the immediate vicinity of the point $x = c$, we have:

->$\int_0^l y_0 u_r dx = \frac{l^4 u_r (c)}{\rho \omega \kappa^2 b^2 m_r^4} \int Y dx,$<-

and for the complete value of $y$ at time $t$,

->$y = \Sigma \left\{ \frac{l^4 u_r (c) u_r (x)}{m_r^4 \kappa^2 b^2 \int \rho \omega u_r^2 dx} \cos \frac{\kappa b}{l^2} m_r^2 t \right\} \int Y dx \dots \dots (2).$<-

->$\int u_r^2 dx$ with $\frac{1}{4} l [u_r (l)]^2.$<-

If we further suppose that the force causing the initial deflection acts at the very end, so that $c = l$, we get:

->$y = 4 \Sigma \left\{ \frac{l^3 u_r (x)}{m_r^4 \kappa^2 b^2 \rho \omega u_r (l)} \cos \frac{\kappa b}{l^2} m_r^2 t \right\} \int Y dx \dots \dots (3).$<-

When $t = 0$, this equation must represent the initial displacement. In cases like this, a problem may arise: how can a series represent an initial displacement that violates a certain condition, when every individual term in that series satisfies the condition $y''' = 0$? <note>The symbol $y'''$ refers to the third derivative, which relates to the "shearing force" in the bar. At a free end, this force should be zero.</note> The reality is that after three rounds of differentiation <note>Differentiation is a calculus operation used here to find the rate of change in the bar's curve.</note> with respect to $x$, the series no longer converges <note>In mathematics, convergence means the sum of the series approaches a specific, finite value.</note> at the point $x = l$. Therefore, we cannot find the value of $y'''$ by differentiating the terms first and then adding them together. The truth of this statement will be clear if we consider a point at a distance $dl$ from the end and replace:

->$u''' (l - dl)$ with $u''' (l) - u^{iv} (l) dl,$<-

# 170.

The forms of the normal functions in various specific cases are obtained by determining the ratios of the four constants in the general solution of:
->$\frac{d^4u}{dx^4} = \frac{m^4}{l^4} u.$<-

If, for the sake of brevity, $x'$ is written for $(mx/l)$, the solution may be put into the form:
->$u = A (\cos x' + \cosh x') + B (\cos x' - \cosh x')$<-
->$+ C (\sin x' + \sinh x') + D (\sin x' - \sinh x') \dots \dots (1),$<-
where $\cosh x$ and $\sinh x$ are the hyperbolic cosine and sine of $x$, defined by the equations:
->$\cosh x = \frac{1}{2}(e^x + e^{-x}), \quad \sinh x = \frac{1}{2}(e^x - e^{-x}) \dots \dots \dots \dots (2).$<-

I have followed the standard notation, although the use of a special symbol could easily be avoided, since:
->$\cosh x = \cos ix, \quad \sinh x = - i \sin ix \dots \dots \dots \dots (3),$<-
where $i = \sqrt{(-1)}$. If this were done, the connection between the formulas of circular and hyperbolic trigonometry would be more apparent. The rules for differentiation are expressed in the equations:
->$\frac{d}{dx} \cosh x = \sinh x, \quad \frac{d}{dx} \sinh x = \cosh x$<-
->$\frac{d^2}{dx^2} \cosh x = \cosh x, \quad \frac{d^2}{dx^2} \sinh x = \sinh x.$<-

When differentiating equation (1) any number of times, the same four compound functions that appear there are continually reproduced. The only one of them that does not become zero <note>original: "vanish"</note> when $x'$ is zero is $\cos x' + \cosh x'$, which then has a value of 2.

Let us first consider the case in which both ends of the bar are free. Since the second and third derivatives ($d^2u/dx^2$ and $d^3u/dx^3$) become zero <note>original: "vanish"</note> when $x$ is zero, it follows that $B = 0$ and $D = 0$, so that:
->$u = A (\cos x' + \cosh x') + C (\sin x' + \sinh x') \dots \dots \dots (4).$<-

# 170. [NORMAL FUNCTIONS FOR A FREE-FREE BAR]

We still have to satisfy the necessary conditions when $x = l$, or $x' = m$. These yield:

->$\left. \begin{aligned} A (-\cos m + \cosh m) + C (-\sin m + \sinh m) = 0 \\ A (\phantom{-}\sin m + \sinh m) + C (-\cos m + \cosh m) = 0 \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots(5),$<-

equations which require for their consistency <note>original: "compatibility"</note> that:

->$(\cosh m - \cos m)^2 = \sinh^2 m - \sin^2 m,$<-

or, by virtue of the relation:

->$\cosh^2 m - \sinh^2 m = 1 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(6),$<-
->$\cos m \cosh m = 1 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(7).$<-

This is the equation whose roots provide the admissible values of $m$. If equation (7) is satisfied, the two ratios of $A : C$ given in (5) are equal, and either of them may be substituted into (4). Omitting the constant multiplier, we have for the normal function <note>The "normal function" describes the shape of the bar during a specific mode of vibration.</note>:

->$\begin{aligned} u = &(\sin m - \sinh m) \left\{ \cos \frac{mx}{l} + \cosh \frac{mx}{l} \right\} \\ &- (\cos m - \cosh m) \left\{ \sin \frac{mx}{l} + \sinh \frac{mx}{l} \right\} \dots\dots\dots (8), \end{aligned}$<-

or, if preferred:

->$\begin{aligned} u = &(\cos m - \cosh m) \left\{ \cos \frac{mx}{l} + \cosh \frac{mx}{l} \right\} \\ &+ (\sin m + \sinh m) \left\{ \sin \frac{mx}{l} + \sinh \frac{mx}{l} \right\} \dots\dots\dots (9); \end{aligned}$<-

and the simple harmonic component of this type is expressed by:

->$$y = Pu \cos \left( \frac{\kappa b}{l^2} m^2 t + \epsilon \right) \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(10).$$<-

# 171.

The frequency of the vibration is $\frac{\kappa b}{2\pi l^2} m^2$, where $b$ is a velocity depending only on the material from which the bar is formed, and $m$ is a dimensionless number <note>original: "abstract number"</note>. Hence, for a given material and mode of vibration, the frequency varies directly with $\kappa$—the radius of gyration <note>The radius of gyration ($\kappa$) represents the distribution of the cross-sectional area around the bending axis; for a rectangular bar of thickness $t$, $\kappa = t / \sqrt{12}$.</note> of the section about an axis perpendicular to the plane of bending—and inversely with the *square* of the length. These results might have been predicted using dimensional analysis <note>original: "argument from dimensions"</note>, if one considers that the frequency is necessarily determined by the value of $l$, together with the value of $\kappa b$—the only quantity involving space, time, and mass that occurs in the governing equations.

# 171. [APPLICATIONS OF THE VIBRATION EQUATION]

...the differential equation. If all the properties of a bar are known except for its absolute size, the frequency of vibration varies inversely with its linear dimensions.

These laws have an important application to tuning forks, whose prongs vibrate like rods that are fixed at the ends where they join the stem <note>original: "stalk"</note> and are free at the other ends. Thus, the vibration period of forks made of the same material and shape varies according to their linear dimensions. The period is approximately independent of the thickness perpendicular to the plane of bending, but it varies inversely with the thickness within the plane of bending. When the thickness is fixed, the period is proportional to the square of the length.

To lower the pitch of a fork for temporary purposes, we may load the ends of the prongs with soft wax, or file away the metal near the base, which weakens the "spring" of the fork. To raise the pitch, the ends of the prongs, which provide the inertia <note>In this context, inertia refers to the mass that resists changes in motion.</note>, may be filed down.

The value of *b* <note>The variable *b* represents the velocity of longitudinal waves in the material, determined by its elasticity and density.</note> reaches its maximum in the case of steel, for which it is about 5,237 meters per second. For brass, the velocity is lower by a ratio of approximately 1.5 to 1; therefore, a tuning fork made of brass would be about a musical fifth lower in pitch than one made of steel.

[For the design of steel vibrators and for rough calculations of frequency—especially when below the limit of human hearing—the theoretical formula is often convenient. If the cross-section of the bar is rectangular with a thickness *t* in the plane of vibration, then $k^2 = \frac{1}{12}t^2$. Using the value of *b* mentioned above, and the values of *m* given later, we obtain the following for the fundamental frequency <note>original: "gravest mode"</note>:

->(clamped-free) frequency = 84,590 $t/l^2$,<-
->(free-free) frequency = 538,400 $t/l^2$,<-

where *l* (length) and *t* (thickness) are expressed in centimeters.

The first of these formulas can be used to calculate the pitch of steel tuning forks.

The lateral vibrations of a bar can be excited by a blow, such as when a tuning fork is struck against a pad. This method is also used for the harmonicon <note>A percussion instrument consisting of a series of glass or metal bars, similar to a modern glockenspiel.</note>, in which strips of metal or glass are supported at the nodes <note>Nodes are the specific points on a vibrating bar that remain stationary during vibration.</note> in such a way that the free vibrations are only slightly hindered.
