-> $J_n(z) = \frac{z^n}{2^n \Gamma(n+1)} \left\{ 1 - \frac{z^2}{2(2n+2)} + \frac{z^4}{2 \cdot 4(2n+2)(2n+4)} \right.$ <-
-> $- \left. \frac{z^6}{2 \cdot 4 \cdot 6(2n+2)(2n+4)(2n+6)} + \dots \dots \right\} \dots \dots \dots (5),$ <-

From this formula, we can easily derive the following relationships between functions of consecutive orders:
-> $J_0'(z) = -J_1(z) \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (6),$ <-
-> $2J_n'(z) = J_{n-1}(z) - J_{n+1}(z) \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (7),$ <-
-> $\frac{2n}{z} J_n(z) = J_{n-1}(z) + J_{n+1}(z) \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (8).$ <-

When $n$ is an integer, $J_n(z)$ can be expressed by the definite integral:
-> $J_n(z) = \frac{1}{\pi} \int_0^\pi \cos(z \sin \omega - n\omega) d\omega \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (9),$ <-
which is Bessel's original form. From this expression, it is obvious that $J_n$ and its derivatives <note>original: "differential coefficients"; in modern calculus, these are the slopes or rates of change of the function.</note> with respect to $z$ are always less than one.

The power series (5) <note>original: "ascending series"; a series where the powers of the variable $z$ increase.</note>, though infinite, converges for all values of $n$ and $z$. However, when $z$ is large, the convergence does not begin for a long time, which makes the series useless for numerical calculations. In such cases, another series that progresses by descending powers of $z$ <note>original: "descending series"; a series where the variable $z$ appears in the denominator, used for approximating values when $z$ is very large.</note> can be used instead. This series is:
-> $J_n(z) = \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi z}} \left\{ 1 - \frac{(1^2 - 4n^2)(3^2 - 4n^2)}{1 \cdot 2 \cdot (8z)^2} + \dots \dots \right\} \cos \left( z - \frac{\pi}{4} - n\frac{\pi}{2} \right)$ <-
-> $+ \sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi z}} \left\{ \frac{1^2 - 4n^2}{1 \cdot 8z} - \frac{(1^2 - 4n^2)(3^2 - 4n^2)(5^2 - 4n^2)}{1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3 \cdot (8z)^3} + \dots \dots \right\}$ <-
-> $\times \sin \left( z - \frac{\pi}{4} - n\frac{\pi}{2} \right) \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (10);$ <-
This series ends if $2n$ is equal to an odd integer. Otherwise, it continues to infinity and eventually becomes divergent. Nevertheless, when $z$ is large, the part of the series that does converge can be used for calculation; it can be proved that the sum of any number of terms differs from the true value of the function by less than the last term included. We will have the opportunity later, in connection with another problem, to consider how this descending series is derived.

# VIBRATIONS OF MEMBRANES. [201.]

**201.** In accordance with the notation for Bessel functions, the expression for a <term>normal component vibration</term> <note>Also known as a "normal mode," this is a natural pattern of vibration where every part of the membrane moves at the same frequency.</note> may therefore be written as:
->*w* = *P J<sub>n</sub>* (*kr*) cos *n* (*θ* + *α*) cos (*pt* + *ε*) ...........(1);<-
and the <term>boundary condition</term> <note>The physical requirement that the membrane be fixed and motionless at its outer edge (where the radius r = a).</note> requires that
->*J<sub>n</sub>* (*ka*) = 0 ....................................(2),<-
an equation whose roots <note>The specific values that satisfy the equation.</note> provide the admissible values of *k*, and therefore of *p* <note>In this context, *k* relates to the spatial wave number and *p* relates to the temporal frequency of the vibration.</note>.

The complete expression for the displacement *w* is obtained by combining the particular solutions found in equation (1) with all admissible values of *k* and *n*. This result is necessarily general enough to cover any initial circumstances that may be imagined. We conclude that any function of the radius *r* and the angle *θ* may be expanded, within the limits of the circle where *r* = *a*, into the following series:
->*w* = ΣΣ *J<sub>n</sub>* (*kr*) {*φ* cos *nθ* + *ψ* sin *nθ*} ........... (3).<-

For every <term>integral</term> <note>original: "integral value"; meaning a whole number or integer.</note> value of *n*, there is a series of values for *k*, given by equation (2); and for each of these, the constants *φ* and *ψ* are arbitrary.

The determination of these constants is carried out in the usual way. Since the energy of the motion is equal to
->½ *ρ* ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>*a*</sup> ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>2π</sup> *ẇ*² *r dθ dr* ........................... (4),<-
<note>Here, *ρ* represents the density of the membrane and *ẇ* (w-dot) represents its velocity, which is the rate of change of displacement *w* over time.</note> and when expressed by means of the <term>normal coordinates</term> <note>A set of coordinates that simplify the description of a system's vibration by treating each mode independently.</note> can only involve their squares, it follows that the product of any two of the terms in equation (3) becomes zero (vanishes) when integrated over the area of the circle. Thus, if we multiply equation (3) by *J<sub>n</sub>* (*kr*) cos *nθ* and integrate, we find:
∫<sub>0</sub><sup>*a*</sup> ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>2π</sup> *w J<sub>n</sub>* (*kr*) cos *nθ r dr dθ*
->= *φ* ∫∫ [*J<sub>n</sub>* (*kr*)]² cos² *nθ r dr dθ* = *φ* · π ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>*a*</sup> [*J<sub>n</sub>* (*kr*)]² *r dr* ......(5),<-
by which *φ* is determined. The corresponding formula for *ψ* is obtained by substituting sin *nθ* for cos *nθ*. A method of evaluating the integral on the right side will be provided presently. Since *φ* and *ψ* each contain two terms—one proportional to cos *pt* and the other to sin *pt*—it is now evident how the solution may be adapted so as to agree with any arbitrary initial values of displacement (*w*) and velocity (*ẇ*).

<summary>This page explains how to use Bessel functions to describe the vibration of a circular membrane, showing how any initial state can be represented as a sum of these functions. It also provides a method for calculating the constants in this series based on the energy of the system and the principle of orthogonality.</summary>

# CIRCULAR BOUNDARY. [202.]

**202.** Let us now examine more closely the character of the <term>fundamental vibrations</term> <note>These are the natural patterns of vibration, or "normal modes," in which every part of the membrane moves at the same frequency.</note>. If $n = 0$, then $w$ (the displacement) is a function of the radius $r$ only; that is to say, the motion is symmetrical with respect to the center of the membrane. The <term>nodes</term> <note>Lines or points on the vibrating surface that remain completely stationary.</note>, if there are any, are the concentric circles defined by the equation:
-> $J_0(kr) = 0$ .............................. (1). <-

When $n$ has an <term>integral</term> <note>A whole number.</note> value other than zero, $w$ is a function of the angle $\theta$ as well as the radius $r$, and the equation for the nodal system takes the form:
-> $J_n(kr) \cos n(\theta - \alpha) = 0$ ........................ (2). <-

The nodal system is thus divisible into two parts. The first consists of the concentric circles represented by:
-> $J_n(kr) = 0$ .............................. (3), <-

and the second consists of the diameters:
-> $\theta = \alpha + (2m + 1)\pi/2n$ ........................ (4), <-

where $m$ is an integer. There are $n$ such diameters, and they are arranged uniformly around the center; in other respects, their position is arbitrary. The radii of the circular nodes will be investigated further on.

**203.** The important <term>integral formula</term> <note>A mathematical expression involving integration, here used to show that different vibration modes are "orthogonal" or independent of one another.</note>:
-> $\int_0^a J_n(kr) J_n(k'r) r dr = 0$ ........................ (1), <-

where $k$ and $k'$ are different roots of
-> $J_n(ka) = 0$ .............................. (2), <-

may be verified analytically by using the differential equations satisfied by $J_n(kr)$ and $J_n(k'r)$. However, it is both simpler and more instructive to begin with a more general problem, where the boundary of the membrane is not restricted to being circular.

The <term>variational equation of motion</term> <note>A method in physics (based on the Principle of Least Action) used to derive the equations of motion by looking at small changes, or "variations," in the energy of the system.</note> is:
-> $\delta V + \rho \iint \ddot{w} \delta w \, dx \, dy = 0$ ........................ (3) <-

where
-> $V = \frac{1}{2} T_1 \iint \{ (\frac{dw}{dx})^2 + (\frac{dw}{dy})^2 \} \, dx \, dy$ ................. (4), <-

and therefore
-> $\delta V = T_1 \iint \{ \frac{dw}{dx} \frac{d\delta w}{dx} + \frac{dw}{dy} \frac{d\delta w}{dy} \} \, dx \, dy$ ................. (5). <-

<summary>This page describes the nodal patterns of a vibrating circular membrane, which consist of concentric circles and diameters, and introduces the mathematical framework for proving the independence of these vibration modes using variational principles.</summary>

<keywords>circular membrane, nodal lines, Bessel functions, fundamental vibrations, variational equation, integral formula, symmetry</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the mathematical proof from the previous page, demonstrating that different patterns of vibration in a membrane are independent of one another (orthogonal) and providing a formula to calculate the intensity of these vibrations.</meta>

# VIBRATIONS OF MEMBRANES [203.]

In these equations, $w$ refers to the actual motion, and $\delta w$ to a hypothetical displacement consistent with the conditions to which the system is subjected. Let us now suppose that the system is performing one of its <term>normal component vibrations</term> <note>The natural patterns of vibration, or "normal modes," in which the entire membrane moves at the same frequency.</note>, so that $w = u$, and
->$\ddot{u} + p^2 u = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(6),$<-
while $\delta w$ is proportional to another <term>normal function</term> <note>A mathematical function describing the shape of a specific vibration mode.</note> $v$.

Since $k = p/c$ <note>Where $k$ relates to the wave number, $p$ to frequency, and $c$ to the speed of the wave.</note>, we get from equation (3):
->$k^2 \iint u v dx dy = \iint \{ \frac{du}{dx} \frac{dv}{dx} + \frac{du}{dy} \frac{dv}{dy} \} dx dy \dots\dots\dots\dots(7).$<-
The integral on the right is <term>symmetrical</term> <note>The result is the same regardless of whether $u$ or $v$ comes first.</note> with respect to $u$ and $v$, and thus
->$(k'^2 - k^2) \iint u v dx dy = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(8),$<-
where $k'^2$ has the same relationship to $v$ that $k^2$ has to $u$.

Accordingly, if the normal vibrations represented by $u$ and $v$ have different periods,
->$\iint u v dx dy = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(9).$<-
In obtaining this result, we have made no assumption regarding the <term>boundary conditions</term> <note>The physical constraints at the edges of the membrane, such as whether it is fixed or free.</note> beyond what is implied by the absence of reactions against acceleration; if such reactions existed, they would appear in the fundamental equation (3).

If in equation (8) we suppose $k' = k$, the equation is satisfied <term>identically</term> <note>Meaning both sides equal zero, which is true but doesn't help solve for the value of the integral.</note>, and we cannot determine the value of $\iint u^2 dx dy$. In order to evaluate this integral, we must follow a different approach.

If $u$ and $v$ are functions satisfying the equations $\nabla^2 u + k^2 u = 0$ and $\nabla^2 v + k'^2 v = 0$ within a certain <term>contour</term> <note>The boundary or outline of the membrane.</note>, we have:
->$(k'^2 - k^2) \iint u v dx dy = \iint (v \nabla^2 u - u \nabla^2 v) dx dy$<-
->$= \int (v \frac{du}{dn} - u \frac{dv}{dn}) ds \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(10),$<-
by <term>Green's theorem</term> <note>original: "Green's theorem"; a fundamental theorem in calculus used to relate a volume or area integral to a boundary integral.</note>. Let us now suppose that $v$ is derived from $u$ by slightly varying $k$, so that:
->$v = u + \frac{du}{dk} \delta k, \quad k' = k + \delta k;$<-
substituting these into equation (10), we find:
->$2k \iint u^2 dx dy = \int (\frac{du}{dk} \frac{du}{dn} - u \frac{d^2 u}{dn dk}) ds \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(11).$<-

<summary>This page derives the orthogonality of normal vibration modes in a membrane, proving that modes with different periods do not interfere with one another. It also uses Green's theorem to provide a method for calculating the integral of the square of a normal function.</summary>
<keywords>vibrations of membranes, normal functions, Green's theorem, orthogonality, boundary conditions, integral calculus, differential equations</keywords>

# VALUES OF INTEGRATED SQUARES

<margin>Section 203.</margin>

Or, if $u$ reaches zero (vanishes) at the boundary:

-> $2k \iint u^2 dx \, dy = \int \frac{du}{dk} \frac{du}{dn} ds$ ........................ (12) <-
<note>Equation 12 relates the total energy of the vibration over the whole surface to the rate of change at the boundary. Here, $dn$ refers to the direction perpendicular to the boundary, and $ds$ is a small segment of the boundary line.</note>

To apply this to a circular area with a radius of $r$, we use:

-> $\left. \begin{aligned} u &= \cos n\theta \, J_n(kr) \\ v &= \cos n\theta \, J_n(k'r) \end{aligned} \right\}$ ........................ (13) <-
<note>$J_n$ represents a Bessel function of the first kind, which describes the radial patterns of a vibrating circular drumhead.</note>

By substituting these into polar coordinates and integrating with respect to the angle $\theta$, we get from equation (10):

-> $(k'^2 - k^2) \int_0^r J_n(kr) J_n(k'r) \, r dr$ <-
-> $= r J_n(k'r) \frac{d}{dr} J_n(kr) - r J_n(kr) \frac{d}{dr} J_n(k'r)$ ............ (14) <-

Consequently, if

-> $\frac{d}{dr} J_n(k'r) : J_n(k'r) = \frac{d}{dr} J_n(kr) : J_n(kr)$ <-

and $k$ and $k'$ are different values, then

-> $\int_0^r J_n(kr) J_n(k'r) \, r dr = 0$ ........................ (15) <-

This equation was first proved by the mathematician Fourier for the specific case where
-> $J_n(kr) = J_n(k'r) = 0$. <-

Again, from equation (11):

-> $2k \int_0^r J_n^2(kr) \, r dr = r \frac{dJ}{dk} \frac{dJ}{dr} - rJ \frac{d^2J}{dr \, dk}$ <-
-> $= kr^2 J'^2 - kr^2 J \left( J'' + \frac{1}{kr} J' \right)$ <-

where the primes (dashes) denote <term>differentiation</term> <note>The mathematical process of finding the rate of change of a function.</note> with respect to $kr$. Now, since

-> $J'' + \frac{1}{kr} J' + \left( 1 - \frac{n^2}{k^2 r^2} \right) J = 0$ <-

we find that

-> $2 \int_0^r J_n^2(kr) \, r dr = r^2 J_n'^2(kr) + r^2 \left( 1 - \frac{n^2}{k^2 r^2} \right) J_n^2(kr)$ ...... (16) <-

This result applies generally. However, if we are looking at membranes with fixed boundaries (where the edge cannot move), then $J_n(kr) = 0$, and the formula simplifies to:

-> $2 \int_0^r J_n^2(kr) \, r dr = r^2 J_n'^2(kr)$ ........................ (17) <-

### VIBRATIONS OF MEMBRANES

**204.** We can use the result we just obtained to simplify the expressions for **$T$** <note>Kinetic energy: the energy of the membrane in motion.</note> and **$V$** <note>Potential energy: the energy stored in the membrane due to its tension and displacement.</note>. From the expression for displacement **$w$**:

-> $w = \Sigma \Sigma \{ \phi_{mn} J_n (k_{mn} r) \cos n\theta + \psi_{mn} J_n (k_{mn} r) \sin n\theta \} \dots \dots \dots (1),$ <-

we find that:

-> $T = \frac{1}{4} \rho \pi a^2 \Sigma \Sigma {J_n}'^2 (k_{mn} a) \{ \dot{\phi}_{mn}^2 + \dot{\psi}_{mn}^2 \} \dots \dots \dots (2),$ <-

-> $V = \frac{1}{4} \rho \pi a^2 \Sigma \Sigma p_{mn}^2 {J_n}'^2 (k_{mn} a) \{ \phi_{mn}^2 + \psi_{mn}^2 \} \dots \dots \dots (3);$ <-

from which we derive the normal <term>equation of motion</term>:

-> $\ddot{\phi}_{mn} + p_{mn}^2 \phi_{mn} = \frac{2 \Phi_{mn}}{\rho \pi a^2 {J_n}'^2 (k_{mn} a)} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (4),$ <-

and a similar equation for $\psi_{mn}$. The value of $\Phi_{mn}$ is found by considering that $\Phi_{mn} \delta \phi_{mn}$ represents the work done by the <term>applied forces</term> <note>original: "impressed forces"</note> during a hypothetical displacement $\delta \phi_{mn}$. Therefore, if $Z$ is the applied force calculated per unit of area:

-> $\Phi_{mn} = \iint Z J_n (k_{mn} r) \cos n\theta \, r dr d\theta \dots \dots \dots (5).$ <-

These expressions and equations do not apply to the case where $n = 0$, because in that instance, $\phi$ and $\psi$ are combined <note>original: "amalgamated"; when $n=0$, the angular components $\cos(0)$ and $\sin(0)$ simplify, merging the variables.</note>. In that case, we have:

-> $\left. \begin{aligned} T &= \frac{1}{2} \rho \pi a^2 {J_0}'^2 (k_{m0} a) \dot{\phi}_{m0}^2 \\ V &= \frac{1}{2} \rho \pi a^2 p_{m0}^2 {J_0}'^2 (k_{m0} a) \phi_{m0}^2 \end{aligned} \right\} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (6),$ <-

-> $\ddot{\phi}_{m0} + p_{m0}^2 \phi_{m0} = \frac{\Phi_{m0}}{\rho \pi a^2 {J_0}'^2 (k_{m0} a)} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (7).$ <-

As an example, let us assume that the initial velocities are zero, and the starting shape <note>original: "initial configuration"</note> is the one formed under the influence of a constant pressure $Z$; thus:

-> $\Phi_{m0} = Z \cdot 2\pi \int_0^a J_0 (k_{m0} r) \, r dr.$ <-

Now, according to the differential equation:

-> $r J_0 (kr) = - \{ r {J_0}'' (kr) + \frac{1}{k} {J_0}' (kr) \},$ <-

and therefore:

-> $\int_0^a J_0 (kr) \, r dr = - \frac{a}{k} {J_0}' (ka) \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (8);$ <-

so that:

-> $\Phi_{m0} = - \frac{2\pi a}{k_{m0}} Z {J_0}' (k_{m0} a).$ <-

Substituting this into equation (7), we see that the initial value of $\phi_{m0}$ is:

-> $(\phi_{m0})_{t=0} = \frac{-2Z}{k_{m0} p_{m0}^2 \rho a {J_0}' (k_{m0} a)} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (9).$ <-

<summary>This page derives the kinetic and potential energy equations for a vibrating circular membrane and establishes its general equation of motion. It specifically calculates the initial displacement of a membrane when subjected to a uniform external pressure.</summary>
<keywords>vibrations of membranes, equation of motion, Bessel functions, kinetic energy, potential energy, applied force, circular membrane, displacement</keywords>

# SPECIAL PROBLEMS.

For values of $n$ other than zero, the force component $\Phi$ and the initial value of the coefficient $\phi_{mn}$ become zero <note>original: "vanish"</note>. The state of the system at time $t$ is expressed by:

->$\phi_{m0} = (\phi_{m0})_{t=0} \cdot \cos p_{m0}t$ ....................(10),<-
->$w = \Sigma \phi_{m0} J_0 (k_{m0}r)$ ............................(11),<-

the summation extending to all the allowed <note>original: "admissible"</note> values of $k_{m0}$.

As an example of **forced vibrations** <note>Forced vibrations occur when an external periodic force drives a system to vibrate at a specific frequency.</note>, we may suppose that $Z$—which remains constant across the surface—varies as a **harmonic function** of time. This can be taken to represent roughly the conditions of a small membrane set in vibration by a series of sound waves <note>original: "train of aerial waves"</note>. If $Z = \cos qt$, we find, following the same logic as before:

->$w = \frac{2}{\rho a} \cos qt \Sigma \frac{J_0 (k_{m0}r)}{k_{m0} (q^2 - {p_{m0}}^2) J_0' (k_{m0}a)}$ ............(12).<-

The forced vibration is, of course, independent of the angle $\theta$. It can be seen that while none of the symmetrical natural vibration components are missing, their relative importance varies greatly—especially if the frequency of the external force ($q$) is very close to one of the membrane's natural frequencies ($p_{m0}$). If the frequencies are nearly identical, the effect of **dissipative forces** <note>original: "dissipative forces"; forces like friction or air resistance that drain energy from the vibration (damping).</note> must be included in the calculation.

[Again, suppose that the force is applied locally at the center. By equation (5):

->$\Phi_{m0} = Z_1 \cos qt$ ............................(13),<-

if $Z_1 \cos qt$ represents the total force at time $t$. From equation (7):

->$\phi_{m0} = \frac{Z_1 \cos qt}{\rho \pi a^2 ({p_{m0}}^2 - q^2) {J_0'}^2 (k_{m0} a)}$ ............(14),<-

and the displacement $w$ is then given by equation (11). This mathematical series converges (reaches a stable sum) unless $r = 0$.

In this method, $k = q/c$, and the ratio of constants by which the two functions of $r$ are multiplied is determined by the conditions at the edge of the membrane. When the frequency $q$ matches one of the values of $p$, the second function disappears from the solution.]

If we arrange these values (excluding zero) in order of size and call them $z_n^{(1)}, z_n^{(2)}, z_n^{(3)} \dots \dots z_n^{(s)} \dots \dots$, then we find the allowed <note>original: "admissible"</note> values of $p$ by multiplying the quantities $z_n^{(s)}$ by $c/a$. The specific <note>original: "particular"</note> solution may then be written as:

-> $w = J_n \left( z_n^{(s)} \frac{r}{a} \right) \{ A_n^{(s)} \cos n\theta + B_n^{(s)} \sin n\theta \} \cos \left\{ \frac{c}{a} z_n^{(s)} t - \epsilon_n^{(s)} \right\} \dots (1).$ <-

The lowest pitch <note>original: "tone"</note> of the group $n$ corresponds to $z_n^{(1)}$. Because in this case $J_n(z_n^{(1)} r/a)$ does not disappear <note>original: "vanish"</note> for any value of $r$ less than $a$, there is no interior **nodal circle** <note>A nodal circle is a circular line on the membrane's surface that remains perfectly still while the rest of the membrane vibrates.</note>. If we set $s = 2$, $J_n$ will disappear when:

-> $z_n^{(2)} \frac{r}{a} = z_n^{(1)},$ <-

which means:

-> $r = a \frac{z_n^{(1)}}{z_n^{(2)}},$ <-

This result represents the radius of the single interior nodal circle. Similarly, if we take the root $z_n^{(s)}$, we obtain a vibration with $s - 1$ nodal circles (not counting the outer boundary) with radii of:

-> $a \frac{z_n^{(1)}}{z_n^{(s)}}, a \frac{z_n^{(2)}}{z_n^{(s)}}, \dots \dots a \frac{z_n^{(s-1)}}{z_n^{(s)}}.$ <-

All the roots of the equation $J_n(ka) = 0$ are **real numbers**. To prove this, suppose for a moment that $ka = \lambda + i\mu$ is a root <note>where $i$ represents an imaginary number</note>. In that case, $k'a = \lambda - i\mu$ must also be a root, and thus, according to Equation 14 in Section 203:

-> $4i\lambda\mu \int_0^a J_n(kr) J_n(k'r) r dr = 0.$ <-

Since $J_n(kr)$ and $J_n(k'r)$ are **conjugate complex quantities** <note>original: "conjugate complex quantities"; pairs of numbers with the same real part but opposite imaginary parts</note> whose product is necessarily positive, the equation above requires that either $\lambda$ or $\mu$ must be zero <note>original: "vanish"</note>. We can see that $\lambda$ cannot be zero because if $ka$ were a purely imaginary number, every term in the mathematical series for $J_n$ would be positive; therefore, the total sum of the series could not be zero. We must conclude that $\mu = 0$, meaning that $k$ is a real number$^1$. We could reach the same conclusion by noting that only **periodic functions** <note>original: "circular functions"; functions like sine and cosine that repeat at regular intervals</note> of time can be used in the mathematical description of a natural vibration component.

The equation $J_n(z) = 0$ has no duplicate roots (except for zero). From equations 7 and 8 in Section 200, we find:

-> $J_n' = \frac{n}{z} J_n - J_{n+1},$ <-

# VIBRATIONS OF MEMBRANES

...the lowest frequency <note>original: "gravest"</note> as 1.0 <note>original: "unity"</note>, together with the radii of the circular nodes expressed as fractions of the membrane's total radius. In the case of six nodal diameters, the frequency stated is the result of a rough calculation I performed myself.

The tones corresponding to the various fundamental modes <note>A "normal mode" is a natural pattern of vibration.</note> of the circular membrane do not belong to a standard harmonic scale, but there are one or two approximately harmonic relations which may be worth noticing. For example:

->$\frac{4}{3} \times 1\cdot594 = 2\cdot125 \approx 2\cdot136$<-
->$\frac{5}{3} \times 1\cdot594 = 2\cdot657 \approx 2\cdot653$<-
->$2 \times 1\cdot594 = 3\cdot188 \approx 3\cdot156$<-

Because of these ratios, the four lowest modes with nodal diameters <note>These are the patterns where the membrane is divided by straight lines passing through the center.</note> would produce a consonant chord <note>A set of notes that sound pleasant together.</note>.

The area of the membrane is divided into segments by the nodal system in such a way that the "sign" or phase of the vibration changes whenever a node is crossed. In those modes of vibration that have nodal diameters, there is clearly no displacement of the membrane's center of mass <note>original: "centre of inertia"</note>. However, in the case of symmetrical vibrations (where the pattern is the same all the way around), the displacement of the center of mass is proportional to:

->$\int_{0}^{a} J_{0}(kr) \, r dr = - \int_{0}^{a} \left\{ J_{0}''(kr) + \frac{1}{kr} J_{0}'(kr) \right\} \, r dr = - \frac{a}{k} J_{0}'(ka)$<-

This is an expression that never equals zero for any of the possible values of $k$, because the mathematical functions $J_{0}'(z)$ and $J_{0}(z)$ <note>These are specific types of Bessel functions used to calculate waves in circular objects.</note> cannot both be zero at the same time. Therefore, in all symmetrical modes, the center of mass of the membrane does move.

**207.** Up until now, we have assumed the circular area of the membrane is a complete, solid disk with only the outer edge fixed. However, it is clear that our theory also provides solutions for other problems—for example, cases where a membrane is bounded by two concentric circles, creating a ring shape. To create a complete theory for a membrane in the form of a ring, we would need to use the "second" Bessel function <note>A more complex mathematical tool used when the center of the circle is removed.</note>.

The problem of a membrane in the shape of a semi-circle can also be considered solved. Any mode of vibration that a semi-circle is capable of must also be applicable to the...

# FIXED RADIUS

...this also applies to a complete circle. To understand this, imagine any point in the matching half-circle having the exact opposite motion of its "mirror image" across the dividing diameter line. In this case, that diameter line will naturally stay still <term>nodal</term> without needing any physical force to hold it in place. Similar logic applies to any wedge-shaped section <term>sector</term> where the angle is a whole-number fraction <note>original: "aliquot part"</note> of 180 degrees <note>original: "two right angles"</note>.

When the angle of the sector is any random size <note>original: "arbitrary"</note>, we can solve the problem using Bessel's functions of a fractional order. If the fixed edges of the sector <note>original: "fixed radii"</note> are at angles $\theta = 0$ and $\theta = \beta$, the specific solution is:

-> $w = P J_{\nu\pi/\beta}(kr) \sin \frac{\nu\pi\theta}{\beta} \cos (pt - \epsilon) \dots\dots\dots (1),$ <-

where $\nu$ is a whole number <term>integer</term>. We can see that if the angle $\beta$ is a whole-number fraction of 180 degrees ($\pi$), then the term $\nu\pi/\beta$ is also a whole number. In this case, the solution is the same as the ones we already found for the complete circle.

An interesting case occurs when the angle $\beta$ equals 360 degrees ($2\pi$). This describes a complete circle where a single radius line (at $\theta = 0$) is forced to stay still <note>original: "constrained to be nodal"</note>.

<image-desc>Fig. 38. A circle with a single horizontal radius drawn from the center to the right edge.</image-desc>

We have:
-> $w = P J_{\frac{1}{2}\nu}(kr) \sin \frac{1}{2}\nu\theta \cos (pt - \epsilon).$ <-

When $\nu$ is an even number, we get vibration patterns <term>modes of vibration</term> that could happen naturally even without forcing the radius to stay still. However, when $\nu$ is an odd number, new types of vibration appear. In these cases, the mathematical series for the function $J$ actually ends <note>original: "terminates"</note>, meaning the solution can be written in a simpler, finite form. For example, when $\nu = 1$:

-> $w = P \frac{\sin kr}{\sqrt{(kr)}} \sin \frac{1}{2}\theta \cos (pt - \epsilon) \dots\dots\dots (2).$ <-

The values of $k$ are given by:
-> $\sin ka = 0, \text{ or } ka = s\pi.$ <-

Because of this, the circular nodes divide the fixed radius into equal sections, and the resulting set of tones forms a harmonic scale <note>A harmonic scale consists of frequencies that are whole-number multiples of a fundamental base frequency.</note>. In the lowest frequency mode <note>original: "gravest mode"</note>, the entire membrane is always pushed to the same side of its resting position <term>equilibrium position</term> at any given moment. It is quite surprising <note>original: "remarkable"</note> that forcing the radius $\theta = 0$ to stay still actually makes the mathematical problem easier to solve than it was before.

# VIBRATIONS OF MEMBRANES

If we set $\nu = 3$, the solution is:
-> $w = P \frac{1}{\sqrt{(kr)}} \left( \frac{\sin kr}{kr} - \cos kr \right) \sin \frac{3}{2} \theta \cos (pt - \epsilon) \dots \dots \dots (3).$ <-

In this case, the nodal radii <term>nodal radii: lines extending from the center of the membrane that remain stationary during vibration</term> are (as shown in Fig. 39):
-> $\theta = \frac{2}{3} \pi, \quad \theta = \frac{4}{3} \pi;$ <-
and the possible tones are determined by the equation:
-> $\tan ka = ka \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (4).$ <-

To calculate the solutions <term>roots</term> of $\tan x = x$, we may assume:
-> $x = (s + \frac{1}{2}) \pi - y = X - y,$ <-
where $y$ is a positive value that is small when $x$ is large.

Substituting this, we find $\cot y = X - y,$
from which:
-> $y = \frac{1}{X} \left( 1 + \frac{y}{X} + \frac{y^2}{X^2} + \dots \right) - \frac{y^3}{3} - \frac{2y^5}{15} - \frac{17y^7}{315} - \dots$ <-

This equation is to be solved by successive approximation <note>Successive approximation is a mathematical method of starting with an estimate and repeatedly refining it to get closer to the true value.</note>. It will easily be found that:
-> $y = X^{-1} + \frac{2}{3} X^{-3} + \frac{13}{15} X^{-5} + \frac{146}{105} X^{-7} + \dots,$ <-
so that the roots of $\tan x = x$ are given by:
-> $x = X - X^{-1} - \frac{2}{3} X^{-3} - \frac{13}{15} X^{-5} - \frac{146}{105} X^{-7} - \dots \dots \dots (5),$ <-
where $X = (s + \frac{1}{2}) \pi.$

In the first quadrant (0 to 90 degrees), there is no solution after zero since $\tan x$ is always greater than $x$. In the second quadrant (90 to 180 degrees), there is no solution because the signs of $x$ and $\tan x$ are opposite. The first solution after zero is therefore in the third quadrant, corresponding to $s = 1$. Even in this case, the mathematical series converges <term>converges: approaches a definite limit</term> enough to provide the value of the root with considerable accuracy; for higher values of $s$, the series is as accurate as could be desired. The actual values of $x/\pi$ are 1.4303, 2.4590, 3.4709, 4.4747, 5.4818, 6.4844, etc. <note>original: "&c."</note>

# EFFECT OF A SMALL LOAD

Consider a small mass <term>load: an additional mass attached to a specific point on the vibrating surface</term> $M$ attached to the membrane at a point defined by the radius vector <term>radius vector: the distance from the center of the circular membrane to a specific point</term> $r'$.

First, we will consider the symmetrical modes <note>original: "types"</note> ($n = 0$), which we can assume still apply despite the presence of the mass $M$. The kinetic energy $T$ (as seen in § 204, equation 6) is changed from

$\frac{1}{2} \rho \pi a^2 J_0'^{2} (k_{m0} a) \dot{\phi}_{m0}^2$ to $\frac{1}{2} \rho \pi a^2 J_0'^{2} (k_{m0} a) \dot{\phi}_{m0}^2 + \frac{1}{2} M \dot{\phi}_{m0}^2 J_0^2 (k_{m0} r')$,

and therefore

-> $p_{m0}^2 : P_{m0}^2 = 1 - \frac{M}{\rho \pi a^2} \frac{J_0^2 (k_{m0} r')}{J_0'^{2} (k_{m0} a)} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (1),$ <-

where $P_{m0}^2$ represents the frequency value when there is no load.

The non-symmetrical vibration modes <note>original: "unsymmetrical normal types"</note> are not fully fixed for the unloaded membrane; however, for our purposes, they must be chosen to make the resulting periods either a maximum or a minimum. This means we choose them so that the effect of the load is either as large or as small as possible. Since adding a load can never raise the pitch <note>pitch: the frequency of the vibration; adding mass increases inertia, which always lowers the frequency</note>, it is clear that the influence of the load is at its minimum (zero) when the mode is shaped so that a nodal diameter <term>nodal diameter: a straight line across the membrane that remains stationary during vibration</term> (any one will do) passes through the point where the load is attached. We must assume the unloaded membrane has two identical periods, one of which remains unchanged by the addition of the load. The other mode is chosen so that the change in period is as great as possible. This occurs when the radius vector $r'$ is positioned exactly halfway between two adjacent nodal diameters. Thus, if $r'$ corresponds to $\theta = 0$, we should use:

-> $w = \phi_{mn} J_n (k_{mn} r) \cos n \theta;$ <-

so that (according to § 204, equation 2):

-> $T = \frac{1}{2} \rho \pi a^2 \dot{\phi}_{mn}^2 J_n'^{2} (k_{mn} a) + \frac{1}{2} M \dot{\phi}_{mn}^2 J_n^2 (k_{mn} r').$ <-

The altered frequency $p_{mn}^2$ is therefore given by:

-> $p_{mn}^2 : P_{mn}^2 = 1 - \frac{2M}{\rho \pi a^2} \frac{J_n^2 (k_{mn} r')}{J_n'^{2} (k_{mn} a)} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (2).$ <-

Naturally, if $r'$ is located such that the load sits on one of the nodal circles <term>nodal circles: circular lines on the membrane that do not move during vibration</term>, neither period is affected.

For example, suppose $M$ is placed at the center of the membrane. The Bessel function $J_n (0)$ equals zero, except when $n = 0$; and $J_0 (0) = 1$. Consequently, only the symmetrical vibrations have their pitch influenced by a central load. For those vibrations, according to equation (1):

-> $p_{m0}^2 : P_{m0}^2 = 1 - \frac{M}{J_0'^{2} (k_{m0} a) \rho \pi a^2} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (3).$ <-

Based on equation (6) in § 200, we know that ->$J_0'(z) = - J_1(z)$,<-
so applying the formula only requires knowing the values of the Bessel function $J_1(z)$ at the points where $J_0(z)$ equals zero (see § 200). For the lowest vibration mode <note>original: "gravest mode"</note>, the value of $J_0'(k_{m0}a)$ is $0.51903^1$. When the value of $k_{m0}a$ is large <note>original: "considerable"</note>, the squared value 
->$J_1^2(k_{m0}a) = 2 \div \pi k_{m0}a$<-
is approximately correct. This shows that for higher-frequency components, the added load has a greater influence on changing the pitch <note>pitch: the frequency of the vibration</note>.

We can calculate how a small irregularity disturbs the nodal system <term>nodal system: the pattern of lines or points on a vibrating surface that remain perfectly still</term> using the formulas from § 90. The most obvious effect is that the straight nodal diameters break up into hyperbolic curves. This happens because the irregularity introduces additional symmetrical vibrations. In many cases, this disturbance is made more likely when some of the natural vibration periods are very close to one another.

**209.** Next, we will investigate how the natural vibrations of a uniform membrane are affected when its shape departs slightly from a perfect circle.

Whatever the shape of the boundary might be, the displacement $w$ satisfies the following equation:
->$\frac{d^2w}{dr^2} + \frac{1}{r} \frac{dw}{dr} + \frac{1}{r^2} \frac{d^2w}{d\theta^2} + k^2w = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(1)$,<-
where $k$ is a constant to be determined. According to Fourier's theorem <term>Fourier's theorem: a mathematical principle stating that any complex periodic wave can be represented as a sum of simple sine and cosine waves</term>, $w$ can be expanded into the following series:
->$w = w_0 + w_1 \cos (\theta + \alpha_1) + w_2 \cos 2 (\theta + \alpha_2) + \dots\dots$<-
->$+ w_n \cos n (\theta + \alpha_n) + \dots\dots,$<-
where $w_0, w_1,$ etc., are functions of the radius $r$ only. By substituting these into equation (1), we see that $w_n$ must satisfy:
->$\frac{d^2w_n}{dr^2} + \frac{1}{r} \frac{dw_n}{dr} + \left(k^2 - \frac{n^2}{r^2}\right) w_n = 0,$<-
the solution for which is:
->$w_n \propto J_n(kr);$<-
because, as noted in § 200, the alternative mathematical function of $r$ cannot be used here <note>Rayleigh refers to Bessel functions of the second kind, which are excluded because they would imply an infinite displacement at the center of the membrane</note>.

The general expression for the displacement $w$ can therefore be written as:
->$w = A_0 J_0(kr) + J_1(kr) (A_1 \cos \theta + B_1 \sin \theta)$<-
->$+ \dots + J_n(kr) (A_n \cos n\theta + B_n \sin n\theta) + \dots\dots\dots(2).$<-
At every point on the boundary, the displacement $w$ must equal zero <note>original: "vanish"</note>.

### NEARLY CIRCULAR BOUNDARY

In the case of a nearly circular membrane, the radius vector <term>radius vector: the distance from the center point to the edge at a specific angle</term> is nearly constant. We may define the radius as $r = a + \delta r$, where $a$ is the average radius and $\delta r$ is a small variation that changes depending on the angle $\theta$. Therefore, the boundary condition <note>original: "boundary condition" - the mathematical requirement that the membrane must be fixed at its edge</note> is:

-> $0 = A_0 [J_0(ka) + k \delta r J_0'(ka)] + \dots \dots$ <-
-> $+ [J_n(ka) + k \delta r J_n'(ka)] [A_n \cos n\theta + B_n \sin n\theta]$ <-
-> $+ \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (3),$ <-

which must hold true for all values of $\theta$.

Let us first consider those modes of vibration that are nearly symmetrical, for which we can assume approximately:

-> $w = A_0 J_0(kr).$ <-

All the remaining coefficients are small compared to $A_0$, since the type of vibration can only differ slightly from what it would be if the boundary were a perfect circle. Thus, if we ignore the squares of these small quantities, equation (3) becomes:

-> $A_0 [J_0(ka) + k \delta r J_0'(ka)] + J_1(ka) [A_1 \cos \theta + B_1 \sin \theta]$ <-
-> $+ \dots + J_n(ka) [A_n \cos n\theta + B_n \sin n\theta] + \dots = 0 \dots \dots (4).$ <-

If we integrate this equation with respect to $\theta$ between the limits of $0$ and $2\pi$ <note>0 and 360 degrees</note>, we obtain:

-> $2\pi J_0(ka) + J_0'(ka) \int_0^{2\pi} k \delta r d\theta = 0,$ <-

or

-> $J_0 \left\{ ka + k \int_0^{2\pi} \delta r \frac{d\theta}{2\pi} \right\} = 0 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (5),$ <-

which shows that the pitch <note>pitch: the frequency of the vibration</note> of the vibration is approximately the same as if the radius vector were uniform and set at its mean value.

This result allows us to form a rough estimate of the pitch of any membrane whose boundary is not excessively elongated. If $\sigma$ represents the area, so that $\rho \sigma$ is the total mass of the membrane, the frequency of the lowest tone <note>original: "gravest tone"</note> is approximately:

-> $(2\pi)^{-1} \times 2.404 \times \sqrt{\frac{\pi T_1}{\sigma \rho}} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (6)^1.$ <-

In order to investigate how the vibration pattern changes, we may—

Multiply equation (4) by $\cos n\theta$ or $\sin n\theta$, and then integrate as before. This results in:

> $\left. \begin{aligned} A_0 J_0'(ka) \int_0^{2\pi} k \delta r \cos n\theta \, d\theta + \pi A_n J_n(ka) = 0 \\ A_0 J_0'(ka) \int_0^{2\pi} k \delta r \sin n\theta \, d\theta + \pi B_n J_n(ka) = 0 \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots(7),$

which determine the ratios $A_n : A_0$ and $B_n : A_0$.

If $\delta r = \delta r_0 + \delta r_1 + \dots + \delta r_n + \dots$ is a Fourier expansion <term>Fourier expansion: a mathematical method of representing a complex shape or wave as a sum of simpler sine and cosine waves</term>, the final expression for the displacement $w$ may be written as:

-> $w : A_0 = J_0(kr)$ <-
-> $- k J_0'(ka) \left\{ \frac{J_1(kr) \delta r_1}{J_1(ka)} + \dots + \frac{J_n(kr) \delta r_n}{J_n(ka)} + \dots \right\} \dots\dots(8).$ <-

When the vibration is not approximately symmetrical, the question becomes more complicated. The normal modes <term>normal modes: the natural patterns or shapes in which a system tends to vibrate when disturbed</term> for a truly circular membrane are to some extent indeterminate, but the irregularity in the boundary will, in general, remove this indeterminacy. The position of the nodal diameters <term>nodal diameters: lines across a circular membrane that remain stationary while the rest of the membrane vibrates</term> must be chosen so that the resulting periods of vibration have maximum or minimum values. Let us, however, suppose that the approximate type of vibration is:

-> $w = A_\nu J_\nu(kr) \cos \nu\theta \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (9),$ <-

and afterwards investigate how the initial line <note>The reference line where the angle $\theta$ equals zero</note> must be taken in order that this form may hold good.

Treating all the remaining coefficients as small in comparison with $A_\nu$, we get from equation (4):

-> $A_0 J_0(ka) + \dots + A_\nu [J_\nu(ka) + k \delta r J_\nu'(ka)] \cos \nu\theta$ <-
-> $+ B_\nu J_\nu(ka) \sin \nu\theta + \dots\dots$ <-
-> $+ J_n(ka) [A_n \cos n\theta + B_n \cos n\theta] + \dots = 0 \dots\dots (10).$ <-

Multiplying by $\cos \nu\theta$ and integrating:

-> $\pi J_\nu(ka) + k J_\nu'(ka) \int_0^{2\pi} \delta r \cos^2 \nu\theta \, d\theta = 0,$ <-

or

-> $J_\nu \left[ ka + k \int_0^{2\pi} \delta r \cos^2 \nu\theta \frac{d\theta}{\pi} \right] = 0,$ <-

which shows <note>original: "shews"</note> that the effective radius of the membrane is:

-> $a + \int_0^{2\pi} \delta r \cos^2 \nu\theta \frac{d\theta}{\pi} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(11).$ <-

The ratios of **A<sub>n</sub>** and **B<sub>n</sub>** to **A** can be found, as previously shown, by integrating equation (10) after multiplying it by **cos nθ** and **sin nθ**.

However, the most interesting point is the pitch <note>original: "pitch"; here referring to the vibrational frequency</note>. The reference line <note>original: "initial line"</note> must be chosen such that expression (11) reaches its maximum or minimum value. If we relate this to a line fixed in space by substituting **θ - α** for **θ**, we must consider how the following quantity depends on **α**:

->$\int_{0}^{2\pi} \delta r \cos^2 \nu (\theta - \alpha) d\theta,$<-

which can also be written as:

->$\cos^2 \nu\alpha \int_{0}^{2\pi} \delta r \cos^2 \nu\theta d\theta + 2 \cos \nu\alpha \sin \nu\alpha \int_{0}^{2\pi} \delta r \cos \nu\theta \sin \nu\theta d\theta$<-
->$+ \sin^2 \nu\alpha \int_{0}^{2\pi} \delta r \sin^2 \nu\theta d\theta \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(12),$<-

and takes the form:

->**A cos² να + 2B cos να sin να + C sin² να**,<-

where **A**, **B**, and **C** do not depend on **α**. Consequently, there are two possible positions for the nodal diameters <term>nodal diameters: stationary lines across the membrane that do not move while the rest of the surface vibrates</term>: one results in a maximum period of vibration, and the other results in a minimum. The diameters of one set divide the angles between the diameters of the other set exactly in half.

However, there are cases where the natural patterns of vibration <term>normal modes: the basic ways a system naturally vibrates</term> remain undefined. This occurs when expression (12) does not change regardless of the value of **α**. This happens if the change in radius (**δr**) is constant, or if **δr** is proportional to **cos νθ**. For instance, if **δr** were proportional to **cos 2θ**—meaning the boundary was slightly oval or elliptical—the system of nodes for **n = 2** (consisting of a pair of perpendicular diameters) could be in any position, at least within this level of mathematical approximation. However, the single diameter corresponding to **n = 1** must align with one of the main axes of the ellipse, and the vibration periods will differ between the two axes.

The shape can be none other than a circle. In the case where the shape is nearly circular, a mathematical proof <note>original: "analytical demonstration"</note> can be provided, the outline of which follows.

The general value of $w$ <note>$w$ represents the displacement of the membrane</note> being
-> $w = A_0 J_0(kr) + \dots + J_n(kr) (A_n \cos n\theta + B \sin n\theta) + \dots \dots (1),$ <-
in which, for the present purpose, the coefficients $A_1, B_1, \dots$ are small relative to $A_0$, we find from the condition that $w$ becomes zero <note>original: "vanishes"</note> when $r = a + \delta r$:
-> $A_0 J_0(ka) + k A_0 J_0'(ka) \delta r + \frac{1}{2} k^2 A_0 J_0''(ka) . (\delta r)^2 + \dots$ <-
-> $+ \Sigma [\{J_n(ka) + k J_n'(ka) \delta r + \dots \} \{A_n \cos n\theta + B_n \sin n\theta\}] = 0 \dots (2).$ <-
Therefore, if 
-> $\delta r = \alpha_1 \cos \theta + \beta_1 \sin \theta + \dots + \alpha_n \cos n\theta + \beta_n \sin n\theta + \dots \dots (3),$ <-
we obtain, by integrating with respect to $\theta$ from $0$ to $2\pi$:
-> $2 A_0 J_0 + \frac{1}{2} k^2 A_0 J_0'' \sum_{n=1}^{n=\infty} (\alpha_n^2 + \beta_n^2)$ <-
-> $+ k \sum_{n=1}^{n=\infty} [(\alpha_n A_n + \beta_n B_n) J_n'] = 0 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (4),$ <-
from which we see, as before, that if the squares of the small quantities are ignored, $J_0(ka) = 0$. This means that at this level of approximation, the average radius <note>original: "mean radius"</note> is also the effective radius <term>effective radius: the radius of a perfect circle that would vibrate at the same frequency as the irregular shape</term>. In order to obtain a more precise approximation, we first determine the ratios $A_n : A_0$ and $B_n : A_0$ by multiplying equation (2) by $\cos n\theta$ and $\sin n\theta$, and then integrating between the limits of $0$ and $2\pi$. Thus:
-> $A_n J_n = - k \alpha_n A_0 J_0', \quad B_n J_n = - k \beta_n A_0 J_0' \dots \dots \dots (5).$ <-
By substituting these values into equation (4), we obtain:
-> $J_0(ka) = \frac{1}{2} k^2 \sum_{n=1}^{n=\infty} \left[ (\alpha_n^2 + \beta_n^2) \left\{ \frac{J_n' J_0'}{J_n} - \frac{1}{2} J_0'' \right\} \right] \dots \dots (6).$ <-
Since $J_0$ <term>Bessel function: a mathematical function used to describe the vibration of circular membranes</term> satisfies the fundamental equation:
-> $J_0'' + \frac{1}{ka} J_0' + J_0 = 0 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (7),$ <-
and in this case $J_0$ is approximately $0$, we may replace $J_0''$ with $-\frac{1}{ka} J_0'$. Equation (6) then becomes:
-> $J_0(ka) = \frac{1}{2} k^2 J_0' \sum_{n=1}^{n=\infty} \left[ (\alpha_n^2 + \beta_n^2) \left\{ \frac{J_n'}{J_n} + \frac{1}{2ka} \right\} \right] \dots \dots (8).$ <-

## FORM OF THE MAXIMUM PERIOD

Let us now suppose that $a + da$ is the equivalent radius <term>equivalent radius: the radius of a perfectly circular membrane that would vibrate at the same frequency as the irregular one</term> of the membrane, so that:

-> $J_0 [k(a + da)] = J_0(ka) + J_0'(ka) kda = 0.$ <-

Then, using equation (8), we find:

-> $da = -\frac{1}{2} k \sum_{n=1}^{n=\infty} \left[ (\alpha_n^2 + \beta_n^2) \left\{ \frac{J_n'}{J_n} + \frac{1}{2ka} \right\} \right] \dots \dots \dots (9).$ <-

Again, if $a + da'$ is the radius of a perfectly circular membrane of equal area:

-> $da' = \frac{1}{4a} \sum_{n=1}^{n=\infty} (\alpha_n^2 + \beta_n^2) \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (10);$ <-

so that:

-> $da' - da = \frac{1}{2a} \sum_{n=1}^{n=\infty} \left[ (\alpha_n^2 + \beta_n^2) \left\{ 1 + ka \frac{J_n'(ka)}{J_n(ka)} \right\} \right] \dots \dots (11).$ <-

The question now concerns the sign of the right-hand side of the equation. If $n = 1$, and we substitute $z$ for $ka$:

-> $1 + z \frac{J_n'(z)}{J_n(z)}$ <-

approximately becomes zero according to equation (7), since in general $J_1 = -J_0'$, and in this case $J_0(z)$ is nearly zero. Thus $da' - da = 0$, as would clearly be expected, since this specific term represents simply a shift in the circle's position without changing the actual shape of the boundary. When $n = 2$, according to equation (8) in section 200:

-> $J_2 = \frac{2}{z} J_1 - J_0,$ <-

From this and equation (7), we find that when $J_0 = 0$:

-> $\frac{J_2'}{J_2} = \frac{z^2 - 4}{2z} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (12),$ <-

from which it follows:

-> $da' - da = \frac{1}{2a} (\alpha_2^2 + \beta_2^2) \left( \frac{z^2}{2} - 1 \right) \dots \dots \dots \dots (13),$ <-

This value is positive, because $z = 2.404$ <note>The value 2.404 is the first root of the Bessel function $J_0$, representing the fundamental mode of a circular membrane</note>.

We still need to prove that:

-> $1 + z \frac{J_n'(z)}{J_n(z)}$ <-

is positive for all integer values of $n$ greater than 2, when $z = 2.404$.

<meta>This page continues the mathematical proof regarding the vibration of nearly circular membranes. It establishes that a perfect circle has a lower fundamental frequency (pitch) than any other shape of the same area by examining the properties of Bessel functions.</meta>

### VIBRATIONS OF MEMBRANES

To achieve this, we can use a theorem found in Riemann’s *Partial Differential Equations* <note>original: *Partielle Differentialgleichungen*; referring to the work of Bernhard Riemann, a German mathematician</note>. The theorem states that neither the Bessel function $J_n$ nor its derivative $J_n'$ has a root (aside from zero) that is less than $n$. We can express the differential equation for $J_n$ in this form:

->$\frac{d^2 J_n(z)}{d(\log z)^2} + (z^2 - n^2) J_n(z) = 0;$<-

Initially, $J_n$ and $J_n'$ (as well as $dJ_n/d \log z$) are positive. Consequently, $dJ_n/d \log z$ starts by increasing and continues to do so until $z = n$. This makes it clear that within the range from $z = 0$ to $z = n$, neither $J_n$ nor $J_n'$ can vanish <term>vanish: in mathematics, to reach a value of zero</term>. Since both $J_n$ and $J_n'$ remain positive until $z = n$, it follows that when $n$ is an integer greater than 2.404, the difference $da' - da$ is positive. 

We can conclude that, unless all the deformation terms $\alpha_2, \beta_2, \alpha_3, \dots$ are zero, $da'$ is greater than $da$. This shows that for any membrane with a nearly circular shape, the circle with the same area is larger than the circle with the same pitch. <note>In other words, a circle of a given area vibrates more slowly—has a lower pitch—than any other shape of the same area.</note>

We have already seen that we can get a good estimate of a nearly circular membrane's pitch based solely on its area. However, using equation (9), we can achieve an even more accurate approximation. Let us apply this method to an ellipse with a semi-major axis $R$ and eccentricity $e$ <term>eccentricity: a measure of how much a shape deviates from being a perfect circle</term>.

The polar equation for the boundary is:

->$r = R \{ 1 - \frac{1}{4} e^2 - \frac{7}{64} e^4 + \dots \dots + \frac{1}{4} e^2 \cos 2\theta + \dots \dots \} \dots \dots (14);$<-

Using the notation from this section, we have:

->$a = R (1 - \frac{1}{4} e^2 - \frac{7}{64} e^4), \quad \alpha_2 = \frac{1}{4} e^2 R.$<-

Therefore, by equation (9):

->$da = - \frac{e^4 R}{32} \cdot kR \cdot \{ \frac{J_2'(z)}{J_2(z)} + \frac{1}{2z} \},$<-

or by equation (12), given that $kR = z = 2.404$:

->$da = - \frac{2.779}{64} e^4 R.$<-

Thus, the radius of the circle with the same pitch is:

->$a + da = R \{ 1 - \frac{1}{4} e^2 - \frac{9.779 e^4}{64} \} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (15),$<-

where the term containing $e^4$ should be accurate.

## ELLIPTICAL BOUNDARY

The result can also be expressed using the eccentricity $e$ and the area $\sigma$ <note>$\sigma$ is the Greek letter sigma, representing the area of the membrane</note>. We have:

-> $R = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma}{\pi}} \left( 1 + \frac{1}{4} e^2 + \frac{5}{32} e^4 \right)$, <-

and thus:

-> $a + da = \sqrt{\frac{\sigma}{\pi}} \left( 1 - \frac{3 \cdot 779}{64} e^4 \right) \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (16)$, <-

from which we see how small the influence of a moderate eccentricity is when the area is already known.

**211.** When the fixed boundary of a membrane is neither straight nor circular, determining its vibrations presents difficulties that generally cannot be overcome without using mathematical functions that have not yet been discussed or listed in tables. A partial exception is made for an elliptic boundary; however, for the purposes of this book, the problem is not important enough to justify introducing such complicated analysis. Readers are instead referred to the original investigation by M. Mathieu¹.

[The method depends on the use of conjugate functions <term>conjugate functions: mathematical pairings used to transform coordinates from one system to another while preserving certain geometric properties</term>. If

-> $x + iy = c \cos (\xi + i\eta) \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (1)$, <-

then the curves where $\eta$ is a constant are confocal ellipses <term>confocal: sharing the same focus points</term>, and the curves where $\xi$ is a constant are confocal hyperbolas. In terms of $\xi$ and $\eta$, the fundamental equation $(\nabla^2 + k^2) u = 0$ becomes:

-> $\frac{d^2u}{d\xi^2} + \frac{d^2u}{d\eta^2} + k'^2 (\cosh^2 \eta - \cos^2 \xi) u = 0 \dots \dots \dots \dots (2)$, <-

where $k' = kc$.

The solution to equation (2) can be found in the following form:

-> $u = \Xi(\xi) \cdot \text{H}(\eta) \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (3)$, <-

in which $\Xi$ is a function of $\xi$ only, and $\text{H}$ is a function of $\eta$ only, provided that:

-> $\frac{d^2\Xi}{d\xi^2} - (k'^2 \cos^2 \xi - a) \Xi = 0 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (4)$, <-

-> $\frac{d^2\text{H}}{d\eta^2} + (k'^2 \cosh^2 \eta - a) \text{H} = 0 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (5)$, <-

# VIBRATIONS OF MEMBRANES

Michell¹ has shown <note>original: "shewn"</note> that the elliptic transformation (1) is the only one that yields an equation capable of being satisfied in the form (3).]

Solvable cases may be created by means of the general solution:

->*w* = *A*₀ *J*₀ (*kr*) + ... + (*Aₙ* cos *nθ* + *Bₙ* sin *nθ*) *Jₙ* (*kr*) + ......<-

For example, we might take:

->*w* = *J*₀ (*kr*) - *λ J*₁ (*kr*) cos *θ*,<-

and by assigning different values to *λ* <note>the Greek letter lambda</note>, we can trace the various boundary shapes to which this solution applies.

Useful information can sometimes be obtained from the theorem in Section 88, which allows us to prove that any contraction of the fixed boundary of a vibrating membrane must cause an increase in pitch <note>original: "elevation of pitch"</note>. This is because the new state can be thought of as differing from the old one simply by the addition of an extra constraint. We can imagine springs, which have no mass of their own, forcing the line of the proposed boundary toward its equilibrium position and gradually becoming stiffer. At each step, the vibrations become more rapid until they reach a limit, which corresponds to the infinite stiffness of the springs and the absolute fixity of their points of application. It is not necessary for the part of the membrane being cut off to have the same density as the rest, or even any density at all.

For instance, the pitch of a regular polygon lies between the pitches of its inscribed and circumscribed circles. However, closer limits would be obtained by substituting the circumscribed circle with a circle of equal area, according to the result of Section 210. In the case of a hexagon, the ratio of the radius of the circle of equal area to the radius of the inscribed circle is 1.050; therefore, the average of these two limits cannot differ from the true value by more than 2.5 percent. In the same way, we might conclude that a 60-degree sector of a circle has a lower pitch <note>original: "graver form"</note> than the equilateral triangle formed by replacing the circle's arc with a straight chord.

It will therefore be seen that there was not much left to be done in 1866; nevertheless, the research paper <note>original: "memoir"</note> of Bourget already referred to contains a useful discussion of the problem accompanied by very complete numerical results, though not all of them were new.

**213.** In his experimental investigations, M. Bourget used various materials, of which paper proved to be as good as any. The paper is soaked in water, and after removing the excess <note>original: "superfluous"</note> moisture with blotting paper, it is placed on a wooden frame whose edges have been previously coated with glue. The shrinking <note>original: "contraction"</note> of the paper as it dries produces the necessary tension, but many failures may occur before a satisfactory result is obtained. Even a well-stretched membrane requires considerable care in use, as it is prone to great variations in pitch due to the changing humidity <note>original: "varying moisture"</note> of the atmosphere. The vibrations are triggered by organ pipes—of which it is necessary to have a series tuned to small intervals of pitch—and they are made visible to the eye by means of a little sand scattered on the membrane. If the vibration is sufficiently strong, the sand accumulates on the nodal lines <note>areas of a vibrating surface that remain stationary</note>, whose form is thus defined with more or less precision. Any inequality in the tension shows itself by the circles becoming elliptical.

The principal results of the experiment are the following:

A circular membrane cannot vibrate in unison with every sound. It can only place itself in unison with sounds higher <note>original: "more acute"</note> than the sound heard when the membrane is gently tapped.

As theory indicates, these possible sounds are separated by smaller and smaller intervals the higher they become.

The nodal lines are only formed distinctly in response to certain definite sounds. A little above or below these pitches, confusion follows, and when the pitch of the pipe is decidedly altered, the membrane remains unmoved. There is not, as Savart <note>Félix Savart (1791–1841), a French physicist known for his work in acoustics</note> supposed, a continuous transition from one system of nodal lines to another.

The nodal lines are circles or diameters, or combinations of circles and diameters, just as theory requires. However, when the—

# OBSERVATIONS OF MONSIEUR BOURGET.

If the number of diameters exceeds two, the sand tends to pile up in a disorganized way toward the center of the membrane, and the nodes <note>lines or points on a vibrating surface that remain stationary</note> are not clearly defined.

The same general laws were verified by Messieurs Bernard and Bourget for square membranes¹; these authors believe that the results of theory are decisively established, contradicting the views of Savart, who argued that a membrane was capable of responding to any sound, regardless of its pitch. However, I must point out here that the distinction between **forced** and **free** vibrations does not seem to have been sufficiently kept in mind. When a membrane is set in motion by sound waves originating from an organ pipe, the vibration is, technically speaking, *forced*. Theory does not claim that the membrane is only capable of vibrating at certain defined frequencies, but rather that it is only capable of vibrating *freely* at those frequencies <note>vibrating on its own after the initial force is removed</note>. When, however, the timing <note>original: "period"</note> of the external force is not roughly equal to one of the membrane's natural periods, the resulting vibration may be too small to detect <note>original: "insensible"</note>.

In Savart's experiments, the sound of the pipe was two or three octaves higher than the lowest <note>original: "gravest"</note> tone of the membrane. Accordingly, it was never far from unison with one of the many overtones <note>higher-frequency tones produced by the same object</note>. Messieurs Bourget and Bernard conducted their experiments under more favorable conditions. When they played a pipe at a pitch somewhat lower than the lowest tone of the membrane, the sand remained still. However, it was thrown into violent vibration as unison <note>matching frequencies</note> was approached. As soon as the pipe was significantly higher than the membrane, the sand returned to rest. 

They modified the experiment by first tuning a pipe about a third higher than the membrane in its natural state. The membrane was then heated until its tension increased enough to raise the pitch above that of the pipe. As the membrane cooled, the pitch gradually fell. The moment the frequencies matched <note>original: "the point of coincidence"</note> was revealed by the violent motion of the sand, which had been noticeably still at the beginning and end of the experiment.

Monsieur Bourget found that theory and observation agreed well regarding the radii of the circular nodes, though the test was not highly precise because the bands of sand had a noticeable width. However, the relative pitch of the various simple tones differed significantly from the theoretical estimates. The

# FORCED VIBRATIONS.

**213 *a*.** The forced vibrations of square and circular membranes have been further studied through experiments by Elsas¹, who confirmed Savart’s conclusions regarding the responsiveness of a membrane to sounds of any pitch <note>original: "arbitrary pitch"</note>. In these experiments, the vibrations of a tuning fork were transmitted to the membrane by a light thread attached perpendicularly <note>original: "normally"</note> at the center. The positions of the nodal curves <term>nodal curves: lines on a vibrating surface that remain still while the rest of the surface moves</term> and the points of maximum vibration were traced in the usual way using sand and lycopodium <term>lycopodium: a fine, light powder made from plant spores, used to visualize vibration patterns</term>. A series of illustrations accompanies the report <note>original: "memoir"</note>, showing the effect of sounds as the pitch progressively rises.

In many cases, the curves found in the experiments do not show the symmetry required by the assumed conditions. For example, in the case of a square membrane, all the curves should relate to the four corners in the same way; in the case of a circular membrane, all the curves should be circles. This discrepancy is likely due to the difficulty of achieving perfectly equal tension across the membrane. If there is any irregularity, it will introduce modes of vibration that should not be present—specifically those that have nodes at the point where the vibration is applied—especially when the vibration periods are nearly identical. Furthermore, an irregularity may disrupt the balance between two modes of theoretically identical pitch which should be activated to the same degree. In fact, passing through such a point of isochronism <term>isochronism: the state of having the same frequency or timing</term> is expected to be highly unstable unless there are moderate damping <note>original: "dissipative"</note> forces.

The theoretical solutions to these questions have already been given (in sections 196 and 204), but they would require much more development to accurately determine the nodal curves for periods that are not included among the natural frequencies <note>original: "natural periods"</note>. However, the general progression of the phenomenon can be followed without difficulty.

If the forced frequency is lower than the lowest natural frequency, the vibration has no internal nodes. This is because a nodal line, if it existed, would necessarily be either an endless loop or end at the boundary², dividing the membrane into two parts. Of—

# VIBRATIONS OF PLATES. [215.]

**215.** We will now calculate the variation <note>original: "variation"; in calculus, a variation refers to a small change in a function or variable.</note> of the potential energy *V*. It should first be noted that the second term in the expression for *V*—specifically the surface integral $\iint \frac{dS}{\rho_1 \rho_2}$—represents the *total curvature* of the plate. Consequently, this term depends only on the conditions at the plate's edge.

-> $\delta V = \frac{2qh^3}{3(1 - \mu^2)} \iint \left\{ \nabla^2 w \cdot \nabla^2 \delta w - (1 - \mu) \delta \frac{1}{\rho_1 \rho_2} \right\} dS \dots \dots (1);$ <-

Thus, we must consider these two variations:

-> $\iint \nabla^2 w \cdot \nabla^2 \delta w \cdot dS$  and  $\iint \delta (\rho_1 \rho_2)^{-1} dS.$ <-

Now, applying Green's theorem <note>original: "Green's theorem"; a mathematical principle used to relate a double integral over a region to a line integral around its boundary.</note>:

$\iint \nabla^2 w \cdot \nabla^2 \delta w \cdot dS = \iint \nabla^4 w \cdot \delta w \cdot dS$
-> $- \int \frac{d \nabla^2 w}{dn} \cdot \delta w \cdot ds + \int \nabla^2 w \frac{d \delta w}{dn} ds \dots \dots \dots \dots (2),$ <-

In this equation, *ds* represents a segment of the boundary line, and *d/dn* indicates the rate of change (differentiation) relative to the normal <term>normal: a line perpendicular to the edge</term> of the boundary, pointing outward.

Transforming the second part is more complex. We have:

-> $\delta \iint \frac{dS}{\rho_1 \rho_2} = \iint \left\{ \frac{d^2 w}{dx^2} \frac{d^2 \delta w}{dy^2} + \frac{d^2 w}{dy^2} \frac{d^2 \delta w}{dx^2} - 2 \frac{d^2 w}{dx dy} \frac{d^2 \delta w}{dx dy} \right\} dS.$ <-

The expression being integrated can be rewritten as:

-> $\frac{d}{dy} \left( \frac{d \delta w}{dy} \frac{d^2 w}{dx^2} - \frac{d \delta w}{dx} \frac{d^2 w}{dx dy} \right) + \frac{d}{dx} \left( \frac{d \delta w}{dx} \frac{d^2 w}{dy^2} - \frac{d \delta w}{dy} \frac{d^2 w}{dx dy} \right).$ <-

Now, if *F* is any function of *x* and *y*:

> $\left. \begin{aligned} \iint \frac{dF}{dy} dx dy &= \int F \sin \theta ds \\ \iint \frac{dF}{dx} dx dy &= \int F \cos \theta ds \end{aligned} \right\} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (3),$

where $\theta$ is the angle between the x-axis and the outward-pointing normal, and the integration on the right side covers the entire boundary. By using these relationships, we find:

-> $\delta \iint \frac{dS}{\rho_1 \rho_2} = \int ds \sin \theta \left\{ \frac{d \delta w}{dy} \frac{d^2 w}{dx^2} - \frac{d \delta w}{dx} \frac{d^2 w}{dx dy} \right\}$ <-
-> $+ \int ds \cos \theta \left\{ \frac{d \delta w}{dx} \frac{d^2 w}{dy^2} - \frac{d \delta w}{dy} \frac{d^2 w}{dx dy} \right\}.$ <-

<vocab>total curvature, Green's theorem, variation, differentiation, normal, boundary, integration</vocab>

# EXPRESSION FOR THE VARIATION OF POTENTIAL ENERGY ($\delta V$)

**215.** If we substitute the values for $\frac{d\delta w}{dx}$ and $\frac{d\delta w}{dy}$ in terms of $\frac{d\delta w}{dn}$ <term>normal derivative: the rate of change in a direction perpendicular to the boundary</term> and $\frac{d\delta w}{ds}$ <term>tangential derivative: the rate of change along the boundary line</term> using the following equations (refer to Fig. 40):

$$\left. \begin{aligned} \frac{d\delta w}{dx} = \frac{d\delta w}{dn} \cos \theta - \frac{d\delta w}{ds} \sin \theta \\ \frac{d\delta w}{dy} = \frac{d\delta w}{dn} \sin \theta + \frac{d\delta w}{ds} \cos \theta \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots (4),$$

->Fig. 40.<-

<image-desc>A geometric diagram showing a coordinate system with an origin O and horizontal axis x. A line radiates from O at an angle θ. At a point on this line, a local coordinate system is established with axes labeled 'n' (normal) and 's' (tangential), where 'n' is perpendicular to the radial line and 's' is tangent to the curve.</image-desc>

we obtain:

$$\delta \iint \frac{dS}{\rho_1 \rho_2} = \int ds \frac{d\delta w}{dn} \left\{ \sin^2 \theta \frac{d^2w}{dx^2} + \cos^2 \theta \frac{d^2w}{dy^2} - 2 \sin \theta \cos \theta \frac{d^2w}{dx dy} \right\}$$
$$+ \int ds \frac{d\delta w}{ds} \left\{ \cos \theta \sin \theta \left( \frac{d^2w}{dx^2} - \frac{d^2w}{dy^2} \right) + (\sin^2 \theta - \cos^2 \theta) \frac{d^2w}{dx dy} \right\} \dots (5).$$

The second integral, by using integration by parts <note>original: "partial integration"; a method in calculus used to simplify the product of functions within an integral</note> with respect to the boundary segment *s*, can be rewritten in this form:

$$\int \delta w \frac{d}{ds} \left\{ \cos \theta \sin \theta \left( \frac{d^2w}{dy^2} - \frac{d^2w}{dx^2} \right) + (\cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \theta) \frac{d^2w}{dx dy} \right\} ds.$$

By collecting and rearranging our results, we find the full expression for the variation of the potential energy $\delta V$:

$$\delta V = \frac{2qh^3}{3(1 - \mu^2)} \left[ \iint \nabla^4 w \delta w dS \right.$$
$$- \int \delta w ds \left\{ \frac{d\nabla^2 w}{dn} + (1 - \mu) \frac{d}{ds} \left( \cos \theta \sin \theta \left( \frac{d^2w}{dy^2} - \frac{d^2w}{dx^2} \right) \right. \right.$$
$$\left. \left. + (\cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \theta) \frac{d^2w}{dx dy} \right) \right\}$$
$$+ \int \frac{d\delta w}{dn} ds \left\{ \mu \nabla^2 w + (1 - \mu) \left( \cos^2 \theta \frac{d^2w}{dx^2} + \sin^2 \theta \frac{d^2w}{dy^2} \right. \right.$$
$$\left. \left. \left. + 2 \cos \theta \sin \theta \frac{d^2w}{dx dy} \right) \right\} \right] \dots (6).$$

The resulting formula (Equation 6) is essential for determining the equations of motion and the boundary conditions for elastic surfaces.</summary>

# VIBRATIONS OF PLATES

There will now be no difficulty in forming the equations of motion. If $\rho$ is the volume density, and $Z \cdot \rho \cdot 2h \cdot dS$ is the transverse force <note>transverse force: a force acting perpendicular to the surface of the plate</note> acting on the element $dS$, then:

->$\delta V - \iint 2Z\rho h \delta w dS + \iint 2\rho h \ddot{w} \delta w dS = 0 \dots\dots\dots(7)^1$<-

is the general variational equation. This must be true regardless of what function $\delta w$ is supposed to be, provided it is consistent with the physical makeup of the system. Hence, by the principles of the Calculus of Variations <note>Calculus of Variations: a field of mathematical analysis that uses small variations in functions to find maxima and minima, often used in physics to find the path or state of least energy</note>:

->$\frac{qh^2}{3\rho(1 - \mu^2)} \nabla^4 w - Z + \ddot{w} = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(8),$<-

at every point of the plate.

If the edges of the plate are free, there is no restriction on the hypothetical boundary values of $\delta w$ and $d\delta w/dn$. Therefore, the coefficients of these quantities in the expression for $\delta V$ must vanish <note>original: "vanish"; in mathematics, this means to equal zero</note>. The conditions to be satisfied at a free edge are thus:

$\left. \begin{aligned} \frac{d\nabla^2 w}{dn} + (1 - \mu) \frac{d}{ds} \left\{ \cos \theta \sin \theta \left( \frac{d^2 w}{dy^2} - \frac{d^2 w}{dx^2} \right) \right. \\ \left. + (\cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \theta) \frac{d^2 w}{dx dy} \right\} = 0 \\ \mu \nabla^2 w + (1 - \mu) \left\{ \cos^2 \theta \frac{d^2 w}{dx^2} + \sin^2 \theta \frac{d^2 w}{dy^2} \right. \\ \left. + 2 \cos \theta \sin \theta \frac{d^2 w}{dx dy} \right\} = 0 \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots(9).$

If the whole circumference of the plate is clamped, $\delta w = 0$ and $d\delta w/dn = 0$, and the requirements of the boundary conditions are already met. If the edge is "supported"$^2$, then $\delta w = 0$, but $d\delta w/dn$ is arbitrary <term>arbitrary: in this context, the value is not fixed by a physical constraint and can vary freely</term>. In this case, the second of the equations in (9) must be satisfied by $w$.

**216.** The boundary equations may be simplified by removing the external elements involved in the use of Cartesian coordinates <term>Cartesian coordinates: the standard (x, y) grid system</term>. Taking the $x$-axis parallel to the normal <term>normal: a line perpendicular to a curve or surface</term> of the bounding curve, we see that we may write:

->$\cos^2 \theta \frac{d^2 w}{dx^2} + \sin^2 \theta \frac{d^2 w}{dy^2} + 2 \cos \theta \sin \theta \frac{d^2 w}{dx dy} = \frac{d^2 w}{dn^2}.$<-

Also, ->$\nabla^2 w = \frac{d^2 w}{dn^2} + \frac{d^2 w}{d\sigma^2} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(1),$<-

# CONDITIONS FOR A FREE EDGE

[Section 216.]

In this context, $\sigma$ represents a fixed axis that coincides with the tangent at the specific point being studied. Generally, the second derivative with respect to the fixed tangent ($d^2w/d\sigma^2$) is different from the second derivative along the arc of the curve itself ($d^2w/ds^2$). To find the relationship between them, we can proceed as follows: expand $w$ using Maclaurin's theorem <note>Maclaurin's theorem: a way to represent a function as an infinite sum of terms calculated from the values of its derivatives at a single point</note> in increasing powers of the small quantities $n$ (the normal) and $\sigma$ (the tangent), and then substitute for $n$ and $\sigma$ using their values expressed in terms of $s$, the arc of the curve.

Thus, in general:

-> $w = w_0 + \frac{dw}{dn_0}n + \frac{dw}{d\sigma_0}\sigma + \frac{1}{2}\frac{d^2w}{dn_0^2}n^2 + \frac{d^2w}{dn_0 d\sigma_0}n\sigma + \frac{1}{2}\frac{d^2w}{d\sigma_0^2}\sigma^2 + \dots,$ <-

However, along the curve, $\sigma = s + \text{cubes}$ <note>original: "cubes"; this refers to mathematical terms of the third order or higher, such as $s^3$</note>, and $n = -\frac{1}{2}s^2/\rho + \dots$, where $\rho$ is the radius of curvature <note>radius of curvature: the radius of a circle that most closely matches the curve at a specific point; it indicates how sharply the edge is bending</note>. Accordingly, for points located on the curve:

-> $w = w_0 - \frac{1}{2}\frac{dw}{dn_0}\frac{s^2}{\rho} + \frac{dw}{d\sigma_0}s + \frac{1}{2}\frac{d^2w}{d\sigma_0^2}s^2 + \text{terms of the order } s^3,$ <-

and therefore:

-> $\frac{d^2w}{ds^2} = \frac{d^2w}{d\sigma^2} - \frac{1}{\rho}\frac{dw}{dn} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(2);$ <-

from which, using equation (1) <note>Equation (1) likely refers to the standard expression for the Laplacian operator in these coordinates: $\nabla^2w = \frac{d^2w}{dn^2} + \frac{d^2w}{d\sigma^2}$</note>, we get:

-> $\nabla^2w = \frac{d^2w}{dn^2} + \frac{1}{\rho}\frac{dw}{dn} + \frac{d^2w}{ds^2} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(3).$ <-

We conclude that the second boundary condition in equation (9) of § 215 can be expressed as:

-> $\frac{d^2w}{dn^2} + \mu \left( \frac{1}{\rho}\frac{dw}{dn} + \frac{d^2w}{ds^2} \right) = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(4).$ <note>$\mu$: Poisson's ratio, a constant representing the elastic properties of the plate material</note> <-

In the same way, by setting $\theta = 0$, we see that the expression:

-> $\cos \theta \sin \theta \left( \frac{d^2w}{dy^2} - \frac{d^2w}{dx^2} \right) + (\cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \theta) \frac{d^2w}{dx dy}$ <-

is equivalent to $d^2w/dn d\sigma$, assuming that the axes of $n$ and $\sigma$ are fixed. The first boundary condition now becomes:

-> $\frac{d}{dn} \nabla^2w + (1 - \mu) \frac{d}{ds} \left( \frac{d^2w}{dn d\sigma} \right) = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(5).$ <-

If we apply these equations to a rectangle whose sides are parallel to the coordinate axes, we obtain the conditions to be satisfied along the edges parallel to the $y$-axis:

-> $\left. \begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dx} \left\{ \frac{d^2w}{dx^2} + (2 - \mu) \frac{d^2w}{dy^2} \right\} = 0 \\ \frac{d^2w}{dx^2} + \mu \frac{d^2w}{dy^2} = 0 \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(6).$ <-

# VIBRATIONS OF PLATES. [216.]

In this case, the distinction between $\sigma$ and $s$ disappears, and $\rho$, the radius of curvature, is infinitely great. The conditions for the other pair of edges are found by interchanging $x$ and $y$. These results may be obtained just as well directly from equation (9) in Section 215, without the preliminary transformation.

**217.** If we assume $Z = 0$ <note>original: "suppose $Z = 0$"; in this context, $Z$ represents the external force acting on the plate</note>, and write
->$\frac{qh^2}{3\rho(1-\mu^2)} = c^4$ ............................(1),<-
the general equation becomes
->$\ddot{w} + c^4 \nabla^4 w = 0$ ............................(2),<-
or, if $w$ is proportional to $\cos(pt - \epsilon)$,
->$\nabla^4 w = k^4 w$ ............................(3),<-
where
->$k^4 = p^2/c^4$ ............................(4).<-

Any two values of $w$, such as $u$ and $v$, which correspond to the same boundary conditions, are conjugate <note>conjugate: in modern terms, this refers to the "orthogonality" of the vibration modes, meaning different modes of vibration do not interfere with one another's energy</note>; that is to say,
->$\iint uv dS = 0$ ............................(5),<-
provided that the periods are different. In order to prove this from the ordinary differential equation (3), we would have to retrace the steps by which equation (3) was obtained. This is the method adopted by Kirchhoff <note>Gustav Kirchhoff (1824–1887), a German physicist known for his work on electricity and the mechanics of plates</note> for the circular disc, but it is much simpler and more direct to use the variational equation:
->$\delta V + 2\rho h \iint \ddot{w} \delta w dS = 0$ ............................(6),<-
in which $w$ refers to the actual motion, and $\delta w$ refers to an arbitrary displacement consistent with the nature of the system. $\delta V$ <note>the variation of the potential energy</note> is a symmetrical function of $w$ and $\delta w$, as may be seen from Section 215, or from the general character of $V$ (Section 94).

If we now assume in the first place that $w = u$ and $\delta w = v$, we have
->$\delta V = 2\rho h p^2 \iint uv dS;$<-
and in like manner if we set $w = v$ and $\delta w = u$—which we are equally entitled to do—we find
->$\delta V = 2\rho h p'^2 \iint uv dS,$<-
