# CONJUGATE PROPERTY.

From which it follows:
->$(p^2 - p'^2) \iint uv dS = 0$ ........................(7).<-

This proof is valid regardless of the shape of the boundary, and whether the edge is clamped, supported, or free, in its entirety or in part.

As with the case of membranes in the previous chapter, equation (7) can be used to prove that the possible values of $p^2$ <note>The square of the frequency of vibration</note> are real numbers; however, this is already clear from physical principles.

**218.** To apply this to a circular disc, it is necessary to express the equations using polar coordinates <note>A coordinate system where each point on a plane is determined by a distance from a central point (the radius, $r$) and an angle from a fixed direction ($\theta$)</note>. Taking the center of the disc as the origin (or pole), the general equation that must be satisfied at every point on the surface is:

->$(\nabla^4 - k^4) w = 0$ ........................(1),<-

where (§ 200) ->$\nabla^2 = \frac{d^2}{dr^2} + \frac{1}{r} \frac{d}{dr} + \frac{1}{r^2} \frac{d^2}{d\theta^2}$.<-

To express the boundary condition (§ 216) for a free edge (where the radius $r = a$), we have:

->$\frac{d}{dn} \nabla^2 w = \frac{d}{dr} \nabla^2 w$, $\frac{d}{ds} \left( \frac{d^2 w}{dn d\sigma} \right) = \frac{d}{ad\theta} \frac{d}{dr} \left( \frac{dw}{rd\theta} \right)$, $\frac{d^2 w}{ds^2} = \frac{d^2 w}{a^2 d\theta^2}$,<-

$\rho = \text{radius of curvature} = a$; and thus:

> $\left. \begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dr} \left( \frac{d^2 w}{dr^2} + \frac{1}{r} \frac{dw}{dr} \right) + \frac{d^2}{d\theta^2} \left( \frac{2 - \mu}{a^2} \frac{dw}{dr} - \frac{3 - \mu}{a^3} w \right) = 0 \\ \frac{d^2 w}{dr^2} + \mu \left( \frac{1}{a} \frac{dw}{dr} + \frac{1}{a^2} \frac{d^2 w}{d\theta^2} \right) = 0 \end{aligned} \right\}$ .........(2).

Once the derivatives <note>original: "differentiations"</note> are calculated, $r$ is to be set equal to $a$.

If $w$ is expanded into a Fourier series <note>A way to represent a complex periodic function as a sum of simple sine and cosine waves</note>:

->$w = w_0 + w_1 + ... + w_n + ...$,<-

each term must satisfy equation (2) individually. Therefore, since:

->$w_n \propto \cos (n\theta - \alpha)$,<-

the following equations must hold:

> $\left. \begin{aligned} \frac{d}{dr} \left( \frac{d^2 w_n}{dr^2} + \frac{1}{r} \frac{dw_n}{dr} \right) - n^2 \left( \frac{2 - \mu}{a^2} \frac{dw_n}{dr} - \frac{3 - \mu}{a^3} w_n \right) = 0 \\ \frac{d^2 w_n}{dr^2} + \mu \left( \frac{1}{a} \frac{dw_n}{dr} - \frac{n^2}{a^2} w_n \right) = 0 \end{aligned} \right\}$ ......(3).

# VIBRATIONS OF PLATES. [Section 218.]

The surface differential equation <note>The fundamental equation describing the physical behavior of the plate's surface</note> may be written as:
->$(\nabla^2 + k^2) (\nabla^2 - k^2) w = 0,$<-
which, for the general term of the Fourier expansion <note>A way to represent complex periodic functions as a sum of simpler sine and cosine waves</note>, becomes:
->$\left(\frac{d^2}{dr^2} + \frac{1}{r} \frac{d}{dr} - \frac{n^2}{r^2} + k^2\right) \left(\frac{d^2}{dr^2} + \frac{1}{r} \frac{d}{dr} - \frac{n^2}{r^2} - k^2\right) w_n = 0,$<-
showing that the complete value of $w_n$ will be obtained by adding together, with arbitrary constants placed in front, the general solutions of:
->$\left(\frac{d^2}{dr^2} + \frac{1}{r} \frac{d}{dr} - \frac{n^2}{r^2} \pm k^2\right) w_n = 0$ ........................(4).<-

The equation using the plus sign (+) is the same as the one found in the case of the vibrations of circular membranes. As concluded in the previous chapter, the solution applicable to this problem is $w_n \propto J_n (kr)$ <note>$J_n$ represents the Bessel function of the first kind</note>; the second function of $r$ <note>the Neumann function</note> is inadmissible here because it becomes infinite at the center of the disc.

In the same way, the solution of the equation using the minus sign (-) is $w_n \propto J_n (ikr)$, where $i = \sqrt{-1}$ <note>the imaginary unit</note> as usual. [See § 221 a.]

The simple vibration is thus:
->$w_n = \cos n\theta \{ \alpha J_n (kr) + \beta J_n (ikr) \} + \sin n\theta \{ \gamma J_n (kr) + \delta J_n (ikr) \}.$<-

The two boundary equations will determine the valid values of $k$ and the values that must be assigned to the ratios $\alpha : \beta$ and $\gamma : \delta$. From the form of these equations, it is evident that we must have:
->$\alpha : \beta = \gamma : \delta,$<-
and thus $w_n$ may be expressed in the form:
->$w_n = P \cos (n\theta - \alpha) \{ J_n (kr) + \lambda J_n (ikr) \} \cos (pt - \epsilon)$......(5).<-

As in the case of a membrane, the nodal system <note>The pattern of lines on the plate that remain stationary during vibration</note> is composed of $n$ diameters symmetrically distributed around the center, but otherwise arbitrary, denoted by:
->$\cos (n\theta - \alpha) = 0$ ..............................(6),<-
together with the concentric circles, whose equation is:
->$J_n (kr) + \lambda J_n (ikr) = 0$..........................(7).<-

**219.** In order to determine $\lambda$ and $k$, we must introduce the boundary conditions. When the edge is free, we obtain the following from Equation (3) in Section 218:
->$\left. \begin{aligned} -\lambda &= \frac{n^2 (\mu - 1) \{ ka J_n' (ka) - J_n (ka) \} - k^3 a^3 J_n' (ka)}{n^2 (\mu - 1) \{ ika J_n' (ika) - J_n (ika) \} + ik^3 a^3 J_n' (ika)} \\ -\lambda &= \frac{(\mu - 1) \{ ka J_n' (ka) - n^2 J_n (ka) \} - k^2 a^2 J_n (ka)}{(\mu - 1) \{ ika J_n' (ika) - n^2 J_n (ika) \} + k^2 a^2 J_n (ika)} \end{aligned} \right\} \dots(1),$<-

### POLAR CO-ORDINATES.

In this derivation, use has been made of the differential equations satisfied by the Bessel functions <note>Mathematical functions used to describe the behavior of waves or heat in circular or cylindrical objects</note> $J_n(kr)$ and $J_n(ikr)$. In each of the fractions on the right-hand side, the denominator may be derived from the numerator by substituting $ik$ for $k$. By eliminating $\lambda$ <note>The Greek letter lambda, here representing a constant in the equation</note>, we obtain the equation whose roots provide the admissible values of $k$.

When $n = 0$, the result takes a simpler form, namely:

-> $2(1 - \mu) + ika \frac{J_0(ika)}{J_0'(ika)} + ka \frac{J_0(ka)}{J_0'(ka)} = 0 \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(2).$ <-

This, of course, could have been obtained more easily by ignoring $n$ from the beginning.

Calculating the lowest root for each value of $n$ is difficult and, without appropriate tables, must be performed using the ascending series expansions for the functions $J_n(kr)$ and $J_n(ikr)$. For the higher roots, one may instead use the semi-convergent descending series for these same functions. Kirchhoff <note>original: "Kirchhoff" — Gustav Kirchhoff (1824–1887), a German physicist renowned for his work on spectroscopy and electricity</note> finds that:

-> $\tan(ka - \frac{1}{2}n\pi) = \frac{B/(8ka) + C/(8ka)^2 - D/(8ka)^3 + \dots}{A + B/(8ka) + D/(8ka)^2 + \dots} \dots\dots(3),$ <-

where
> $A = \gamma = (1 - \mu)^{-1},$
> $B = \gamma(1 - 4n^2) - 8,$
> $C = \gamma(1 - 4n^2)(9 - 4n^2) + 48(1 + 4n^2),$
> $D = -\gamma \frac{1}{3} \{(1 - 4n^2)(9 - 4n^2)(13 - 4n^2)\} + 8(9 + 136n^2 + 80n^4).$

When $ka$ is large,
-> $\tan(ka - \frac{1}{2}n\pi) = 0$ approximately; <-

from which it follows that:
-> $ka = \frac{1}{2}\pi(n + 2h) \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(4),$ <-

where $h$ is an integer.

A numerical comparison shows that $h$ is identical to the number of circular nodes <note>The lines or circles on a vibrating surface that remain completely still</note>. Equation (4) expresses a law discovered by Chladni <note>Ernst Chladni (1756–1827), often called the "father of acoustics" for his visual demonstrations of vibrating plates</note>: that the frequencies corresponding to patterns with a given number of nodal diameters are—with the exception of the lowest—approximately proportional to the squares of consecutive even or odd numbers, depending on whether the number of the diameters is itself even or odd. Within the range where equation (4) applies, we also see that the pitch is approximately the same when any number is subtracted from $h$, provided twice that number be

***

The most general movement of a uniform circular plate is expressed by layering—with various strengths (amplitudes) and timings (phases)—the individual vibration components we have already investigated. Determining the exact amplitude and phase that match any initial displacement or velocity is achieved in the same way as the similar problem for a vibrating membrane. This is done using the unique properties of the mathematical functions proven in section 217.

**221.** When a plate is perfectly symmetrical, whether it is made of uniform material or not, theory suggests—and experiments confirm—that the position of the nodal diameters <note>The stationary lines that cross through the center of the disc like spokes on a wheel</note> is flexible. Their position depends entirely on how the plate is held and how it is made to vibrate. By changing the point where the plate is supported, any chosen diameter can be made into a nodal line. 

However, it is usually a different story when there is any noticeable lack of exact symmetry. In a perfectly symmetrical plate, two modes of vibration might have identical timings (periods) and can be combined in any way while remaining simple harmonic <note>A pure, consistent vibration like a steady musical note</note>. If symmetry is lost, these two modes separate and begin to vibrate at different frequencies. 

At the same time, the position of the nodal diameters becomes fixed, or rather limited to only two possibilities. One set of diameters is found by rotating the other set by half the angle that exists between two neighboring diameters in the same set. This assumes that the lack of uniformity is small; otherwise, the pattern of vibrations will no longer look like approximate circles and diameters at all. The cause of this deviation might be an irregularity in the material, the thickness, or the shape of

# OSCILLATION OF NODES

<margin>Section 221</margin>

...which represents a fixed <term>nodal system</term> <note>original: "nodal system"; a pattern of points or lines in a vibrating object that remain stationary while the rest of the object moves.</note>
->$\theta = \alpha + m (\pi/n)$..............................(3),<-

in any arbitrary position depending on where the bow is applied. The nodal system remains similarly fixed, despite the variable $\epsilon$ <note>$\epsilon$ represents the phase difference between two vibrations.</note>, when $\alpha$ is chosen so that $\cos n\alpha = 0$ or $\sin n\alpha = 0$. But in general, there is no fixed nodal system. When $\epsilon$ is a multiple of $2\pi$—that is, when the two vibrations are restored to the same <term>phase</term> <note>original: "phase"; the specific stage or position in a cycle of a periodic motion.</note>—there is a nodal system represented by equation (3). And when $\epsilon$ is an odd multiple of $\pi$, so that the two vibrations are in opposite phases, we have in place of equation (2):
->$\sin n(\theta + \alpha) \cos pt$..............................(4),<-
with a nodal system
->$\theta = -\alpha + m (\pi/n)$..............................(5).<-

In these cases, a nodal system exists, and in a sense, the system may be said to oscillate between the positions given by (3) and (5). However, it must not be overlooked that at intermediate times, there is no true nodal system at all. For example, when $\epsilon = \frac{1}{2}\pi$ <note>a 90-degree phase shift</note>, equation (1) becomes:
->$\cos n\alpha \sin n\theta \cos pt + \sin n\alpha \cos n\theta \sin pt$.<-

The <term>squared amplitude</term> <note>original: "squared amplitude"; a mathematical value representing the intensity or energy of the vibration at a specific point.</note> of this motion is:
->$\cos^2 n\alpha \sin^2 n\theta + \sin^2 n\alpha \cos^2 n\theta$,<-

a quantity which never reaches zero for any value of $\theta$. In general, the squared amplitude is:
->$\cos^2 n\alpha \sin^2 n\theta + \sin^2 n\alpha \cos^2 n\theta - 2 \cos n\alpha \sin n\alpha \cos n\theta \sin n\theta \cos \epsilon$,<-

or, as it may also be written:
->$\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2} \cos 2n\alpha \cos 2n\theta - \frac{1}{2} \sin 2n\alpha \sin 2n\theta \cos \epsilon$...........(6).<-

This quantity is at a maximum or a minimum when:
->$\tan 2n\theta = \cos \epsilon \tan 2n\alpha$........................(7).<-

The point of minimum motion thus oscillates back and forth between $\theta = +\alpha$ and $\theta = -\alpha$; but as we have seen, it is only in these extreme positions that the minimum is actually zero.

A similar phenomenon occurs during the free vibrations of a <term>circular membrane</term> <note>original: "circular membrane"; a thin, flat material stretched over a circular frame, like a drumhead.</note>, or indeed any <term>system of revolution</term> <note>original: "system of revolution"; an object that is perfectly symmetrical around a central axis.</note> where the position of <term>nodal lines</term> <note>original: "nodal lines"; lines on a vibrating surface that remain still while the rest of the surface moves.</note> is arbitrary as long as the symmetry is complete.

<summary>This page explains that when two vibrations are combined, the points of no motion (nodes) usually shift or disappear unless the vibrations are in specific phases. The author demonstrates mathematically how these "nodes" appear to oscillate back and forth in symmetrical vibrating systems like drumheads.</summary>
<keywords>oscillation of nodes, nodal system, phase difference, squared amplitude, circular membrane, vibration physics, symmetry</keywords>

368 [222. VIBRATIONS OF PLATES.

It should be remembered that the vibrations excited by a bow are not, strictly speaking, free vibrations, and that their timing <note>original: "periods"; the time taken for one complete vibration</note> is therefore liable to a certain modification. It may be that under the action of the bow, two or more separate natural component vibrations occur at the same time. The whole motion may behave as a simple harmonic vibration because of the external force, even though the natural timing would be a little different. Such an explanation is suggested by the regular character of the patterns obtained in certain cases.

Another cause of deviation may perhaps be found in the way the plates are supported. The requirements of scientific theory are often difficult to meet in actual experiments. When this is so, we may have to be content with an imperfect comparison; but we must remember that a discrepancy may be the fault of the experiment just as much as the theory.

[In the ordinary use of sand to investigate the vibrations of flat plates and membranes, the movement toward the nodes <note>points on a vibrating surface that remain stationary</note> is irregular in its character. If a grain of sand is located anywhere other than at a node, it is made to jump by a sufficiently vigorous transverse <note>sideways or up-and-down</note> vibration. The result may be a movement either toward or away from a node; but after a succession of such jumps, the grain ultimately finds its way to a node as the only place where it can remain undisturbed. Grains which have already arrived at a node remain there, while others are constantly shifting their position.

It was found by Savart that very fine powder, such as lycopodium <note>a fine, dust-like powder made from clubmoss spores</note>, behaves differently from sand. Instead of collecting at the nodes, it heaps itself up at the places of greatest motion <note>known as antinodes</note>. This effect was traced by Faraday¹ to the influence of air currents, which are themselves the result of the vibration. In a vacuum, all powders move to the nodes.

In some cases, the movement of sand to the nodes, or to some of them, takes place in a more direct manner as the result of friction. Thus, in his investigation of the longitudinal <note>lengthwise</note> vibrations of thin, narrow strips of glass held horizontally, Savart² observed the marking of nodes apparently dependent upon an accompaniment of vibrations of a transverse character. The special peculiarity of this phenomenon was the lack of correspondence between the lines traced by sand upon the two faces of the glass when tested—

# VIBRATIONS OF PLATES [223.]

The subject was taken up again by Kirchhoff¹, who first provided the **two** equations appropriate for a free edge and completed the theory of the vibrations of a circular disc.

**224.** The correctness of Kirchhoff’s boundary equations has been disputed by Mathieu², who, without explaining where he considers Kirchhoff’s error to lie, has substituted a different set of equations. He proves that if $u$ and $u'$ are two normal functions <note>normal functions: in this context, these represent the spatial distribution or "shape" of displacement for specific modes of vibration</note>, so that $w = u \cos pt$ and $w = u' \cos p't$ are possible vibrations, then:

$(p^2 - p'^2) \iint uu' dx dy$
->$= c^4 \int ds \left\{ u' \frac{d\nabla^2 u}{dn} - \nabla^2 u \frac{du'}{dn} - \nabla^2 u' \frac{du}{dn} + u \frac{d\nabla^2 u'}{dn} \right\} \dots \dots \dots (1).$<-

This follows if it is admitted that $u$ and $u'$ satisfy their respective equations:
->$c^4 \nabla^4 u = p^2 u, \quad c^4 \nabla^4 u' = p'^2 u'.$<-

Since the left-hand side of the equation is zero, the same must be true of the right-hand side; and this, according to Mathieu, cannot be the case unless at all points of the boundary both $u$ and $u'$ satisfy one of the four following pairs of equations:

| Pair 1 | Pair 2 | Pair 3 | Pair 4 |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $u = 0$ | $\nabla^2 u = 0$ | $u = 0$ | $\frac{du}{dn} = 0$ |
| $\frac{du}{dn} = 0$ | $\frac{d(\nabla^2 u)}{dn} = 0$ | $\nabla^2 u = 0$ | $\frac{d(\nabla^2 u)}{dn} = 0$ |

The second pair would seem the most likely for a free edge, but it is found to lead to an impossibility. Since the first and third pairs are obviously inadmissible, Mathieu concludes that the fourth pair of equations must be those which really express the condition of a free edge. He is not deterred in his belief in this result by the fact that the corresponding conditions for the free end of a bar would be $du/dx = 0$ and $d^3u/dx^3 = 0$. The first of these is contradicted by even the simplest observation of the vibration of a large tuning fork <note>tuning fork: a two-pronged steel device that vibrates at a specific pitch when struck, used here as a practical example of a vibrating bar with free ends</note>.

¹ *Crelle*, vol. <term>40</term> p. 51. **On the equilibrium and motion of an elastic plate** <note>original: "Ueber das Gleichgewicht und die Bewegung einer elastischen Scheibe"</note>.
² *Liouville*, vol. <term>14</term> 1869.

<header>HISTORY OF THE PROBLEM.</header>

The fact is that although any of the four pairs of equations would secure the disappearance <note>original: "evanescence"; meaning the state of vanishing or becoming zero</note> of the boundary integral in equation (1), it does not follow conversely that the integral can be made to vanish in no other way; and such a conclusion is disproved by Kirchhoff's investigation. There are, besides, innumerable other cases in which the integral in question would vanish; all that is really necessary is that the boundary supports <note>original: "appliances"</note> should be either at rest, or devoid of inertia <note>inertia: the tendency of an object to resist changes in its state of motion; here, meaning the supports have no mass that affects the vibration</note>.

**225.** The vibrations of a rectangular plate, whose edge is *supported*, may be easily investigated theoretically; the normal functions <note>normal functions: the mathematical descriptions of the specific shapes a plate takes when vibrating at a single resonant frequency</note> are identical with those applicable to a membrane of the same shape whose boundary is fixed. If we assume

-> $w = \sin \frac{m \pi x}{a} \sin \frac{n \pi y}{b} \cos pt \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (1),$ <-

we see that at all points of the boundary,

-> $w = 0, \quad d^2 w / dx^2 = 0, \quad d^2 w / dy^2 = 0,$ <-

which secure the fulfillment of the necessary conditions (§ 215). The value of $p$, found by substitution in $c^4 \nabla^4 w = p^2 w$,

is -> $p = c^2 \pi^2 \left( \frac{m^2}{a^2} + \frac{n^2}{b^2} \right) \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (2),$ <-

showing <note>original: "shewing"</note> that the analogy to the membrane does not extend to the sequence of tones <note>sequence of tones: the mathematical relationship between the fundamental frequency and its higher overtones</note>.

It is not necessary to repeat here the discussion of the primary and derived nodal systems given in Chapter IX. It is enough to observe that if two of the fundamental modes in equation (1) have the same period <note>period: the time it takes to complete one full vibration cycle</note> in the case of the membrane, they must also have the same period in the case of the plate. The derived nodal systems are accordingly identical in the two cases.

The generality of the value of $w$ obtained by combining <note>original: "compounding"</note> with arbitrary amplitudes and phases all possible particular solutions of the form (1) requires no fresh discussion.

Unless the contrary assertion had been made, it would have seemed unnecessary to say that the nodes of a *supported* plate have nothing to do with the ordinary Chladni's figures <note>Chladni's figures: the geometric patterns formed by sand or powder on a vibrating plate, first demonstrated by Ernst Chladni</note>, which belong to a plate whose edges are free.

...for which $\mu$ <note>Poisson's ratio, which measures the ratio of transverse contraction to longitudinal extension</note> vanishes. The investigation of the problem under this condition is therefore not without interest, though the results will not be strictly applicable to ordinary glass or metal plates, for which the value of $\mu$ is about 1/3.$^1$

If $u_1, u_2,$ etc., denote the normal functions <note>Mathematical descriptions of the natural modes of vibration for a system</note> for a free bar investigated in Chapter 8, corresponding to 2, 3, etc. nodes, the vibrations of a rectangular plate will be expressed by

-> $w = u_1(x/a), \quad w = u_2(x/a), \text{ etc.},$ <-
or
-> $w = u_1(y/b), \quad w = u_2(y/b), \text{ etc.}$ <-

In each of these primitive modes, the nodal system <note>The set of points or lines that remain stationary while the rest of the plate vibrates</note> is composed of straight lines parallel to one or the other of the edges of the rectangle. When $b = a$, the rectangle becomes a square, and the vibrations

-> $w = u_n(x/a), \quad w = u_n(y/a),$ <-

having necessarily the same period, may be combined in any proportion, while the whole motion still remains simple harmonic. Whatever the proportion may be, the resulting nodal curve will of necessity pass through the points determined by

-> $u_n(x/a) = 0, \quad u_n(y/a) = 0.$ <-

Now let us consider more particularly the case where $n = 1$. The nodal system of the primitive mode, $w = u_1(x/a)$, consists of a pair of straight lines parallel to $y$, whose distance from the nearest edge is $0.2242 a$. The points in which these lines are met by the corresponding pair for $w = u_1(y/a)$ are those through which the nodal curve of the compound vibration must in all cases pass. It is evident that they are symmetrically arranged on the diagonals of the square. If the two primitive vibrations are taken to be equal, but in opposite phases (or, algebraically, with equal and opposite amplitudes), we have

-> $w = u_1(x/a) - u_1(y/a) \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (3),$ <-

yielding a pitch that is somewhat too high. The lowest <note>original: "gravest"</note> mode following this occurs when the diagonals are nodes <term>nodes: lines on a vibrating surface that remain stationary while the rest of the surface moves</term>. The pitch for this mode, if $\mu = 0$ <note>$\mu$ refers to Poisson's ratio, a measure of how much a material thins when stretched</note>, would be given by:
->$p'^2 = \frac{qh^2}{\rho a^4} \frac{(4 \cdot 7300)^4}{3} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots (5)$<-

(see Section 174).

We may conclude that if the material of the plate were such that $\mu = 0$, the interval between the two lowest tones would be slightly greater than the ratio 1.318. Chladni <note>Ernst Chladni (1756–1827), the "father of acoustics," who used sand to visualize these vibration patterns</note> determined the interval to be a fifth <note>In acoustics, a "fifth" represents a frequency ratio of 3:2, or 1.5</note>.

**229.** The existence of vibration modes where the two shortest diameters <note>The lines passing through the midpoints of the square's sides</note> are nodes can be deduced from the following logic. In Figure 48, suppose that $GH$ is a plate where the edges $HO$ and $GO$ are supported, and the edges $GC$ and $CH$ are free. Since this plate tends toward a specific position of equilibrium, it must be capable of vibrating in certain fundamental modes. Focusing on one of these, let us imagine a distribution of displacement ($w$) over the three remaining quadrants. This distribution is such that in any two adjoining quadrants, the values of $w$ are equal and opposite at points that are mirror images of each other across the dividing line. If the entire plate vibrates according to this pattern, no external force will be needed to keep the lines $GE$ and $FH$ stationary <note>original: "fixed"</note>; therefore, the entire plate may be considered "free." The same logic can be used to prove that modes exist in which the diagonals are nodes, or in which both the diagonals and the diameters just mentioned are nodal lines simultaneously.

It is divided into four quadrants by a horizontal line FH and a vertical line GE, which intersect at a central point O. The lines GE and FH represent the diameters/nodes discussed in the text.</image-desc>

# PRINCIPLE OF SYMMETRY.
<meta>229.] at top left</meta>

The principle of symmetry may also be applied to other shapes of plates. We might thus infer the possibility of nodal diameters <term>nodal diameters: lines of no movement that pass through the center of a circular or symmetrical plate</term> in a circle, or of nodal principal axes in an ellipse. When the boundary is a regular hexagon, it is easy to see that Figures 49, 50, and 51 represent possible vibration forms.

![Three diagrams of regular hexagons showing nodal lines. Fig. 49 shows a hexagon with one vertical dashed line and one horizontal dashed line intersecting at the center. Fig. 50 shows a hexagon with three dashed lines intersecting at the center, connecting opposite vertices. Fig. 51 shows a hexagon with three dashed lines intersecting at the center, connecting the midpoints of opposite sides.](fig49_50_51.png)

->Fig. 49. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Fig. 50. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Fig. 51.<-

It is interesting to trace the continuity of Chladni’s figures <term>Chladni’s figures: patterns formed by sand on a vibrating plate that reveal its nodal lines</term> as the shape of the plate is gradually altered. In a circle, for example, when there are two perpendicular nodal diameters, it does not matter—in terms of the pitch and the type of vibration—in what position they are placed. As the circle is transformed into a square by extending the corners, the position of these diameters becomes fixed. In the two possible positions, the pitch of the vibration is different because the projecting corners do not have the same effect in both cases. The vibration of a square plate shown in Fig. 42 corresponds to that of a circle when there is one circular node. The relationship between the lower-pitched <note>original: "graver"</note> modes of a hexagon or an ellipse and those of a circle may be traced in the same way.

**230.** For plates of uniform material and thickness and of fixed shape, the period of the vibration in any fundamental mode is proportional to <note>original: "varies as"</note> the square of the linear dimension, provided, of course, that the boundary conditions are the same in all the cases compared. When the edges are clamped, we may go further and assert that the removal of *any* external portion results in <note>original: "is attended by"</note> a rise of pitch, whether the material and the thickness are uniform or not.

Let $AB$ be a part of a clamped edge (it is of no consequence whether the rest of the boundary is clamped or not), and

->Fig. 52.<-

### VIBRATIONS OF PLATES.
<meta>230.] at top right</meta>

Suppose the piece $ACBD$ is removed, and the new edge $ADB$ is also clamped. The pitch of any fundamental vibration <term>fundamental vibration: the lowest frequency at which an object naturally vibrates</term> is higher <note>original: "sharper"</note> than it was before the change. This is evident because the altered vibrations could be obtained from the original system by introducing a constraint <term>constraint: a physical restriction on movement</term> that clamps the edge $ADB$. The effect of the constraint is to raise the pitch of every component; since the portion $ACBD$ is flat and at rest throughout the motion, it may be removed. To follow the sequence of changes with greater security from error, it is best to imagine the line of clamping advancing by stages between the two positions $ACB$ and $ADB$. For example, the pitch of a uniform clamped plate in the form of a regular hexagon is lower than that of the inscribed circle but higher than that of the circumscribed circle.

When a plate is free, it is not true that an addition to the edge always increases the period <term>period: the time it takes for one complete cycle of vibration</term>. To prove this, it is sufficient to look at a specific case.

$AB$ is a narrow, thin plate that has no inertia <term>inertia: the resistance of an object to any change in its motion</term> itself but carries loads at $A, B$, and $C$. It is clear that the addition to the breadth

->Fig. 53.<-

![A diagram labeled Fig. 53 showing a narrow rectangular plate with three points marked A, C, and B. The rectangle is enclosed by a dotted line indicating an expansion of its breadth.](fig53.png)

indicated by the dotted line would increase the stiffness of the bar, and therefore *reduce* the period of vibration. The same consideration shows that for a uniform free plate of a given area, there is no lower limit of pitch; for by a sufficient elongation, the period of the lowest <note>original: "gravest"</note> component may be made to exceed any measurable quantity. When the edges are clamped, the shape that produces the lowest pitch is undoubtedly the circle.

If all the dimensions of a plate, including the thickness, are altered in the same proportion, the period is proportional to the linear dimension, as is the case for every solid body vibrating due to its own elasticity.

The period also varies inversely as the square root of Young’s modulus <term>Young’s modulus: a measure of the stiffness of a solid material</term>, if the Poisson's ratio ($\mu$) is constant, and directly as the square root of the mass per unit of volume (density) of the substance.

It also outlines the physical laws relating a plate's dimensions and material properties to its period of vibration.</summary>

## CYLINDER OR RING
<margin>231.</margin>

**231.** While experimenting with square plates of thin wood where the grain ran parallel to one pair of sides, Wheatstone¹ found that the pitch of the vibrations changed depending on whether the nearly straight nodal lines <term>nodal lines: the parts of a vibrating surface that remain still during vibration</term> were parallel or perpendicular to the wood's grain. This effect happens because the wood’s stiffness—specifically its flexural rigidity <term>flexural rigidity: the resistance of a material to bending</term>—varies in these two directions. Because these two sets of vibrations have different periods <note>period: the time it takes for one complete cycle of vibration</note>, they cannot be combined in the usual way. Consequently, it is impossible to make such a wooden plate vibrate with diagonal nodal lines. However, this inequality of periods can be eliminated <note>original: "obviated"</note> by changing the ratio of the plate's side lengths; once the periods match, the usual method of superposition <term>superposition: the overlapping or combining of different vibration patterns</term>—which creates diagonal nodal lines—becomes possible again. Wheatstone verified this through his experiments.

A further application of the principle of superposition was developed by König². In order for two modes of vibration to combine, it is only necessary that their periods match. It is clear that the sides of a rectangular plate can be sized in such a ratio that, for example, a vibration with two nodes parallel to one pair of sides matches the pitch of a vibration with three nodes parallel to the other pair. In such a case, new nodal patterns <note>original: "figures"</note> emerge from the combination of these two primary modes of vibration.

**232.** When considering the vibrations of a plate that is naturally curved, the problem generally becomes much more difficult. However, there is one case where the complexity of the curvature is more than compensated for by the absence of a free edge. This case is particularly interesting because it serves as the best model for a bell that can be analyzed with simple mathematical methods.

A long cylindrical shell with a circular cross-section and uniform thickness is clearly capable of flexural <note>original: "flexural" — referring to vibrations that involve bending or flexing the material</note> vibrations. In this state, the central axis of the cylinder remains still and the surface stays cylindrical, while the movement of every part is perpendicular to the lines that form the cylinder's length. The problem can therefore be treated as a two-dimensional one, focusing on the potential and kinetic energies of the various ways the cross-section can deform. This same analysis also applies to the vibrations of a ring, which is formed by rotating a small enclosed area around an external axis (see section 192 a).

² *Poggendorff's Annalen der Physik*, 1864, vol. 122, p. 238. <note>The original text erroneously printed 1884, but volume 122 corresponds to 1864.</note>

# VIBRATIONS OF PLATES

<margin>232.</margin>

**232.** A cylinder or ring is capable of two types of vibrations. These depend, respectively, on how much the material can stretch (extensibility) and its resistance to bending (flexural rigidity). These are similar to the longitudinal <note>longitudinal: vibrations where the particles move back and forth in the same direction the wave travels</note> and lateral <note>lateral: vibrations where the particles move side-to-side, perpendicular to the wave's path</note> vibrations seen in straight bars. 

However, when the cylinder is thin, the forces that resist bending are very small compared to the forces that oppose stretching. Just as with straight bars, the vibrations caused by bending are lower in pitch <note>original: "graver"</note> and more significant than those caused by the material's resistance to stretching. In the extreme case of an infinitely thin shell or ring, these bending vibrations become completely independent of any stretching of the circumference as a whole. We can calculate these vibrations by assuming that every part of the circumference keeps its original natural length throughout the entire motion.

Although the vibrations we are about to discuss are similar to the transverse <term>transverse: moving or situated across something</term> vibrations of straight bars—because both depend on the resistance to bending—we must not make the common mistake of assuming they move only in a "normal" direction <term>normal: in physics, this means moving perpendicularly (at a right angle) to the surface</term>. It is easy to see that if every particle in a cylinder or ring moved only along the radius (inward or outward), the circumference would have to stretch. This would contradict our condition that no stretching occurs. To satisfy this "no-extension" condition, it is necessary to recognize that each part of the circumference moves both along the curve (tangential motion) and perpendicular to it (normal motion). The relative size of these two movements must satisfy a specific differential equation. Our first step will be to investigate this equation.

**233.** Let the original radius of the circle be *a*. We will define the resting position <note>original: "equilibrium position"</note> of any small section of the circumference using the angle $\theta$. While in motion, let the polar coordinates <term>polar coordinates: a way of describing a point's location using a distance (r) and an angle (θ)</term> of that section become:

-> $r = a + \delta r, \quad \phi = \theta + \delta \theta.$ <-

If $ds$ represents the length of the arc of the deformed curve that corresponds to the original section $a d\theta$, we have:

-> $(ds)^2 = (a d\theta)^2 = (d\delta r)^2 + r^2 (d\theta + d\delta \theta)^2;$ <-

From this, we find—by ignoring the squares of the tiny changes $\delta r$ and $\delta \theta$—the following result:

-> $\frac{\delta r}{a} + \frac{d\delta \theta}{d\theta} = 0 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (1)$ <-

This is the relationship we require.

<summary>This page explains that thin cylinders and rings vibrate primarily through bending rather than stretching, and it derives a mathematical equation to show that these vibrations must involve both radial and tangential movement to keep the circumference length constant.</summary>

<keywords>vibrations, flexural rigidity, cylinders, rings, transverse vibrations, normal motion, tangential motion, differential equations, polar coordinates</keywords>

# POTENTIAL AND KINETIC ENERGIES
<sig>R. 25</sig>
<meta>catchword: 233.]</meta>

In whatever way the original circle is deformed at time $t$, the change in radius ($\delta r$) may be expanded by Fourier's theorem <note>Fourier's theorem: a mathematical method used to represent complex periodic waveforms as a sum of simple sine and cosine waves.</note> in the following series:

->$\delta r = a \{ A_1 \cos \theta + B_1 \sin \theta + A_2 \cos 2\theta + B_2 \sin 2\theta + \dots$<-
->$+ A_s \cos s\theta + B_s \sin s\theta + \dots \} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (2),$<-

And the corresponding tangential displacement <note>tangential displacement: movement along the curve of the circle rather than inward or outward.</note> required by the condition of no extension <note>condition of no extension: the assumption that the total length of the circle's circumference does not change during vibration.</note> will be:

->$\delta \theta = - A_1 \sin \theta + B_1 \cos \theta + \dots - \frac{A_s}{s} \sin s\theta + \frac{B_s}{s} \cos s\theta - \dots \dots (3),$<-

with any constant that might be added to $\delta \theta$ being omitted.

If $\sigma a d\theta$ represents the mass of the element <note>element: an infinitesimally small section of the ring.</note> $a d\theta$, the kinetic energy $T$ of the entire motion will be:

->$T = \frac{1}{2} \sigma a \int_0^{2\pi} \left\{ \left( \frac{d \delta r}{dt} \right)^2 + a^2 \left( \frac{d \delta \theta}{dt} \right)^2 \right\} d\theta$<-
->$= \frac{1}{2} \sigma \pi a^3 \left\{ 2 \left( \dot{A}_1^2 + \dot{B}_1^2 \right) + \frac{5}{4} \left( \dot{A}_2^2 + \dot{B}_2^2 \right) + \dots \right.$<-
->$\left. + \left( 1 + \frac{1}{s^2} \right) \left( \dot{A}_s^2 + \dot{B}_s^2 \right) + \dots \right\} \dots \dots \dots \dots (4),$<-

where the products of the coordinates $A_s$ and $B_s$ disappear during the process of integration <note>integration: a mathematical process used here to sum up the energy across every part of the circle.</note>.

We now have to calculate the form of the potential energy $V$. Let $\rho$ be the radius of curvature <note>radius of curvature: the radius of a circle that best fits the curve of the deformed ring at a specific point.</note> of any element $ds$; then for the corresponding element of $V$ we may use $\frac{1}{2} B ds \{ \delta (1/\rho) \}^2$, where $B$ is a constant depending on the material and on the thickness. Thus:

->$V = \frac{1}{2} B a \int_0^{2\pi} \left( \delta \frac{1}{\rho} \right)^2 d\theta \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (5).$<-

Now,
->$1/\rho = u + d^2u/d\phi^2,$<-
and
->$u = \frac{1}{r} = \frac{1}{a} \{ 1 - A_1 \cos \phi - B_1 \sin \phi - \dots \},$<-

because in the small terms the distinction between $\phi$ and $\theta$ may be ignored.

Hence,
->$\delta \frac{1}{\rho} = \frac{1}{a} \Sigma \{ (s^2 - 1) (A_s \cos s\phi + B_s \sin s\phi) \},$<-

# VIBRATIONS OF PLATES. [234.]

**234.** When $s = 1$, the frequency is zero, as might have been anticipated. The principal mode of vibration corresponds to $s = 2$ and has four nodes, each distant from the others by 90°. These so-called nodes are not, however, places of absolute rest, for the tangential motion <note>original: "tangential motion"; motion along the circumference of the ring or plate.</note> is at its maximum there. In fact, the tangential vibration at these points is half the maximum normal motion <note>original: "normal motion"; motion perpendicular to the surface, moving inward and outward.</note>. In general, for the $s^{th}$ term, the maximum tangential motion is $(1/s)$ of the maximum normal motion and occurs at the nodes of the latter.

When a bell-shaped body is sounded by a blow, the point where the blow is applied is a place of maximum normal motion for the resulting vibrations. The same is true when the vibrations are excited by a violin bow, as is generally done in lecture-room experiments. Bells made of glass, such as finger-glasses, are however more easily thrown into regular vibration by friction with a wetted finger carried around the circumference. The pitch of the resulting sound is the same as the sound produced <note>original: "elicited"</note> by a tap with the soft part of the finger. However, because the tangential motion of a vibrating bell has been very generally ignored, the production of sound in this manner has been viewed as a difficulty. It is now hardly necessary to point out that the effect of the friction is, in the first instance, to excite tangential motion, and that the point where the friction is applied is the place where the tangential motion is greatest, and therefore where the normal motion vanishes.

**235.** The existence of tangential vibration in a bell was verified in the following manner. A so-called air-pump receiver <note>A heavy glass jar, typically bell-shaped, used in vacuum experiments.</note> was securely fastened to a table with the open end facing upward and set into vibration with a moistened finger. A small chip in the rim, reflecting the light of a candle, created a bright spot whose motion could be observed with a Coddington lens <note>A type of magnifying lens that provides a wide field of view and high magnification.</note> suitably fixed in place. As the finger was moved around, the line of vibration was seen to rotate with an angular velocity double that of the finger; and the amount of excursion <note>The distance the spot of light moved, representing the amplitude of the vibration.</note> (indicated by the length of the line of light), though variable, was finite in every position. There was, however, some difficulty in observing the correspondence between the momentary direction of vibration and the position of the point of excitement. To achieve this satisfactorily, it was found necessary to apply the friction in the neighborhood of a single point. It then became evident that the spot moved tangentially when the bell was...

# TANGENTIAL MOTION

<margin>Section 235</margin>

...[vibrations were] started at points distant from that location by 0, 90, 180, or 270 degrees; and normally when the friction was applied at the intermediate points corresponding to 45, 135, 225, and 315 degrees. Sometimes care is required to make the bell vibrate in its lowest possible pitch <note>original: "gravest mode"</note> without a noticeable mix of higher overtones.

If a small weight is added to any point on the rim, the vibration period increases slightly (lowering the pitch). This increase varies depending on whether the weighted point matches a node <term>a point on a vibrating body that remains stationary</term> of the normal or the tangential motion; the effect is greater in the case of tangential motion. Therefore, the sound produced depends on where the vibration is started. In general, both tones are heard, and their interaction creates *beats* <note>rhythmic pulses in sound volume caused by two similar frequencies interfering with each other</note>, the frequency of which is equal to the difference between the frequencies of the two tones. This phenomenon is often observed in the case of large bells.

**235 *a*.** In determining the number of nodal meridians <term>vertical lines on the bell's surface that do not move during vibration</term> (represented as 2*s*) corresponding to any particular tone of a bell, one can take advantage of beats. These may be caused by accidental irregularities in the bell's casting or introduced intentionally by adding a weight (compare sections 208 and 209). By tapping cautiously around a circle of latitude <note>a horizontal ring around the circumference of the bell</note>, one can investigate the places where the beats disappear, which happens when one of the two component tones is not triggered. 

However, a decision should not be made too hastily. The beats might be inaudible simply because of an unsuitable position of the ear or the mouth of the resonator <note>a tool used to amplify specific frequencies</note> used with the ear. By moving around the bell, a position is soon found where the observation can be made most effectively. Near the spot where the blow is struck, there is a loop <term>an antinode; a point of maximum vibration</term> of the vibration that is most active, and a coincident node of the vibration that is least active. When the ear is positioned opposite a node of the first vibration (and therefore opposite a loop of the second), the original imbalance is corrected, and distinct beats may be heard even if the blow is only slightly off from a nodal point. 

Accurately determining two consecutive places where no beats are generated is all that is strictly necessary for this purpose. The ratio of the entire circumference of the horizontal circle to the distance (the arc) between the two points in question is, in fact, 4*s*. For example, if the distance between consecutive points proved to be 45°, we would conclude that *s* = 2, which describes a case where the bell's circular shape deforms into an ellipse. To ensure greater security against error, it is advisable in practice to determine a larger...

In the process described above for determining nodes, we assume that the listener can clearly hear the specific tone corresponding to the vibration being studied. For this purpose, the beats are helpful because they help direct the listener's attention. However, when dealing with more difficult subjects, such as church bells, it is advisable to use resonators. A set of von Helmholtz’s <note>Hermann von Helmholtz (1821–1894), a German physicist who invented resonators to identify specific frequencies in complex sounds</note> design, manufactured by König, are very convenient. One should choose a resonator with a pitch slightly higher than the tone being examined and tune it by moving a finger across the aperture. Without the accuracy provided by resonators, determining the correct octave is very uncertain.

The only class of bells for which an approximate theory can be provided are those with thin walls (see sections 233 and 235 c). The following glass bells may be considered examples:

->I. $c'$, $e''\flat$, $c'''\#$.<-
->II. $a$, $c''\#$, $b''$.<-
->III. $f'\#$, $b''$.<-

The value of $s$ <note>half the number of nodal meridians</note> for the lowest tone <note>original: "gravest tone"</note> was 2, for the second tone it was 3, and for the third tone it was 4.

Similar observations have been made on a so-called "hemispherical bell" of nearly uniform thickness, weighing about 3 hundredweight <note>original: "cwt"; a unit of weight equal to 112 pounds in the UK</note>. Four tones could be plainly heard:

->$e\flat$, $f'\#$, $e''$, $b''$,<-

The pitch was identified using a harmonium. The lowest tone has a long duration. When the bell is struck by a hard object, the higher tones are at first louder <note>original: "predominant"</note>, but after a time they die away and leave the $e\flat$ tone alone. If the object striking the bell is soft, the initial loudness of the higher tones is less noticeable.

By the method described, there was no difficulty in showing that the four tones correspond respectively to $s = 2, 3, 4, 5$. Thus, for the lowest tone, the vibration is elliptical with 4 nodal meridians <term>vertical lines on the bell's surface that do not move during vibration</term>; for the next tone there are 6 nodal meridians, and so on.

# BELLS

Tapping along a meridian <note>original: "meridian"; here, a vertical line running from the top (crown) to the bottom (rim) of the bell</note> showed that the sounds became less clear as the edge was moved away from, and this happened in a continuous manner with no indication of a nodal circle of latitude <note>a horizontal ring around the bell that remains stationary during vibration</note>. A question we will return to regarding church bells arises here: which of the various simultaneous tones determines the pitch of the bell as a whole? It appears to be the third tone in the series, as the bell-founders identified the pitch as *E* natural.

In church bells, there is a great concentration of metal at the "sound-bow" <note>the thickened part of the bell's rim where the clapper strikes</note>. This concentration is so significant that we can hardly expect the bell to behave the same way as thin, uniform bells. However, the method already described is sufficient to determine the number of nodal meridians <note>vertical lines on the bell's surface that do not vibrate</note> for all the more important tones. From a bell weighing 6 cwt. <note>hundredweight; 6 cwt. is approximately 672 pounds or 305 kilograms</note> made by the founders Mears and Stainbank, six tones could be identified, namely:

->*e'*, *c''*, *f''+*, *b''b*, *d'''*, *f'''*<-
->(4) (4) (6) (6) (8)<-

The pitch of this bell, as specified by the makers, is *d''*. Therefore, it is the fifth tone in the series above that characterizes the overall pitch of the bell. The number of nodal meridians in the various components is indicated within the parentheses. For example, in the case of the tone *e'*, there are 4 nodal meridians. A similar examination along a meridian showed that there was no nodal circle of latitude. At the same time, differences in intensity were observed. This tone is most fully developed when the blow is delivered about midway between the crown <note>the top of the bell</note> and the rim.

The next tone is *c''*. Observation showed that for this vibration, there are also four—and only four—nodal meridians. However, in this case, there is a well-defined nodal circle of latitude, located about a quarter of the way up from the rim toward the crown. When heard through a resonator <note>a device used to isolate and amplify specific sound frequencies</note>, this tone disappears when the bell is struck exactly on a point of this circle, but it returns with even a very small displacement to either side. The nodal circle and the four meridians divide the surface into segments; within each segment, the vibration moves in a single direction <note>original: "normal motion is of one sign"</note>.

The tone *f''* corresponds to 6 nodal meridians. There is no well-defined nodal circle. The sound is indeed very faint when the tap is moved far from the sound-bow; it was thought to reach its minimum intensity when a position about halfway up the bell was reached.

-> $E\flat' - 2$, &nbsp;&nbsp; $d'' - 6$, &nbsp;&nbsp; $f'' + 4$, &nbsp;&nbsp; $B\flat'' - B''$, &nbsp;&nbsp; $d'''$, &nbsp;&nbsp; $g'''$. <-

# CURVED PLATES OR SHELLS.

...or bending <note>original: flexural</note>, and (§ 44) their frequencies are proportional to the thickness *h*, so that the sounds become deeper <note>original: graver</note> without limit as the thickness is reduced.

We can think of vibrations of the first class as depending on the term of order *h*, and vibrations of the second class as depending on the term of order $h^3$ <note>thickness cubed</note>, in the mathematical expression for potential energy. Generally, both terms occur, and it is only in the theoretical limit—as the shell becomes infinitely thin—that the separation into two distinct classes becomes absolute. This is a question that has sometimes caused difficulty. In the case of stretching <note>original: extensional</note> vibrations, the idea that the $h^3$ term should be negligible compared to the *h* term seems reasonable enough. But is it permissible, when dealing with the other class of vibrations, to omit the *h* term while keeping the $h^3$ term?

The question may be illustrated by considering a problem of static equilibrium <note>original: statical problem</note>. It is a general principle of mechanics (§ 74) that if specific displacements (which are not enough on their own to determine the final shape) are produced in a system originally in equilibrium by corresponding forces, the resulting change in shape <note>original: deformation</note> is determined by the condition that the potential energy shall be as small as possible. Apply this principle to the case of an elastic shell, where the given displacements are of a type that do not, by themselves, involve a stretching of the middle surface. The resulting change in shape will, in general, include both stretching and bending, and any expression for the energy will take this form:

->*Ah* (stretching <note>original: extension</note>)² + *Bh*³ (bending)²...............(1).<-

This energy is to be as small as possible. Therefore, when the thickness is diminished without limit, the actual displacement will be one of pure bending, if such a movement exists that is consistent with the given conditions.

At first sight, it may well appear strange that of the two terms, the one proportional to the cube of the thickness is to be kept, while the one proportional to the first power may be neglected. The fact, however, is that the large potential energy that would accompany any stretching of the middle surface is the very reason why such stretching does not occur. The comparative largeness of the coefficient (proportional to *h*) is more than canceled out by the smallness of the stretching itself, as the energy is proportional to the square of that stretching.

<summary>This page explains the mathematical distinction between stretching and bending vibrations in thin elastic shells, arguing that as a shell becomes thinner, its movements consist almost entirely of pure bending. The author demonstrates that stretching is minimized because it would require a disproportionately large amount of potential energy.</summary>
<keywords>elastic shells, potential energy, flexural vibrations, extensional vibrations, thickness (h), mechanics, deformation, bending vs stretching</keywords>

# CURVED PLATES OR SHELLS [Section 235 c.]

First, let us assume simply that the surface is a surface of revolution <note>A surface of revolution is a shape formed by rotating a two-dimensional curve around a central axis, like a bowl or a cooling tower.</note>, and that any point on it is defined by the cylindrical coordinates <term>cylindrical coordinates: A system of three-dimensional coordinates ($z$, $r$, $\phi$) where $z$ is the height, $r$ is the radius from the axis, and $\phi$ is the angle of rotation.</term> $z$, $r$, and $\phi$. After the surface undergoes deformation <note>original: "deformation"; the process of changing shape due to applied stress.</note>, the coordinates of this point become $z + \delta z$, $r + \delta r$, and $\phi + \delta \phi$, respectively. If $ds$ represents an infinitesimal segment of a curve (an element of arc) on the surface, then:

->$(ds + d\delta s)^2 = (dz + d\delta z)^2 + (r + \delta r)^2 (d\phi + d\delta \phi)^2 + (dr + d\delta r)^2,$<-

from which it follows that:

->$ds\ d\delta s = dz\ d\delta z + r^2 d\phi\ d\delta \phi + r \delta r (d\phi)^2 + dr\ d\delta r \dots \dots (1).$<-

In this context, we treat $z$ and $\phi$ as independent variables, so that, for example:

->$d\delta z = \frac{d\delta z}{dz} dz + \frac{d\delta z}{d\phi} d\phi;$<-

while:

->$dr = \frac{dr}{dz} dz + \frac{dr}{d\phi} d\phi,$<-

where we assume by our hypothesis that $dr/d\phi = 0$ <note>Since the surface is symmetrical around its axis, the radius does not change as you move around the angle $\phi$.</note>. Consequently:

->$\frac{d\delta s}{ds} = \frac{(dz)^2}{(ds)^2} \left\{ \frac{d\delta z}{dz} + \frac{dr}{dz} \frac{d\delta r}{dz} \right\} + \frac{(d\phi)^2}{(ds)^2} \left\{ r^2 \frac{d\delta \phi}{d\phi} + r \delta r \right\}$<-

->$+ \frac{dz d\phi}{(ds)^2} \left\{ \frac{d\delta z}{d\phi} + r^2 \frac{d\delta \phi}{dz} + \frac{dr}{dz} \frac{d\delta r}{d\phi} \right\} \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (2),$<-

where $d\delta s/ds$ represents the extension <term>extension: The stretching or fractional change in length of a segment.</term> of the element $ds$. If there is no stretching of any arc on the surface, equation (2) must equal zero regardless of the values of $dz$ and $d\phi$. Thus:

->$\frac{d\delta z}{dz} + \frac{dr}{dz} \frac{d\delta r}{dz} = 0 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (3),$<-

->$r \frac{d\delta \phi}{d\phi} + \delta r = 0 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (4),$<-

->$\frac{d\delta z}{d\phi} + r^2 \frac{d\delta \phi}{dz} + \frac{dr}{dz} \frac{d\delta r}{d\phi} = 0 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (5).$<-

By eliminating <note>original: "elimination"; the algebraic process of removing a variable from a system of equations to simplify them.</note> $\delta r$ from these, we find:

->$\frac{d\delta z}{dz} - \frac{dr}{dz} \frac{d}{dz} \left( r \frac{d\delta \phi}{d\phi} \right) = 0,$<-

->$\frac{d\delta z}{d\phi} + r^2 \frac{d\delta \phi}{dz} - r \frac{dr}{dz} \frac{d^2 \delta \phi}{d\phi^2} = 0;$<-

and again, by eliminating $\delta z$, we arrive at:

->$\frac{d}{dz} \left( r^2 \frac{d\delta \phi}{dz} \right) - r \frac{d^2 r}{dz^2} \frac{d^2 \delta \phi}{d\phi^2} = 0 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (6).$<-

# CONDITIONS OF INEXTENSION

If the thickness and the shape of the boundary (or boundaries) are symmetrical around the axis, the normal functions <note>Normal functions describe the natural patterns or "modes" in which a system vibrates.</note> of the system can be found by assuming that the change in the angle, $\delta\phi$, is proportional to $\cos s\phi$ or $\sin s\phi$. The equation for $\delta\phi$ can then be written as:

->$r^2 \frac{d}{dz} \left( r^2 \frac{d\delta\phi}{dz} \right) + s^2 r^2 \frac{d^2r}{dz^2} \delta\phi = 0$ ..................... (7). <-

We can see that the conditions of inextension <note>Inextension refers to a type of deformation where the surface of the object does not stretch or compress, only bends.</note> significantly help determine the shape of these normal functions.

The simplest application of this is the case of a cylinder where the radius $r$ is constant (let us call this constant value $a$). In this case, equations (3), (4), (5), and (7) simplify to:

-> $\frac{d\delta z}{dz} = 0, \quad \delta r + a \frac{d\delta\phi}{d\phi} = 0, \quad \frac{d\delta z}{d\phi} + a^2 \frac{d\delta\phi}{dz} = 0 ...... (8),$ <-

-> $\frac{d^2\delta\phi}{dz^2} = 0$ ................................. (9). <-

According to equation (9), if $\delta\phi$ is proportional to $\cos s\phi$, we may assume:

-> $a\delta\phi = (A_s a + B_s z) \cos s\phi$ ... .....................(10), <-

and then, using equation (8):

-> $\delta r = s (A_s a + B_s z) \sin s\phi$ ... .....................(11), <-

-> $\delta z = - s^{-1} B_s a \sin s\phi$ ... ...........................(12). <-

Similar terms, using new arbitrary constants, can be added by substituting $s\phi + \frac{1}{2}\pi$ for $s\phi$. If $B_s = 0$, the displacement <note>Displacement refers to the distance and direction a point on the surface moves from its original position during vibration.</note> occurs in only two dimensions (see section 233).

If a disc that cannot stretch is attached to the cylinder at $z = 0$ to form a cup shape, the displacements $\delta r$ and $\delta\phi$ must be zero at that value of $z$ (except in the case where $s = 1$). Therefore, $A_s = 0$, and:

-> $a\delta\phi = B_s z \cos s\phi, \enspace \delta r = s B_s z \sin s\phi, \enspace \delta z = - s^{-1} B_s a \sin s\phi ... (13).$ <-

Furthermore, in the case of a cone, where the radius $r$ is equal to $\tan \gamma \cdot z$, equations (3), (4), (5), and (7) become:

-> $\left. \begin{aligned} \frac{d\delta z}{dz} + \tan \gamma \frac{d\delta r}{dz} = 0, \quad z \tan \gamma \frac{d\delta\phi}{d\phi} + \delta r = 0 \\ \frac{d\delta z}{d\phi} + z^2 \tan^2 \gamma \frac{d\delta\phi}{dz} + \tan \gamma \frac{d\delta r}{d\phi} = 0 \end{aligned} \right\} ...... (14),$ <-

-> $\frac{d}{dz} \left( z^2 \frac{d\delta\phi}{dz} \right) = 0$ ................................. (15). <-

# CURVED PLATES OR SHELLS. [Section 235 c]

If we assume, as is standard, that the change in the angle ($\delta\phi$) is proportional to $\cos s\phi$, we obtain the following solution for equation (15):
->$\delta\phi = (A_s + B_s z^{-1}) \cos s\phi$ ........................(16),<-
and the values corresponding to it are:
->$\delta r = s \tan \gamma (A_s z + B_s) \sin s\phi$ ........................(17),<-
->$\delta z = \tan^2 \gamma [s^{-1} B_s - s (A_s z + B_s)] \sin s\phi$ ......(18).<-
If the cone is complete all the way to its point <note>original: "vertex"</note> at $z = 0$, then the constant $B_s$ must be zero, so that:
->$\delta\phi = A_s \cos s\phi$........................(19),<-
->$\delta r = s A_s r \sin s\phi$........................(20),<-
->$\delta z = - s A_s \tan \gamma r \sin s\phi$........................(21).<-

For both the cone and the cylinder, the second term in the general equation (7) becomes zero <note>original: "vanishes"</note>. We can find a much broader range of solvable cases by assuming that the surface is shaped such that:
->$r^3 \frac{d^2r}{dz^2} = \text{constant}$ ........................ (22),<-
This is an equation that is generally satisfied by surfaces of the second degree <note>Surfaces of the second degree, also known as quadric surfaces, include shapes like spheres, ellipsoids, and paraboloids.</note>. If we have the following equation:
->$\frac{z^2}{a^2} + \frac{r^2}{b^2} = 1$ ........................(23),<-
we will find that:
->$r^3 \frac{d^2r}{dz^2} = -\frac{b^4}{a^2}$ ........................(24);<-
and thus equation (7) takes this form:
->$\frac{d^2\delta\phi}{d\alpha^2} - \frac{s^2b^4}{a^2} \delta\phi = 0$ ........................(25),<-
provided that $\delta\phi$ is proportional to $\cos s\phi$, and $\alpha$ is defined by:
->$\alpha = \int r^{-2} dz$........................(26),<-
or in this specific case:
->$\alpha = \frac{a}{2b^2} \log \frac{a + z}{a - z}$ ........................(27).<-
The solution for equation (25) is:
->$\delta\phi = \left[ A \left( \frac{a + z}{a - z} \right)^{-\frac{1}{2}s} + B \left( \frac{a + z}{a - z} \right)^{+\frac{1}{2}s} \right] \cos s\phi$........(28).<-
The corresponding values for the change in radius ($\delta r$) and the vertical displacement ($\delta z$) are to be obtained from equations (4) and (5).

<summary>This page provides the mathematical solutions for the deformation of cones and other second-degree surfaces (like ellipsoids) under the condition of inextension. It demonstrates how specific geometric properties allow complex physical equations to be solved more easily.</summary>
<keywords>curved plates, shells, cone, cylinder, surfaces of the second degree, quadric surfaces, differential equations, vertex, inextension</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the mathematical analysis of how surfaces of revolution (shapes created by rotating a curve around an axis) can be deformed or "bent" without stretching. It applies general equations to specific shapes, including the parabola and the sphere.</meta>

# NORMAL MODES

If the surface is complete through the vertex <note>The highest point or peak of the surface.</note> (where $z = a$), the term multiplied by $B$ must vanish <note>original: "disappear"</note>. Thus, omitting the constant multiplier, we can take:

->$\delta\phi = \left(\frac{a - z}{a + z}\right)^{\frac{1}{2}s} \cos s\phi$ ........................(29);<-

from which, using equations (4) and (5), we obtain:

->$\delta r = \frac{sb}{a} \frac{(a - z)^{\frac{1}{2}s + \frac{1}{2}}}{(a + z)^{\frac{1}{2}s - \frac{1}{2}}} \sin s\phi$........................(30),<-

->$\delta z = (sz + a) \frac{b^2 (a - z)^{\frac{1}{2}s}}{a^2 (a + z)^{\frac{1}{2}s}} \sin s\phi$..................(31).<-

If we measure the distance $z'$ from the vertex, so that $z' = a - z$, we can write the equations as:

->$\delta\phi = \left(\frac{z'}{r}\right)^s \cos s\phi$....................................(32),<-

->$\delta r = sr \left(\frac{z'}{r}\right)^s \sin s\phi$....................................(33),<-

->$\delta z = -\delta z' = \frac{b^2}{a^2} \left\{ (s + 1) a - sz' \right\} \left(\frac{z'}{r}\right)^s \sin s\phi$ ......(34).<-

For a parabola, the values $a$ and $b$ are infinite, while $b^2/a = 2a'$ and $r^2 = 4a'z'$. Thus, we can take: <margin>¹ On the Infinitesimal Bending of Surfaces of Revolution. *Proceedings of the Mathematical Society*, vol. xiii. p. 4, 1881.</margin>

->$\delta\phi = r^s \cos s\phi, \quad \delta r = sr^{s+1} \sin s\phi, \quad \delta z' = -2 (s + 1) a'r^s \sin s\phi$...(35).<-

We will now consider the important case of the sphere, for which, in equation (23), $b = a$. Letting $\theta$ represent the angle between the radius vector and the axis, we have $z = a \cos \theta$ and $r = a \sin \theta$. Therefore, from equations (29), (30), and (31), we find:

->$\delta\phi = \cos s\phi \tan^s \frac{1}{2}\theta$....................................(36),<-

->$\delta r/a = s \sin s\phi \sin \theta \tan^s \frac{1}{2}\theta$........................(37),<-

->$\delta z/a = (1 + s \cos \theta) \sin s\phi \tan^s \frac{1}{2}\theta$..................(38).<-

The other terms of the full solution, which correspond to equation (28), are obtained by changing the sign of $s$.

In the equations above, the displacements are resolved <note>Broken down into directional components.</note> parallel and perpendicular to the axis where $\theta = 0$. However, it is usually more convenient to resolve them along the normal <note>The direction perpendicular to the surface at any given point.</note> and the meridian <note>The curve formed by the intersection of the surface with a plane containing its axis of revolution, similar to a line of longitude.</note>. If the components in these directions are represented by $w$ and $a\delta\theta$, we have:

->$w = \delta r \sin \theta + \delta z \cos \theta, \quad a\delta\theta = \delta r \cos \theta - \delta z \sin \theta;$<-

<summary>This page derives the mathematical formulas for the "normal modes" or natural patterns of deformation for parabolic and spherical surfaces that occur without stretching. It concludes by translating these coordinate-based displacements into physical directions like the "normal" and "meridian" of the surface.</summary>

<keywords>infinitesimal bending, surfaces of revolution, parabola, sphere, vertex, normal, meridian, displacement components</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the mathematical derivation of deformations in curved surfaces, moving from spherical coordinates to the specific case of a cylindrical shell to determine its potential energy.</meta>

# CURVED PLATES OR SHELLS. [235 c.

so that altogether
$\delta\phi = \cos s\phi [A_s \tan^s \frac{1}{2}\theta + B_s \cot^s \frac{1}{2}\theta] \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(39),$
$\delta\theta = -\sin s\phi \sin \theta [A_s \tan^s \frac{1}{2}\theta - B_s \cot^s \frac{1}{2}\theta] \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(40),$
$w/a = \sin s\phi [A_s (s + \cos \theta) \tan^s \frac{1}{2}\theta + B_s (s - \cos \theta) \cot^s \frac{1}{2}\theta] \dots(41).$

We may add more terms to the equations above by substituting $s\phi + \frac{1}{2}\pi$ for $s\phi$ and changing the arbitrary constants.

**235 d.** We will now apply the equations from Section 235 c to the main ways a cylindrical surface stretches, in order to create a formula for its potential energy. We will label the axial extension (stretching along the length) as $\epsilon_1$, the circumferential extension (stretching around the perimeter) as $\epsilon_2$, and the shear <term>shear: a deformation where parallel internal surfaces slide past one another</term> as $\varpi$. The first of these is given by equation (2) in Section 235 c, if we assume that $d\phi = 0$ and $dz/ds = 1$. Since for a cylinder the radius does not change along its length ($dr/dz = 0$), we find:
$\epsilon_1 = \frac{d\delta z}{dz} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(1).$

In the same way:
$\epsilon_2 = \frac{\delta r}{a} + \frac{d\delta\phi}{d\phi} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(2).$

We can find the value of the shear by looking at the difference in how the two diagonals of an infinitesimal <note>extremely small</note> square (with sides $dz$ and $ad\phi$) stretch. It is:
$\varpi = \frac{1}{a} \frac{d\delta z}{d\phi} + a \frac{d\delta\phi}{dz} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(3).$

The next part of the problem—namely <note>original: "viz."</note>, expressing the potential energy using $\epsilon_1$, $\epsilon_2$, and $\varpi$—belongs to the general theory of elasticity and can only be covered briefly here. However, it is helpful to show the main steps of the analysis, and we refer readers to the textbooks by Thomson and Tait <note>William Thomson (Lord Kelvin) and Peter Guthrie Tait, authors of *Treatise on Natural Philosophy* (1867).</note> and by Love <note>Augustus Edward Hough Love, a famous mathematician known for his work on elasticity.</note> for further explanations. Using the notation from the former (*Natural Philosophy*, § 694), the general equations in three dimensions are:
$na = S, \quad nb = T, \quad nc = U \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(4),$
$\left. \begin{aligned} Me &= P - \sigma (Q + R) \\ Mf &= Q - \sigma (R + P) \\ Mg &= R - \sigma (P + Q) \end{aligned} \right\} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(5),$

where $\sigma = \frac{m - n}{2m} \dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots\dots(6)^1.$

---
$^1$ $M$ is Young's modulus <term>Young's modulus: a measure of a material's stiffness under tension or compression</term>, $\sigma$ is Poisson's ratio <term>Poisson's ratio: the ratio of how much a material thins when it is stretched</term>, $n$ is the constant of rigidity, and $(m - \frac{1}{3}n)$ is the constant of compressibility.

<summary>This page applies general deformation formulas to a cylindrical surface to define axial extension, circumferential extension, and shear. It introduces the fundamental equations of elasticity used to calculate the potential energy of the shell.</summary>
<keywords>cylindrical surface, potential energy, shear, axial extension, Young's modulus, Poisson's ratio, elasticity theory, Thomson and Tait</keywords>

# CYLINDRICAL SHELL.
<margin>235 d.</margin>

The energy $w$ per unit of volume is given by
$2w = (m + n) (e^2 + f^2 + g^2)$
->$+ 2 (m - n) (fg + ge + ef) + n (a^2 + b^2 + c^2) \dots \dots (7).$<-

When applying this to a thin plate (or lamina) <note>original: lamina; a thin layer or plate of material</note> assumed to be parallel to the $xy$ plane, we set the stresses $R = 0$, $S = 0$, $T = 0$, so that
->$g = - \sigma \frac{e + f}{1 - \sigma}, \quad a = 0, \quad b = 0 \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (8).$<-

Thus, in terms of the extensions $e$ and $f$ (parallel to $x$ and $y$) and the shear $c$ <term>shear: a deformation where parallel internal surfaces slide past one another</term>, we obtain
->$w = n \left\{ e^2 + f^2 + \frac{m - n}{m + n} (e + f)^2 + \frac{1}{2} c^2 \right\} \dots \dots \dots \dots (9).$<-

This value represents the energy calculated per unit volume. To adapt this formula for our use, we must multiply it by the thickness ($2h$). Therefore, using the notation introduced at the start of this section, the energy per unit area for a shell with thickness $2h$ is:
->$2nh \left\{ \epsilon_1^2 + \epsilon_2^2 + \frac{1}{2} \varpi^2 + \frac{m - n}{m + n} (\epsilon_1 + \epsilon_2)^2 \right\} \dots \dots \dots (10).$<-

This expression can be applied to both curved and flat plates, as any changes caused by curvature would involve higher powers of $h$ <note>Since $h$ represents half the thickness and is very small, its higher powers (like $h^2$ or $h^3$) become negligible in these specific calculations</note>. The same principle applies to the energy involved in bending.

**235 e.** We are now ready to investigate the extensional vibrations <term>extensional vibrations: vibrations that cause the material to stretch and compress along its surface rather than just bending</term> of an infinite cylindrical shell, assuming these vibrations are periodic in relation to both the length $z$ and the angle $\phi$. It is convenient to use single letters to represent the displacements parallel to $z$, $\phi$, and $r$. We will use:
->$\delta z = u, \quad a \delta \phi = v, \quad \delta r = w \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (1).$<-

We assume these functions are proportional to the sines or cosines of $jz/a$ and $s\phi$. We can create various combinations, such as the following example$^1$:
$u = U \cos s\phi \cos jz/a, \quad v = V \sin s\phi \sin jz/a,$
->$w = W \cos s\phi \sin jz/a \dots \dots (2);$<-
so that from equations (1), (2), and (3) in Section 235 d, we find:
->$a.\epsilon_1 = - jU \cos s\phi \sin jz/a \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (3),$<-
->$a.\epsilon_2 = (W + sV) \cos s\phi \sin jz/a \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (4),$<-
->$a.\varpi = (- sU + jV) \sin s\phi \cos jz/a \dots \dots \dots \dots \dots (5).$<-

---
$^1$ We can, of course, add $\pi/2$ <note>original: $\frac{1}{2}\pi$</note> to $s\phi$, $jz/a$, or both, as needed <note>Adding $\pi/2$ to the angle in a sine or cosine function effectively switches it between a sine and a cosine, allowing for different starting phases of the vibration</note>.

<summary>This page calculates the potential energy per unit area for a cylindrical shell by adapting formulas for thin plates and establishes the fundamental displacement equations for studying how these shells vibrate and stretch.</summary>
<keywords>cylindrical shell, potential energy, extensional vibrations, shear, elasticity, displacement functions, lamina</keywords>

--- Page 425 ---
<meta>This page continues the mathematical analysis of cylindrical shells, specifically calculating energy values and deriving frequency equations for their vibrations based on the previous section's energy formulas.</meta>

# CURVED PLATES OR SHELLS. [235 e.]

The potential energy per unit area is therefore given by equation (10) in § 235 d:

$2nha^{-2} \left[ \cos^2 s\phi \sin^2 jz/a \left\{ j^2 U^2 + (W + sV)^2 + \frac{m-n}{m+n} (W + sV - jU)^2 \right\} \right.$
$\left. + \frac{1}{2} \sin^2 s\phi \cos^2 jz/a (-sU + jV)^2 \right] ......(6).$

Furthermore, if $\rho$ represents the volume density, the kinetic energy per unit area is:

$\rho h \left[ \left( \frac{dU}{dt} \right)^2 \cos^2 s\phi \cos^2 jz/a + \left( \frac{dV}{dt} \right)^2 \sin^2 s\phi \sin^2 jz/a \right.$
$\left. + \left( \frac{dW}{dt} \right)^2 \cos^2 s\phi \sin^2 jz/a \right] ......(7).$

When integrating equations (6) and (7) with respect to $z$ and $\phi$, the mean value of the square of each sine or cosine is $\frac{1}{2}$.<note>Footnote 1</note> We can then apply Lagrange's method <note>Lagrange's method: a systematic way to derive the equations of motion for a complex system using its total energy</note>, treating $U$, $V$, and $W$ as independent generalized coordinates. If the vibration is of the type $\cos pt$, and we let $p^2 \rho / n = k^2$, the resulting equations can be written as:

$\{ 2(N+1)j^2 + s^2 - k^2 a^2 \} U - (2N+1)jsV - 2NjW = 0...(8),$
$-(2N+1)jsU + \{ j^2 + 2(N+1)s^2 - k^2 a^2 \} V + 2(N+1)sW = 0...(9),$
$-2NjU + 2(N+1)sV + \{ 2(N+1) - k^2 a^2 \} W = 0...(10),$

where -> $N = \frac{m-n}{m+n}$ ..............................(11). <-

The frequency equation is the one that describes when the determinant of this set of three equations vanishes <note>original: evanescence; in this context, it means the determinant equals zero, which is necessary to find the natural frequencies of the system</note>. After reduction, it can be written as:

$[k^2 a^2 - j^2 - s^2] \{ k^2 a^2 [k^2 a^2 - 2(N+1)(j^2 + s^2 + 1)]$
$+ 4(2N+1)j^2 \} + 4(2N+1)j^2 s^2 = 0......(12).$<note>Footnote 2</note>

Naturally, these equations also include the theory of the extensional vibrations <term>extensional vibrations: vibrations where the material stretches and compresses along its surface</term> of a flat plate, for which the radius $a$ is infinite ($a = \infty$). In this application, it is convenient to let $a\phi = y$, $s/a = \beta$, and $j/a = \gamma$. The displacements are then:

$u = U \cos \beta y \cos \gamma z, \quad v = V \sin \beta y \sin \gamma z, \quad w = W \cos \beta y \sin \gamma z$
$... (13).$

---

$^1$ In the physical problem of a simple cylinder, the range of integration for $\phi$ is from $0$ to $2\pi$; but mathematically, we are not limited to one revolution. We can imagine the shell to consist of several overlapping layers <note>original: superposed convolutions</note>, and in that case, $s$ is not required to be a whole number.

$^2$ *Note on the Free Vibrations of an infinitely long Cylindrical Shell.* Proceedings of the Royal Society, vol. 45, p. 446, 1889.

<summary>This page derives the potential and kinetic energy for a cylindrical shell to establish a system of equations for its vibrations. These equations are then used to formulate a frequency equation that describes the natural vibration patterns of both curved and flat plates.</summary>
<keywords>potential energy, kinetic energy, Lagrange's method, frequency equation, cylindrical shell, extensional vibrations, generalized coordinates</keywords>
